author: Daniel Linwood
context_before: Our masked autoencoder (MAE) is a simple autoencoding approach that reconstructs the original signal given its partial observation. Like all autoencoders, our approach has an encoder that maps the observed signal to a latent representation, and a decoder that reconstructs the original signal from the latent representation. Unlike classical autoencoders, we adopt an asymmetric design that allows the encoder to operate only on the partial, observed signal (without mask tokens) and a lightweight decoder that reconstructs the full signal from the latent representation and mask tokens. Figure 1 illustrates the idea, introduced next.
context_after: MAE encoder. Our encoder is a ViT [16] but applied only on visible, unmasked patches. Just as in a standard ViT, our encoder embeds patches by a linear projection with added positional embeddings, and then processes the resulting set via a series of Transformer blocks. However, our encoder only operates on a small subset (e.g., 25%) of the full set. Masked patches are removed; no mask tokens are used. This allows us to train very large encoders with only a fraction of compute and memory. The full set is handled by a lightweight decoder, described next.
a: Masking. Following ViT [16], we divide an image into regular non-overlapping patches. Then we sample a subset of patches and mask (i.e., remove) the remaining ones. Our sampling strategy is straightforward: we sample random patches without replacement, following a uniform distribution. We simply refer to this as “random sampling”. Random sampling with a high masking ratio (i.e., the ratio of removed patches) largely eliminates redundancy, thus creating a task that cannot be easily solved by extrapolation from visible neighboring patches (see Figures 2 – 4). The uniform distribution prevents a potential center bias (i.e., more masked patches near the image center). Finally, the highly sparse input creates an opportunity for designing an efficient encoder, introduced next.
b: Our approach is an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder operates only on the visible subset of patches, producing latent representations for those patches; masked patches are simply removed and no mask tokens are introduced at this stage. A lightweight decoder then takes as input the encoded visible patches together with a set of learnable mask tokens, placed at the positions of the masked patches, and reconstructs the original image in pixel space. This asymmetry is central: the heavy encoder sees only the small observed fraction of the signal, while the shallow decoder handles the full set of tokens and performs the reconstruction task. As a result, the encoder can be very large, since its computation and memory scale with the number of visible patches rather than the full image, and the overall pretraining remains efficient. The reconstruction target is the pixels of the masked patches, and the loss is computed only on the masked positions, so the model is trained to infer the missing content from the visible context. This design shifts most of the modeling burden to the encoder while keeping the decoder minimal, enabling scalable and effective self-supervised pretraining.

author: Daniel Linwood
context_before: This paper shows that masked autoencoders (MAE) are scalable self-supervised learners for computer vision. Our MAE approach is simple: we mask random patches of the input image and reconstruct the missing pixels. It is based on two core designs. First, we develop an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture, with an encoder that operates only on the visible subset of patches (without mask tokens), along with a lightweight decoder that reconstructs the original image from the latent representation and mask tokens. Second, we find that masking a high proportion of the input image, e.g., 75%, yields a nontrivial and meaningful self-supervisory task. Coupling these two designs enables us to train large models efficiently and effectively: we accelerate training (by 3× or more) and improve accuracy. Our scalable approach allows for learning high-capacity models that generalize well: e.g., a vanilla ViT-Huge model achieves the best accuracy (87.8%) among methods that use only ImageNet-1K data. Transfer performance in downstream tasks outperforms supervised pretraining and shows promising scaling behavior.
context_after: This appetite for data has been successfully addressed in natural language processing (NLP) by self-supervised pretraining. The solutions, based on autoregressive language modeling in GPT [47, 48, 4] and masked autoencoding in BERT [14], are conceptually simple: they remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content. These methods now enable training of generalizable NLP models containing over one hundred billion parameters [4].
a: Deep learning has witnessed an explosion of architectures of continuously growing capability and capacity [33, 25, 57]. Aided by the rapid gains in hardware, models today can easily overfit one million images [13] and begin to demand hundreds of millions of—often publicly inaccessible—labeled images [16].
b: The self-supervised approach in our masked autoencoder (MAE) is similar in spirit to these NLP techniques: we remove a portion of the data and learn to predict the removed content, in our case random patches of an image. This idea, however, has not yet been as successful in computer vision as in NLP, largely because the signals available in images are continuous and highly redundant, unlike the discrete tokens of language.

author: Daniel Linwood
context_before: Self-supervised learning approaches have seen significant interest in computer vision, often focusing on different pretext tasks for pre-training [15, 61, 42, 70, 45, 17]. Recently, contrastive learning [3, 22] has been popular, e.g., [62, 43, 23, 7], which models image similarity and dissimilarity (or only similarity [21, 8]) between two or more views. Contrastive and related methods strongly depend on data augmentation [7, 21, 8]. Autoencoding pursues a conceptually different direction, and it exhibits different behaviors as we will present.
context_after: Masking. Following ViT [16], we divide an image into regular non-overlapping patches. Then we sample a subset of patches and mask (i.e., remove) the remaining ones. Our sampling strategy is straightforward: we sample random patches without replacement, following a uniform distribution. We simply refer to this as “random sampling”. Random sampling with a high masking ratio (i.e., the ratio of removed patches) largely eliminates redundancy, thus creating a task that cannot be easily solved by extrapolation from visible neighboring patches (see Figures 2 – 4). The uniform distribution prevents a potential center bias (i.e., more masked patches near the image center). Finally, the highly sparse input creates an opportunity for designing an efficient encoder, introduced next.
a: Our masked autoencoder (MAE) is a simple autoencoding approach that reconstructs the original signal given its partial observation. Like all autoencoders, our approach has an encoder that maps the observed signal to a latent representation, and a decoder that reconstructs the original signal from the latent representation. Unlike classical autoencoders, we adopt an asymmetric design that allows the encoder to operate only on the partial, observed signal (without mask tokens) and a lightweight decoder that reconstructs the full signal from the latent representation and mask tokens. Figure 1 illustrates the idea, introduced next.
b: Autoencoding is a classical method for self-supervised learning [46, 47, 48]. It has been used in vision [49, 50, 26, 40, 41, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. In this paper, we study the autoencoding paradigm in the context of self-supervised learning for computer vision. We introduce a simple approach: we mask random patches of the input image and reconstruct the missing pixels. It is based on two core designs. First, we develop an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture, with an encoder that operates only on the visible subset of patches (without mask tokens), along with a lightweight decoder that reconstructs the original image from the latent representation and mask tokens. Second, we find that masking a high proportion of the input image, e.g., 75%, yields a nontrivial and meaningful self-supervisory task. Coupling these two designs enables us to train large models efficiently and effectively: we accelerate training (by 3× or more) and improve accuracy. Our scalable approach allows for learning high-capacity models that generalize well: e.g., a vanilla ViT-Huge model achieves the best accuracy (87.8%) among methods that use only ImageNet-1K data. Transfer performance in downstream tasks outperforms supervised pre-training and shows promising scaling behavior.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Discuss placing batch normalization after residual addition. Compare this design with alternatives and explain how the resulting post-addition transformation affects signal propagation.
a:
BN after addition. Before turning f into an identity mapping, we go the opposite way by adopting BN after addition (Fig. 4(b)). In this case f involves BN and ReLU. The results become considerably worse than the baseline (Table 2). Unlike the original design, now the BN layer alters the signal that passes through the shortcut and impedes information propagation, as reflected by the difficulties on reducing training loss at the beginning of training (Fib. 6 left).

ReLU before addition. A na¨ıve choice of making f into an identity mapping is to move the ReLU before addition (Fig. 4(c)). However, this leads to a non-negative output from the transform F, while intuitively a “residual” function should take values in (−∞, +∞). As a result, the forward propagated signal is monotonically increasing. This may impact the representational ability, and the result is worse (7.84%, Table 2) than the baseline. We expect to have a residual function taking values in (−∞, +∞). This condition is satisfied by other Residual Units including the following ones.
b: Placing batch normalization after the residual addition, as in the original ResNet, yields BN(x + F(x)). The addition happens in the identity path's native scale, so the shortcut remains a clean, parameter-free identity; BN then renormalizes the combined signal before the next block. This gives strong forward normalization and keeps gradients well-conditioned through deep stacks, but the transformation sits on the main highway: every block rescales and shifts the residual stream, so the identity mapping is no longer exact, and the forward signal's variance is repeatedly reset rather than accumulated. Alternatives differ mainly in where normalization interrupts the path. Pre-activation ResNets compute x + F(BN(x)), leaving the shortcut untouched end-to-end; signal and gradient propagate additively with no post-addition rescaling, which improves optimization at extreme depth but weakens per-layer normalization of the summed stream. Another option normalizes only the branch, BN(F(x)), preserving an exact identity but allowing the residual sum's variance to grow with depth. Post-addition BN thus trades an exact identity for controlled activation statistics: it bounds the post-sum signal, stabilizes early training, and dampens variance drift, at the cost of a slightly distorted shortcut and a scale-sensitive interaction between branch and identity contributions.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Review related work for masked image modeling. Relate language-model pretraining to the difficulty of defining useful image tokens, and distinguish modern masked reconstruction from classical denoising autoencoders.
a:
Masked language modeling and its autoregressive counterparts, e.g., BERT [14] and GPT [47, 48, 4], are highly successful methods for pre-training in NLP. These methods hold out a portion of the input sequence and train models to predict the missing content. These methods have been shown to scale excellently [4] and a large abundance of evidence indicates that these pre-trained representations generalize well to various downstream tasks.

Autoencoding is a classical method for learning representations. It has an encoder that maps an input to a latent representation and a decoder that reconstructs the input. For example, PCA and k-means are autoencoders [29]. Denoising autoencoders (DAE) [58] are a class of autoencoders that corrupt an input signal and learn to reconstruct the original, uncorrupted signal. A series of methods can be thought of as a generalized DAE under different corruptions, e.g., masking pixels [59, 46, 6] or removing color channels [70]. Our MAE is a form of denoising autoencoding, but different from the classical DAE in numerous ways.
b: Masked image modeling (MIM) is motivated by the success of masked language modeling (MLM) in NLP, where predicting masked tokens from context yields strong pretraining. Extending this to vision is not straightforward: language has a discrete vocabulary, so masking and prediction are well-defined, whereas images are continuous and lack a natural tokenization. This difficulty in defining useful image tokens has shaped the field. Early approaches relied on pixel-level reconstruction, but pixels are low-level and redundant, making the pretext task less semantically meaningful. Later work explored discrete visual tokens via tokenizers or clustering, and feature-level targets from a teacher network, to make prediction more structured. Modern masked reconstruction differs from classical denoising autoencoders in both objective and setting. Denoising autoencoders typically corrupt inputs with noise and train to recover the clean signal, often with shallow or moderate capacity and for representation learning or generation. Modern MIM instead masks a large, structured fraction of patches, operates on transformer backbones at scale, and predicts masked content—sometimes in pixel space, sometimes in feature or token space—to learn transferable representations for downstream tasks. The emphasis on high masking ratios, asymmetric encoder-decoder designs, and semantic targets distinguishes current methods from classical denoising.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Describe a controlled comparison of plain and residual ImageNet models. Explain architectural choices that permit a fair comparison and compare computational complexity with conventional deep convolutional architectures.
a:
We have tested various plain/residual nets, and have observed consistent phenomena. To provide instances for discussion, we describe two models for ImageNet as follows.

Plain Network. Our plain baselines (Fig. 3, middle) are mainly inspired by the philosophy of VGG nets [40] (Fig. 3, left). The convolutional layers mostly have 3×3 filters and follow two simple design rules: (i) for the same output feature map size, the layers have the same number of filters; and (ii) if the feature map size is halved, the number of filters is doubled so as to preserve the time complexity per layer. We perform downsampling directly by convolutional layers that have a stride of 2. The network ends with a global average pooling layer and a 1000-way fully-connected layer with softmax. The total number of weighted layers is 34 in Fig. 3 (middle). It is worth noticing that our model has fewer filters and lower complexity than VGG nets [40] (Fig. 3, left). Our 34- layer baseline has 3.6 billion FLOPs (multiply-adds), which is only 18% of VGG-19 (19.6 billion FLOPs).
b: We compare plain and residual networks under controlled settings on ImageNet. The plain network stacks 3×3 convolutions with batch normalization and ReLU, downsampling by strided convolution; the residual version inserts identity shortcuts over every two layers, adding no parameters and negligible computation. To ensure fairness, both use the same depth (34 layers), same width schedule, same input resolution (224×224), same augmentation, optimization, and training schedule; shortcuts are parameter-free identities, with 1×1 convolutions used only when dimensions change, and these are excluded from the comparison or matched in the plain baseline. Under this control, the plain deep network exhibits higher training error than its shallower counterpart, indicating an optimization difficulty rather than overfitting, while the residual network trains more easily and achieves lower error. Computationally, residual blocks add only element-wise additions, so FLOPs and parameter counts are essentially identical to the plain counterpart and comparable to conventional deep convolutional architectures of similar depth and width; the gains arise from improved optimization, not increased model capacity.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Discuss whether residual pre-activation can reduce overfitting. Describe how training and held-out error can distinguish regularization from optimization and explain what this enables for increasing model depth.
a:
Reducing overfitting. Another impact of using the proposed pre-activation unit is on regularization, as shown in Fig. 6 (right). The pre-activation version reaches slightly higher training loss at convergence, but produces lower test error. This phenomenon is observed on ResNet-110, ResNet-110(1-layer), and ResNet-164 on both CIFAR-10 and 100. This is presumably caused by BN’s regularization effect [8]. In the original Residual Unit (Fig. 4(a)), although the BN normalizes the signal, this is soon added to the shortcut and thus the merged signal is not normalized. This unnormalized signal is then used as the input of the next weight layer. On the contrary, in our pre-activation version, the inputs to all weight layers have been normalized.

Comparisons on CIFAR-10/100. Table 4 compares the state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR-10/100, where we achieve competitive results. We note that we do not specially tailor the network width or filter sizes, nor use regularization techniques (such as dropout) which are very effective for these small datasets. We obtain these results via a simple but essential concept — going deeper. These results demonstrate the potential of pushing the limits of depth.
b:
Pre-activation residual blocks can reduce overfitting, but not as a primary mechanism. In the original residual formulation, the identity shortcut passes through the addition after the second batch normalization and ReLU, so the residual branch output is added to an already-normalized signal. In the pre-activation variant, BN and ReLU precede the convolutions, leaving the shortcut path clean and unobstructed. This improves optimization: gradients flow more directly through the identity mapping, and very deep networks become easier to train. The regularization effect is secondary. Because each block’s residual branch is normalized before the convolution, the learned function is better conditioned; the network can more easily represent near-identity mappings, which mildly constrains the effective complexity of each block and can reduce overfitting in practice. But the dominant benefit is optimization, not explicit regularization.

Training and held-out error distinguish these two effects. If both training and held-out error decrease, the change improved optimization—the model fits the data better without harming generalization. If training error decreases while held-out error rises, the change increased effective capacity and overfitting. If training error is roughly unchanged but held-out error falls, the change acted as a regularizer. Pre-activation typically shows the first pattern: lower training error and comparable or lower held-out error, indicating better optimization rather than stronger regularization.

This distinction enables increasing depth. When held-out error tracks training error downward as depth grows, deeper models are not merely memorizing; they are learning more generalizable features. Pre-activation makes this regime accessible by removing optimization barriers at extreme depth, so additional layers can be added without the degradation problem masking their potential. The result is that depth can be scaled to improve accuracy, with held-out error serving as the check that the gain is genuine generalization rather than overfitting.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Compare linear probing and end-to-end fine-tuning as assessments of self-supervised visual representations. Explain why relative performance may depend on the evaluation protocol and what this implies for large masked autoencoders.
a:
These observations suggest that linear separability is not the sole metric for evaluating representation quality. It has also been observed (e.g., [8]) that linear probing is not well correlated with transfer learning performance, e.g., for object detection. To our knowledge, linear evaluation is not often used in NLP for benchmarking pre-training.

We evaluate transfer learning in downstream tasks using the pre-trained models in Table 3. Object detection and segmentation. We fine-tune Mask R-CNN [24] end-to-end on COCO [37]. The ViT backbone is adapted for use with FPN [36] (see A.3). We apply this approach for all entries in Table 4. We report box AP for object detection and mask AP for instance segmentation.

Compared to supervised pre-training, our MAE performs better under all configurations (Table 4). With the smaller ViT-B, our MAE is 2.4 points higher than supervised pretraining (50.3 vs. 47.9, APbox). More significantly, with the larger ViT-L, our MAE pre-training outperforms supervised pre-training by 4.0 points (53.3 vs. 49.3).
b:
Linear probing and end-to-end fine-tuning measure different things. Linear probing freezes the representation and fits a linear classifier, so it isolates the quality of features as a fixed embedding: it rewards representations that are already linearly separable and low-dimensional in their discriminative directions. End-to-end fine-tuning updates all parameters, so it measures the representation's potential as an initialization—how well the network can adapt when the features are allowed to move.

Relative performance can therefore depend on the protocol. A representation that is linearly separable but lacks fine-grained, task-specific structure may look strong under linear probing yet gain little from fine-tuning. Conversely, features that are entangled or high-dimensional may be weak under a linear readout but become effective once the backbone is adapted. Protocol choices—learning rate schedules, layer-wise decay, normalization, augmentation, and training length—also interact with the representation's statistics, so rankings are not protocol-invariant. Linear probing and fine-tuning should be read as complementary diagnostics, not as a single score.

For large masked autoencoders this matters. Such models learn rich, high-capacity features from reconstruction; their representations are often not optimized for a linear readout, so linear probing can understate their transferability, while fine-tuning reveals their strength. Reporting only one protocol risks misleading conclusions about scaling. The implication is to evaluate large MAEs with both protocols, tune each fairly, and interpret linear probing as a lower bound on feature usability rather than a definitive assessment.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Write a research abstract introducing masked image reconstruction with an asymmetric encoder and decoder. Motivate a high masking ratio and summarize why the method scales effectively for visual representation learning.
a: This paper shows that masked autoencoders (MAE) are scalable self-supervised learners for computer vision. Our MAE approach is simple: we mask random patches of the input image and reconstruct the missing pixels. It is based on two core designs. First, we develop an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture, with an encoder that operates only on the visible subset of patches (without mask tokens), along with a lightweight decoder that reconstructs the original image from the latent representation and mask tokens. Second, we find that masking a high proportion of the input image, e.g., 75%, yields a nontrivial and meaningful self-supervisory task. Coupling these two designs enables us to train large models efficiently and effectively: we accelerate training (by 3× or more) and improve accuracy. Our scalable approach allows for learning high-capacity models that generalize well: e.g., a vanilla ViT-Huge model achieves the best accuracy (87.8%) among methods that use only ImageNet-1K data. Transfer performance in downstream tasks outperforms supervised pretraining and shows promising scaling behavior.
b: We present a simple, effective, and scalable approach to visual representation learning: masked image reconstruction with an asymmetric encoder–decoder architecture. Our method masks a large fraction of image patches and learns by reconstructing the missing pixels from the visible remainder. Crucially, the encoder operates only on unmasked patches, while a lightweight decoder reconstructs the full image from the encoded visible patches and mask tokens. This asymmetry decouples representation learning from reconstruction: the heavy encoder never processes mask tokens, and the shallow decoder handles the reconstruction task, substantially reducing compute and memory relative to symmetric designs. We motivate a high masking ratio, e.g., 75%, because images are spatially redundant: random masking at low ratios leaves the reconstruction task nearly trivial, allowing the model to exploit local interpolation rather than learning semantic structure. A high ratio removes most low-level content and forces the encoder to infer global context and object-level regularities from sparse visible evidence, yielding representations that transfer well. The design scales effectively along model size and data: the encoder's cost depends only on the visible subset, so larger encoders remain tractable; the decoder stays small and can be discarded after pretraining, leaving a standard encoder for downstream tasks; and reconstruction targets derived from pixels require no extra labels or pretrained networks. These properties make the method a practical path to general-purpose visual representations.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Describe a reproducible ImageNet training and evaluation protocol for image classification. Cover input resizing and augmentation, optimization settings, and the distinction between training and evaluation preprocessing.
a: Our implementation for ImageNet follows the practice in [21, 40]. The image is resized with its shorter side randomly sampled in [256, 480] for scale augmentation [40]. A 224×224 crop is randomly sampled from an image or its horizontal flip, with the per-pixel mean subtracted [21]. The standard color augmentation in [21] is used. We adopt batch normalization (BN) [16] right after each convolution and before activation, following [16]. We initialize the weights as in [12] and train all plain/residual nets from scratch. We use SGD with a mini-batch size of 256. The learning rate starts from 0.1 and is divided by 10 when the error plateaus, and the models are trained for up to 60 × 104 iterations. We use a weight decay of 0.0001 and a momentum of 0.9. We do not use dropout [13], following the practice in [16]. In testing, for comparison studies we adopt the standard 10-crop testing [21]. For best results, we adopt the fullyconvolutional form as in [40, 12], and average the scores at multiple scales (images are resized such that the shorter side is in {224, 256, 384, 480, 640}).
b:
For reproducible ImageNet classification training, fix the input pipeline first. Decode images to RGB, resize the shorter side to 256 pixels with bicubic interpolation, then take a 224×224 center crop for evaluation. For training, use the same resize to 256 and then random crop to 224×224, with random horizontal flip. Optionally add mild color jitter or RandAugment, but keep the recipe fixed and documented. Normalize with the dataset mean and standard deviation after converting to float in [0,1]. The key distinction is that training preprocessing is stochastic and evaluation preprocessing is deterministic: at test time, resize shorter side to 256, center-crop 224, and do not flip or jitter. For multi-crop evaluation, average logits over the center crop and its horizontal flip, and report both single-crop and multi-crop numbers.

For optimization, use SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 1e-4, and a batch size of 1024 or 4096 depending on hardware, scaling the learning rate linearly. A standard baseline is initial learning rate 0.1 for batch size 256, with cosine decay or a step schedule dropping by 10× at 30, 60, and 90 epochs over 90–100 epochs. Use label smoothing 0.1, no dropout in the classifier, and initialize the final fully connected layer with small weights. Train in mixed precision where supported, but keep the optimizer state in FP32. Log the exact number of epochs, warmup (e.g., 5 epochs linear warmup), and whether BN statistics are frozen during fine-tuning.

For reproducibility, set all random seeds, enable deterministic cuDNN where possible, and record library versions, augmentation parameters, and the exact resize/crop implementation. Evaluate top-1 and top-5 accuracy on the 50,000-image validation set using the deterministic pipeline, and report mean and standard deviation over at least three seeds. Do not tune on the validation set without a held-out protocol; if needed, split off a small validation subset or use cross-validation. Finally, save the final checkpoint and the exact preprocessing configuration so that reported numbers can be regenerated bit-for-bit.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Present ablations for a masked image autoencoder. Compare predicting visual tokens and pixels and analyze the effects of corruption and alternate reconstruction or sampling choices. Do not invent exact measurements.
a:
We also compare an MAE variant that predicts tokens, the target used in BEiT [2]. Specifically for this variant, we use the DALLE pre-trained dVAE [50] as the tokenizer, following [2]. Here the MAE decoder predicts the token indices using cross-entropy loss. This tokenization improves fine-tuning accuracy by 0.4% vs. unnormalized pixels, but has no advantage vs. normalized pixels. It also reduces linear probing accuracy. In §5 we further show that tokenization is not necessary in transfer learning.

Our pixel-based MAE is much simpler than tokenization. The dVAE tokenizer requires one more pre-training stage, which may depend on extra data (250M images [50]). The dVAE encoder is a large convolutional network (40% FLOPs of ViT-L) and adds nontrivial overhead. Using pixels does not suffer from these problems.

Data augmentation. Table 1e studies the influence of data augmentation on our MAE pre-training.

Our MAE works well using cropping-only augmentation, either fixed-size or random-size (both having random horizontal flipping). Adding color jittering degrades the results and so we do not use it in other experiments.
b:
We ablate the masked image autoencoder along two axes: reconstruction target and corruption/sampling design. For the target, we compare predicting visual tokens versus raw pixels under the same masking ratio and encoder-decoder capacity. Token prediction treats each patch as a discrete class and optimizes cross-entropy over the visible context; pixel prediction regresses normalized patch values with an MSE-style loss. The token target emphasizes semantic abstraction and typically yields stronger linear-probe representations, while the pixel target retains low-level detail and can be more sensitive to high-frequency texture. Neither dominates universally: the gap depends on masking ratio, patch size, and decoder width, so we report trends rather than fixed deltas.

For corruption, we vary the masking ratio and masking strategy (random versus structured/block-wise). Higher ratios increase the difficulty of the pretext task and generally improve transfer up to a point, after which optimization degrades because too little context remains. Block-wise masking removes contiguous regions and encourages longer-range reasoning; random masking spreads evidence more evenly. We also compare replacing masked patches with a learnable mask token versus simple removal/zeroing, and find the learnable token stabilizes training and clarifies the visible/masked distinction.

For reconstruction and sampling, we contrast a lightweight decoder against a heavier one, and full reconstruction against partial or shallow decoding. A shallow decoder suffices for token targets but may underfit pixel targets. We further compare uniform patch sampling with importance- or saliency-guided sampling; uniform sampling is simpler and robust, while guided sampling can focus capacity on informative regions at the cost of added complexity. Overall, token targets with random masking and a lightweight decoder form a strong default, and the ablations show the design is governed by trade-offs among abstraction, detail, and task difficulty rather than a single optimal configuration.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Write a related-work section on residual representations in recognition and iterative optimization. Explain how expressing quantities through residuals can make a problem easier to solve.
a: Residual Representations. In image recognition, VLAD [18] is a representation that encodes by the residual vectors with respect to a dictionary, and Fisher Vector [30] can be formulated as a probabilistic version [18] of VLAD. Both of them are powerful shallow representations for image retrieval and classification [4, 47]. For vector quantization, encoding residual vectors [17] is shown to be more effective than encoding original vectors. In low-level vision and computer graphics, for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs), the widely used Multigrid method [3] reformulates the system as subproblems at multiple scales, where each subproblem is responsible for the residual solution between a coarser and a finer scale. An alternative to Multigrid is hierarchical basis preconditioning [44, 45], which relies on variables that represent residual vectors between two scales. It has been shown [3, 44, 45] that these solvers converge much faster than standard solvers that are unaware of the residual nature of the solutions. These methods suggest that a good reformulation or preconditioning can simplify the optimization.
b:
## Related Work

**Residual representations in recognition.** Representing signals by residuals has a long history in recognition. Classical coding methods such as Fisher vectors and VLAD encode an image as a set of differences between local descriptors and a learned dictionary, and this residual encoding consistently outperforms encoding the descriptors themselves. In low-level vision, steerable filters and wavelet transforms decompose signals into residual subbands, and the JPEG image compression standard stores residuals relative to predictions. These methods share a common insight: the residual between a signal and a prediction is often smaller and more structured than the signal, and therefore easier to model.

**Residual representations in optimization.** In numerical analysis, multigrid methods reformulate a linear system so that the solver operates on residuals between the current estimate and the target; the coarse-grid correction is driven entirely by these residuals, which makes the problem far better conditioned. Similarly, Newton-type methods solve for updates relative to the current point rather than for the solution directly, and preconditioning rewrites a system in terms of a residual that is easier to invert. Domain decomposition and residual correction schemes follow the same principle: expressing the unknown as a correction to an approximate solution simplifies the optimization.

**Residual connections.** Highway networks first introduced gated shortcut connections that allow information to bypass layers. Our residual formulation differs in that the shortcut is identity and ungated, and we show that this simple construction enables the training of extremely deep networks by making the layers learn residual functions with reference to the input, rather than unreferenced functions. This connects the recognition and optimization perspectives: the network's layers solve a sequence of residual correction problems, and the identity mapping provides a well-conditioned path for both forward and backward signals.

author: Daniel Linwood
task: Summarize the motivation for studying signal propagation in deep residual networks. Connect identity shortcuts and pre-activation to the practical training of very deep networks, and outline a reproducible CIFAR training setup.
a:
This paper investigates the propagation formulations behind the connection mechanisms of deep residual networks. Our derivations imply that identity shortcut connections and identity after-addition activation are essential for making information propagation smooth. Ablation experiments demonstrate phenomena that are consistent with our derivations. We also present 1000-layer deep networks that can be easily trained and achieve improved accuracy.

Appendix: Implementation Details The implementation details and hyperparameters are the same as those in [1]. On CIFAR we use only the translation and flipping augmentation in [1] for training. The learning rate starts from 0.1, and is divided by 10 at 32k and 48k iterations. Following [1], for all CIFAR experiments we warm up the training by using a smaller learning rate of 0.01 at the beginning 400 iterations and go back to 0.1 after that, although we remark that this is not necessary for our proposed Residual Unit. The mini-batch size is 128 on 2 GPUs (64 each), the weight decay is 0.0001, the momentum is 0.9, and the weights are initialized as in [23].
b:
The motivation is simple: if we want to train networks of hundreds or thousands of layers, we must understand how signals propagate through them. In plain networks, repeated multiplication by weight matrices shrinks or amplifies signals layer by layer, so deep models are hard to optimize. Residual networks change this picture: an identity shortcut creates a path where the signal can pass through unchanged, and gradients can flow back directly. This makes optimization of very deep models practical rather than hopeless.

The key design choice is pre-activation. Placing batch normalization and ReLU before the convolution, and keeping the shortcut as a clean identity, gives an unobstructed signal path. The residual branch then learns a correction to the identity, and the forward and backward signals do not get repeatedly distorted. This is why pre-activation residual blocks train more reliably and generalize better at extreme depth.

For a reproducible CIFAR setup: use the CIFAR-10 dataset with standard augmentation—random crop with padding and horizontal flip—and per-pixel mean subtraction. Train residual networks with pre-activation blocks, 3×3 convolutions, and a stem of 16 filters. Use SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 1e-4, batch size 128, and a step learning rate schedule starting at 0.1, dropping by 10× at fixed epochs. Report results over multiple seeds and fixed preprocessing so comparisons are fair. This setup isolates the effect of depth and shortcut design.

author: Daniel Linwood
context_before: Mask sampling strategy. In Table 1f we compare different mask sampling strategies, illustrated in Figure 6.

We trained and evaluated models on a large corpus of Associated Press news text, using a standard next-word prediction objective. The corpus was split into a training set and a held-out test set; all models were trained on the same training portion and evaluated on the same test portion, with perplexity as the primary metric. Neural models were feed-forward networks with a fixed context window of preceding words mapped to learned distributed embeddings and a hidden layer, trained by stochastic gradient descent with cross-entropy loss. Words outside the vocabulary were thus treated uniformly, and perplexities were computed over the same reduced vocabulary for all models to keep comparisons fair. We also report results with the full vocabulary where feasible, noting that unknown-word handling affects conventional and neural models differently, since neural models can generalize through shared embeddings while n-gram models cannot.

task: Describe numerical stability concerns in calculating softmax probabilities in a parallel neural language model. Explain a stable implementation and how computational overhead affects scaling.
a:
There could be a numerical problem in the computation of the exponentials in the forward phase, whereby all the p j could be numerically zero, or one of them could be too large for computing the exponential (step 1(c)ii above). To avoid this problem, the usual solution is to subtract the maximum of the y j’s before taking the exponentials in the softmax. Thus we have added an extra Allreduce operation to share among the M processors the maximum of the y j’s, before computing the exponentials in p j.Letqi be the maximum of the y j’s in block i. Then the overall maximum Q = maxi qi is collectively computed and shared among the M processors. The exponentials are then computed as follows: p j← ey j−Q (instead of step 1(c)ii) to guarantee that at least one of the p j’s will be numerically non-zero, and the maximum of the exponential’s argument is 1.

By comparing clock time of the parallel version with clock time on a single processor, we found that the communication overhead was only 1/15th of the total time (for one training epoch): thus we get an almost perfect speed-up through parallelization, using this algorithm on a fast network.
b:
In a parallel neural language model, softmax probabilities are computed as p_i = exp(z_i) / Σ_j exp(z_j) over a large vocabulary partitioned across devices. Two numerical hazards dominate. First, exponentials overflow: for logits above roughly 88 in float32, exp(z) becomes inf, producing inf/inf = NaN and poisoning gradients. Second, underflow: when all logits are very negative, every exp(z) rounds to zero, yielding 0/0 and losing the entire distribution. Parallel reduction compounds this because partial sums and maxima are exchanged across workers; a single overflowing shard corrupts the global denominator, and non-associative floating-point addition makes results order- and topology-dependent, so different ranks may disagree.

The standard stable implementation subtracts the maximum logit before exponentiating: m = max_j z_j, then p_i = exp(z_i − m) / Σ_j exp(z_j − m). This keeps the largest exponent at 1 and all others in (0, 1], eliminating overflow and preserving relative precision; the denominator is at least 1, so no division by zero. In a parallel setting, m must be a global maximum, obtained by an all-reduce max across shards before the local exp and sum, followed by an all-reduce sum of denominators. For numerical care, accumulate the denominator in float32 or higher even under mixed-precision training, and consider log-sum-exp form for the log-probability used in the loss: log p_i = (z_i − m) − log Σ_j exp(z_j − m), which avoids materializing normalized probabilities.

The overhead is real. The global max and sum each require a collective communication step whose latency grows with the number of shards and the interconnect; on many accelerators this synchronization can dominate the softmax when the per-shard compute is small. Memory traffic for the extra pass over logits and the temporary exp buffer adds bandwidth pressure. As vocabulary and model parallelism scale, these collectives become a scaling bottleneck: latency-bound all-reduces do not shrink with more devices, and stragglers force the whole group to wait. Mitigations include fusing max and sum into a single online (streaming) softmax pass, using hierarchical or tree reductions, overlapping communication with computation, and computing the softmax denominator in a lower precision where safe. The trade-off is that every stabilization step buys numerical robustness at the cost of synchronization, so the design must balance precision guarantees against the communication budget at scale.

a:
We believe that the main reason for these improvements is that the proposed approach allows to take advantage of the learned distributed representation to ﬁght the curse of dimensionality with its own weapons: each training sentence informs the model about a combinatorial number of other sentences.

There is probably much more to be done to improve the model, at the level of architecture, computational efﬁciency, and taking advantage of prior knowledge. An important priority of future research should be to improve speed-up techniques5 as well as ways to increase capacity without increasing training time too much (to deal with corpora with hundreds of millions of words or more). A simple idea to take advantage of temporal structure and extend the size of the input window to include possibly a whole paragraph (without increasing too much the number of parameters or computation time) is to use a time-delay and possibly recurrent neural networks. Evaluations of the type of models presented here in applicative contexts would also be useful, but see work already done by Schwenk and Gauvain (2002) for improvements in speech recognition word error rate.
b: Distributed word representations map each word to a dense continuous vector, so words with similar meanings occupy nearby regions of the space. This geometric structure lets a neural language model share statistical strength across words: instead of treating each word as an isolated symbol, the model can interpolate between related words and represent the context as a smooth function of the vectors. Because the context is encoded in a fixed-dimensional continuous space, the model can condition on a longer history without a combinatorial explosion in the number of parameters. The hidden state summarizes many preceding words through learned nonlinear combinations, so longer contexts become usable in practice, whereas a purely symbolic n-gram model would require an exponential number of distinct contexts. The implications are important. Generalization improves because unseen word sequences can be handled through similarity in representation space, reducing the curse of dimensionality. Recognition tasks, such as speech or handwriting recognition, benefit because the language model assigns better probabilities to plausible word sequences and can integrate evidence over longer spans, improving disambiguation and robustness to noise.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Describe how to evaluate and compare a neural probabilistic language model and n-gram baselines using test perplexity. Discuss convergence and the implications of architectural choices without fabricating measurements.
a: Below are measures of test set perplexity (geometric average of 1/ ˆP(wt|wt−11 )) for different models P. Apparent convergence of the stochastic gradient ascent procedure was obtained after around 10ˆ to 20 epochs for the Brown corpus. On the AP News corpus we were not able to see signs of over- ﬁtting (on the validation set), possibly because we ran only 5 epochs (over 3 weeks using 40 CPUs). Early stopping on the validation set was used, but was necessary only in our Brown experiments. A weight decay penalty of 10−4 was used in the Brown experiments and a weight decay of 10−5 was used in the APNews experiments (selected by a few trials, based on validation set perplexity). Table 1 summarizes the results obtained on the Brown corpus. All the back-off models of the table are modiﬁed Kneser-Ney n-grams, which worked signiﬁcantly better than standard back-off models. When m is speciﬁed for a back-off model in the table, a class-based n-gram is used (m is the number of word classes). Random initialization of the word features was done (similarly to initialization of neural network weights), but we suspect that better results might be obtained with a knowledge-based initialization.
b:
Evaluate all models on an identical held-out test set, using the same vocabulary, tokenization, and sentence boundaries, with out-of-vocabulary words mapped consistently. Compute test perplexity as the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token, ensuring the n-gram baselines use the same smoothing and backoff scheme across orders. Report perplexity only after fixing hyperparameters on validation data, and compare models at matched training conditions rather than at arbitrary checkpoints.

Convergence matters: neural models may still be improving when n-gram counts have stabilized, so monitor validation perplexity over epochs and compare at convergence or at a pre-declared compute budget. Note that perplexity is comparable only under the same vocabulary and normalization; differences in context length, embedding size, hidden units, and regularization change the effective model class and should be reported alongside results.

Architectural choices—context window, depth, activation, and parameter sharing—affect both convergence speed and final perplexity, but their impact must be measured empirically rather than assumed. Use confidence intervals from multiple seeds and paired tests on per-token log-likelihoods to judge whether gaps are meaningful.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Compare shared-memory and distributed-memory strategies for data-parallel training of a neural language model. Discuss synchronization, communication cost, and how an implementation might address them.
a:
In the case of a shared-memory processor, parallelization is easily achieved, thanks to the very low communication overhead between processors, through the shared memory. In that case we have chosen a data-parallel implementation in which each processor works on a different subset of the data. Each processor computes the gradient for its examples, and performs stochastic gradient updates on the parameters of the model, which are simply stored in a shared-memory area. Our ﬁrst implementation was extremely slow and relied on synchronization commands to make sure that each processor would not write at the same time as another one in one of the above parameter subsets. Most of the cycles of each processor were spent waiting for another processor to release a lock on the write access to the parameters.

Instead we have chosen an asynchronous implementation where each processor can write at any time in the shared-memory area. Sometimes, part of an update on the parameter vector by one of the processors is lost, being overwritten by the update of another processor, and this introduces a bit of noise in the parameter updates. However, this noise seems to be very small and did not apparently slow down training.
b:
In data-parallel training, each worker holds a replica of the model and processes a distinct shard of the batch, then gradients must be reconciled. Under shared memory (single node, multiple devices or threads), synchronization is cheap: workers write to a common buffer and use barriers or atomic operations, with the interconnect (PCIe/NVLink, or L3 cache) offering high bandwidth and low latency. The dominant cost is contention and serialization at the parameter server or reduction tree, plus cache-coherence traffic. A practical implementation uses a hierarchical all-reduce: intra-node reduction via shared buffers or NCCL over NVLink, overlapping gradient computation with communication, and bucketing small tensors to amortize launch overhead.

Under distributed memory (multiple nodes), each process has private address space, so synchronization requires explicit message passing (MPI, NCCL, or gRPC). Communication cost scales with model size and node count: a ring all-reduce moves roughly 2(N−1)/N times the gradient volume per worker, and latency grows with hop count and network congestion. Bandwidth, not latency, dominates for large models. Implementations address this with gradient compression (quantization, sparsification, error feedback), larger effective batches to improve compute-to-communication ratio, and asynchronous or stale-gradient schemes (with convergence caveats). Overlapping backward-pass gradient production with all-reduce, using communication hooks per layer, hides much of the cost. Hybrid strategies—intra-node shared-memory reduction plus inter-node ring—are standard. The key trade-off: shared memory minimizes synchronization overhead but caps scale at one node's resources; distributed memory scales out but demands careful overlap, compression, and topology-aware collective design to keep communication off the critical path.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Review earlier work on vector representations of words and documents. Relate information retrieval and distributional approaches to the task of learning a language probability model.
a: The idea of using a vector-space representation for words has been well exploited in the area of information retrieval (for example see work by Schutze, 1993), where feature vectors for words are learned on the basis of their probability of co-occurring in the same documents (Latent Semantic Indexing, see Deerwester et al., 1990). An important difference is that here we look for a representation for words that is helpful in representing compactly the probability distribution of word sequences from natural language text. Experiments suggest that learning jointly the representation (word features) and the model is very useful. We tried (unsuccessfully) using as ﬁxed word features for each word w the ﬁrst principal components of the co-occurrence frequencies of w with the words occurring in text around the occurrence of w. This is similar to what has been done with documents for information retrieval with LSI. The idea of using a continuous representation for words has however been exploited successfully by Bellegarda (1997) in the context of an n-gram based statistical language model, using LSI to dynamically identify the topic of discourse.
b: Earlier work on distributed representations—most notably neural probabilistic language models and word embeddings—established that words and documents can be mapped to dense vectors whose geometry encodes semantic and syntactic regularities. These distributional approaches rest on the hypothesis that contexts of use determine meaning, and they learn representations by predicting co-occurrence or context. Information retrieval offers a complementary tradition: documents are represented as sparse term vectors, and similarity is measured in a vector space, with weighting schemes such as tf-idf capturing term importance. Both traditions share the intuition that proximity in representation space corresponds to semantic or topical relatedness, yet they differ in supervision and sparsity. Relating them to language probability modeling, one can view a language model as assigning probability to sequences via representations of context; IR can supply document-level context and relevance signals, while distributional embeddings provide smoothed, low-dimensional features that mitigate data sparsity. Combining the two suggests models in which word and document vectors jointly parameterize conditional probabilities, allowing retrieval evidence to inform lexical prediction and vice versa.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Discuss why the computation of output probabilities in a neural language model can be expensive even when its parameter count scales reasonably. Motivate parallel computation.
a:
Although the number of parameters scales nicely, i.e. linearly with the size of the input window and linearly with the size of the vocabulary, the amount of computation required for obtaining the output probabilities is much greater than that required from n-gram models. The main reason is that with n-gram models, obtaining a particular P(wt|wt−1,...,wt−n+1) does not require the computation of the probabilities for all the words in the vocabulary, because of the easy normalization (performed when training the model) enjoyed by the linear combinations of relative frequencies. The main computational bottleneck with the neural implementation is the computation of the activations of the output layer.

Running the model (both training and testing) on a parallel computer is a way to reduce computation time. We have explored parallelization on two types of platforms: shared-memory processor machines and Linux clusters with a fast network.
b: The expense arises because the output distribution is normalized over the entire vocabulary: computing p(w | context) requires a softmax over all V output logits, so cost per prediction scales with V (and with the dimension of the final hidden layer), not merely with the number of parameters. In large-vocabulary settings, this normalization and the dense matrix multiplication producing all logits dominate, even if the model's parameter count is modest. This motivates parallel computation: the logits and softmax can be partitioned across vocabulary shards and processed concurrently across devices or cores, with only a reduction for the normalization constant. Parallelism thus converts a serial per-token bottleneck into a scalable operation, improving throughput and making training and inference practical for large vocabularies.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Introduce the generalization and computational problems in estimating distributions over word sequences. Motivate a neural approach using learned representations and relate it to alternative approaches.
a:
There are many approaches that have been proposed to address these two issues, and we will brieﬂy explain in Section 1.2 the relations between the approach proposed here and some of these earlier approaches. We will ﬁrst discuss what is the basic idea of the proposed approach. A more formal presentation will follow in Section 2, using an implementation of these ideas that relies on shared-parameter multi-layer neural networks. Another contribution of this paper concerns the challenge of training such very large neural networks (with millions of parameters) for very large data sets (with millions or tens of millions of examples). Finally, an important contribution of this paper is to show that training such large-scale model is expensive but feasible, scales to large contexts, and yields good comparative results (Section 4).

Many operations in this paper are in matrix notation, with lower case v denoting a column vector and v′ its transpose, A j the j-th row of a matrix A,andx.y = x′y.
b:
Estimating distributions over word sequences is fundamentally hard for two reasons. First, generalization: natural language is combinatorially vast, and any finite corpus leaves most possible sequences unseen, so a model must assign sensible probability to novel combinations rather than merely memorizing observed ones. Second, computation: exact normalization over all sequences of a given length is intractable, and even tractable factorizations face the curse of dimensionality as context grows. Classical n-gram models address computation through Markov assumptions but suffer sharply from data sparsity, requiring smoothing and backoff heuristics that generalize poorly.

A neural approach instead learns distributed representations of words and composes them into a continuous representation of context, from which the next-word distribution is predicted. Because similar words and contexts map to nearby vectors, statistical strength is shared across semantically related events, yielding better generalization to unseen sequences without explicit smoothing. The model remains a proper conditional distribution, normalized locally over the vocabulary at each step, so computation stays tractable while conditioning on a richer, learned summary of history.

This relates to alternatives in instructive ways. It generalizes n-gram and class-based models by replacing discrete counts with learned features; it connects to log-bilinear and energy-based formulations; and it anticipates later architectures that trade the fixed context window for recurrent or attention-based representations. Empirically, such models achieve substantially lower perplexity, demonstrating that learned representations mitigate both the sparsity and the dimensionality problems that limit count-based estimation.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Explain how an energy-based neural language model can assign probabilities to words absent from a fixed vocabulary, including how contextual information and features may help.
a: Out-of-vocabulary words. An advantage of this architecture over the previous one is that it can easily deal with out-of-vocabulary words (and even assign them a probability!). The main idea is to ﬁrst guess an initial feature vector for such a word, by taking a weighted convex combination of the feature vectors of other words that could have occurred in the same context, with weights proportional to their conditional probability. Suppose that the network assigned a probability ˆP(i|wt−1t−n+1) to words i∈ V in context wt−1t−n+1, and that in this context we observe a new word j⁄∈ V . We initialize the feature vector C( j) for j as follows: C( j)← ∑i∈V C(i) ˆP(i|wt−1t−n+1). We can then incorporate j in V and re-compute probabilities for this slightly larger set (which only requires a renormalization for all the words, except for word i, which requires a pass through the neural network). This feature vector C(i) can then be used in the input context part when we try to predict the probabilities of words that follow word i.
b:
An energy-based language model assigns probabilities through a normalized distribution over candidate next tokens: for context \(c\) and candidate \(w\), \(p(w \mid c) = \exp(-E(w,c)) / Z(c)\), where \(Z(c) = \sum_{w'} \exp(-E(w',c))\). With a fixed vocabulary, \(Z\) sums only over known words, and out-of-vocabulary words receive zero probability. To handle absent words, the key move is to define the energy over a compositional representation of the word rather than over a vocabulary index. A word can be represented by features—characters or subword units, morphemes, phonological form, spelling patterns, or embeddings from a character-level encoder. The energy function then scores any candidate string by composing these features with the context representation, so an unseen word is not an undefined index but a point in a continuous feature space that the model can evaluate.

Contextual information enters through the context encoding, which modulates how features are weighted. For example, a character-level encoder can produce a representation \(r(w)\) for any string, and the energy can be a learned compatibility between \(r(w)\) and a context vector \(h(c)\), such as \(E(w,c) = -f(r(w), h(c))\). This lets the model generalize: an unseen word sharing morphology or spelling with known words, and fitting the syntactic or semantic expectations of the context, receives a lower energy and thus higher probability. Features can also include type-level cues—suffixes signaling part of speech, prefixes, or similarity to known embeddings—so the model can assign sensible mass to plausible novel forms.

The normalization \(Z(c)\) is the remaining challenge, since summing over all possible strings is intractable. Practical approaches use negative sampling, contrastive estimation, or a candidate generator that proposes plausible strings, with the energy reranking them; the partition function can then be approximated over this candidate set or learned via noise-contrastive objectives. The result is a model that assigns graded probabilities to words outside the fixed vocabulary, guided by compositional features and context, rather than treating them as impossible.

author: Elias Montclair
task: Introduce a probabilistic sequence model for a large finite word vocabulary. Explain how a fixed word history and learned vector features can define the next-word distribution.
a:
The training set is a sequence w1···wT of words wt∈ V , where the vocabulary V is a large but ﬁnite set. The objective is to learn a good model f (wt,··· ,wt−n+1)= ˆP(wt|wt−11 ), in the sense that it gives high out-of-sample likelihood. Below, we report the geometric average of 1/ ˆP(wt|wt−11 ), also known as perplexity, which is also the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood. The only constraint on the model is that for any choice of wt−11 , ∑|V|i=1 f (i,wt−1,··· ,wt−n+1)=1, with f > 0. By the product of these conditional probabilities, one obtains a model of the joint probability of sequences of words.

We decompose the function f (wt,··· ,wt−n+1)= ˆP(wt|wt−11 ) in two parts: 1. A mapping C from any element i of V to a real vector C(i)∈ Rm. It represents the distributed feature vectors associated with each word in the vocabulary. In practice, C is represented by a|V|×m matrix of free parameters. 2. The probability function over words, expressed with C: a function g maps an input sequence of feature vectors for words in context, (C(wt−n+1),··· ,C(wt−1)), to a conditional probability distribution over words in V for the next word wt. The output of g is a vector whose i-th element estimates the probability ˆP(wt = i|wt−11 ) as in Figure 1.
b:
A probabilistic sequence model over a large finite vocabulary assigns to every word sequence a probability, and by the chain rule it decomposes that probability into a product of conditional next-word distributions. For a fixed word history, the model must specify a distribution over the next word, and the central question is how to parameterize this conditional distribution compactly when the vocabulary is large.

The approach is to associate each word in the vocabulary with a learned real-valued vector, a distributed feature representation. These vectors are not hand-designed; they are parameters learned jointly with the rest of the model from data. Words that behave similarly in context acquire similar vectors, so the representation shares statistical strength across words that occur rarely, which is essential for a large finite vocabulary.

Given a fixed history of preceding words, the model maps the history to a context representation. Each word in the history is replaced by its feature vector, and these vectors are combined — for instance by concatenation followed by one or more learned transformations — into a fixed-dimensional summary of the history. The context representation is thus a function of the particular history, computed from the same shared word vectors used throughout the model.

The next-word distribution is then defined by a scoring function over the vocabulary. For each candidate word, a score is computed from the context representation and that word's feature vector, typically through an inner product or a small learned network. Applying a softmax over the scores yields a proper probability distribution over the finite vocabulary, normalized so that the probabilities of all words sum to one. The parameters are the word vectors and the transformation weights, and they are trained by maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences, equivalently minimizing the cross-entropy between the model distribution and the empirical next-word frequencies.

This design has several desirable properties. Because the distribution is defined through continuous features rather than a separate parameter per history-word pair, the model generalizes to histories and words unseen in training. The number of parameters grows with the vocabulary size and the feature dimension, not with the number of possible histories, so it remains tractable for large vocabularies. Smoothing is implicit: a word never observed after a given history still receives a sensible probability if its features are close to those of words that were observed in that context. The fixed history assumption makes the conditional distribution well defined and permits efficient computation, while the learned vectors provide the sharing that makes estimation feasible from finite data.

author: Arthur Westmere
context_before: The objects of these seven rights make up the whole of a man's estate.
context_after:
duction to Moral Philosophy, 1747, p. 224.

THERE are two principles which induce men to enter into a civil society, which we shall call the principles of authority and utility. At the head of every small society or association of men, we find a person of superior abilities. In a warlike society he is a man of superior strength, and in a polished one of superior mental capacity. Age and a long possession of power have also a tendency to strengthen authority. Age is naturally in our imagination connected with wisdom and experience, and a continuance in power bestows a kind of right to the exercise of it. But superior wealth still more than any of these qualities contributes to confer authority. This proceeds not from any dependence that the poor have upon the rich, for in general the poor are independent, and support themselves by their labour, yet, though they expect no benefit from them, they have a strong propensity to pay them respect. This principle is fully explained in the Theory of Moral Sentiments  , where it is shown that it arises from our sympathy with our superiors being greater than that with our equals or inferiors: we admire their happy situation, enter into it with pleasure, and endeavour to promote it  .

Among the great, as superior abilities of body and mind are not so easily judged of by others, it is more convenient, as it is more common, to give the preference to riches. It is evident that an old family, that is, one which has been long distinguished by its wealth, has more authority than any other. An upstart is always disagreeable, we envy his superiority over us and think ourselves [as] well entitled to wealth as he  . If I am told that a man's grandfather was very poor and dependent on my family, I will grudge very much to see his grandson in a station above me, and will not be much disposed to submit to his authority. Superior age, superior abilities of body and of mind, ancient family and superior wealth seem to be the four things that give one man authority over another  .

The second principle which induces men to obey the civil magistrate is utility. Every one is sensible of the necessity of this principle to preserve justice and peace in the society. By civil institutions the poorest may get redress of injuries from the wealthiest and most powerful; and though there may be some irregularities in particular cases, as undoubtedly there are, yet we submit to them to avoid greater evils. It is the sense of public utility, more than of private, which influences men to obedience. It may sometimes be for my interest to disobey, and to wish government overturned, but I am sensible that other men are of a different opinion from me, and would not assist me in the enterprise. I therefore submit to its decision for the good of the whole.

If government has been of a long standing in a country, and if it be supported by proper revenues, and be at the same time in the hands of a man of great abilities, authority is then in perfection.

In all governments both these principles take place in some degree, but in a monarchy the principle of authority prevails, and in a democracy that of utility. In Britain, which is a mixed government, the factions formed some time ago, under the names of Whig and Tory, were influenced by these principles, the former submitted to government on account of its utility and the advantages which they derived from it, while the latter pretended that it was of divine institution, and to offend against it was equally criminal as for a child to rebel against its parent. Men in general follow these principles according to their natural dispositions. In a man of a bold, daring and bustling turn the principle of utility is predominant, and a peaceable easy turn of mind usually is pleased with a tame submission to superiority  .

It has been a common doctrine in this country that contract is the foundation of allegiance to the civil magistrate  . But that this is not the case will appear from the following reasons.

In the first place the doctrine of an original contract is peculiar to Great Britain, yet government takes place where it was never thought of, which is even the case with the greater part of people in this country  . Ask a common porter or day-labourer why he obeys the civil magistrate, he will tell you that it is right to do so, that he sees others do it, that he would be punished if he refused to do it, or perhaps that it is a sin against God not to do it. But you will never hear him mention a contract as the foundation of his obedience.

Secondly, when certain powers of government were at first entrusted to certain persons upon certain conditions, it is true that the obedience of those who entrusted it might be founded on a contract, but their posterity have nothing to do with it, they are not conscious of it, and therefore cannot be bound by it. It may indeed be said that by remaining in the country you tacitly consent to the contract and are bound by it. But how can you avoid staying in it? You were not consulted whether you should be born in it or not. And how can you get out of it? Most people know no other language nor country, are poor, and obliged to stay not far from the place where they were born, to labour for a subsistence. They cannot, therefore, be said to give any consent to a contract, though they may have the strongest sense of obedience. To say that by staying in a country a man agrees to a contract of obedience to government is just the same with carrying a man into a ship and after he is at a distance from land to tell him that by being in the ship  he has contracted to obey the master  . The foundation of a duty cannot be a principle with which mankind is entirely unacquainted. They must have some idea, however confused, of the principle upon which they act.

fully inculcated,' Hume, 'Of the Original Contract,' Essays, 1748, p. 293.

 ‘Can we seriously say that a poor peasant or artisan has a free choice to leave his own country when he knows no foreign language or manners, and lives from day to day by the small wages he acquires? We may as well assert that a man by remaining in a vessel freely consents to the dominion of the master; though he was carried on board while asleep.' Hume, Essays, 1748, p. 299.

But again, upon the supposition of an original contract, by leaving the state you expressly declare that you will no longer continue a subject of it and are freed from the obligation which you owed it. Yet every state claims its own subjects and punishes them for such practices  , which would be the highest injustice if their living in the country implies a consent to a former agreement. Again, if there be such a thing as an original contract, aliens who come into a country, preferring it to others, give the most express consent to it. Yet a state always suspects aliens as retaining a prejudice in favour of their mother country, and they are never so much depended upon as free-born subjects  . So much is the English law influenced by this principle that no alien can hold a place under the government, even though he should be naturalized by act of parliament  . Besides, if such a contract were supposed, why should the state require an oath of allegiance, whenever a man enters on any office? For if they supposed a previous contract, what occasion is there for renewing it? Breach of allegiance or high treason is a much greater crime, and more severely punished, in all nations, than breach of contract, in which no more but fulfilment is required. They must, therefore, be on a different footing, the less can by no means involve in it the greater contract. Contract is not therefore the principle of obedience to civil government, but the principles of authority and utility formerly explained.

We shall now endeavour to explain the nature of government, its different forms, what circumstances gave occasion for it, and by what it is maintained.

The forms of government, however various, may not improperly be reduced to these three, monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical. These may be blended in a great number of ways, and we usually denominate the government from that one which prevails.

Monarchical government is where the supreme power and authority is vested in one who can do what he pleases, make peace and war, impose taxes, and the like.

Aristocratical government is where a certain order of people in the state, either of the richest or of certain families, have it in their power to choose magistrates who are to have the management of the state.

Democratic government is where the management of affairs belongs to the whole body of the people together.

These two last forms may be called republican, and then the division of government is into monarchical and republican.
a: The origin of natural rights is quite evident. That a person has a right to have his body free from injury and his liberty free from infringement unless there be a proper cause, nobody doubts. But acquired rights such as property require more explanation. Property and civil government very much depend on one another. The preservation of property and the inequality of possession first formed it, and the state of property must always vary with the form of government. The civilians begin with considering government and then treat of property and other rights. Others  who have written on this subject begin with the latter and then consider family and civil government. There are several advantages peculiar to each of these methods, though that of the civil law seems upon the whole preferable.
b: The seven rights are life, liberty, reputation, property, and the protection of one's person, goods, and family; together they constitute the estate of every man, and the security of them is the great end of civil government.
