 corn. In the price of linen we must add to this price the wages of the
 flax-dresser, of the spinner, of the weaver, of the bleacher, etc.
 together with the profits of their respective employers.

 As any particular commodity comes to be more manufactured, that part of
 the price which resolves itself into wages and profit, comes to be greater
 in proportion to that which resolves itself into rent. In the progress of
 the manufacture, not only the number of profits increase, but every
 subsequent profit is greater than the foregoing; because the capital from
 which it is derived must always be greater. The capital which employs the
 weavers, for example, must be greater than that which employs the
 spinners; because it not only replaces that capital with its profits, but
 pays, besides, the wages of the weavers: and the profits must always bear
 some proportion to the capital.

 In the most improved societies, however, there are always a few
 commodities of which the price resolves itself into two parts only: the
 wages of labour, and the profits of stock; and a still smaller number, in
 which it consists altogether in the wages of labour. In the price of
 sea-fish, for example, one part pays the labour of the fisherman, and the
 other the profits of the capital employed in the fishery. Rent very seldom
 makes any part of it, though it does sometimes, as I shall shew hereafter.
 It is otherwise, at least through the greater part of Europe, in river
 fisheries. A salmon fishery pays a rent; and rent, though it cannot well
 be called the rent of land, makes a part of the price of a salmon, as well
 as wares and profit. In some parts of Scotland, a few poor people make a
 trade of gathering, along the sea-shore, those little variegated stones
 commonly known by the name of Scotch pebbles. The price which is paid to
 them by the stone-cutter, is altogether the wages of their labour; neither
 rent nor profit makes any part of it.

 But the whole price of any commodity must still finally resolve itself
 into some one or other or all of those three parts; as whatever part of it
 remains after paying the rent of the land, and the price of the whole
 labour employed in raising, manufacturing, and bringing it to market, must
 necessarily be profit to somebody.

 As the price or exchangeable value of every particular commodity, taken
 separately, resolves itself into some one or other, or all of those three
 parts; so that of all the commodities which compose the whole annual
 produce of the labour of every country, taken complexly, must resolve
 itself into the same three parts, and be parcelled out among different
 inhabitants of the country, either as the wages of their labour, the
 profits of their stock, or the rent of their land. The whole of what is
 annually either collected or produced by the labour of every society, or,
 what comes to the same thing, the whole price of it, is in this manner
 originally distributed among some of its different members. Wages, profit,
 and rent, are the three original sources of all revenue, as well as of all
 exchangeable value. All other revenue is ultimately derived from some one
 or other of these.

 Whoever derives his revenue from a fund which is his own, must draw it
 either from his labour, from his stock, or from his land. The revenue
 derived from labour is called wages; that derived from stock, by the
 person who manages or employs it, is called profit; that derived from it
 by the person who does not employ it himself, but lends it to another, is
 called the interest or the use of money. It is the compensation which the
 borrower pays to the lender, for the profit which he has an opportunity of
 making by the use of the money. Part of that profit naturally belongs to
 the borrower, who runs the risk and takes the trouble of employing it, and
 part to the lender, who affords him the opportunity of making this profit.
 The interest of money is always a derivative revenue, which, if it is not
 paid from the profit which is made by the use of the money, must be paid
 from some other source of revenue, unless perhaps the borrower is a
 spendthrift, who contracts a second debt in order to pay the interest of
 the first. The revenue which proceeds altogether from land, is called
 rent, and belongs to the landlord. The revenue of the farmer is derived
 partly from his labour, and partly from his stock. To him, land is only
 the instrument which enables him to earn the wages of this labour, and to
 make the profits of this stock. All taxes, and all the revenue which is
 founded upon them, all salaries, pensions, and annuities of every kind,
 are ultimately derived from some one or other of those three original
 sources of revenue, and are paid either immediately or mediately from the
 wages of labour, the profits of stock, or the rent of land.

 When those three different sorts of revenue belong to different persons,
 they are readily distinguished; but when they belong to the same, they are
 sometimes confounded with one another, at least in common language.

 A gentleman who farms a part of his own estate, after paying the expense
 of cultivation, should gain both the rent of the landlord and the profit
 of the farmer. He is apt to denominate, however, his whole gain, profit,
 and thus confounds rent with profit, at least in common language. The
 greater part of our North American and West Indian planters are in this
 situation. They farm, the greater part of them, their own estates: and
 accordingly we seldom hear of the rent of a plantation, but frequently of
 its profit.

 Common farmers seldom employ any overseer to direct the general operations
 of the farm. They generally, too, work a good deal with their own hands,
 as ploughmen, harrowers, etc. What remains of the crop, after paying the
 rent, therefore, should not only replace to them their stock employed in
 cultivation, together with its ordinary profits, but pay them the wages
 which are due to them, both as labourers and overseers. Whatever remains,
 however, after paying the rent and keeping up the stock, is called profit.
 But wages evidently make a part of it. The farmer, by saving these wages,
 must necessarily gain them. Wages, therefore, are in this case confounded
 with profit.

 An independent manufacturer, who has stock enough both to purchase
 materials, and to maintain himself till he can carry his work to market,
 should gain both the wages of a journeyman who works under a master, and
 the profit which that master makes by the sale of that journeyman’s work.
 His whole gains, however, are commonly called profit, and wages are, in
 this case, too, confounded with profit.

 A gardener who cultivates his own garden with his own hands, unites in his
 own person the three different characters, of landlord, farmer, and
 labourer. His produce, therefore, should pay him the rent of the first,
 the profit of the second, and the wages of the third. The whole, however,
 is commonly considered as the earnings of his labour. Both rent and profit
 are, in this case, confounded with wages.

 As in a civilized country there are but few commodities of which the
 exchangeable value arises from labour only, rent and profit contributing
 largely to that of the far greater part of them, so the annual produce of
 its labour will always be sufficient to purchase or command a much greater
 quantity of labour than what was employed in raising, preparing, and
 bringing that produce to market. If the society were annually to employ
 all the labour which it can annually purchase, as the quantity of labour
 would increase greatly every year, so the produce of every succeeding year
 would be of vastly greater value than that of the foregoing. But there is
 no country in which the whole annual produce is employed in maintaining
 the industrious. The idle everywhere consume a great part of it; and,
 according to the different proportions in which it is annually divided
 between those two different orders of people, its ordinary or average
 value must either annually increase or diminish, or continue the same from
 one year to another.
b:
The establishment of private property in land introduces a distinction among the several parts into which the price of commodities naturally resolves itself, which does not exist, or exists only in a very imperfect manner, in the rude state of society. Before land is appropriated, and before stock has accumulated, the whole produce of labour belongs to the labourer; he has neither landlord nor master to share with him. But as soon as the soil becomes private property, the landlord demands a rent for the use of it, and this rent constitutes the first deduction from the produce of the labour bestowed upon it. The farmer, in order to cultivate, must obtain stock, and the owner of that stock expects a profit proportioned to its value; this profit is a second deduction. The price of the commodity must therefore be sufficient to replace the stock employed, together with its ordinary profit, and to pay the rent of the land, before any part can remain to the labourer. In every improved society, accordingly, the price of almost every commodity resolves itself into three component parts: wages, profit, and rent; and in the price of some commodities a fourth part, the interest of money, may appear as a distinct item, though in strictness it is only a derivative of profit.

The wages of labour are the recompense of the labourer for his work, and are regulated, in the ordinary course of things, by the demand for labour and the supply of it, or, more precisely, by the proportion between the funds destined for the maintenance of labour and the number of those who are to be maintained. Where the demand for labour is increasing, wages are liberal; where it is stationary, they are moderate; where it is declining, they are scanty. It is to be observed, however, that the liberal reward of labour is both the effect and the cause of increasing national wealth; it is not the quantity of gold and silver, but the quantity of the necessaries and conveniences of life which the labourer can purchase with his wages, that constitutes their real value. The money price of labour may rise while its real price falls, if the price of provisions rises still faster; and hence no judgment concerning the condition of the labouring poor can be formed from the money wages alone, without a comparison with the prices of those commodities upon which they are expended.

Profit is the revenue derived from the employment of stock, and is distinguished from wages by the circumstance that it is regulated by the value of the stock employed, not by the labour bestowed. The rate of profit, however, is not so easily ascertained as the rate of wages or rent, because the stock employed is frequently concealed, and the same person may be both labourer and proprietor. It is to be remembered, likewise, that profit is not the same thing as the interest of money, though the two commonly bear a certain proportion to one another. The ordinary rate of profit varies with the state of the society: it is high in rude and newly settled countries, where stock is scarce and the demand for it great; it is low in rich and improved countries, where competition among the owners of stock reduces it; and it is perhaps never so low as in countries which are declining, where the demand for stock is less than the supply. The profit of stock, therefore, is a component part of price which varies inversely, in a general sense, with the opulence of the society, though particular branches of trade may be more or less profitable according to circumstances.

Rent is the price paid for the use of land, and is the revenue of the landlord. It is to be distinguished from the profits of the farmer, who is the capitalist employed in cultivation. Rent, considered as the price paid for the use of land, is naturally the highest which the tenant can afford to pay, consistent with the ordinary profit of the stock employed in cultivation. It is not, therefore, a constituent part of the price of the produce in the same sense as wages and profit; for the price of the produce is not raised by the payment of rent, but rent arises because the price is sufficient to pay it. In this respect rent differs essentially from wages and profit, which must be paid in order that the commodity may be produced at all. If the price of corn were not sufficient to replace the stock of the farmer with its ordinary profit, and to pay the rent of the landlord, the land would not be cultivated; but if it is sufficient, the rent is the surplus which remains after the other two are paid. Hence it follows that rent is not a cause of the high price of corn, but an effect of it; and that the interest of the landlord is strictly connected with the general prosperity of the society, since whatever tends to raise the price of produce tends to raise rent.

The three parts into which the price of commodities resolves itself are not merely nominal distinctions; they are real and distinct revenues, accruing to three different orders of men, and the proportion which they bear to one another varies with the state of the society and the nature of the commodity. In some commodities, such as those produced by the labour of a single person without the aid of stock or land, the whole price resolves itself into wages; but in the improved state of society such commodities are few. In others, the price resolves itself into wages and profit, without rent, as in the case of manufactured goods produced by stock employed in a house or workshop, where no land is concerned. In others again, as in the rude produce of the soil, all three parts enter into the price. The distinction is of importance not only to the theory of price, but to the theory of revenue; for the annual produce of the land and labour of a country is distributed among these three orders, and the wealth of the society depends upon the proportion which each receives, and upon the manner in which the whole is employed.

It is to be observed, however, that the component parts of price are not to be confounded with the sources of revenue. Wages, profit, and rent are revenues to the individuals who receive them; but the revenue of the society is not the sum of the prices of all commodities, for the same commodity may be counted more than once in the progress of its production. The corn which is used to feed the labourer is a part of the price of the commodity which the labourer produces; but the value of the corn is not to be added to the value of the commodity without a double reckoning. The true measure of the wealth of a nation is the annual produce of its land and labour, and the revenue of the society is the surplus which remains after the maintenance of the productive labourers has been deducted. This surplus, which is the fund destined for the maintenance of the unproductive labourers and for the enjoyments of the proprietors, is not the same thing as the gross produce, and the distinction between gross and neat revenue is of the utmost importance in judging of the effects of different systems of policy.

The conditions upon which these conclusions depend are chiefly these: that the society is in a progressive, stationary, or declining state, and that the commodity in question is produced under circumstances of ordinary competition. In a progressive society, wages are high, profits are moderate, and rents are rising; in a stationary society, wages are moderate, profits are low, and rents are at their height; in a declining society, wages are low, profits are low, and rents are falling. These are general tendencies, not universal laws; for particular circumstances, such as the discovery of new markets, the interruption of commerce, or the operation of monopolies, may produce effects contrary to the general course. The rent of land, for instance, is not always proportioned to the fertility of the soil, but depends also upon the situation of the market and the means of conveyance; and the profit of stock may be raised for a time by the exclusion of competition, though it is naturally reduced by the increase of stock. It is a common error to suppose that the price of commodities is raised by the payment of rent, or that the interest of the landlord is opposed to that of the consumer; the truth is that rent is the effect, not the cause, of the high price of produce, and that the landlord is benefited by whatever promotes the general prosperity.

A further distinction is to be made between the real and the nominal price of commodities. The real price is the quantity of labour which the commodity can purchase or command; the nominal price is the quantity of money for which it can be exchanged. The real price is the same in all ages and countries, and is the true measure of value; the nominal price is different, and depends upon the quantity of gold and silver in circulation. Hence the wages of labour, the profits of stock, and the rent of land, considered as revenues, are to be estimated by their real, not their nominal, amount; for it is the command over the necessaries and conveniences of life which constitutes their real value. The price of provisions, therefore, is the principal circumstance which regulates the real wages of labour; and the money price of labour is commonly adjusted, though not immediately or exactly, to the money price of provisions.

It is proper likewise to observe that the distinction between wages, profit, and rent is not merely an analytical device for the explanation of price, but corresponds to the actual distribution of the annual produce among the three great orders of the community. The labourers, the proprietors of stock, and the proprietors of land, are the three original orders into which every civilized society is divided, and the revenue of each is derived from a different source. The interest of the first is connected with the general interest of the society, since the demand for labour increases with the increase of wealth; the interest of the second is also connected with the general interest, though in a different manner, for profit is diminished by the increase of stock; and the interest of the third is connected with the general interest in a still more intimate manner, for rent rises with the improvement of the country. But the interest of the merchants and manufacturers is not always the same with that of the society, and their clamour for restrictions upon foreign trade is frequently the clamour of a particular order for a monopoly against the public.

In applying these principles to particular cases, it is necessary to distinguish between the conclusions which hold universally and those which depend upon the special circumstances of the country or the commodity. The general proposition that the price of every commodity resolves itself into wages, profit, and rent, or into some two of them, is true in the improved state of society; but in the rude state of society the whole price resolves itself into wages, and in the case of some commodities produced by the labour of a single person, the same is true even in an improved society. The general proposition that rent is not a component part of price in the same sense as wages and profit is true of the rent of land in its ordinary acceptation; but the rent of houses and buildings is of a different nature, and is a part of the price of the commodity produced, since the building is a part of the stock employed. The general proposition that the rate of profit is reduced by the increase of stock is true in the ordinary course of things; but it may be counteracted for a time by improvements in the arts, by the discovery of new branches of trade, or by the acquisition of new territory.

These considerations suggest that the analysis of price and revenue is not a matter of mere speculation, but has a direct bearing upon the practical questions of policy. The taxes which are imposed upon the several parts of price fall ultimately upon the revenue of the community, and the effect of a tax upon wages, profit, or rent is different according to the manner in which it operates. A tax upon wages, for instance, tends to raise wages and to lower profit; a tax upon profit tends to discourage industry and to reduce the stock employed; a tax upon rent falls upon the landlord, and is the least inconvenient of all taxes, since it does not interfere with the industry of the people. The system of natural liberty, which proposes that every man should be left perfectly free to pursue his own interest in his own way, is founded upon the observation that the interests of the three orders are, in the main, connected with the general interest of the society, and that the interference of government is more likely to obstruct than to promote the increase of wealth.

I conclude, therefore, that the establishment of private property in land, by introducing rent as a distinct revenue, and by rendering necessary the accumulation of stock and the payment of profit, has divided the price of commodities into three component parts, and has distributed the annual produce of the society among three orders of men. The wages of labour, the profits of stock, and the rent of land are the three original sources of all revenue, and the proportion which they bear to one another is the principal circumstance which determines the condition of the different orders of the community. The general conclusions which I have laid down are founded upon the nature of things, and are confirmed by the experience of all nations; but in applying them to particular cases, regard must be had to the circumstances of the society, to the nature of the commodity, and to the operation of those causes which may for a time counteract the general tendency. It is by attending to these distinctions that we are enabled to judge correctly of the effects of different systems of policy, and to distinguish the real from the nominal price of commodities, the revenue of the society from its gross produce, and the interest of the landlord and the labourer from the interest of the merchant and the manufacturer.

author: Arthur Westmere
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，分析对伤害的报复情感与法律救济的关系，讨论人身自由保护、财产侵占和返还制度。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
Our resentment naturally falls upon inanimate as well as animate objects, and in many places the sword or instrument that had killed any person was considered as execrable, and accordingly was destroyed, particularly among the Athenians. By the English law if a man fell from a house and was killed, the house was forfeited by the law of deodand  . Deodand signifies to be given to the devil, by the same sort of metaphor that the scripture uses where it is said he blessed God in his heart, that is, he cursed him. Afterwards the clergy applied deodands to charitable uses. If a man was killed by an object at rest, only the part by which he was killed was forfeited.

¹ 'And forasmuch as when any person is convicted for any felony within the benefit of clergy, upon his prayer to have the benefit thereof allowed to him it hath been used to administer a book to him to try whether he can read as a clerk, which by experience is found to be of no use, be it therefore enacted' that such person 'shall not be required to read, but without any reading shall be allowed, taken, and reputed to be and punished as a clerk convict.' 5 and 6 Ann. cap. 6 (6 Ann. cap. 9 in Statutes of the Realm). The indulgence had already been extended to women (who were of course incapable of obtaining benefit of clergy) by 3 W. and M. cap. 9. The account of the origin of benefit of clergy in the text is far from accurate.

If he was killed [by falling] from the wheel of a wagon standing, only that wheel was deodand, but if the wagon was in motion, the whole team was forfeited. It was long questioned if a ship was forfeited by a man being killed in it, but as mariners are so much exposed, it was thought hard that it should  .

A person may also be injured in his body by demem- bration, mutilation, assault and battery, or restraint on his liberty. Maiming and mutilation originally by the Roman law were compensated for in the same way with murder, and if the person was incapable, with the assistance of his friends, to pay the compensation, he was given over to the person maimed, to be maimed in the same manner, as we are acquainted by the Salic law, which gives us the form of their procedure. In the same manner all hurts among many nations, particularly among the Lombards, were compounded for; they paid so much for a tooth, so much more if it was a foretooth, so much for two teeth, but, what is very remarkable, though twenty were knocked out, the injured person could claim no more than the price of three. They had a precise sum for every member of the body. Among the Romans, if a man could not pay his composition, he was obliged to make satisfaction by the law of retaliation ; he received as many blows as he gave. An eye went for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. This custom continued long, and is in general reasonable, but in some cases it is not proper. If a man got his arm broken in wrestling, it was hard that another's should be broken for it in cold blood. In some cases it was impracticable, as when a man causes an abortion in a woman, he could not be punished in the same manner. This custom by degrees went out, and pecuniary fines, according to the circumstances of him who was to pay them, were introduced, and the praetor at Rome caused them to be received, but in some countries it continued longer, and there are remains of it

in Holland to this day. When a person was maimed in any member that rendered him incapable of military service  , the punishment was more severe.

By the Coventry Act, maiming in the face from malice or forethought was punished with death  . The reason of this was that Sir John Coventry had spoken impertinently against the king in parliament. The Prince of Wales, with some others, probably not without the king's permission, laid wait for him, and cut his ears and his face  . The parliament immediately enacted that maiming in the face from forethought should be punishable with death. There was never one, however, executed upon this law but one Cook, who lay in wait to murder his brother, but did not get it executed, only he maimed him in the face. He was therefore by the Coventry Act found guilty of deliberate malice. He pled that his intention was to murder, not to maim, but the court from the instrument he used found that he intended to maim as well as murder  . A man may also be injured by assault and battery. When a person is put to bodily fear it is assault, and when he is actually beat it is battery. Originally no assault by words subjected to punishment, unless there was likewise a shaking of the fist, drawing an instrument or something of this kind. A composition was the first punishment for these crimes, but now it is fine and imprisonment.

A man may further be injured in his body by restraining his liberty, therefore the laws of every country are particularly careful of securing it. No magistrate in this country has an arbitrary power of imprisonment. It is indeed reasonable that he should have it in his power to imprison when there is ground of suspicion, though an innocent man may sometimes suffer a little by it. Nothing is more difficult than perfectly to secure liberty. If the person can bring some circumstances to alleviate the suspicion, he may be set at liberty upon bail, unless it be a capital crime. If the bail be not sufficient, it is unjust in the magistrate to accept of it, but if it be, he is punishable if he do not. If a person be wrongously kept in prison beyond the time when he ought to have been tried, he has so much a day according to his station.

In England, if a person be confined the day after the assizes, forty  days after he may have the benefit of the Habeas Corpus Act, that is, he may be carried to London at his own expense, but if he cannot afford this, he must wait till the next assizes. In Scotland there is no occasion for the Habeas Corpus Act. A person may be tried by the sheriff if he pleases, and at any rate can be carried to Edinburgh to the king's court. All this is for the security of liberty in free governments, but in despotic governments the will of the magistrate is law.

It is to be observed with respect to what is done through fear, that a bond given from this principle is not binding; no obligation is valid unless the person acted voluntar[il]y. However if a person is threatened to be pursued  , and gives a bond to avoid it, the bond is valid, and the fear is not considered as a metus iniustus.

A rape or forcible marriage is capital, because the woman is so dishonoured that no other punishment can be a sufficient retaliation. Though forcible marriage be forbidden by law, yet if the woman afterwards consent, the friends can have no appeal, yet the king may pursue it.

A man may be injured in his reputation, by affronts, by words, and by writings. An affront in company is a real injury; if the affront be offered in words it is a verbal injury; if in writing it is a written injury. In all these the law gives redress. Affronts by the old law were punished in the same manner with assault and battery. Affronts in company are most atrocious crimes; the trifling fine of five or ten pounds is by no means an adequate compensation for them. Where the law denies justice, we are naturally led to take it ourselves. This introduced duelling in Europe, which brings along with it an additional injury; I must not only receive a box on the ear, but I am obliged to expose my life, or become altogether odious. It is to be observed that in Socrates' time the affront of giving the lie was little thought of; he does it himself without any ceremony.

Verbal injuries are redressed both by ancient and modern laws. When a person is accused by words, it sustains a process before a court of justice. If he be accused of forgery, theft, or any crime, as he may be subjected to great damages, he is entitled to sufficient redress. In the same manner if a person's right or title be slandered he suffers an injury. If I say you have no more right to your own house than I have, it is an injury, as it may excite those who have pretended titles. Though it be true, this is only an alleviation, and will not secure me from a prosecution. There are some offences that are only prosecuted in spiritual courts, as if a person call a woman a whore.

Written injuries are subjected to severer punishments than verbal ones, as they are more deliberate malice.

Abusive words in a libel give a process, though the same words would not if spoken. Libels and satires are punished according to the nature of the government. In aristocratical governments they are punished severely. Little petty princes may be quite destroyed by abusive libels, whereas kings and ministers of state in a free country, being far out of their reach, cannot be hurt by them. In  governments, and in Rome for a long time, they were not punished. Augustus at last revived the law subjecting the authors to a capital punishment  . In general people of circumstances take no notice of such libels unless it be absolutely necessary to clear themselves of some crime.

A person may be injured in his estate, real or personal. With regard to his real estate he may be injured either in his moveables or immoveables. In his immoveables he may be injured by arson or forcible entry. Arson is wilful fire-raising  either in the house of another, or in our own, so as to affect that of another. By the Roman, English and Scotch law this is punished capitally. If the fire be occasioned by negligence no punishment is inflicted. Forcible entry is the violently putting a man out of his estate. The laws are so strict on this head that the person ousted may retake his own by violence  . This was occasioned by the feudal customs, by which it was very common for barons and their vassals to deprive one another of their possessions, and this was the only way [that] then could be fallen on to get it restored. Afterwards it was enacted that if any person could prove that he was violent[ly] dispossessed, his estate should be restored  . But if the violent possessor had kept it three years, the old possessor must prove not only that he was dispossessed by violence, but that he has a real right to it, before it be restored  .
b:
The sentiment of retaliation for injury, which nature has implanted in every breast and which the civil magistrate can never entirely extinguish, stands in a relation to legal remedy that is at once its origin, its measure, and its perpetual rival. It is worth observing that the desire to return harm upon him who has done harm is the foundation upon which the whole edifice of justice is raised; yet the same passion, when left to its own direction, is the source of the wildest injustice. From this paradox arises the necessity of a distinct and regular administration of law, and the peculiar difficulty of every system of jurisprudence, which must borrow its vigour from a passion it can neither safely indulge nor wholly suppress.

Consider first the nature of that sentiment. When a man is injured in his person or his property, the immediate and natural movement of his mind is resentment, and resentment naturally demands that the author of the injury should suffer in his turn. This demand is not in itself unreasonable. The violator of the laws of justice, as I have elsewhere observed, is conscious that he deserves to be punished, and the spectator who enters into the sentiments of the sufferer feels the same indignation. There is therefore in the human breast a natural sense of desert, which approves of punishment proportioned to the offence, and which no refinement of policy can wholly erase. The first legislators of mankind did not create this sentiment; they found it, and they found likewise that to leave its execution to the injured party was to establish a war of every man against his neighbour.

Hence the institution of courts of justice, and hence the general principle that the magistrate is the avenger of the injuries of the weak, and that the remedy for wrong is to be sought not in private vengeance but in public authority. The law, in taking upon itself the punishment of crimes and the redress of civil injuries, does in effect say to the injured man: your resentment is just, but it is dangerous; commit it to us, and we will satisfy it according to rule. In this substitution lies the whole difference between a state of civility and a state of barbarism. Where the law is weak, the injured party and his kin become the executioners of their own cause; where it is strong, the sword is taken from the private hand and placed in that of the magistrate.

Yet the relation between the passion and the remedy is not one of simple substitution. The law, in most nations, has found it expedient to allow the natural resentment a certain scope, and to model its remedies upon the shape of that resentment. Thus in the matter of pecuniary reparation, the damages awarded are not always measured by the mere value of the thing lost, but sometimes by the circumstances of insult and contumely which accompanied the loss; and in the punishment of crimes, the law frequently graduates the penalty according to the degree of indignation which the offence naturally excites, rather than according to any precise calculation of the public detriment. This accommodation of legal rule to natural sentiment is prudent, because a law which should altogether contradict the moral feelings of the people would be obeyed with reluctance, and would lose that hold upon the affections which is the surest foundation of obedience. But it is likewise dangerous, because the sentiment, when once admitted as a measure, is apt to claim more than its due, and to demand punishments disproportioned to the offence and remedies beyond the injury sustained.

From these general considerations let us descend to the particular heads of remedy which the question proposes: the protection of personal liberty, the restitution of property taken by wrong, and the vindication of possession.

Of personal liberty, it may be said that it is of all rights the most sacred, because it is the foundation of every other. A man deprived of his liberty is deprived of the power of acquiring property, of performing contracts, and of discharging the duties of a citizen. The injury therefore which consists in the unlawful imprisonment or detention of the person is of a nature to excite the strongest resentment, and the law has accordingly provided remedies of a peculiar character. In the first place, it is not left to the party injured to pursue his remedy by the ordinary and dilatory forms of action, but a summary writ is given, by which the person detaining another is commanded forthwith to produce the body of the party detained, and to show by what authority he holds him. This remedy is founded upon the principle that the loss of liberty, even for a short time, is a mischief not to be compensated by money; and that the law, if it cannot restore the time lost, ought at least to restore the liberty without delay, and to punish the usurpation of it with severity.

Here we may observe a distinction between the remedy for the detention of the person and the remedy for the detention of a thing. In the latter case, the owner may generally be compensated by the restitution of the thing, or by damages equivalent to its value; and if the thing be returned, the injury is in a great measure repaired. But in the case of personal liberty, the injury is not capable of complete reparation; for the time during which a man has been deprived of his freedom can never be restored to him, and the apprehension and suffering attending the restraint are not to be estimated by any pecuniary standard. The law therefore, in this instance, does not content itself with compensation, but adds punishment; and it has been held, in many systems of jurisprudence, that even the consent of the party detained shall not always be pleaded in bar of the remedy, because the law presumes that consent to be obtained by fraud or by force, and because the liberty of the subject is a matter in which the public has an interest distinct from that of the individual. This last point deserves attention, for it shows that the protection of liberty is not merely a private right but a public concern; and it explains why the remedies for it are often more summary and more penal than those which are provided for the mere recovery of property.

Of property taken by wrong, and of the remedy of restitution, the principle is more simple, though the application is attended with many difficulties. The natural sentiment of the owner is to demand back his own, and the law of most nations has given him an action for the recovery of the specific thing, where the thing can be identified, and an action for damages where it cannot. The action for the specific recovery is founded upon the notion that the property of the thing remains in the owner notwithstanding the wrongful taking; for the wrongdoer acquires no dominion by his wrong, and the possession of the thief is not the possession of the owner. Hence, if the thing be found in the hands of the wrongdoer, or of any person who has not acquired it by a bona fide purchase in market overt, the owner may reclaim it. This is the remedy which the law calls restitution, and it is of great antiquity, being derived from the plainest dictates of natural justice.

But here a question of some subtlety arises, which has much exercised the courts and the writers upon jurisprudence. What shall be done where the thing has passed into the hands of a third person, who has purchased it fairly and without knowledge of the wrong? The natural resentment of the owner would pursue the thing into whatever hands it may have come; but the convenience of commerce, and the security of honest purchasers, have in most nations introduced a limitation. In England, by the custom of markets overt, a sale in open market gave a good title to the buyer, provided the sale was fair and the buyer ignorant of the wrong; and though this custom has been in great measure abolished by later statutes, the principle which it embodied, namely, that the innocent purchaser shall not be made to suffer for the fraud of another, is still admitted in many cases. The true ground of distinction seems to be this: where the owner has by his own negligence or imprudence enabled the wrongdoer to appear as the owner, the loss ought rather to fall upon him than upon the innocent buyer; but where the owner has been guilty of no negligence, and the thing has been taken from him by force or stealth, the buyer who has dealt with the thief ought not to be protected, because he has trusted a person who had no title, and the law will not compel the true owner to bear the loss occasioned by that misplaced confidence. This reasoning is not without its difficulties, for it is often hard to say what constitutes negligence in the owner; and different nations have settled the point differently, according as they have been more solicitous for the security of property or for the facility of commerce.

The restitution of the specific thing is, however, not always possible; and where it is not, the law gives damages, which are to be measured by the value of the thing at the time of the wrong, together with a compensation for the loss sustained by the detention. But here the natural sentiment of the injured party is apt to demand more than the law can give. He demands not only the value of his property, but a penalty upon the wrongdoer; and the law, in some cases, has yielded to this demand, by giving damages beyond the mere value, under the name of vindictive or exemplary damages. Whether this be wise is a question of policy rather than of strict justice. In a state where the law is weak, and where the wrongdoer is often able to escape the criminal process, such exemplary damages may be necessary to deter from wrong; but where the criminal law is vigorously administered, they are apt to be excessive, and to give to the injured party a profit beyond his loss, which is contrary to the first principles of justice.

Of the vindication of possession, the doctrine is closely connected with the foregoing. Possession, as the civilians say, is the natural foundation of property; and the law protects possession even where the title is doubtful, because the peace of society requires that no man should be permitted to redress himself by force. Hence the remedy of ejectment, and the various remedies for the recovery of land, are not founded merely upon the right of property, but upon the right of possession; and a person who has been ousted from the possession of land may recover it, though his title be not perfect, against a mere wrongdoer who has no title at all. The reason is that the law, in the first instance, presumes the possession to be rightful, and casts the burden of proof upon him who disturbs it. This is agreeable to the natural sentiment of mankind, which regards the actual occupant as the owner until the contrary be shown; and it is likewise agreeable to the public utility, because it prevents the multiplication of suits and the disturbance of the public peace.

But the protection of possession is not to be confounded with the protection of property. A man may have possession without a good title, and he may have a good title without possession. The law protects the former against force, but it does not thereby confirm his title; and the true owner may recover the possession by the proper action, and may then be restored to the full enjoyment of his right. The distinction is of importance in practice, because it explains why a person who has been wrongfully dispossessed may recover possession without proving his title, while a person who claims the property must prove his title. The one remedy is founded upon the natural resentment of the possessor at being disturbed, and is summary and possessory; the other is founded upon the right of property, and is more deliberate and more strictly examined.

From these several heads of remedy, let us return to the general question of the relation between the sentiment of retaliation and the legal remedy. The conclusion which seems to follow from the whole is this: that the sentiment of retaliation is the natural and original source of the remedy, but that it is not the measure of it. The law adopts the sentiment so far as to give a remedy for every injury, and to proportion the remedy in some degree to the indignation which the injury naturally excites; but it does not leave the execution of the remedy to the party injured, nor does it permit him to take satisfaction beyond what the law allows. The law, in short, is the substitute for private vengeance, and it is a substitute which is not perfect, but which is the best that human wisdom has been able to devise.

This conclusion, however, must be understood with certain limitations. In the first place, it holds only where the law is regularly administered and where the courts are accessible to all. In a country where the law is expensive, dilatory, and uncertain, the natural sentiment of resentment will often break out into private violence, and the remedy of the courts will be despised. In the second place, the conclusion holds only in a general sense; for in particular cases the law may be obliged to depart from the natural sentiment, as where it protects the innocent purchaser, or where it refuses to give exemplary damages, or where it allows the wrongdoer to escape on account of some technical defect. In such cases the injured party may feel that the law has not satisfied his resentment, and he may be tempted to seek his remedy elsewhere. It is the part of a wise legislator to diminish these occasions of dissatisfaction, by making the remedy as complete and as speedy as the nature of things will admit.

There is likewise another consideration which deserves attention. The sentiment of retaliation, though it be the origin of the remedy, is not the only principle which the law consults. The law consults likewise the public utility, the security of commerce, the peace of society, and the reformation of the offender. These principles sometimes coincide with the sentiment of retaliation, and sometimes they oppose it. Where they oppose it, the law ought to follow the public utility rather than the sentiment, because the sentiment is but the feeling of an individual, whereas the public utility is the interest of all. Thus, in the case of the innocent purchaser, the law protects him, not because the owner has no just cause of complaint, but because the security of commerce is of more importance than the satisfaction of the owner's resentment. In like manner, in the punishment of crimes, the law often inflicts a milder punishment than the natural sentiment would demand, because it consults the reformation of the offender and the prevention of future crimes.

It may be asked, however, whether the sentiment of retaliation, when thus checked and regulated by the law, is not in danger of being extinguished, and whether the extinction of it would not be a public misfortune. To this I answer that the sentiment, in its proper degree, is useful and even necessary to the administration of justice. A people without resentment at wrong would be a people without indignation at injustice, and the laws would be feebly executed. But the sentiment, to be useful, must be under the direction of reason and law; it must be confined to the punishment of real injuries, and it must not be allowed to extend to the innocent. The law, therefore, does not aim at extinguishing the sentiment, but at regulating it; and it is a good sign of a well-ordered society when the people are more disposed to appeal to the courts than to take vengeance into their own hands.

Upon the whole, then, we may conclude that the sentiment of retaliation is the natural foundation of legal remedy; that the law adopts and regulates it, but does not follow it implicitly; that the protection of personal liberty, the restitution of property, and the vindication of possession are severally founded upon this sentiment, combined with considerations of public utility; and that in particular cases the law may depart from the sentiment, either to protect the innocent or to promote the general welfare. These conclusions are general, and are subject to the particular circumstances of each society; for the laws of nations differ according to their manners, their commerce, and their form of government, and what is expedient in one country may be inexpedient in another. The true wisdom of the legislator consists in accommodating the remedy to the sentiment of the people, so far as may be consistent with justice, and in correcting the sentiment where it is excessive, without attempting to destroy it altogether.

author: Arthur Westmere
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察个人如何评价自己的过去行为，讨论他人的预期判断、社会经验和一般道德规则的形成。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
A great part, perhaps the greatest part, of human happiness and misery arises from the view of our past conduct, and from the degree of approbation or disapprobation which we feel from the consideration of it. But in whatever manner it may affect us, our sentiments of this kind have always some secret reference either to what are, or to what upon a certain condition would be, or to what we imagine ought to be the sentiments of others. We examine it as we imagine an impartial spectator would examine it. If upon placing ourselves in his situation we thoroughly enter into all the passions and motives which influenced it, we approve of it by sympathy with the approbation of this supposed equitable judge. If otherwise, we enter into his disapprobation and condemn it.

Was it possible that a human creature could grow up to manhood in some solitary place without any communication with his own species, he could no more think of his own character, of the propriety or demerit of his own sentiments and conduct, of the beauty or deformity of his own mind, than of the beauty or deformity of his own face. All these are objects which he cannot easily see, which naturally he does not look at; and with regard to which he is provided with no mirror which can present them to his view. Bring him into society, and he is immediately provided with the mirror which he wanted before. It is placed in the countenance and behaviour of those he lives with, which always mark when they enter into, and when they disapprove of his sentiments; and it is here that he first views the propriety and impropriety of his own passions, the beauty and deformity of his own mind. To a man who from his birth was a stranger to society, the objects of his passions, the external bodies which either pleased or hurt him, would occupy his whole attention. The passions themselves, the desires or aversions, the joys or sorrows, which those objects excited, though of all things the most immediately present to him, could scarce ever be the objects of his thoughts. The idea of them could never interest him so much as to call upon his attentive consideration. The consideration of his joy could in him excite no new joy, nor that of his sorrow any new sorrow, though the consideration of the causes of those passions might often excite both. Bring him into society, and all his own passions will immediately become the causes of new passions. He will observe that mankind approve of some of them, and are disgusted by others. He will be elevated in the one case, and cast down in the other; his desires and aversions, his joys and sorrows will now often become the causes of new desires and new aversions, new joys and new sorrows: they will now therefore interest him deeply, and often call upon his most attentive consideration.

Our first ideas of personal beauty and deformity, are drawn from the shape and appearance of others, not from our own. We soon become sensible, however, that others exercise the same criticism upon us. We are pleased when they approve of our figure, and are disobliged when they seem to be disgusted. We become anxious to know how far our appearance deserves either their blame or approbation. We examine our own persons limb by limb, and by placing ourselves before a looking-glass, or by some such expedient, endeavour, as much as possible, to view ourselves at the distance and with the eyes of other people. If after this examination we are satisfied with our own appearance, we can more easily support the most disadvantageous judgments of others: if, on the contrary, we are sensible that we are the natural objects of distaste, every appearance of their disapprobation mortifies us beyond all measure. A man who is tolerably handsome, will allow you to laugh at any little irregularity in his person; but all such jokes are commonly insupportable to one who is really deformed. It is evident, however, that we are anxious about our own beauty and deformity only on account of its effect upon others. If we had no connexion with society, we should be altogether indifferent about either.

In the same manner our first moral criticisms are exercised upon the characters and conduct of other people; and we are all very forward to observe how each of these affects us. But we soon learn, that others are equally frank with regard to our own. We become anxious to know how far we deserve their censure or applause, and whether to them we must necessarily appear those agreeable or disagreeable creatures which they represent us. We begin upon this account to examine our own passions and conduct, and to consider how these must appear to them, by considering how they would appear to us if in their situation. We suppose ourselves the spectators of our own behaviour, and endeavour to imagine what effect it would, in this light, produce upon us. This is the only looking-glass by which we can, in some measure, with the eyes of others, scrutinize the propriety of our own conduct. If in this view it pleases us, we are tolerably satisfied. We can be more indifferent about the applause, and, in some measure, despise the censure of others; secure that, however misunderstood or misrepresented, we are the natural and proper objects of approbation. On the contrary, if we are displeased with it, we are often upon that very account more anxious to gain their approbation, and, provided we have not already, as they say, shaken hands with infamy, we are altogether distracted at the thoughts of their censure, which then strikes us with double severity.

When I endeavour to examine my own conduct, when I endeavour to pass sentence upon it, and either to approve or condemn it, it is evident that, in all such cases, I divide myself, as it were, into two persons, and that I, the examiner and judge, represent a different character from that other I, the person whose conduct is examined into and judged of. The first is the spectator, whose sentiments with regard to my own conduct I endeavour to enter into, by placing myself in his situation, and by considering how it would appear to me when seen from that particular point of view. The second is the agent, the person whom I properly call myself, and of whose conduct, under the character of a spectator, I was endeavouring to form some opinion. The first is the judge; the second the pannel. But that the judge should, in every respect, be the same with the pannel, is as impossible, as that the cause should, in every respect, be the same with the effect.

To be amiable and to be meritorious, that is, to deserve love and to deserve reward, are the great characters of virtue, and to be odious and punishable, of vice. But all these characters have an immediate reference to the sentiments of others. Virtue is not said to be amiable or to be meritorious, because it is the object of its own love, or of its own gratitude; but because it excites those sentiments in other men. The consciousness that it is the object of such favourable regards is the source of that inward tranquillity and self-satisfaction with which it is naturally attended, as the suspicion of the contrary gives occasion to the torments of vice. What so great happiness as to be beloved, and to know that we deserve to be beloved? What so great misery as to be hated, and to know that we deserve to be hated?

Man is considered as a moral, because he is regarded as an accountable being. But an accountable being, as the word expresses, is a being that must give an account of its actions to some other, and that consequently must regulate them according to the good liking of this other. Man is accountable to God and his fellow-creatures. But though he is, no doubt, principally accountable to God; in the order of time, he must necessarily conceive himself as accountable to his fellow-creatures, before he can form any idea of the Deity, or of the rules by which that divine being will judge of his conduct. A child surely conceives itself as accountable to its parents, and is elevated or cast down by the thought of their merited approbation or disapprobation, long before it forms any idea of its accountableness to the Deity, or of the rules by which that divine being will judge of its conduct.
b:
When a man comes to review his own past conduct, he does so, in the first instance, by placing himself in the position of an impartial spectator: he endeavours to see his actions as they would appear to one who had no share in the passions that prompted them, and whose judgment is not warped by self-love. The judgment he forms is therefore not a simple recollection of what he did, but a moral appraisal conducted through a borrowed perspective. This borrowed perspective is not invented afresh on each occasion. It is supplied by experience—his own and that of others—and by the general rules which that experience has gradually established in his mind.

The mechanism deserves careful attention. A child, before he has learned to compare his conduct with any rule, feels chiefly the pleasure or pain of immediate consequences: the approbation or displeasure of those about him. He observes that certain actions are followed by the resentment of his companions, others by their gratitude; and he comes to associate the former with the expectation of blame, the latter with the expectation of praise. What he expects from others is thus the first standard by which he measures himself. The expectation is not merely a prediction of how they will behave; it is a prediction accompanied by a sense of what they ought to feel, and this sense is gradually detached from the particular persons whose favour or resentment he has actually experienced. When he has seen many instances of resentment directed at cruelty, and of gratitude directed at kindness, he forms the general proposition that cruelty deserves blame and kindness deserves praise, even where no particular person is present to feel either sentiment.

The formation of such general rules is thus a work of time and of social intercourse. It is not that men first perceive the rule and then apply it; rather, they first feel particular approvals and disapprovals, and the rule is the sediment left by many such feelings. The rule acquires authority because it corrects the partiality of particular judgments. In a single instance, our resentment may be excessive because we are the injured party; our approbation may be excessive because we are the beneficiary. The general rule, being formed from the concurring sentiments of many spectators in many situations, represents what the impartial spectator would feel, and it is to this corrected standard that the wise and virtuous man endeavours to bring his own conduct. The man of weak character, on the other hand, judges each case by the passion of the moment, and his self-appraisal fluctuates with his circumstances.

Here a distinction must be drawn between the general conclusion and the particular judgment. The general conclusion is that actions of a certain kind—say, breaches of promise—are blameable, and that a man who has committed such a breach ought to feel remorse and to repair the injury. This conclusion holds irrespective of the agent's present convenience or of the particular excuses he may invent. But the particular judgment—how much blame attaches to this breach, in this situation, by this agent—depends on conditions that the general rule cannot fully specify: the degree of deliberation, the strength of the temptation, the harm actually done, the agent's opportunities for knowing better, and the character of the person injured. The impartial spectator, in forming his particular judgment, must weigh all these circumstances; and different impartial spectators, if equally informed and equally free from bias, will generally converge, though they may not perfectly agree.

It is worth asking what other explanations might be offered for the phenomenon. One might say that the agent's self-appraisal is simply the internalized voice of external authority—that he judges himself as his parents or his society once judged him, and that the appearance of an impartial spectator is an illusion. There is truth in this: the sentiments of those about us are the original materials out of which conscience is formed. But the explanation is incomplete, for it cannot account for the fact that men sometimes condemn themselves by a standard higher than that of their society, or that they appeal from the judgment of their neighbours to a tribunal within. Another explanation would derive the whole from self-interest: that a man calls his conduct good when it is useful to him, and bad when it is harmful. But this fails to explain the remorse of a man who has injured another secretly and with impunity, where no self-interested motive prompts the condemnation. A third explanation would make the judgment a matter of mere custom, so that what is blamed in one country is praised in another, and there is no impartial spectator but only the local one. Custom undoubtedly shapes the content of many rules, but the form of the judgment—the appeal to an imagined spectator who is neither self nor other—appears to be universal, and the differences between societies are differences in what the spectator is thought to approve, not in the practice of appealing to him.

The connection between the expectation of others and the formation of general rules may be illustrated by a familiar case. A merchant who has been cheated by a partner reviews the transaction. He feels resentment, and he expects that others, if they knew the facts, would share it. But he also knows that his resentment may be inflamed by his loss, and he therefore asks what an indifferent person would think. If he concludes that he was indeed wronged, his resentment is approved; if he concludes that he was careless or that the partner acted within his rights, his resentment is condemned, and he feels shame for having entertained it. The general rule—that fraud deserves resentment and that carelessness does not—is what enables him to make this correction. The rule was not given to him at birth; it was built up from his experience of similar cases and from the concurring judgments of those he has known. And the particular judgment he now forms depends on conditions the rule leaves open: whether the partner concealed anything, whether the merchant had means of checking the accounts, and what the custom of the trade permits.

It should be observed that the impartial spectator is not a real person, and the standard he represents is not a standard of perfect wisdom. It is the standard of the ordinary, informed, unbiased spectator—the man who knows the facts and is not himself involved. This is why the general rules of morality are, as it were, the common sense of mankind, and why they are felt to be binding even when no external sanction enforces them. The agent who has violated them feels a peculiar uneasiness, which we call remorse, arising from the consciousness that he has rendered himself the proper object of the resentment of his fellows, and that he has fallen short of what the impartial spectator within him approves. This remorse is not merely a fear of punishment; it is a sentiment of desert, and it is the strongest of all the checks to wrongdoing.

The account here given has an important consequence for the understanding of moral knowledge. We do not first know the rule and then apply it; we first feel, and the rule is an abstraction from many feelings. Hence the general conclusion is always somewhat indeterminate, and its application to particular cases requires a kind of judgment that cannot be reduced to rule. The man of experience and reflection applies the rule with discrimination; the inexperienced man applies it mechanically, and either condemns where he ought to excuse or excuses where he ought to condemn. This is why the study of particular cases, and the comparison of our own judgments with those of others, is necessary to the formation of a sound moral taste. It is also why the rules themselves are subject to revision as experience extends: a rule that seemed adequate in a simpler state of society may be found too crude when new circumstances arise.

Finally, the connection between self-appraisal and the expectation of others is reciprocal. We judge ourselves by the standard we have learned from others, but we also contribute to the standard by which others judge. When a man acts in a manner that the impartial spectator approves, he strengthens the general rule; when he acts otherwise, he weakens it, or at least he provides an example that others may follow. The moral rules of a society are thus not a fixed inheritance but a living product, maintained and modified by the conduct and judgments of its members. The individual who reviews his past conduct is therefore engaged in a task that is at once personal and public: he is measuring himself against a standard that he has helped to form, and his judgment, if it is sound, will in turn contribute to the standard by which others measure themselves.

author: Arthur Westmere
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察人们想象显贵生活的方式，讨论社会地位、个人风度与公众认可之间的联系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
When we consider the condition of the great, in those delusive colours in which the imagination is apt to paint it, it seems to be almost the abstract idea of a perfect and happy state. It is the very state which, in all our waking dreams and idle reveries, we had sketched out to ourselves as the final object of all our desires. We feel, therefore, a peculiar sympathy with the satisfaction of those who are in it. We favour all their inclinations, and forward all their wishes. What pity, we think, that any thing should spoil and corrupt so agreeable a situation! We could even wish them immortal; and it seems hard to us, that death should at last put an end to such perfect enjoyment. It is cruel, we think, in Nature, to compel them from their exalted stations to that humble, but hospitable home, which she has provided for all her children. Great King, live for ever! is the compliment, which after the manner of eastern adulation, we should readily make them, if experience did not teach us its absurdity. Every calamity that befalls them, every injury that is done them, excites in the breast of the spectator ten times more compassion and resentment than he would have felt, had the same things happened to other men. It is the misfortunes of Kings only which afford the proper subjects for tragedy. They resemble, in this respect, the misfortunes of lovers. Those two situations are the chief which interest us upon the theatre; because, in spite of all that reason and experience can tell us to the contrary, the prejudices of the imagination attach to these two states a happiness superior to any other. To disturb, or to put an end to such perfect enjoyment, seems to be the most atrocious of all injuries. The traitor who conspires against the life of his monarch, is thought a greater monster than any other murderer. All the innocent blood that was shed in the civil wars, provoked less indignation than the death of Charles I. A stranger to human nature, who saw the indifference of men about the misery of their inferiors, and the regret and indignation which they feel for the misfortunes and sufferings of those above them, would be apt to imagine, that pain must be more agonizing, and the convulsions of death more terrible to persons of higher rank, than to those of meaner stations.

Upon this disposition of mankind, to go along with all the passions of the rich and the powerful, is founded the distinction of ranks, and the order of society. Our obsequiousness to our superiors more frequently arises from our admiration for the advantages of their situation, than from any private expectations of benefit from their good-will. Their benefits can extend but to a few; but their fortunes interest almost every body. We are eager to assist them in compleating a system of happiness that approaches so near to perfection; and we desire to serve them for their own sake, without any other recompense but the vanity or the honour of obliging them. Neither is our deference to their inclinations founded chiefly, or altogether, upon a regard to the utility of such submission, and to the order of society, which is best supported by it. Even when the order of society seems to require that we should oppose them, we can hardly bring ourselves to do it. That kings are the servants of the people, to be obeyed, resisted, deposed, or punished, as the public conveniency may require, is the doctrine of reason and philosophy; but it is not the doctrine of Nature. Nature would teach us to submit to them, for their own sake, to tremble and bow down before their exalted station, to regard their smile as a reward sufficient to compensate any services, and to dread their displeasure, though no other evil was to follow from it, as the severest of all mortifications. To treat them in any respect as men, to reason and dispute with them upon ordinary occasions, requires such resolution, that there are few men whose magnanimity can support them in it, unless they are likewise assisted by familiarity and acquaintance. The strongest motives, the most furious passions, fear, hatred, and resentment, are scarce sufficient to balance this natural disposition to respect them: and their conduct must, either justly or unjustly, have excited the highest degree of all those passions, before the bulk of the people can be brought to oppose them with violence, or to desire to see them either punished or deposed. Even when the people have been brought this length, they are apt to relent every moment, and easily relapse into their habitual state of deference to those whom they have been accustomed to look upon as their natural superiors. They cannot stand the mortification of their monarch. Compassion soon takes the place of resentment, they forget all past provocations, their old principles of loyalty revive, and they run to re-establish the ruined authority of their old master, with the same violence with which they had opposed it. The death of Charles I. brought about the Restoration of the royal family. Compassion for James II. when he was seized by the populace in making his escape on ship-board, had almost prevented the Revolution, and made it go on more heavily than before.

Do the great seem insensible of the easy price at which they may acquire the public admiration; or do they seem to imagine that to them, as to other men, it must be the purchase either of sweat or of blood? By what important accomplishments is the young nobleman instructed to support the dignity of his rank, and to render himself worthy of that superiority over his fellow-citizens, to which the virtue of his ancestors had raised them? Is it by knowledge, by industry, by patience, by self-denial, or by virtue of any kind? As all his words, as all his motions are attended to, he learns an habitual regard to every circumstance of ordinary behaviour, and studies to perform all those small duties with the most exact propriety. As he is conscious how much he is observed, and how much mankind are disposed to favour all his inclinations, he acts, upon the most indifferent occasions, with that freedom and elevation which the thought of this naturally inspires. His air, his manner, his deportment, all mark that elegant and graceful sense of his own superiority, which those who are born to inferior stations can hardly ever arrive at: these are the arts by which he proposes to make mankind more easily submit to his authority, and to govern their inclinations according to his own pleasure: and in this he is seldom disappointed. These arts, supported by rank and pre-eminence, are, upon ordinary occasions, sufficient to govern the world. Lewis XIV. during the greater part of his reign, was regarded, not only in France, but over all Europe, as the most perfect model of a great prince. But what were the talents and virtues by which he acquired this great reputation? Was it by the scrupulous and inflexible justice of all his undertakings, by the immense dangers and difficulties with which they were attended, or by the unwearied and unrelenting application with which he pursued them? Was it by his extensive knowledge, by his exquisite judgment, or by his heroic valour? It was by none of these qualities. But he was, first of all, the most powerful prince in Europe, and consequently held the highest rank among kings; and then, says his historian, “he surpassed all his courtiers in the gracefulness of his shape, and the majestic beauty of his features. The sound of his voice, noble and affecting, gained those hearts which his presence intimidated. He had a step and deportment which could suit only him and his rank, and which would have been ridiculous in any other person. The embarrassment which he occasioned to those who spoke to him, flattered that secret satisfaction with which he felt his own superiority. The old officer, who was confounded and faultered in asking him a favour, and not being able to conclude his discourse, said to him, Sir, your majesty, I hope, will believe that I do not tremble thus before your enemies: had no difficulty to obtain what he demanded.” These frivolous accomplishments, supported by his rank, and, no doubt, too, by a degree of other talents and virtues, which seems, however, not to have been much above mediocrity, established this prince in the esteem of his own age, and have drawn, even from posterity, a good deal of respect for his memory. Compared with those of his own times, and in his own presence, no other virtue, it seems, appeared to have any merit. Knowledge, industry, valour, and beneficence, trembled, were abashed, and lost all dignity before them.
b:
That the imagination of the condition of the great and the fortunate is among the most active and most consequential operations of the human mind will scarcely be denied by anyone who has attended to the ordinary course of conversation. We do not merely observe the rich and the exalted; we enter, by a kind of sympathetic anticipation, into their situation, and we clothe it with pleasures which perhaps they never feel. The palace, the equipage, the retinue, the deference of inferiors, the easy command of every convenience—these are imagined as constituting a state of happiness almost superior to the condition of humanity. And from this imagination, rather than from any cool calculation of the satisfactions actually enjoyed, arises a great part of that emulation which sets every man in motion, and which is the hidden spring of industry, of ambition, and of the whole busy scene of human life.

It is to be remarked, however, that the pleasure we derive from contemplating such a condition is not chiefly a pleasure of the senses. The conveniences of the great are not, in kind, different from those of the meanest; a bed is a bed, and hunger is appeased by food in every rank. What chiefly distinguishes the condition of the exalted in our imagination is the consideration which attends it—the observation, the regard, the applause of mankind. The rich man is admired because he is rich; his equipage is agreeable not merely as a convenience but as a badge of distinction; and the satisfaction which we ascribe to him is less the enjoyment of what he possesses than the consciousness of being the object of general esteem. Hence it is that the loss of fortune is felt as a loss of standing, and that men of spirit have been known to bear the privation of many comforts with composure, while they could not endure the mortification of being overlooked.

From this connection between wealth and public regard there follows a consequence of some importance: the qualities which procure esteem are not always the qualities which deserve it, and the imagination is perpetually disposed to confound them. We are apt to regard the man of high station as possessing, in a peculiar degree, the virtues which become his station; we expect from him magnanimity, dignity, and a certain elevation of sentiment; and the expectation itself disposes us to see these qualities where they are but faintly, or perhaps not at all, present. The splendour of the condition reflects a borrowed lustre upon the person; the office dignifies the man, and we ascribe to the individual what belongs to the situation. This is the origin of that general deference which is paid to rank and title, and of the facility with which mankind are disposed to believe that those who are placed above them are also above them in merit.

Yet it must not be concluded that this disposition is altogether irrational or pernicious. In the ordinary course of things, the man who is raised to high station has passed through a course of discipline which tends to form the very qualities we expect; the habits of command produce dignity, the necessity of presiding over others produces self-command, and the observation to which he is exposed produces a certain care of his conduct. The presumption, therefore, is not without foundation; it is a general rule, drawn from experience, that the station and the character are frequently united, though the union is neither universal nor necessary. It is the nature of such general rules, indeed, to be liable to exceptions; and the mischief arises when the rule is applied with confidence to a particular case in which the conditions that support it are wanting. The deference which is due to the office is easily transferred to the person; and the person, sheltered by the office, may escape that scrutiny to which his conduct would otherwise be exposed.

The manner or air of a man—what is commonly called his address—operates in a similar way, though by a different mechanism. A graceful and composed deportment is agreeable in itself, and it is likewise a sign of those qualities which fit a man for society: of self-command, of attention to others, of a mind not wholly occupied with its own concerns. Hence the man of pleasing address is received with favour, and his opinions are listened to with a regard which they might not otherwise obtain. But here too the sign is not infallible.
