A studied politeness may conceal a cold and interested heart; an easy confidence may be the effect of assurance rather than of merit; and the world, which judges by appearances, is often deceived. The connection between the outward manner and the inward disposition is a connection of frequent, not of constant, conjunction; and the man who trusts to it in a particular instance may be mistaken.

It is proper likewise to observe that the imagination of the condition of the great is affected by the peculiar circumstances of the imaginer. To the man who has known want, the plenty of the rich appears in colours heightened by contrast; to him the freedom from anxiety which wealth appears to bestow is the most enviable of all possessions, and he is apt to forget that wealth brings anxieties of its own. To the man born in a humble station, the dignity of the great is a thing almost sacred; he approaches it with awe, and is disposed to magnify every circumstance which distinguishes it. On the other hand, one who has been long conversant with the great is apt to see them as they are, and to estimate their condition more coolly; his imagination is less inflamed, and he is less disposed to ascribe to them a happiness which he has had occasion to see interrupted by the same infirmities which disturb the peace of other men. The same object, therefore, is contemplated with different feelings by different persons; and the general conclusion that high station is attended with high enjoyment must be understood with an allowance for the situation and temper of him who forms the judgment.

There is likewise a further consideration, which deserves to be weighed. The applause of the public is not a simple thing; it is composed of the sentiments of many individuals, each of whom is influenced by his own imagination, his own interests, and his own peculiar habits of thinking. A reputation, therefore, may be raised or depressed by causes which have little relation to the real merit of the person who is its object. The fashion of the times, the prejudices of a party, the partiality of friends, the envy of rivals—all these enter into the composition of public esteem, and render it a very uncertain measure of desert. Hence the wise man will not repose his happiness upon it; he will receive it with moderation, and he will not be cast down by the want of it. Yet he will not despise it altogether; for the approbation of mankind is a natural and laudable object of desire, and the man who is wholly indifferent to it is perhaps deficient in that social sympathy which is the foundation of virtue.

It may be asked, then, upon what principle the love of distinction is to be justified, if the distinction itself is so uncertain and the imagination which pursues it so liable to error. The answer is, that the love of distinction is not, in its origin, a vicious passion. It is the desire of being the object of that sympathetic regard which is natural to man; and it is connected with the desire of being worthy of regard. The error lies not in the desire, but in the means by which it is pursued, and in the estimation which is formed of the condition in which it is supposed to be attained. The man who seeks to be admired for qualities which he does not possess, or who values himself upon a station to which he has no merit to recommend him, is justly exposed to contempt; but the man who labours to render himself the proper object of esteem, and who receives the esteem of others as the reward of his labours, acts upon a principle which is consonant to nature and conducive to the good of society.

The conclusion, therefore, which I would draw is this: that the imagination of the condition of the great is a powerful and almost universal principle of human conduct; that it operates chiefly by associating the idea of happiness with the idea of public consideration; that the connection between station, manner, and merit is a connection of frequent but not of necessary conjunction; and that the judgments which men form of the happiness of others are always to be understood as subject to the peculiar circumstances and temper of him who forms them. In general, it may be affirmed that the pursuit of distinction is a natural and useful passion, since it calls forth industry and cultivates the virtues which fit men for society; but in particular instances it is liable to be misled by appearances, and to mistake the splendour of the situation for the merit of the person. The wise man, therefore, will neither be dazzled by the one nor deceived by the other; he will estimate the condition of the great with a just allowance for the cares which attend it, and the esteem of the public with a just allowance for the causes which may exaggerate or diminish it; and he will seek rather to deserve approbation than to obtain it, remembering that the applause of the world is at best a doubtful and uncertain good, while the consciousness of deserving it is a satisfaction which depends upon himself.

author: Arthur Westmere
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察生活资料价格变化如何影响劳动积极性，讨论工资、劳动供给和制造业产出的关系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
In cheap years it is pretended, workmen are generally more idle, and in
 dear times more industrious than ordinary. A plentiful subsistence,
 therefore, it has been concluded, relaxes, and a scanty one quickens their
 industry. That a little more plenty than ordinary may render some workmen
 idle, cannot be well doubted; but that it should have this effect upon the
 greater part, or that men in general should work better when they are ill
 fed, than when they are well fed, when they are disheartened than when
 they are in good spirits, when they are frequently sick than when they are
 generally in good health, seems not very probable. Years of dearth, it is
 to be observed, are generally among the common people years of sickness
 and mortality, which cannot fail to diminish the produce of their
 industry.

 In years of plenty, servants frequently leave their masters, and trust
 their subsistence to what they can make by their own industry. But the
 same cheapness of provisions, by increasing the fund which is destined for
 the maintenance of servants, encourages masters, farmers especially, to
 employ a greater number. Farmers, upon such occasions, expect more profit
 from their corn by maintaining a few more labouring servants, than by
 selling it at a low price in the market. The demand for servants
 increases, while the number of those who offer to supply that demand
 diminishes. The price of labour, therefore, frequently rises in cheap
 years.

 In years of scarcity, the difficulty and uncertainty of subsistence make
 all such people eager to return to service. But the high price of
 provisions, by diminishing the funds destined for the maintenance of
 servants, disposes masters rather to diminish than to increase the number
 of those they have. In dear years, too, poor independent workmen
 frequently consume the little stock with which they had used to supply
 themselves with the materials of their work, and are obliged to become
 journeymen for subsistence. More people want employment than easily get
 it; many are willing to take it upon lower terms than ordinary; and the
 wages of both servants and journeymen frequently sink in dear years.

 Masters of all sorts, therefore, frequently make better bargains with
 their servants in dear than in cheap years, and find them more humble and
 dependent in the former than in the latter. They naturally, therefore,
 commend the former as more favourable to industry. Landlords and farmers,
 besides, two of the largest classes of masters, have another reason for
 being pleased with dear years. The rents of the one, and the profits of
 the other, depend very much upon the price of provisions. Nothing can be
 more absurd, however, than to imagine that men in general should work less
 when they work for themselves, than when they work for other people. A
 poor independent workman will generally be more industrious than even a
 journeyman who works by the piece. The one enjoys the whole produce of his
 own industry, the other shares it with his master. The one, in his
 separate independent state, is less liable to the temptations of bad
 company, which, in large manufactories, so frequently ruin the morals of
 the other. The superiority of the independent workman over those servants
 who are hired by the month or by the year, and whose wages and maintenance
 are the same, whether they do much or do little, is likely to be still
 greater. Cheap years tend to increase the proportion of independent
 workmen to journeymen and servants of all kinds, and dear years to
 diminish it.

 A French author of great knowledge and ingenuity, Mr Messance, receiver of
 the tallies in the election of St Etienne, endeavours to shew that the
 poor do more work in cheap than in dear years, by comparing the quantity
 and value of the goods made upon those different occasions in three
 different manufactures; one of coarse woollens, carried on at Elbeuf; one
 of linen, and another of silk, both which extend through the whole
 generality of Rouen. It appears from his account, which is copied from the
 registers of the public offices, that the quantity and value of the goods
 made in all those three manufactories has generally been greater in cheap
 than in dear years, and that it has always been greatest in the cheapest,
 and least in the dearest years. All the three seem to be stationary
 manufactures, or which, though their produce may vary somewhat from year
 to year, are, upon the whole, neither going backwards nor forwards.

 The manufacture of linen in Scotland, and that of coarse woollens in the
 West Riding of Yorkshire, are growing manufactures, of which the produce
 is generally, though with some variations, increasing both in quantity and
 value. Upon examining, however, the accounts which have been published of
 their annual produce, I have not been able to observe that its variations
 have had any sensible connection with the dearness or cheapness of the
 seasons. In 1740, a year of great scarcity, both manufactures, indeed,
 appear to have declined very considerably. But in 1756, another year of
 great scarcity, the Scotch manufactures made more than ordinary advances.
 The Yorkshire manufacture, indeed, declined, and its produce did not rise
 to what it had been in 1755, till 1766, after the repeal of the American
 stamp act. In that and the following year, it greatly exceeded what it had
 ever been before, and it has continued to advance ever since.

 The produce of all great manufactures for distant sale must necessarily
 depend, not so much upon the dearness or cheapness of the seasons in the
 countries where they are carried on, as upon the circumstances which
 affect the demand in the countries where they are consumed; upon peace or
 war, upon the prosperity or declension of other rival manufactures and
 upon the good or bad humour of their principal customers. A great part of
 the extraordinary work, besides, which is probably done in cheap years,
 never enters the public registers of manufactures. The men-servants, who
 leave their masters, become independent labourers. The women return to
 their parents, and commonly spin, in order to make clothes for themselves
 and their families. Even the independent workmen do not always work for
 public sale, but are employed by some of their neighbours in manufactures
 for family use. The produce of their labour, therefore, frequently makes
 no figure in those public registers, of which the records are sometimes
 published with so much parade, and from which our merchants and
 manufacturers would often vainly pretend to announce the prosperity or
 declension of the greatest empires.

 Though the variations in the price of labour not only do not always
 correspond with those in the price of provisions, but are frequently quite
 opposite, we must not, upon this account, imagine that the price of
 provisions has no influence upon that of labour. The money price of labour
 is necessarily regulated by two circumstances; the demand for labour, and
 the price of the necessaries and conveniencies of life. The demand for
 labour, according as it happens to be increasing, stationary, or
 declining, or to require an increasing, stationary, or declining
 population, determines the quantities of the necessaries and conveniencies
 of life which must be given to the labourer; and the money price of labour
 is determined by what is requisite for purchasing this quantity. Though
 the money price of labour, therefore, is sometimes high where the price of
 provisions is low, it would be still higher, the demand continuing the
 same, if the price of provisions was high.

 It is because the demand for labour increases in years of sudden and
 extraordinary plenty, and diminishes in those of sudden and extraordinary
 scarcity, that the money price of labour sometimes rises in the one, and
 sinks in the other.

 In a year of sudden and extraordinary plenty, there are funds in the hands
 of many of the employers of industry, sufficient to maintain and employ a
 greater number of industrious people than had been employed the year
 before; and this extraordinary number cannot always be had. Those masters,
 therefore, who want more workmen, bid against one another, in order to get
 them, which sometimes raises both the real and the money price of their
 labour.

 The contrary of this happens in a year of sudden and extraordinary
 scarcity. The funds destined for employing industry are less than they had
 been the year before. A considerable number of people are thrown out of
 employment, who bid one against another, in order to get it, which
 sometimes lowers both the real and the money price of labour. In 1740, a
 year of extraordinary scarcity, many people were willing to work for bare
 subsistence. In the succeeding years of plenty, it was more difficult to
 get labourers and servants. The scarcity of a dear year, by diminishing
 the demand for labour, tends to lower its price, as the high price of
 provisions tends to raise it. The plenty of a cheap year, on the contrary,
 by increasing the demand, tends to raise the price of labour, as the
 cheapness of provisions tends to lower it. In the ordinary variations of
 the prices of provisions, those two opposite causes seem to counterbalance
 one another, which is probably, in part, the reason why the wages of
 labour are everywhere so much more steady and permanent than the price of
 provisions.

 The increase in the wages of labour necessarily increases the price of
 many commodities, by increasing that part of it which resolves itself into
 wages, and so far tends to diminish their consumption, both at home and
 abroad. The same cause, however, which raises the wages of labour, the
 increase of stock, tends to increase its productive powers, and to make a
 smaller quantity of labour produce a greater quantity of work. The owner
 of the stock which employs a great number of labourers necessarily
 endeavours, for his own advantage, to make such a proper division and
 distribution of employment, that they may be enabled to produce the
 greatest quantity of work possible. For the same reason, he endeavours to
 supply them with the best machinery which either he or they can think of.
 What takes place among the labourers in a particular workhouse, takes
 place, for the same reason, among those of a great society. The greater
 their number, the more they naturally divide themselves into different
 classes and subdivisions of employments. More heads are occupied in
 inventing the most proper machinery for executing the work of each, and it
 is, therefore, more likely to be invented. There are many commodities,
 therefore, which, in consequence of these improvements, come to be
 produced by so much less labour than before, that the increase of its
 price is more than compensated by the diminution of its quantity.
b:
The price of provisions, or of those necessaries and conveniencies which support the labourer, is among the most powerful, though least immediate, of all the circumstances that regulate the industry of a people. Its influence is seldom confined to the single article whose price has changed; it operates by altering the real recompence of labour, and thereby the disposition of the labourer to exert himself, the terms on which he is willing to be employed, and, through these, the quantity and quality of the manufactures that a country is able to produce. To treat this subject properly, it is necessary to distinguish the several channels through which the price of subsistence acts, to observe how these channels are connected with the wages of labour and the supply of hands, and to mark the conditions upon which the general conclusions depend, together with the other causes that may produce appearances similar to those which are commonly ascribed to the price of provisions alone.

The first and most obvious channel is the real wage. What the labourer receives is nominally a sum of money, but really a command over the necessaries of life. When provisions become dearer, the same money wage purchases less; the labourer is in effect worse paid, though his master's payments may not have been diminished by a single shilling. It is natural to suppose that a reduction in the real recompence of labour should diminish the quantity of labour offered. Yet this supposition is not universally true, and the reason why it is not deserves attention. Where the labourer is already reduced to the bare means of subsistence, a rise in the price of provisions may compel him to work more, not less: he must add to his industry to procure the same quantity of food, and the necessity of the case may extort from him an exertion which no prospect of better payment could have drawn forth. This is the well-known case in which dearness operates as a spur rather than a check, and in which the labouring poor, in the language of common observation, are driven to their work by hunger. But this effect is confined within narrow limits. It supposes a labourer already at the margin of subsistence, a demand for labour that will absorb any additional exertion, and an absence of those combinations and customs by which the hours and the pace of work are frequently fixed. Where these conditions fail, and where the labourer has some little stock or credit upon which to subsist, a rise in the price of provisions will rather diminish than increase the supply of labour; the workman will prefer a little leisure to a diminished pittance, and will not sell his ease at a rate which leaves him no better provision than before.

From this it follows that the relation between the price of provisions and the supply of labour is not a simple and uniform one, but depends upon the level of wages relative to the cost of living, upon the habits and customs of the people, and upon the nature of the employment. In a country where wages are high, and where the labourer enjoys a considerable surplus above mere necessaries, a rise in the price of provisions may be borne for a time without any material diminution of industry; the labourer will retrench his indulgences rather than his work, and the supply of labour will continue nearly the same. In a country where wages are low, and where the labourer is already straitened, the same rise will produce a very different effect: it may either force him to a more severe exertion, as has been said, or it may reduce him to a state of languor and inability, in which the quantity of work performed is diminished, though the hours of attendance may be the same. The difference between these two situations is not a matter of small consequence to the manufacturer, for it determines whether a rise in the price of provisions shall raise or lower the cost of production.

The connection with the wages of labour is here very intimate, and it is necessary to be precise. Wages are not determined by the price of provisions alone, nor by the quantity of money in circulation, nor by the will of the master, but by the contract between the master and the workman, in which the relative necessities of the parties are the governing circumstance. The master, having a stock to support himself, can wait; the workman, having no stock, or a very small one, cannot. This inequality of situation gives the master an advantage in the bargain, and it is the reason why wages are not always raised in proportion to the dearness of provisions. In the long run, however, the price of provisions must have a considerable influence upon wages, because the labourer must live, and the race of labourers cannot be kept up unless their earnings are sufficient to maintain them and to bring up a family. The price of provisions, therefore, enters into the natural price of labour as one of its principal component parts, and the natural price of labour in its turn enters into the price of every manufacture. But the adjustment is slow and irregular. It is retarded by the poverty of the workman, who cannot hold out for better terms; it is accelerated or retarded by the state of the demand for labour; and it is frequently disturbed by laws and regulations relating to the settlement of the poor, to apprenticeships, and to the free circulation of hands from one place to another.

The supply of labour, again, is not to be confounded with the number of labourers. The number of hands may be the same, and yet the quantity of labour actually performed may vary greatly, according as the labourer is well or ill fed, strong or weak, diligent or negligent. A rise in the price of provisions, when it reduces the labourer to a worse diet, may diminish the vigour of his body and the alacrity of his mind, and thus lower the produce of his work without any visible diminution of his numbers. This consideration is of great importance in manufactures, where the work is often delicate, and where the quality of the commodity depends upon the attention and the bodily condition of the workman. A manufacturer who employs a number of hands at low wages, and who finds his profits reduced by the dearness of provisions, may be tempted to reduce wages still further; but this reduction, if it goes beyond a certain point, will defeat its own purpose, for it will impair the health and the industry of his people, and will render the work both less in quantity and worse in quality. It is a maxim, therefore, that the liberal reward of labour is the effect, and not the cause, of great national wealth; and it is also a maxim that the liberal reward of labour, by enabling the labourer to live better, to be stronger, and to work with more cheerfulness, tends to increase the produce of the country, and to lower the real cost of manufactures, though it may raise the money price of some of them.

The effect of the price of provisions upon manufactures is thus seen to be twofold. In the first place, it affects the cost of production through its influence upon wages. A rise in the price of provisions, if it is followed by a rise in wages, will raise the money price of manufactures; but whether it raises their real price, or the quantity of other goods for which they exchange, depends upon whether the rise in wages is general and proportionate, and upon whether the manufactures are exported or consumed at home. In the second place, it affects the supply of labour through its influence upon the condition and the disposition of the workmen. A rise in the price of provisions, when it is not accompanied by a rise in wages, will reduce the real recompence of labour, and may either diminish the quantity of work performed, as has been shown, or may force the workmen to a more severe exertion, according to the circumstances already stated. In the former case, the produce of manufactures is diminished, and the price of the commodity tends to rise; in the latter case, the produce may be increased for a time, and the price may fall, but the fall is purchased at the expense of the health and the strength of the people, and is therefore of short duration.

These conclusions, however, are general, and are subject to several qualifications which it is necessary to state, lest they should be applied too broadly. The first is that the effect of a rise in the price of provisions depends upon the proportion which provisions bear to the whole expenditure of the labourer. If the labourer spends but a small part of his income upon bread, a rise in the price of bread will affect him little; if he spends a great part, it will affect him much. The same rise, therefore, which is a trifle to the workman of a rich country, where wages are high and the necessaries of life are cheap, may be a serious calamity to the workman of a poor country, where wages are low and the necessaries of life are dear. The second qualification is that the effect depends upon the duration of the change. A temporary scarcity, such as that occasioned by a bad harvest, may produce effects very different from those of a permanent rise in the price of provisions. In a temporary scarcity, the labourer may be supported by his little savings, by the credit of the shopkeeper, or by the charity of his neighbours, and the supply of labour may be little affected; in a permanent rise, the whole habits of the people must be altered, and the effect upon wages and upon industry will be more lasting. The third qualification is that the effect depends upon the state of the demand for labour. If the demand is increasing, and the country is advancing in wealth, a rise in the price of provisions may be accompanied by a rise in wages, and the labourer may be better off than before, notwithstanding the dearness of food. If the demand is stationary or declining, the rise in the price of provisions will be felt as a real diminution of the means of subsistence, and will produce the effects which have been described.

There are also other explanations of the appearances which are commonly ascribed to the price of provisions alone, and these must be carefully distinguished. A decline in the industry of a manufacturing town may be occasioned, not by the dearness of provisions, but by a failure of the demand for its particular commodity, by the introduction of machinery, by the removal of a branch of trade to another place, or by the pressure of taxes. A rise in the price of manufactures may be occasioned, not by a rise in wages, but by a rise in the price of the raw material, by the dearness of fuel, by the increased cost of carriage, or by the want of that security and freedom which are necessary to the successful conduct of trade. A diminution in the number of labourers may be occasioned, not by the dearness of provisions, but by the ravages of disease, by the drain of emigration, by the obstructions to marriage arising from the poor laws, or by the natural decay of a population which has been supported by a declining trade. It is the business of the observer to distinguish these several causes, and not to attribute to the price of provisions alone those effects which may proceed from a combination of circumstances. The price of provisions is, indeed, a cause of great importance, and its influence is extensive; but it is not the only cause, and its operation is frequently modified or counteracted by others.

The distinction between the general conclusion and the particular case is here of the utmost importance. The general conclusion is that a rise in the price of provisions, when it is not accompanied by a proportionate rise in wages, tends to diminish the real recompence of labour, and, according to the circumstances of the country and the habits of the people, either to diminish the supply of labour and the produce of manufactures, or to force the labourer to a more severe exertion which is injurious to his health and ultimately to the produce of his work. The particular case is that in which the labourer is already at the margin of subsistence, in which the demand for labour is brisk, and in which the work is such as admits of an increase of exertion without an increase of skill; in this case, a rise in the price of provisions may, for a time, increase the quantity of labour offered and the produce of manufactures, though it will not increase the real recompence of the labourer, and though the increase will be purchased at the expense of his health and his comfort. The general conclusion is that the liberal reward of labour is favourable to the industry of the labourer, and that high wages, by enabling him to live better, tend to increase the produce of the country; the particular case is that in which high wages are accompanied by a rise in the price of provisions so great as to leave the labourer but little better off than before, in which case the effect upon his industry will depend upon the direction in which he chooses to spend his additional earnings, and upon the customs of the place in which he lives.

It may be added that the relation between the price of provisions and the industry of manufactures is not a relation of simple cause and effect, but a relation of mutual dependence. The price of provisions affects wages, wages affect the supply and the condition of labour, and these in turn affect the produce and the price of manufactures. But the produce of manufactures, by increasing the wealth of the country, may increase the demand for labour, and may raise wages, and may thus enable the labourer to purchase a greater quantity of provisions, even at a higher price. The improvement of agriculture, again, by increasing the quantity of provisions, may lower their price, and may thus raise the real recompence of labour, and may increase the produce of manufactures. The whole is a system of reciprocal action, in which no one part can be understood without a reference to the others; and the observer who confines his attention to a single link in the chain will be apt to mistake the nature of the connection, and to ascribe to one cause what is in reality the effect of many.

Upon the whole, therefore, it may be concluded that the price of provisions is a circumstance of great moment to the industry of a country, but that its operation is not uniform and cannot be reduced to a simple rule. It acts through the real wage, through the condition and the disposition of the labourer, and through the supply of labour; and its effects upon manufactures are determined by the proportion which provisions bear to the labourer's expenditure, by the duration of the change, by the state of the demand for labour, and by the habits and customs of the people. The general conclusion, that a rise in the price of provisions, when it is not accompanied by a rise in wages, tends to diminish the real recompence of labour and to check the produce of manufactures, is subject to the particular exception, that where the labourer is already at the margin of subsistence and the demand for labour is brisk, the same cause may for a time force him to a more severe exertion and may increase the produce, though at the expense of his health and his comfort. And the appearances which are commonly ascribed to the price of provisions alone may frequently be occasioned by other causes, such as the failure of demand, the introduction of machinery, the pressure of taxes, or the obstructions to the free circulation of labour. It is by distinguishing these several causes, and by marking the conditions upon which the operation of each depends, that we are enabled to form a just judgment of the whole, and to avoid the error of attributing to a single circumstance those effects which are the result of a combination of many.

author: Arthur Westmere
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，讨论伤害他人与正当防卫的评价基础，分析公正、自我克制、悔恨和功绩意识之间的关系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
There can be no proper motive for hurting our neighbour, there can be no incitement to do evil to another, which mankind will go along with, except just indignation for evil which that other has done to us. To disturb his happiness merely because it stands in the way of our own, to take from him what is of real use to him merely because it may be of equal or more use to us, or to indulge, in this manner, at the expence of other people, the natural preference which every man has for his own happiness above that of other people, is what no impartial spectator can go along with. Every man is, no doubt, by nature, first and principally recommended to his own care; and as he is fitter to take care of himself than of any other person, it is fit and right that it should be so. Every man, therefore, is much more deeply interested in whatever immediately concerns himself, than in what concerns any other man: and to hear, perhaps, of the death of another person, with whom we have no particular connexion, will give us less concern, will spoil our stomach, or break our rest much less than a very insignificant disaster which has befallen ourselves. But though the ruin of our neighbour may affect us much less than a very small misfortune of our own, we must not ruin him to prevent that small misfortune, nor even to prevent our own ruin. We must, here, as in all other cases, view ourselves not so much according to that light in which we may naturally appear to ourselves, as according to that in which we naturally appear to others. Though every man may, according to the proverb, be the whole world to himself, to the rest of mankind he is a most insignificant part of it. Though his own happiness may be of more importance to him than that of all the world besides, to every other person it is of no more consequence than that of any other man. Though it may be true, therefore, that every individual, in his own breast, naturally prefers himself to all mankind, yet he dares not look mankind in the face, and avow that he acts according to this principle. He feels that in this preference they can never go along with him, and that how natural soever it may be to him, it must always appear excessive and extravagant to them. When he views himself in the light in which he is conscious that others will view him, he sees that to them he is but one of the multitude in no respect better than any other in it. If he would act so as that the impartial spectator may enter into the principles of his conduct, which is what of all things he has the greatest desire to do, he must, upon this, as upon all other occasions, humble the arrogance of his self-love, and bring it down to something which other men can go along with. They will indulge it so far as to allow him to be more anxious about, and to pursue with more earnest assiduity, his own happiness than that of any other person. Thus far, whenever they place themselves in his situation, they will readily go along with him. In the race for wealth and honours, and preferments, he may run as hard as he can, and strain every nerve and every muscle, in order to outstrip all his competitors. But if he should justle, or throw down any of them, the indulgence of the spectators is entirely at an end. It is a violation of fair play, which they cannot admit of. This man is to them, in every respect, as good as he: they do not enter into that self-love by which he prefers himself so much to this other, and cannot go along with the motive from which he hurt him. They readily, therefore, sympathize with the natural resentment of the injured, and the offender becomes the object of their hatred and indignation. He is sensible that he becomes so, and feels that those sentiments are ready to burst out from all sides against him.

As the greater and more irreparable the evil that is done, the resentment of the sufferer runs naturally the higher, so does likewise the sympathetic indignation of the spectator, as well as the sense of guilt in the agent. Death is the greatest evil which one man can inflict upon another, and excites the highest degree of resentment in those who are immediately connected with the slain. Murder, therefore, is the most atrocious of all crimes which affect individuals only, in the sight both of mankind, and of the person who has committed it. To be deprived of that which we are possessed of, is a greater evil than to be disappointed of what we have only the expectation. Breach of property, therefore, theft and robbery, which take from us what we are possessed of, are greater crimes than breach of contract, which only disappoints us of what we expected. The most sacred laws of justice, therefore, those whose violation seems to call the loudest for vengeance and punishment, are the laws which guard the life and person of our neighbour; the next are those which guard his property and possessions; and last of all come those which guard what are called his personal rights, or what is due to him from the promises of others.

The violator of the more sacred laws of justice can never reflect on the sentiments which mankind must entertain with regard to him, without feeling all the agonies of shame, and horror, and consternation. When his passion is gratified, and he begins coolly to reflect upon his conduct, he can enter into none of the motives which influenced it. They appear now as detestable to him as they did always to other people. By sympathizing with the hatred and abhorrence which other men must entertain for him, he becomes in some measure the object of his own hatred and abhorrence. The situation of the person, who suffered by his injustice, now calls upon his pity. He is grieved at the thought of it; regrets the unhappy effects of his own conduct, and feels at the same time that they have rendered him the proper object of the resentment and indignation of mankind, and of what is the natural consequence of resentment, vengeance and punishment. The thought of this perpetually haunts him, and fills him with terror and amazement. He dares no longer look society in the face, but imagines himself as it were rejected, and thrown out from the affections of all mankind. He cannot hope for the consolation of sympathy in this his greatest, and most dreadful distress. The remembrance of his crimes has shut out all fellow-feelings with him from the hearts of his fellow-creatures. The sentiments which they entertain with regard to him, are the very thing which he is most afraid of. Every thing seems hostile, and he would be glad to fly to some inhospitable desert, where he might never more behold the face of a human creature, nor read in the countenance of mankind the condemnation of his crimes. But solitude is still more dreadful than society. His own thoughts can present him with nothing but what is black, unfortunate, and disastrous, the melancholy forebodings of incomprehensible misery and ruin. The horror of solitude drives him back into society, and he comes again into the presence of mankind, astonished to appear before them, loaded with shame and distracted with fear, in order to supplicate some little protection from the countenance of those very judges, who he knows have already all unanimously condemned him. Such is the nature of that sentiment, which is properly called remorse; of all the sentiments which can enter the human breast the most dreadful. It is made up of shame from the sense of the impropriety of past conduct; of grief for the effects of it; of pity for those who suffer by it; and of the dread and terror of punishment from the consciousness of the justly provoked resentment of all rational creatures.

The opposite behaviour naturally inspires the opposite sentiment. The man who, not from frivolous fancy, but from proper motives, has performed a generous action, when he looks forward to those whom he has served, feels himself to be the natural object of their love and gratitude, and, by sympathy with them, of the esteem and approbation of all mankind. And when he looks backward to the motive from which he acted, and surveys it in the light in which the indifferent spectator will survey it, he still continues to enter into it, and applauds himself by sympathy with the approbation of this supposed impartial judge. In both these points of view his own conduct appears to him every way agreeable. His mind, at the thought of it, is filled with chearfulness, serenity, and composure. He is in friendship and harmony with all mankind, and looks upon his fellow-creatures with confidence and benevolent satisfaction, secure that he has rendered himself worthy of their most favourable regards. In the combination of all these sentiments consists the consciousness of merit, or of deserved reward.
b:
That hurt or injury which one person inflicts upon another is not, in itself, a violation of justice. The same external event—a wound, a deprivation of liberty, a loss of property—may be innocent, excusable, or criminal, according to the intention from which it proceeds and the circumstances in which it is done. The evaluation of injury therefore cannot rest upon the mere magnitude of the harm, but must consider the design of the agent, the provocation received, and the relation in which the parties stand to one another. It is this consideration which renders the theory of self-defence instructive, since it exhibits, in the clearest light, how our moral sentiments adjust themselves to the intentions and situation of the agent, and how the several principles of justice, self-command, remorse, and the sense of merit or demerit are combined in a single judgment.

The foundation of the whole is the sympathetic mechanism by which we approve or disapprove of actions. When we behold a person injured, we enter, by imagination, into the resentment of the sufferer; and when we behold the agent, we enter into the motives which influenced him. Our moral judgment is the result of a certain correspondence or dissonance between these two sympathetic movements. Where the resentment of the sufferer is fully justified by the impropriety of the agent's motive, we call the action unjust and the agent criminal; where the agent's motive is such as we can entirely go along with, the resentment of the sufferer appears unreasonable, and the injury, though real, is not a wrong. Self-defence is the great instance in which the resentment of the sufferer is superseded by our sympathy with the necessary precautions of the defender. The man who is attacked may repel force by force; and we approve of his resistance, not because we delight in the harm done to the aggressor, but because we enter into the natural and justifiable desire of preserving life and limb. The aggressor has placed himself in a situation in which, by the very nature of his undertaking, he has exposed himself to the consequences of a resistance which he himself rendered necessary. The defender acts under a necessity which excludes the imputation of injustice; and the harm he inflicts, being the means of safety and not the object of his desire, is regarded as an accident of the conflict rather than as a violation of right.

Here, then, is a distinction of the first importance: the difference between the intention and the mere material effect. The defender intends his own preservation; the harm to the assailant is foreseen but not desired. The assailant intends the harm to the defender, or at least the submission which can only be procured by the fear of it. It is the intention which gives the colour to the action. This is not to say that the intention alone determines the whole moral character of the transaction; for the circumstances must be such as to make the resistance necessary and proportionate. If a man, under a slight provocation, should repel a blow with a deadly weapon, our sympathy with his resentment would be checked by our sense of the disproportion between the injury threatened and the injury inflicted. The defender is justified only in so far as the means he employs are necessary to avert the evil with which he is threatened; and the judgment of necessity is not a matter of mere private opinion, but must be such as a candid and impartial spectator could go along with. Hence the general conclusion: an injury is unjust when it proceeds from an improper motive, and self-defence is just when it proceeds from a necessary and proportionate resistance to an unjust attack. But this general conclusion must be distinguished from the particular judgment in any given case, which depends upon the apprehension of the agent at the moment, the information available to him, and the degree of danger which a reasonable person in his situation would have perceived.

The relation between justice and self-command now becomes apparent. Justice, in the strict sense, is the virtue which consists in abstaining from what is another's, and in doing no harm to our neighbour. It is a negative virtue, capable of being prescribed by precise rules, and its violation calls for punishment rather than mere blame. But the preservation of justice in the world depends upon the resentment of mankind, and resentment is a passion which, if left to itself, is apt to run to excess. The injured person is tempted to retaliate beyond the measure of the offence; and the spectator, entering into his resentment, is tempted to approve of that excess. It is here that self-command becomes necessary. The man of perfect self-command moderates his resentment to the pitch which the impartial spectator can go along with; he does not suffer the injury to inflame him beyond the degree which the offence deserves. In the case of self-defence, self-command is displayed in the defender's restraining his resistance to what is necessary for his safety, and in his not converting a just defence into a cruel revenge. The man who, having disarmed his assailant, should deliberately kill him, would lose the approbation of the spectator; for the necessity which justified the first blow no longer justifies the second. Thus self-command is not opposed to justice, but is the guardian of it; it preserves the just mean between the excess of resentment and the defect of a servile submission to injury.

From this we may pass to the consideration of remorse, and of its connection with the sense of merit and demerit. Remorse is the sentiment of the man who reflects upon his own conduct and finds that he has acted in a manner which the impartial spectator within his breast cannot approve. It is not merely the fear of punishment, nor merely the regret for a disappointed interest; it is the consciousness of having violated a rule of justice, and of having rendered himself the proper object of the resentment of mankind. The remorse of the aggressor in a case of unjust attack is the natural counterpart of the approbation which we bestow upon the defender. The aggressor, if he has any remaining sense of justice, must feel that he has exposed himself to the just resistance of the person he attacked; and this feeling is the foundation of the distinction between the sense of demerit and the sense of merit. We approve of the defender as meritorious, because his conduct is the proper object of gratitude and approbation; we disapprove of the aggressor as demeritorious, because his conduct is the proper object of resentment and punishment. The sense of merit is the consciousness of having acted so as to deserve the gratitude of mankind; the sense of demerit is the consciousness of having acted so as to deserve their resentment. These sentiments are not arbitrary; they arise from the sympathetic mechanism by which we enter into the feelings of the persons concerned, and they are the foundation of the whole system of rewards and punishments.

It is important, however, to observe that the sense of merit and demerit is not always proportioned to the external harm. A man may do a great harm and yet be little blameable, as in the case of the defender who, in the necessary resistance to an attack, kills the assailant; and a man may do a small harm and yet be highly criminal, as in the case of the man who, from a malignant motive, insults and injures a person who has done him no wrong. The moral judgment depends upon the propriety of the motive, and upon the correspondence between the motive and the circumstances, rather than upon the mere magnitude of the effect. This is the principle which reconciles the severity of justice with the lenity of humanity. Justice requires that the aggressor should be punished, because the resentment of mankind is justly excited against him; but humanity requires that we should consider the temptations and difficulties of his situation, and that we should not impute to him a degree of guilt which the impartial spectator could not go along with. The man who has been provoked beyond human endurance may be excused, though not justified; and the man who has acted from a cool and deliberate malice is the proper object of the severest resentment, though the harm he has done may be comparatively small.

The connection between these several principles may be illustrated by a case which is not a case of self-defence, but which throws light upon the conditions of our judgments. Suppose a man, walking in a public street, is suddenly assaulted by a stranger who attempts to rob him. The man strikes the robber, and the robber falls and is killed. Our judgment upon this transaction depends upon several conditions. First, we must consider whether the danger was imminent and the resistance necessary; if the robber was armed and the defender had no other means of safety, we approve of the resistance. Secondly, we must consider whether the defender used no more force than was necessary; if he continued to strike after the robber was disabled, our approbation is withdrawn. Thirdly, we must consider the knowledge and apprehension of the defender at the moment; if he believed, upon reasonable grounds, that his life was in danger, we excuse him even though the danger was not in fact so great as he supposed. Fourthly, we must consider the character of the robber's intention; if he intended murder as well as robbery, our resentment against him is greater, and our sympathy with the defender is more complete. These conditions show that the judgment of self-defence is not a simple deduction from a general rule, but a complex appreciation of circumstances, motives, and intentions. The general conclusion is that self-defence is justifiable when it is necessary and proportionate; but the particular judgment in any case depends upon the apprehension of the agent, the information available to him, and the degree of danger which a reasonable person in his situation would have perceived.

It may be objected that this account makes the moral judgment too dependent upon the opinion of the spectator, and that it leaves no fixed standard by which to distinguish justice from injustice. To this it may be answered that the impartial spectator is not a mere fiction, but a standard which every man carries within his breast, and which corrects the partiality of self-love. The man who is injured is apt to exaggerate the offence; the man who has injured another is apt to extenuate his own fault. It is by consulting the impartial spectator—by asking what a candid and disinterested person would feel—that we arrive at a just estimate of the case. This standard is not arbitrary, because it is founded upon the uniform constitution of human nature, and because it is confirmed by the common sense of mankind in all ages and nations. The general rules of justice are derived from the particular judgments which we form upon particular cases; and though these rules are not absolutely precise, they are sufficiently determinate for the purposes of human society.

Another possible explanation of the phenomena must be considered, namely, that the approbation of self-defence arises not from sympathy with the defender's motive, but from a regard to the general utility of permitting resistance to violence. Upon this view, we approve of self-defence because a society in which men are permitted to defend themselves is more secure and prosperous than one in which they are not. This explanation has some force, and it is not inconsistent with the account which has been given. But it is not the whole truth. For we approve of the defender even when his resistance is unsuccessful, and even when the particular act of resistance may seem to have increased the evil rather than diminished it. We approve of him because we enter into his natural indignation against the aggressor, and because we sympathise with his desire of safety. The utility of the general practice may confirm our approbation, but it is not the original source of it. The sentiment of justice is anterior to the calculation of utility, and it is felt with a warmth which no calculation of utility can adequately explain.

The same may be said of the sense of merit and demerit. It is not merely a calculation of the probable consequences of rewarding or punishing; it is a sentiment which arises from the sympathetic correspondence between the agent and the spectator. The man who has acted meritoriously feels a conscious dignity and elevation of mind; the man who has acted demeritoriously feels a depression and a dread of the resentment of mankind. These sentiments are the natural attendants of virtue and vice, and they are the foundation of the moral approbation and disapprobation which we bestow upon actions. They are not always proportioned to the external consequences, because they depend upon the intention and the circumstances; and it is this which renders the moral judgment so delicate and so difficult.

In the case of self-defence, the sense of merit is peculiarly interesting. The defender does not feel that he has done a meritorious action in the sense of having conferred a benefit upon mankind; he feels rather that he has done what was necessary for his own preservation, and that he has not violated the rules of justice. His merit consists in his self-command, in his restraining his resentment within the bounds of necessity, and in his not abusing the power which the conflict has given him. The aggressor, on the other hand, feels remorse, not merely because he has failed in his purpose, but because he has violated the rules of justice and has rendered himself the proper object of resentment. If he is a man of any reflection, he must feel that he has exposed himself to the just resistance of the person he attacked, and that his own suffering is the consequence of his own injustice. This remorse is the natural punishment of the aggressor, and it is often more severe than any punishment which the law can inflict.

The distinction between the general conclusion and the particular judgment is of the utmost importance in the theory of self-defence. The general conclusion is that a man may justly defend himself against an unjust attack, and that the harm he inflicts upon the aggressor is not a violation of justice. But the particular judgment in any case depends upon a variety of conditions which cannot be reduced to a precise rule. The law of England, as it is understood by the best authorities, requires that the resistance should be necessary, and that the force used should be proportionate to the danger. But the law itself is obliged to leave much to the discretion of the jury, because the circumstances of each case are different, and because the apprehension of the agent at the moment cannot be exactly measured. The moral judgment is even more delicate than the legal, because it considers the motive and the character of the agent, and not merely the external act. A man may be legally justified in killing another in self-defence, and yet may feel remorse for having done so, if he believes that he might have avoided the conflict by a greater degree of forbearance. The law acquits him, but his own conscience may not acquit him. This shows that the moral judgment is not identical with the legal, and that the sense of merit and demerit is not always proportioned to the external harm.

The relation between justice and self-command may be further illustrated by the case of the man who is insulted and provoked, but who is not attacked. He has no right to kill the insulter, because the provocation, however great, does not threaten his life or his safety. His self-command consists in restraining his resentment within the bounds of the law and of the impartial spectator. If he should kill the insulter, he would be guilty of murder, because the harm he inflicts is disproportionate to the injury he has received. The general conclusion is that the provocation may extenuate the offence, but it cannot justify the killing. The particular judgment depends upon the degree of provocation, the character of the parties, and the circumstances of the case. The man who has been provoked beyond human endurance may be excused, though not justified; and the man who has acted from a cool and deliberate malice is the proper object of the severest resentment.

In conclusion, the evaluation of injury and self-defence rests upon the sympathetic mechanism by which we enter into the motives of the agent and the resentment of the sufferer. The general conclusion is that an injury is unjust when it proceeds from an improper motive, and that self-defence is just when it proceeds from a necessary and proportionate resistance to an unjust attack. But the particular judgment in any case depends upon the apprehension of the agent, the information available to him, and the degree of danger which a reasonable person in his situation would have perceived. The principles of justice, self-command, remorse, and the sense of merit and demerit are intimately connected: justice requires that the aggressor should be punished, self-command moderates the resentment of the defender, remorse is the natural punishment of the aggressor, and the sense of merit and demerit is the foundation of the moral approbation and disapprobation which we bestow upon actions. These principles are not arbitrary, but are founded upon the uniform constitution of human nature, and they are confirmed by the common sense of mankind in all ages and nations. The general rules of justice are sufficiently determinate for the purposes of human society, though they are not absolutely precise; and the particular judgment in any case must be left to the discretion of the impartial spectator, who corrects the partiality of self-love and who is the standard of moral judgment within the breast of every man.

author: Arthur Westmere
context_before: Upon some occasions, indeed, we both punish and approve of punishment, merely from a view to the general interest of society, which, we imagine, cannot otherwise be secured. Of this kind are all the punishments inflicted for breaches of what is called either civil police, or military discipline. Such crimes do not immediately or directly hurt any particular person; but their remote consequences, it is supposed, do produce, or might produce, either a considerable inconveniency, or a great disorder in the society. A centinel, for example, who falls asleep upon his watch, suffers death by the law of war, because such carelessness might endanger the whole army. This severity may, upon many occasions, appear necessary, and, for that reason, just and proper. When the preservation of an individual is inconsistent with the safety of a multitude, nothing can be more just than that the many should be preferred to the one. Yet this punishment, how necessary soever, always appears to be excessively severe. The natural atrocity of the crime seems to be so little, and the punishment so great, that it is with great difficulty that our hearts can reconcile itself to it.
context_after: A man of humanity must recollect himself, must make an effort, and exert his whole firmness and resolution, before he can bring himself either to inflict it, or to go along with it when it is inflicted by others. It is not, however, in this manner, that he looks upon the just punishment of an ungrateful murderer or parricide. His heart, in this case, applauds with ardour, and even with transport, the just retaliation which seems due to such detestable crimes, and which, if, by any accident, they should happen to escape, he would be highly enraged and disappointed. The very different sentiment with which the spectator views those different punishments, is a proof that his approbation of the one is far from being founded upon the same principles with that of the other. He looks upon the centinel as an unfortunate victim, who, indeed, must, and ought to be, devoted to the safety of numbers, but whom still, in his heart, he would be glad to save; and he is only sorry, that the interest of the many should oppose it. But if the murderer should escape from punishment, it would excite his highest indignation, and he would call upon God to avenge, in another world, that crime which the injustice of mankind had neglected to chastise upon earth.
a: Though such carelessness appears very blamable, yet the thought of this crime does not naturally excite any such resentment, as would prompt us to take such dreadful revenge.
b: We feel, therefore, a kind of horror at the sight of it, which no consideration of its necessity can entirely overcome, and which prompts us to lament the cruel exigency that demands such a sacrifice.

It has been considered as of so much importance that a proper number of
 young people should be educated for certain professions, that sometimes
 the public, and sometimes the piety of private founders, have established
 many pensions, scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries, etc. for this

 the education of the greater part of churchmen is paid for in this
 manner. Very few of them are educated altogether at their own expense.
 The long, tedious, and expensive education, therefore, of those who are,
 will not always procure them a suitable reward, the church being crowded
 with people, who, in order to get employment, are willing to accept of a
 much smaller recompence than what such an education would otherwise have
 entitled them to; and in this manner the competition of the poor takes
 away the reward of the rich. It would be indecent, no doubt, to compare
 either a curate or a chaplain with a journeyman in any common trade. The
 pay of a curate or chaplain, however, may very properly be considered as
 of the same nature with the wages of a journeyman. They are all three
 paid for their work according to the contract which they may happen to
 make with their respective superiors. Till after the middle of the
 fourteenth century, five merks, containing about as much silver as ten
 pounds of our present money, was in England the usual pay of a curate or
 a stipendiary parish priest, as we find it regulated by the decrees of
 several different national councils. At the same period, fourpence a-day,
 containing the same quantity of silver as a shilling of our present
 money, was declared to be the pay of a master mason; and threepence
 a-day, equal to ninepence of our present money, that of a journeyman
 mason. {See the Statute of Labourers, 25, Ed. III.} The wages of both
 these labourers, therefore, supposing them to have been constantly
 employed, were much superior to those of the curate.
context_after:
By the 12th of Queen Anne, c.
 12. it is declared, “That whereas, for want of sufficient
 maintenance and encouragement to curates, the cures have, in several
 places, been meanly supplied, the bishop is, therefore, empowered to
 appoint, by writing under his hand and seal, a sufficient certain stipend
 or allowance, not exceeding fifty, and not less than twenty pounds
 a-year”. Forty pounds a-year is reckoned at present very good pay
 for a curate; and, notwithstanding this act of parliament, there are many
 curacies under twenty pounds a-year. There are journeymen shoemakers in

 twenty. This last sum, indeed, does not exceed what is frequently earned

 attempted to regulate the wages of workmen, it has always been rather to

author: Arthur Westmere
context_before: The same principle, the same love of system, the same regard to the beauty of order, of art and contrivance, frequently serves to recommend those institutions, which tend to promote the public welfare. When a patriot exerts himself for the improvement of any part of the public police, his conduct does not always arise from pure sympathy with the happiness of those who are to reap the benefit of it. It is not commonly from a fellow-feeling with carriers and waggoners that a public-spirited man encourages the mending of high roads. When the legislature establishes premiums and other encouragements to advance the linen or woollen manufactures, its conduct seldom proceeds from pure sympathy with the wearer of cheap or fine cloth, and much less from that with the manufacturer, or merchant. The perfection of police, the extension of trade and manufactures, are noble and magnificent objects. The contemplation of them pleases us, and we are interested in whatever can tend to advance them. They make part of the great system of government, and the wheels of the political machine seem to move with more harmony and ease by means of them. We take pleasure in beholding the perfection of so beautiful and grand a system, and we are uneasy till we remove any obstruction that can in the least disturb or encumber the regularity of its motions. All constitutions of government, however, are valued only in proportion, as they tend to promote the happiness of those who live under them. This is their sole use and end. From a certain spirit of system, however, from a certain love of art and contrivance, we sometimes seem to value the means more than the end, and to be eager to promote the happiness of our fellow-creatures, rather from a view to perfect and improve a certain beautiful and orderly system, than from any immediate sense or feeling of what they either suffer or enjoy. There have been men of the greatest public spirit, who have shewn themselves in other respects not very sensible to the feelings of humanity. And on the contrary, there have been men of the greatest humanity, who seem to have been entirely devoid of public spirit.
context_after: Who had ever less humanity, or more public spirit, than the celebrated legislator of Muscovy? The social and well natured James the First of Great Britain seems, on the contrary, to have had scarce any passion, either for the glory, or the interest of his country. Would you awaken the industry of the man, who seems almost dead to ambition, it will often be to no purpose to describe to him the happiness of the rich and the great; to tell him that they are generally sheltered from the sun and the rain, that they are seldom hungry, that they are seldom cold, and that they are rarely exposed to weariness, or to want of any kind. The most eloquent exhortation of this kind will have little effect upon him. If you would hope to succeed, you must describe to him the conveniency and arrangement of the different apartments in their palaces, you must explain to him the propriety of their equipages, and point out to him the number, the order, and the different offices of all their attendants. If any thing is capable of making impression upon him, this will. Yet all these things tend only to keep off the sun and the rain, to save them from hunger and cold, from want and weariness. In the same manner, if you would implant public virtue in the breast of him, who seems heedless of the interest of his country, it will often be to no purpose to tell him, what superior advantages the subjects of a well-governed state enjoy; that they are better lodged, that they are better clothed, that they are better fed. These considerations will commonly make no great impression. You will be more likely to persuade, if you describe the great system of public police which procures these advantages, if you explain the connexions and dependencies of its several parts, their mutual subordination to one another, and their general subserviency to the happiness of the society; if you show how this system might be introduced into his own country, what it is that hinders it from taking place there at present, how those obstructions might be removed, and all the several wheels of the machine of government be made to move with more harmony and smoothness, without grating upon one another, or mutually retarding one another’s motions. It is scarce possible that a man should listen to a discourse of this kind, and not feel himself animated to some degree of public spirit. He will, at least for the moment, feel some desire to remove those obstructions, and to put into motion so beautiful and so orderly a machine. Nothing tends so much to promote public spirit as the study of politics, of the several systems of civil government, their advantages and disadvantages, of the constitution of our own country, its situation, and interest with regard to foreign nations, its commerce, its defence, the disadvantages it labours under, the dangers to which it may be exposed, how to remove the one, and how to guard against the other. Upon this account political disquisitions, if just and reasonable, and practicable, are of all the works of speculation the most useful. Even the weakest and the worst of them are not altogether without their utility. They serve at least to animate the public passions of men, and rouse them to seek out the means of promoting the happiness of the society.
a: Every man may find in the circle of his acquaintance instances both of the one kind and the other.
b: The heroes of literary as well as civil history have been very often no less remarkable for what they have suffered, than for what they have achieved.

context_before: The next step Mr. Law fell upon was the relieving of the public debts, which amounted to 200[o] millions  . As he saw the diminution must needs come, he took another method to keep up his notes. He got a grant of the exclusive privilege of trading to Canada, and established the Mississippi Company. To this he joined the African, the Turkey, and the East India companies. He also farmed the tobacco and all the public revenues of France at 52 millions  , for in France the whole revenue is farmed by one man, who undertakes it and levies it without excisemen, and the farmers there are the richest in the country, and must be skilled in the finances and public revenues  . Mr. Law undertook this, and, having the whole trade of the country monopolized, it was difficult to say what profits he would make. He wanted to lend the government 80 or 90 millions [sterling], which he could easily do by issuing notes to that value, but then he saw that they would soon return upon him. To prevent this, his invention was set on work, and we shall see how far he succeeded. As the company he erected seemed to be in a very flourishing condition, shares were purchased in it at a very considerable rate. He opened a subscription to it at 500 livres, so that a navy ticket or billet d'état purchased a share into it, which raised them to a par, as they had for a long time been far below it. The government of France was never in such a miserable condition as then.
context_after: Never was monarch more degraded than Lewis XIV. After the treaty of Utrecht he had occasion to borrow 8 millions of livres from Holland, and not only to give them his bond for 32 millions, but to get some merchants to be security for him  . Since that was the case, we need not be surprised that the billets d'état sold at great discount, as they bore no interest, and it was quite uncertain when they would be paid. Law published a declaration that one of these, which was granted for 500 livres, should purchase a share in the company, and thus they came again to par. The people still continuing in great expectations of profit, he in a few days opened a new subscription at 5000 livres, and afterwards another at 10,000. At this time he was enabled to lend the government 1600 millions of livres at 3 per cent¹.
a: The interest of the money which should have paid the billets d'état was seized upon for other purposes.
b: Its credit was so low that it could borrow only on the most exorbitant terms.

author: Arthur Westmere
context_before: Had he stopped here, it is probable that he would have answered all engagements, but his future proceedings ruined all. It was impossible that the value of shares could long continue at such a high rate. He thought, however, that it was necessary to do all that he could to keep them up, as the whole fortunes of many people were in the bank. He had issued out notes to double the circulation of the country, which raised the price of everything to an enormous pitch, and consequently the exchange was against France in all foreign trade. This was principally occasioned by his opening an office to purchase 500 livres shares at 9000 livres  , which obliged him to issue out many notes. People of prudence who were concerned opposed this scheme, and indeed it was the first thing that made his bank lose credit, and occasioned its dissolution. As he was not obliged to pay the capital sums, only the annual dividend of 200 livres arising from the profits  , he might have let them fall to their original 500 without any great loss but that of reputation; but his buying up the shares occasioned his issuing out so many notes that they must of necessity return upon him. This was so much the case that he was obliged to open offices in different parts of Paris for the payment of them. When in this manner oppressed, he was making continual changes on the coin, in order to dissuade people from returning on the bank, and disgust them at gold and silver  . He cried up gold, but as coin cannot be kept much above the level of the metal, when it was so much depreciated, it was not taken. If a person had 20,000 guineas, as he was afraid that the coin would not continue at that value, he went to the bank and got it exchanged for notes. The same consideration prevented them from returning upon the bank, as they would there be paid in coin. By this means he not only prevented his notes from coming upon him, but filled his coffers with almost all the gold in the country. In order to accomplish this part of his scheme more perfectly, he most arbitrarily published an edict prohibiting any persons from keeping by them gold or silver, beyond a certain sum  . He also took away the severe penalties that were in force against the exportation of coin, and every person was allowed to export money free from duty  .
context_after: He reasoned with himself, some instrument of change is necessary, paper, gold, and silver, at present are the medium; if gold and silver be utterly exported, paper only remains, and may be rendered the sole instrument of commerce. This he thought he had done effectually when by an edict he had swept a part into his coffers, and cleared the country of the remainder. They would therefore be obliged to take paper. At last, however, after a great number of expedients, he found it was impracticable. By paying out great sums, he kept off ruin for some months, but at last published an edict that all bank notes were to be paid only in one half: and indeed if he had stood to this, as some imagined he might have done, it would have been far better than to have suffered the after consequences. Upon this edict the credit of the bank was entirely broken, and the bank notes all on a sudden sunk to nothing  . This ruined an immense number of people. Britain can never be much hurt by the breaking of a bank, because few people keep notes by them to any value  . A man worth £40,000 will scarce ever have £500 of notes by him. But the breaking of this bank in France occasioned the most dreadful confusion. The greatest part of people had their whole fortunes in notes, and were reduced to a state of beggary. The only people who were safe were the stock-jobbers who had sold out in time, or with their bank notes had purchased all the valuable goods and a great deal of land, though at the highest prices. These made immense fortunes by it.
a: By this means much of it went to Holland.
