The particular application is a matter of time and circumstance: whether, in a given situation, the appropriate remedy is an increase of public investment, a reduction of the rate of interest, a redistribution of income towards those with a higher propensity to consume, or some combination of these. The general conclusion tells us where to look; it does not tell us what we shall find. And it is a mark of the practical man that he knows the difference between a principle and a policy.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，探讨物价上涨对企业经营和劳动收入的影响，区分普遍价格变化与相对价格调整的作用机制。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
It has long been recognised, by the business world and by economists alike, that a period of rising prices acts as a stimulus to enterprise and is beneficial to business men.

In the first place there is the advantage which is the counterpart of the loss to the investing class which we have just examined. When the value of money falls, it is evident that those persons who have engaged to pay fixed sums of money yearly out of the profits of active business must benefit, since their fixed money outgoings will bear a smaller proportion than formerly to their money turnover. This benefit persists not only during the transitional period of change, but also, so far as old loans are con- cerned, when prices have settled down at their new and higher level. For example, the farmers throughout Europe, who had raised by mortgage the funds to purchase the land they farmed, now find themselves almost freed from the burden at the expense of the mort- gagees.

But during the period of change, while prices are rising month by month, the business man has a further and greater source of windfall. Whether he is a merchant or a manufacturer, he will generally buy before he sells, and on at least a part of his stock he will run the risk of price changes. If, therefore, month after month his stock appreciates on his hands, he is always selling at a better price than he expected and securing a windfall profit upon which he had not calculated. In such a period the business of trade becomes unduly easy. Any one who can borrow money and is not exceptionally unlucky must make a profit, which he may have done little to deserve. Thus, when prices are rising, the business man who borrows money is able to repay the lender with what, in terms of real value, not only represents no interest, but is even less than the capital originally advanced.

But if the depreciation of money is a source of gain to the business man, it is also the occasion of opprobrium. To the consumer the business man's exceptional profits appear as the cause (instead of the consequence) of the hated rise of prices. Amidst the rapid fluctuations of his fortunes he himself loses his conservative instincts, and begins to think more of the large gains of the moment than of the lesser, but permanent, profits of normal business. The welfare of his enterprise in the relatively distant future weighs less with him than before, and thoughts are excited of a quick fortune and clearing out. His excessive gains have come to him unsought and without fault or design on his part, but once acquired he does not lightly surrender them, and will struggle to retain his booty. With such impulses and so placed, the business man is himself not free from a suppressed uneasiness. In his heart he loses his former self-confidence in his relation to Society, in his utility and necessity in the economic scheme. He fears the future of his business and his class, and the less secure he feels his fortune to be the tighter he clings to it. The business man, the prop of Society and the builder of the future, to whose activities and rewards there had been accorded, not long ago, an almost religious sanction, he of all men and classes most respectable, praiseworthy, and necessary, with whom interference was not only disastrous but almost impious, was now to suffer sidelong glances, to feel himself suspected and attacked, the victim of unjust and injurious laws,—to become, and know himself half guilty, a profiteer.

No man of spirit will consent to remain poor if he believes his betters to have gained their goods by lucky gambling. To convert the business man into the profiteer is to strike a blow at capitalism, because it destroys the psychological equilibrium which permits the perpetuance of unequal rewards. The economic doctrine of normal profits, vaguely apprehended by every one, is a necessary condition for the justification of capitalism. The business man is only tolerable so long as his gains can be held to bear some relation to what, roughly and in some sense, his activities have contributed to Society.

This, then, is the second disturbance to the existing economic order for which the depreciation of money is responsible. If the fall in the value of money discourages investment, it also discredits enterprise.

Not that the business man was allowed, even during the period of boom, to retain the whole of his exceptional profits. A host of popular remedies vainly attempted to cure the evils of the day; which remedies themselves—subsidies, price and rent fixing, profiteer hunting, and excess profits duties—eventually became not the least part of the evils.

In due course came the depression, with falling prices, which operate on those who hold stocks in a manner exactly opposite to rising prices. Excessive losses, bearing no relation to the efficiency of the business, took the place of windfall gains; and the effort of every one to hold as small stocks as possible brought industry to a standstill, just as previously their efforts to accumulate stocks had over-stimulated it. Unemployment succeeded Profiteering as the problem of the hour.

It has been a commonplace of economic textbooks that wages tend to lag behind prices, with the result that the real earnings of the wage-earner are diminished during a period of rising prices. This has often been true in the past, and may be true even now of certain classes of labour which are ill-placed or ill-organised for improving their position. But in Great Britain, at any rate, and in the United States also, some important sections of labour were able to take advantage of the situation not only to obtain money wages equivalent in purchasing power to what they had before, but to secure a real improvement, to combine this with a diminution in their hours of work (and, so far, of the work done), and to accomplish this (in the case of Great Britain) at a time when the total wealth of the community as a whole had suffered a decrease. This reversal of the usual course has not been due to an accident and is traceable to definite causes.

The organisation of certain classes of labour—railwaymen, miners, dockers, and others—for the purpose of securing wage increases is better than it was. Life in the army, perhaps for the first time in the history of wars, raised in many respects the conventional standard of requirements,—the soldier was better clothed, better shod, and often better fed than the labourer, and his wife, adding in war time a separation allowance to new opportunities to earn, had also enlarged her ideas.

But these influences, while they would have supplied the motive, might have lacked the means to the result if it had not been for another factor—the windfalls of the profiteer. The fact that the business man had been gaining, and gaining notoriously, considerable windfall profits in excess of the normal profits of trade, laid him open to pressure, not only from his employees but from public opinion generally; and enabled him to meet this pressure without financial difficulty. In fact, it was worth his while to pay ransom, and to share with his workmen the good fortune of the day.

Thus the working classes improved their relative position in the years following the war, as against all other classes except that of the "profiteers." In some important cases they improved their absolute position—that is to say, account being taken of shorter hours, increased money wages, and higher prices, some sections of the working classes secured for themselves a higher real remuneration for each unit of effort or work done. But we cannot estimate the stability of this state of affairs, as contrasted with its desirability, unless we know the source from which the increased reward of the working classes was drawn. Was it due to a permanent modification of the economic factors which determine the distribution of the national product between different classes? Or was it due to some temporary and exhaustible influence connected with Inflation and with the resulting disturbance in the standard of value?

The period of depression has exacted its penalty from the working classes more in the form of unemployment than by a lowering of real wages, and State assistance to the unemployed has greatly moderated even this penalty. Money wages have followed prices downwards. But the depression of 1921–22 did not reverse or even greatly diminish the relative advantage gained by the working classes over the middle class during the previous years. In 1923 British wage rates stood at an appreciably higher level above the pre-war rates than did the cost of living, if allowance is made for the shorter hours worked.

If, for any reason right or wrong, the business world expects that prices will fall, the processes of production tend to be inhibited; and if it expects that prices will rise, they tend to be over-stimulated. A fluctuation in the measuring-rod of value does not alter in the least the wealth of the world, the needs of the world, or the productive capacity of the world. It ought not, therefore, to affect the character or the volume of what is produced. A movement of relative prices, that is to say of the comparative prices of different commodities, ought to influence the character of production, because it is an indication that various commodities are not being produced in the exactly right proportions. But this is not true of a change, as such, in the general price level.
b:
The proposition that a general rise of prices is favourable to business enterprise, and unfavourable to the wage-earning classes, is one of those half-truths which, being repeated from hand to hand, acquire in the public mind the authority of an axiom. It is not an axiom; it is a theorem whose validity depends upon conditions which are seldom stated and frequently absent. My purpose here is to disentangle two things which the ordinary discussion confounds: a change in the general level of prices, on the one hand, and a change in the relative prices of particular commodities, on the other. The effects attributed to the first are often in reality the effects of the second; and where the first operates alone, its consequences for business and for labour are far more ambiguous than the popular view allows.

Let us begin with the general case. Suppose all prices and all money incomes—including wages, rents, interest, and salaries—to rise in the same proportion, and to rise simultaneously. Nothing real has occurred. The entrepreneur sells his output dearer and buys his materials dearer; his money profit is greater, but its purchasing power is unchanged. The wage-earner receives more sovereigns, each of which commands fewer goods, and his real wage is where it was. On the strict assumption of universality and simultaneity, therefore, a general price change is a mere change in the unit of account, a matter of bookkeeping and of the inconvenience of adjusting contracts. It has no power to enrich one class at the expense of another. This is the limiting case, and it is worth fixing in the mind, because it shows that every real effect which we are accustomed to ascribe to "rising prices" must arise from some departure from universality or simultaneity—from the fact that prices do not all move together, or do not move at the same time, or that money incomes are fixed by contract for longer or shorter periods.

The first and most important departure is the phenomenon of lag. Incomes fixed in money terms—debts, mortgages, annuities, the remuneration of salaried officials, and, in a lesser degree, wages settled by collective agreement or custom—do not respond instantaneously to a change in the price level. The entrepreneur, on the other hand, stands at the point where prices are made; his selling prices move early, while many of his costs move late. He therefore enjoys, for the interval, what may be called a windfall of the transitional period: his receipts are computed at the new level and a part of his outgoings at the old. This is the genuine kernel of truth in the maxim that rising prices are good for trade. But observe its character: it is a profit of transition, not of equilibrium; it belongs to the interval of adjustment, and it is extinguished precisely in proportion as the adjustment is completed. It is, moreover, a transfer, not a creation. What the entrepreneur gains in this interval is, in the main, what the rentier and the fixed-income receiver lose; and the wage-earner occupies an intermediate position, gaining where his wages are adjusted early and losing where they are adjusted late. The gain to business is thus, in the first instance, a redistribution of command over goods, and only secondarily, and under conditions to be examined, a stimulus to production.

The stimulus to production deserves separate treatment, for it is here that the popular view finds its strongest support. The entrepreneur who finds his receipts outrunning his costs is encouraged to extend his operations; he borrows at a rate of interest which, being fixed in money terms, appears low when prices are rising; the real burden of his existing debts is lightened, and his own net worth, computed in money, is enhanced. There is thus a real, and not merely a distributive, effect, provided—and this proviso is essential—that the additional demand which his expanded operations evoke is not offset by a contraction of demand elsewhere. For the gain of the entrepreneur is the loss of the rentier, and if the rentier, finding his real income diminished, reduces his expenditure, the net addition to total demand may be small or nil. The expansionary effect of rising prices is therefore conditional upon the disposition of the classes whose real incomes are curtailed: upon whether they respond by spending less, and upon whether the banking system is prepared to finance the enlarged volume of transactions. Where these conditions are satisfied, rising prices may sustain activity; where they are not, the redistribution may occur without the stimulus, and the community may find itself with altered shares of a product no larger than before.

I turn now to the second phenomenon, which is commonly confused with the first: a change in relative prices. Here the analysis is altogether different, and the effects are not transitional but permanent, and not merely distributive but genuinely productive or destructive according to the direction of the change. Suppose that the price of a particular commodity rises relatively to the prices of other things, whether because of an increase in demand for it or a diminution of the supply. The producers of that commodity enjoy an advantage which no general inflation could confer: their receipts rise while the prices of what they buy remain, relatively, where they were. Resources are drawn towards that employment; the alteration of relative prices is the mechanism by which a community is informed of a change in the wants of its members or in the conditions of supply, and by which it is induced to reallocate its productive effort accordingly. This is the indispensable function of the price system, and it operates through relative, not through general, changes. A general inflation, so far from performing this function, obscures it; for when all prices are moving, the signals which guide the allocation of resources are muffled, and the entrepreneur can no longer distinguish the rise of his own price, which invites him to expand, from the general rise, which invites him to do nothing of the kind. It is for this reason that inflation is inimical to the efficient conduct of business in the longer run, however agreeable its transitional profits may be to the individual trader. The individual trader sees his own price rising and is deceived; the community suffers because the deception is general.

The effect upon labour income must be analysed with the same distinction. A general rise of prices, in so far as wages lag, diminishes real wages, and to that extent transfers command over goods from the wage-earner to the entrepreneur and to the debtor. This is the sense in which inflation may be said to be "unfavourable to labour." But it is a conclusion which holds only for the interval of lag and only in the measure of the lag; and it is offset, partially or wholly, where wages are adjusted promptly, where the worker's employment is made more secure by the stimulus to trade, or where the alternative to rising prices is a contraction of output and a volume of unemployment which reduces the real income of labour by a greater amount than the lag would have done. The comparison is not between a rising price level and a stable one, but between a rising price level and whatever alternative is actually available; and a judgement which ignores the alternative is not an economic judgement but a rhetorical one.

Nor must it be supposed that relative price changes are uniformly favourable to labour, or that their effect can be read off from the direction of the change. A rise in the relative price of wage-goods, unaccompanied by a rise in money wages, diminishes the real wage of the workers who consume them, while it enriches the producers of those goods; a fall in the relative price of wage-goods does the reverse. The incidence depends upon the pattern of consumption of the classes concerned, upon the elasticity of demand for the commodities whose prices have changed, and upon the mobility of labour between employments. Where labour is immobile, a relative price change which destroys the demand for one kind of skill may depress the wages of that skill for a long period, while the community as a whole enjoys the benefit of the change. Here, as elsewhere, the general conclusion—that relative price changes reallocate income and effort in the direction of the changed conditions—must be distinguished from the particular conclusion, which depends upon the specific commodities, the specific classes, and the specific institutional arrangements under consideration.

Let me state the matter in a form which may serve as a summary. A general rise of prices, taken by itself and in isolation, is a change in the measuring rod; it enriches no class and impoverishes none, except in so far as it is not general, that is to say, except in so far as some incomes are fixed in money terms while others are not. The real effects commonly attributed to it are (a) a transfer from fixed-income receivers and lagging wage-earners to entrepreneurs and debtors, which is transitional in character; (b) a stimulus to production, which is conditional upon the disposition of the losers and upon the availability of credit, and which may be absent or even reversed; and (c) a disturbance of the signalling function of prices, which is injurious to the efficiency of production and therefore, in the longer run, to the real income of all classes, including the entrepreneurial. A change in relative prices, on the other hand, is the means by which a community adjusts its production to its wants; it necessarily benefits some and injures others, and its net effect upon the real income of labour depends upon conditions which cannot be ascertained a priori.

The practical bearing of this analysis is to warn against the loose identification of "rising prices" with "prosperity," and of "stable prices" with "justice." The entrepreneur who welcomes inflation because his profits are enlarged is welcoming a transfer which he will presently find himself obliged to restore, and is assisting at a process which, by confusing the signals of the market, will in the end impair the very activity from which his profits are drawn. The wage-earner who regards every rise of prices as an injury to himself is neglecting the possibility that the alternative may be an injury greater still, and is neglecting also the distinction between a rise which is general and one which is confined to the commodities he buys. The statesman who seeks to stabilise the general level of prices is pursuing a reasonable object, but he should not suppose that stability of the general level is the same thing as stability of the economic system; for the system lives by relative changes, and a policy which suppressed them in the name of stability would suppress the mechanism of adjustment itself.

It remains to observe that the foregoing analysis has been conducted upon assumptions which are themselves conditions. It assumes that the monetary system is such that a general rise of prices can occur without a disproportionate disturbance of the structure of money rates of interest—an assumption which is not always realised, for if the rate of interest is held rigid while prices rise, the real rate falls and the stimulus to borrowing may become excessive, while if it is raised sharply the stimulus may be converted into a check. It assumes, further, that the rise of prices is not of so violent and irregular a character as to destroy the calculability upon which business enterprise depends; for beyond a certain point the entrepreneur can no longer form expectations, and the profit of transition gives place to the losses of confusion. And it assumes that the distributive changes which we have described are not themselves the occasion of further disturbances—of demands for higher money wages which outrun the rise of prices, and so of a cumulative process in which no class gains and all are harassed. These are not refinements of the argument; they are part of it. The conclusion that rising prices favour business and injure labour is true, if at all, only within a narrow range of conditions, and the delineation of that range is the whole of the matter.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察物价预期如何影响生产和财富转移，比较持续上涨与持续下降对经济协调的不同影响。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The fact that the expectation of changes in the general price level affects the processes of production, is deeply rooted in the peculiarities of the existing economic organisation of society. We have already seen that a change in the general level of prices, that is to say a change in the measuring-rod, which fixes the obligation of the borrowers of money (who make the decisions which set production in motion) to the lenders (who are inactive once they have lent their money), effects a redistribution of real wealth between the two groups. Furthermore, the active group can, if they foresee such a change, alter their action in advance in such a way as to minimise their losses to the other group or to increase their gains from it, if and when the expected change in the value of money occurs. If they expect a fall, it may pay them, as a group, to damp production down, although such enforced idleness impoverishes Society as a whole. If they expect a rise, it may pay them to increase their borrowings and to swell production beyond the point where the real return is just sufficient to recompense Society as a whole for the effort made. Sometimes, of course, a change in the measuring-rod, especially if it is unforeseen, may benefit one group at the expense of the other disproportionately to any influence it exerts on the volume of production; but the tendency, in so far as the active group anticipate a change, will be as I have described it. This is simply to say that the intensity of production is largely governed in existing conditions by the anticipated real profit of the entrepreneur. Yet this criterion is the right one for the community as a whole only when the delicate adjustment of interests is not upset by fluctuations in the standard of value.

There is also a considerable risk directly arising out of instability in the value of money. During the lengthy process of production the business world is incurring outgoings in terms of money—paying out in money for wages and other expenses of production—in the expectation of recouping this outlay by disposing of the product for money at a later date. That is to say, the business world as a whole must always be in a position where it stands to gain by a rise of price and to lose by a fall of price. Whether it likes it or not, the technique of production under a régime of money-contract forces the business world always to carry a big speculative position; and if it is reluctant to carry this position, the productive process must be slackened. The argument is not affected by the fact that there is some degree of specialisation of function within the business world, in so far as the professional speculator comes to the assistance of the producer proper by taking over from him a part of his risk.

Now it follows from this, not merely that the actual occurrence of price changes profits some classes and injures others (which has been the theme of the first section of this chapter), but that a general fear of falling prices may inhibit the productive process altogether. For if prices are expected to fall, not enough risk-takers can be found who are willing to carry a speculative “bull” position, and this means that entrepreneurs will be reluctant to embark on lengthy productive processes involving a money outlay long in advance of money recoupment,—whence unemployment. The fact of falling prices injures entrepreneurs; consequently the fear of falling prices causes them to protect themselves by curtailing their operations; yet it is upon the aggregate of their individual estimations of the risk, and their willingness to run the risk, that the activity of production and of employment mainly depends.

There is a further aggravation of the case, in that an expectation about the course of prices tends, if it is widely held, to be cumulative in its results up to a certain point. If prices are expected to rise and the business world acts on this expectation, that very fact causes them to rise for a time and, by verifying the expectation, reinforces it; and similarly, if it expects them to fall. Thus a comparatively weak initial impetus may be adequate to produce a considerable fluctuation.

The best way to cure this mortal disease of individualism must be to provide that there shall never exist any confident expectation either that prices generally are going to fall or that they are going to rise; and also that there shall be no serious risk that a movement, if it does occur, will be a big one. If, unexpectedly and accidentally, a moderate movement were to occur, wealth, though it might be redistributed, would not be diminished thereby.

To procure this result by removing all possible influences towards an initial movement would seem to be a hopeless enterprise. The remedy would lie, rather, in so controlling the standard of value that whenever something occurred which, left to itself, would create an expectation of a change in the general level of prices, the controlling authority should take steps to counteract this expectation by setting in motion some factor of a contrary tendency. Even if such a policy were not wholly successful, either in counteracting expectations or in avoiding actual movements, it would be an improvement on the policy of sitting quietly by whilst a standard of value, governed by chance causes and deliberately removed from central control, produces expectations which paralyse or intoxicate the government of production.

We see, therefore, that rising prices and falling prices each have their characteristic disadvantage. The Inflation which causes the former means Injustice to individuals and to classes,—particularly to rentiers; and is therefore unfavourable to saving. The Deflation which causes falling prices means Impoverishment to labour and to enterprise by leading entrepreneurs to restrict production, in their endeavour to avoid loss to themselves; and is therefore disastrous to employment. The counterparts are, of course, also true,—namely that Deflation means Injustice to borrowers, and that Inflation leads to the over-stimulation of industrial activity. But these results are not so marked as those emphasised above, because borrowers are in a better position to protect themselves from the worst effects of Deflation than lenders are to protect themselves from those of Inflation, and because labour is in a better position to protect itself from over-exertion in good times than from under-employment in bad times.

Thus Inflation is unjust and Deflation is inexpedient. Of the two perhaps Deflation is, if we rule out exaggerated inflations such as that of Germany, the worse; because it is worse, in an impoverished world, to provoke unemployment than to disappoint the rentier. But it is not necessary that we should weigh one evil against the other. It is easier to agree that both are evils to be shunned. The Individualistic Capitalism of to-day, precisely because it entrusts saving to the individual investor and production to the individual employer, presumes a stable measuring-rod of value, and cannot be efficient—perhaps cannot survive—without one.

For these grave causes we must free ourselves from the deep distrust which exists against allowing the regulation of the standard of value to be the subject of deliberate decision. We can no longer afford to leave it in the category of which the distinguishing characteristics are possessed in different degrees by the weather, the birth-rate, and the Constitution,—matters which are settled by natural causes, or are the resultant of the separate action of many individuals acting independently, or require a Revolution to change them.
b:
The influence of price expectations upon production and upon the distribution of wealth is not a single problem but a family of problems, and the attempt to treat it by a single formula has been the source of much confusion. We must distinguish, first, between expectations which are held with confidence and those which are held loosely; secondly, between expectations concerning particular prices and expectations concerning the general level; and thirdly, between a state of affairs in which prices are expected to move persistently in one direction and one in which they are expected to oscillate about a norm. The practical consequences differ profoundly according as the expectation is of a continuing rise or of a continuing fall, and it is with this contrast that I am chiefly concerned.

Let us begin with the entrepreneur. The motive to produce is the expectation of a surplus of proceeds over costs, and this surplus is a matter of money. If the entrepreneur expects the prices of his product to rise relatively to the costs he must incur, the expected profit on a given volume of output is increased, and he is induced to extend his operations and to employ more labour. But here a qualification of the first importance enters. The stimulus depends not on the absolute level of prices but on the relation between the prices expected at the date of sale and the costs contracted for at earlier dates. A general expectation of rising prices operates, therefore, through a divergence between the prospective selling price and the current level of money costs, and it produces its effect most powerfully when money costs are sticky—when wages and rents and the rates of interest on old contracts do not adjust themselves promptly. If all money incomes and all money costs were instantaneously and proportionately adjusted to the expected change in prices, the expectation would have no real effect upon output at all; it would be a mere change in the unit of account. The stimulus to production which we observe in a period of rising prices is thus, in the strict sense, a phenomenon of imperfect adjustment. It arises because the rise of prices outruns the rise of money costs, and it lasts only so long as that lag persists. The profits which it generates are, in part, not a net addition to the community's real income but a transfer to the entrepreneur from those whose money incomes have not yet risen.

This brings me to the second aspect of the matter, the redistribution of wealth. A change in the value of money, actual or expected, is never neutral. It operates upon the relations between debtors and creditors, between those whose incomes are fixed in money and those whose incomes are variable, and between the holders of claims payable in money and the owners of material property. A continuing expectation of rising prices benefits the debtor at the expense of the creditor; it lightens the real burden of past obligations and encourages new borrowing, since the borrower anticipates repaying in a depreciated currency. It favours the trader and the active businessman, whose gains rise with prices, at the expense of the rentier and the salaried person, whose money income is fixed by contract or custom. It discourages the holding of money and of fixed-interest securities, and it turns the community's savings into channels which promise to keep pace with the rise. A continuing expectation of falling prices produces precisely the opposite set of transfers: the real burden of debts is increased, the rentier gains at the expense of the debtor and the trader, and the holding of money yields a profit in real terms which no productive enterprise can easily match. In each case the transfer is not a mere bookkeeping matter; it alters the disposition of the community to spend and to invest, and thereby alters production itself.

Now the difference between the two cases is not symmetrical, and this asymmetry is the heart of the matter. A persistent expectation of rising prices, so long as it is moderate and is not allowed to degenerate into a flight from the currency, can be accompanied by a high level of employment and by an expansion of output. The reason is that the rise of prices operates as a stimulus to enterprise, and the transfers which it effects, though unjust, are in a direction which on the whole favours spending and investment. The expectation of a continuing fall, on the other hand, is attended by a special and cumulative obstacle. When prices are expected to fall, the holding of money becomes profitable; the businessman postpones purchases and the consumer postpones expenditure, since the same money will buy more later. The rate of interest, which measures the reward for parting with money, is not easily brought low enough to offset the expected appreciation of money, for it cannot fall below a certain minimum without inducing lenders to prefer hoarding. The result is that investment is checked, output is curtailed, employment falls, and the fall of prices, by confirming the expectation, generates a further fall. The process is self-reinforcing in a way in which the upward process is not, because the downward movement encounters a floor to the rate of interest which the upward movement does not encounter. This is the ground for the view that deflation is the more dangerous of the two, and that a persistent expectation of falling prices is incompatible with the maintenance of production at its normal level.

But I must guard against the impression that the upward case is one of unqualified benefit. The stimulus of rising prices depends, as I have said, upon the lag of money costs behind prices. As the expectation becomes general and is acted upon, wages and other costs are revised upward, the lag is closed, and the stimulus ceases. If the expectation of rising prices becomes firmly embedded, it may lead to a progressive rise in the demand for money for the purpose of holding goods rather than claims, to speculative accumulation of stocks, and to a flight from the currency which destroys the very basis of contract. The experience of countries which have passed through such a phase is sufficient evidence that the upward movement, once it passes a certain point, ceases to stimulate production and begins to disorganise it. The conclusion, therefore, is not that rising prices are good and falling prices bad in themselves, but that the effect of any price expectation depends upon the character of the expectation, upon the institutions of the community, and upon the presence or absence of the lags and rigidities through which alone a change in the value of money can influence real activity.

It is necessary also to notice that the reasoning I have given rests upon conditions which may not always be present. It assumes a community in which production is carried on by entrepreneurs who borrow money and contract for costs in advance, and in which a substantial part of wealth is held in the form of fixed-money claims. In a community where production is organised without money contracts, or where debts are few and short-lived, the redistributive effects of price movements would be small, and the influence upon production correspondingly weak. It assumes, further, that the monetary authority does not act in such a way as to offset the expectation; a policy which accommodates the demand for money or which alters the rate of interest may modify or reverse the tendencies I have described. And it assumes that the expectation is held with sufficient confidence to influence conduct; where expectations are vague or conflicting, their effect upon production and upon the distribution of wealth may be negligible, and the observed phenomena must be explained by other causes—by changes in the propensity to consume, by technical improvements, by changes in the terms of foreign trade, or by the mere passage of time.

I would sum up the matter thus. The expectation of a continuing rise in prices tends, under the conditions I have specified, to stimulate production by creating a divergence between prospective proceeds and current money costs, and to transfer wealth from creditors and fixed-income receivers to debtors and traders. The expectation of a continuing fall tends to check production by making the holding of money profitable and by defeating the power of the rate of interest to offset the expected appreciation, and to transfer wealth in the opposite direction. The downward tendency is the more to be feared, because it is cumulative and because it encounters a floor to the rate of interest which the upward tendency does not encounter. But these are general tendencies, not universal laws. Their strength depends upon the stickiness of money costs, upon the prevalence of money contracts, upon the confidence with which the expectation is held, and upon the policy of the monetary authority; and where these conditions are absent or are offset by other forces, the conclusions I have drawn must be modified accordingly. The practical moral is that stability of the general level of prices, or at least the avoidance of a persistent expectation of movement in either direction, is favourable to the coordination of production and to the maintenance of a tolerable distribution of wealth; and that where movement is unavoidable, the downward movement is the one which requires the more active and the more deliberate correction.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察国际制度能否支持第一次世界大战后和约的调整，分析法律程序、公共意见与经济重建的关系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
Are any constitutional means open to us for altering the Treaty? President Wilson and General Smuts, who believe that to have secured the Covenant of the League of Nations outweighs much evil in the rest of the Treaty, have indicated that we must look to the League for the gradual evolution of a more tolerable life for Europe.

“There are territorial settlements,” General Smuts wrote in his statement on signing the Peace Treaty, “which will need revision. There are guarantees laid down which we all hope will soon be found out of harmony with the new peaceful temper and unarmed state of our former enemies. There are punishments foreshadowed over most of which a calmer mood may yet prefer to pass the sponge of oblivion. There are indemnities stipulated which cannot be enacted without grave injury to the industrial revival of Europe, and which it will be in the interests of all to render more tolerable and moderate. . . . I am confident that the League of Nations will yet prove the path of escape for Europe out of the ruin brought about by this war.” Without the League, President Wilson informed the Senate when he presented the Treaty to them early in July, 1919, “. . . long-continued supervision of the task of reparation which Germany was to undertake to complete within the next generation might entirely break down;¹ the reconsideration and revision of administrative arrangements and restrictions which the Treaty prescribed, but which it recognized might not provide lasting advantage or be entirely fair if too long enforced, would be impracticable."

Can we look forward with fair hopes to securing from the operation of the League those benefits which two of its principal begetters thus encourage us to expect from it? The relevant passage is to be found in Article XIX. of the Covenant, which runs as follows:

"The Assembly may from time to time advise the reconsideration by Members of the League of treaties which have become inapplicable and the consideration of international conditions whose continuance might endanger the peace of the world."

But alas! Article V. provides that “Except where otherwise expressly provided in this Covenant or by the terms of the present Treaty, decisions at any meeting of the Assembly or of the Council shall require the agreement of all the Members of the League represented at the meeting.” Does not this provision reduce the League, so far as concerns an early reconsideration of any of the terms of the Peace Treaty, into a body merely for wasting time? If all the parties to the Treaty are unanimously of opinion that it requires alteration in a particular sense, it does not need a League and a Covenant to put

the business through. Even when the Assembly of the League is unanimous it can only “advise” reconsideration by the members specially affected.

But the League will operate, say its supporters, by its influence on the public opinion of the world, and the view of the majority will carry decisive weight in practice, even though constitutionally it is of no effect. Let us pray that this be so. Yet the League in the hands of the trained European diplomatist may become an unequaled instrument for obstruction and delay. The revision of Treaties is entrusted primarily, not to the Council, which meets frequently, but to the Assembly, which will meet more rarely and must become, as any one with an experience of large Inter-Ally Conferences must know, an unwieldy polyglot debating society in which the greatest resolution and the best management may fail altogether to bring issues to a head against an opposition in favor of the status quo. There are indeed two disastrous blots on the Covenant,—Article V., which prescribes unanimity, and the much-criticized Article X., by which “The Members of the League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all Members of the League.” These two Articles together go some way to destroy the conception of the League as an instrument of progress, and to equip it from the outset with an almost fatal bias towards the status quo. It is these Articles which have reconciled to the League some of its original opponents, who now hope to make of it another Holy Alliance for the perpetuation of the economic ruin of their enemies and the Balance of Power in their own interests which they believe themselves to have established by the Peace.

But while it would be wrong and foolish to conceal from ourselves in the interests of “idealism” the real difficulties of the position in the special matter of revising treaties, that is no reason for any of us to decry the League, which the wisdom of the world may yet transform into a powerful instrument of peace, and which in Articles XI.-XVII.¹ has already accomplished a great and beneficent achievement. I agree, therefore, that our first efforts for the Revision of the Treaty must be made through the League rather than in any other way, in the hope that the force of general opinion and, if necessary, the use of financial pressure and financial inducements, may be enough to prevent a recalcitrant minority from exercising their right of veto. We must trust the new Governments, whose existence I premise

in the principal Allied countries, to show a pro- founder wisdom and a greater magnanimity than their predecessors.

We have seen in Chapters IV. and V. that there are numerous particulars in which the Treaty is objectionable. I do not intend to enter here into details, or to attempt a revision of the Treaty clause by clause. I limit myself to three great changes which are necessary for the economic life of Europe, relating to Reparation, to Coal and Iron, and to Tariffs.
b:
The question of whether international institutions possess the requisite vitality to sanction and sustain the adjustment of peace treaties following the cataclysm of the Great War is not merely a matter of legal jurisprudence, but a profound inquiry into the stability of the post-war social order. To assume that the rigid architecture of law can, in isolation, accommodate the fluid necessities of economic reconstruction is to misunderstand the fundamental nature of political obligation. We must recognize that the validity of any international settlement rests ultimately not upon the sanctity of parchment, but upon the consent of the governed, a consent which is itself conditioned by the material well-being of the populace and the prevailing currents of public opinion.

In the immediate aftermath of hostilities, the prevailing orthodoxy held that the League of Nations, or any analogous institutional framework, would serve as the arbiter of disputes and the facilitator of necessary revisions. However, this view suffers from a fatal defect: it treats international law as a static code, impervious to the shifting tides of economic reality. In truth, the economic fabric of Europe was torn asunder by the war, creating conditions under which the strict adherence to pre-war economic boundaries and financial obligations became a source of perpetual friction rather than stability. The capacity of international institutions to support treaty adjustment is therefore contingent upon their ability to decouple the legal rigidity of sovereignty from the pragmatic necessities of economic interdependence.

Consider the relationship between legal procedure and public opinion. In the democratic societies of Western Europe, public opinion is no longer a passive recipient of state decree but an active, volatile force. The masses, having borne the disproportionate burden of the conflict, demand a peace that promises not merely the absence of war, but the prospect of economic security and social equity. If the legal procedures established by the peace treaties demand sacrifices that the public perceives as unjust or economically ruinous, the legitimacy of the treaty itself erodes. International institutions, lacking their own coercive power independent of member states, find themselves powerless to enforce adjustments that lack domestic political support. Thus, the efficacy of legal mechanism is subordinate to the psychological and economic climate of the nations concerned.

Furthermore, the process of economic reconstruction cannot be separated from the political framework of the peace. The reparations imposed upon the defeated powers, for instance, were not merely financial transactions but political instruments designed to secure security and justice. Yet, when these financial demands collided with the fragile economic realities of the post-war world, they threatened to undermine the very stability they sought to preserve. Here, the role of international institutions is not to rigidly enforce the letter of the law, but to provide a forum for the flexible interpretation of obligations in light of changing economic circumstances. The failure to recognize this flexibility leads to a paralysis of international cooperation, where legal formalism obstructs the pragmatic adjustments necessary for survival.

It is essential to distinguish between the general principles of international relations and the specific historical context of the post-war period. In general, international institutions derive their authority from the perceived fairness and utility of the rules they uphold. In the specific context of the post-war era, the utility of the peace treaties was inextricably linked to the economic viability of the European continent. If the treaties rendered certain nations economically insolvent, they could not expect to maintain the political loyalty of those nations. The judgment that international institutions can support treaty adjustment depends heavily on the condition that these institutions are empowered to facilitate economic cooperation alongside legal arbitration. Without such empowerment, they remain mere debating societies, incapable of addressing the root causes of international discord.

Other possible explanations might suggest that the failure of the post-war settlement was due primarily to the resurgence of nationalist sentiments or the inherent instability of the balance of power. While these factors are undoubtedly significant, they do not fully account for the specific mechanisms of treaty adjustment. Nationalism itself is often exacerbated by economic distress; the balance of power is difficult to maintain when the economic foundations of the great powers are eroding. Therefore, the economic dimension must be viewed as the substrate upon which political and legal structures rest.

In conclusion, international institutions can support the adjustment of peace treaties only if they are designed to integrate legal procedure with the dynamics of public opinion and economic reconstruction. The rigidity of law must be tempered by the flexibility of economic pragmatism. The peace of the world is not secured by the mere signing of documents, but by the continuous, adaptive management of the interests and aspirations of the peoples involved. To ignore this reality is to invite not merely a pause in hostilities, but a recurrence of the same destructive forces that led to the war itself. The stability of the post-war order depends less on the perfection of its legal codes than on the wisdom with which international institutions navigate the complex interplay of economic necessity and public demand.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，解释投资资产预期收益与资本边际效率的关系，讨论供给价格、贴现及利率比较的意义。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
WHEN a man buys an investment or capital-asset, he purchases the right to the series of prospective returns, which he expects to obtain from selling its output, after deducting the running expenses of obtaining that output, during the life of the asset. This series of annuities $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{n}$ it is convenient to call the prospective yield of the investment.

Over against the prospective yield of the investment we have the supply price of the capital-asset, meaning by this, not the market-price at which an asset of the type in question can actually be purchased in the market, but the price which would just induce a manufacturer newly to produce an additional unit of such assets, i.e. what is sometimes called its replacement cost. The relation between the prospective yield of a capital-asset and its supply price or replacement cost, i.e. the relation between the prospective yield of one more unit of that type of capital and the cost of producing that unit, furnishes us with the marginal efficiency of capital of that type. More precisely, I define the marginal efficiency of capital as being equal to that rate of discount which would make the present value of the series of annuities given by the returns expected from the capital-asset during its life just equal to its supply price. This gives us the marginal efficiencies of particular types of capital-assets. The greatest of these marginal efficiencies can then be regarded as the marginal efficiency of capital in general.

The reader should note that the marginal efficiency of capital is here defined in terms of the expectation of yield and of the current supply price of the capital-asset. It depends on the rate of return expected to be obtainable on money if it were invested in a newly produced asset; not on the historical result of what an investment has yielded on its original cost if we look back on its record after its life is over.

If there is an increased investment in any given type of capital during any period of time, the marginal efficiency of that type of capital will diminish as the investment in it is increased, partly because the prospective yield will fall as the supply of that type of capital is increased, and partly because, as a rule, pressure on the facilities for producing that type of capital will cause its supply price to increase; the second of these factors being usually the more important in producing equilibrium in the short run, but the longer the period in view the more does the first factor take its place. Thus for each type of capital we can build up a schedule, showing by how much investment in it will have to increase within the period, in order that its marginal efficiency should fall to any given figure. We can then aggregate these schedules for all the different types of capital, so as to provide a schedule relating the rate of aggregate investment to the corresponding marginal efficiency of capital in general which that rate of investment will establish. We shall call this the investment demand-schedule; or, alternatively, the schedule of the marginal efficiency of capital.

Now it is obvious that the actual rate of current investment will be pushed to the point where there is no longer any class of capital-asset of which the marginal efficiency exceeds the current rate of interest. In other words, the rate of investment will be pushed to the point on the investment demand-schedule where the marginal efficiency of capital in general is equal to the market rate of interest.

The same thing can also be expressed as follows. If $Q_{r}$ is the prospective yield from an asset at time r, and $d_{r}$ is the present value of $f_{1}$ deferred r years at the current rate of interest, $\Sigma Q_{r} d_{r}$ is the demand price of the investment; and investment will be carried to the point where $\Sigma Q_{r} d_{r}$ becomes equal to the supply price of the investment as defined above. If, on the other hand, $\Sigma Q_{r} d_{r}$ falls short of the supply price, there will be no current investment in the asset in question.

It follows that the inducement to invest depends partly on the investment demand-schedule and partly on the rate of interest. Only at the conclusion of Book IV. will it be possible to take a comprehensive view of the factors determining the rate of investment in their actual complexity. I would, however, ask the reader to note at once that neither the knowledge of an asset's prospective yield nor the knowledge of the marginal efficiency of the asset enables us to deduce either the rate of interest or the present value of the asset. We must ascertain the rate of interest from some other source, and only then can we value the asset by “capitalising” its prospective yield.

How is the above definition of the marginal efficiency of capital related to common usage? The Marginal Productivity or Yield or Efficiency or Utility of Capital are familiar terms which we have all frequently used. But it is not easy by searching the literature of economics to find a clear statement of what economists have usually intended by these terms.

There are at least three ambiguities to clear up. There is, to begin with, the ambiguity whether we are concerned with the increment of physical product per unit of time due to the employment of one more physical unit of capital, or with the increment of value due to the employment of one more value unit of capital. The former involves difficulties as to the definition of the physical unit of capital, which I believe to be both insoluble and unnecessary. It is, of course, possible to say that ten labourers will raise more wheat from a given area when they are in a position to make use of certain additional machines; but I know no means of reducing this to an intelligible arithmetical ratio which does not bring in values. Nevertheless many discussions of this subject seem to be mainly concerned with the physical productivity of capital in some sense, though the writers fail to make themselves clear.

Secondly, there is the question whether the marginal efficiency of capital is some absolute quantity or a ratio. The contexts in which it is used and the practice of treating it as being of the same dimension as the rate of interest seem to require that it should be a ratio. Yet it is not usually made clear what the two terms of the ratio are supposed to be.

Finally, there is the distinction, the neglect of which has been the main cause of confusion and misunderstanding, between the increment of value obtainable by using an additional quantity of capital in the existing situation, and the series of increments which it is expected to obtain over the whole life of the additional capital asset;—i.e. the distinction between $Q_{1}$ and the complete series $Q_{1}$ , $Q_{2}$ ... $Q_{r}$ ... This involves the whole question of the place of expectation in economic theory. Most discussions of the marginal efficiency of capital seem to pay no attention to any member of the series except $Q_{1}$ . Yet this cannot be legitimate except in a static theory, for which all the Q's are equal. The ordinary theory of distribution, where it is assumed that capital is getting now its marginal productivity (in some sense or other), is only valid in a stationary state. The aggregate current return to capital has no direct relationship to its marginal efficiency; whilst its current return at the margin of production (i.e. the return to capital which enters into the supply price of output) is its marginal user cost, which also has no close connection with its marginal efficiency.

There is, as I have said above, a remarkable lack of any clear account of the matter. At the same time I believe that the definition which I have given above is fairly close to what Marshall intended to mean by the term. The phrase which Marshall himself uses is "marginal net efficiency" of a factor of production; or, alternatively, the "marginal utility of capital". The following is a summary of the most relevant passage which I can find in his Principles (6th ed. pp. 519-520). I have run together some non-consecutive sentences to convey the gist of what he says:

"In a certain factory an extra £100 worth of machinery can be applied so as not to involve any other extra expense, and so as to add annually £3 worth to the net output of the factory after allowing for its own wear and tear. If the investors of capital push it into every occupation in which it seems likely to gain a high reward; and if, after this has been done and equilibrium has been found, it still pays and only just pays to employ this machinery, we can infer from this fact that the yearly rate of interest is 3 per cent. But illustrations of this kind merely indicate part of the action of the great causes which govern value. They cannot be made into a theory of interest, any more than into a theory of wages, without reasoning in a circle. . . . Suppose that the rate of interest is 3 per cent. per annum on perfectly good security; and that the hat-making trade absorbs a capital of one million pounds. This implies that the hat-making trade can turn the whole million pounds' worth of capital to so good account that they would pay 3 per cent. per annum net for the use of it rather than go without any of it. There may be machinery which the trade would have refused to dispense with if the rate of interest had been 20 per cent. per annum. If the rate had been 10 per cent., more would have been used; if it had been 6 per cent., still more; if 4 per cent. still more; and finally, the rate being 3 per cent., they use more still. When they have this amount, the marginal utility of the machinery, i.e. the utility of that machinery which it is only just worth their while to employ, is measured by 3 per cent."

It is evident from the above that Marshall was well aware that we are involved in a circular argument if we try to determine along these lines what the rate of interest actually is.¹ In this passage he appears to accept the view set forth above, that the rate of interest determines the point to which new investment will be pushed, given the schedule of the marginal efficiency of capital. If the rate of interest is 3 per cent., this means that no one will pay £100 for a machine unless he hopes thereby to add £3 to his annual net output after allowing for costs and depreciation. But we shall see in Chapter 14 that in other passages Marshall was less cautious—though still drawing back when his argument was leading him on to dubious ground.

Although he does not call it the “marginal efficiency of capital”, Professor Irving Fisher has given in his Theory of Interest (1930) a definition of what he calls “the rate of return over cost” which is identical with my definition. “The rate of return over cost”, he writes,  “is that rate which, employed in computing the present worth of all the costs and the present worth of all the returns, will make these two equal.” Professor Fisher explains that the extent of investment in any direction will depend on a comparison between the rate of return over cost and the rate of interest. To induce new investment “the rate of return over cost must exceed the rate of interest".¹ "This new magnitude (or factor) in our study plays the central rôle on the investment opportunity side of interest theory."² Thus Professor Fisher uses his "rate of return over cost" in the same sense and for precisely the same purpose as I employ "the marginal efficiency of capital".
b:
It is a fundamental error of the classical school to treat the determination of investment as a mechanical adjustment between the supply of savings and the demand for funds, governed solely by the prevailing rate of interest. To understand the true dynamics of capital accumulation, we must penetrate beyond the superficial arithmetic of financial returns and examine the deeper psychological and structural forces that govern the entrepreneur’s decision to commit resources to the future. At the heart of this inquiry lies the concept of the marginal efficiency of capital, a notion which, while seemingly technical, is in reality the pivot upon which the entire structure of employment and economic prosperity turns. The marginal efficiency of capital is defined not as a rate of return in the accounting sense, but as the discount rate that equates the present value of the expected series of returns from a capital asset with its supply price. It is, in essence, the internal rate of return of the project, determined by the intersection of two distinct sets of variables: the prospective yield of the asset and its replacement cost.

To grasp the significance of this relationship, we must first dissect the component of prospective yield. This yield is not a fixed quantity known with certainty; rather, it is a sum of expectations. It depends upon the expected output of the asset over its life and, crucially, upon the expected state of demand for that output. Here we encounter the profound instability inherent in capitalist enterprise. The expectation of future revenue is a construct of the human mind, shaped by the conventions of the market and the fragile psychology of the crowd. When optimism prevails, the expected yields are inflated, and the marginal efficiency of capital rises, inducing a surge in investment. Conversely, when confidence falters, the expected yields collapse, and the marginal efficiency falls, regardless of the physical productivity of the machinery or the technical feasibility of the project. Thus, the marginal efficiency is not merely a function of technology or resource availability; it is a function of confidence, a volatile and subjective variable that defies precise measurement.

The second component, the supply price of the asset, introduces the element of scarcity and cost. As the volume of investment increases, the supply price of capital assets tends to rise. This occurs for two reasons: first, the increased demand for the inputs required to produce capital goods—labor, raw materials, and machinery—drives up their costs; second, the most profitable opportunities are exhausted first, leaving subsequent investments to face higher relative costs or lower yields. Therefore, the marginal efficiency of capital is a decreasing function of the volume of investment. As we employ more capital, the expected return on the next unit of capital diminishes. This diminishing return is not a law of nature in the short run, but a consequence of the rising cost of production and the saturation of the most lucrative avenues for deployment.

The entrepreneur’s decision to invest is then determined by comparing this marginal efficiency of capital with the rate of interest. The rate of interest, in this framework, is not the price of capital, but the price of liquidity. It represents the reward for parting with liquidity for a specified period. The entrepreneur will continue to invest as long as the marginal efficiency of capital exceeds the rate of interest. When the two are equal, the marginal inducement to invest ceases. It is here that the classical error becomes most apparent. The classical economists assumed that a fall in the rate of interest would invariably lead to an increase in investment, thereby equilibrating the market for savings and investment. They treated the rate of interest as a variable that could be adjusted to clear the market, much like the price of a commodity. However, this view neglects the autonomous nature of the marginal efficiency of capital. The rate of interest may fall, but if the marginal efficiency of capital falls faster, or if it remains below the rate of interest despite the decline, investment will not increase. In fact, during a depression, the rate of interest may be at its lowest, yet investment may be at its nadir, because the collapse of expected yields has driven the marginal efficiency of capital into a state of profound insufficiency.

Consider, for instance, a scenario in which technological progress reduces the supply price of a new type of manufacturing equipment, thereby lowering its replacement cost. In isolation, one might expect this to stimulate investment. However, if this technological progress simultaneously renders existing stocks of capital obsolete, or if it is accompanied by a widespread expectation of falling prices for the final goods produced, the prospective yield may plummet. The entrepreneur, observing the falling price of the machine, may also observe the falling price of the goods it produces. If the expected net revenue falls more sharply than the supply price, the marginal efficiency of capital may actually decline, discouraging investment despite the lower cost of the asset. This illustrates the critical interdependence of the two determinants: a change in the supply price does not operate in a vacuum but interacts dynamically with expectations of revenue.

Furthermore, the comparison between the marginal efficiency of capital and the rate of interest is fraught with complications arising from the nature of the rate of interest itself. The rate of interest is determined by the preference for liquidity, which is influenced by the quantity of money and the psychological desire to hold cash. It is not directly determined by the marginal productivity of capital. Therefore, the equilibrium between investment and savings is not a harmonious convergence of two sides of the same coin, but a precarious balance between two independent forces: the expectations of the entrepreneurs and the preferences of the hoarders. If the rate of interest is rigid, or if it falls slower than the marginal efficiency of capital, the result is a deficiency in effective demand. The system may settle at an equilibrium level of employment significantly below full employment, because the marginal efficiency of capital has fallen to a level that cannot be counteracted by any feasible reduction in the interest rate.

It is essential to distinguish between the general conclusion and the specific circumstances under which it holds. In the long run, we may assume that expectations are realized and that the economy adjusts to its fundamental constraints. However, the long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the short run, the marginal efficiency of capital is dominated by the volatility of expectations. The "animal spirits" of the entrepreneur—the spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction—play a decisive role. If these spirits are dampened, the marginal efficiency of capital collapses, and no amount of monetary easing can restore investment to its full-employment level. This is the liquidity trap, not merely in the sense that monetary policy becomes ineffective, but in the sense that the fundamental inducement to invest has been extinguished by pessimism.

Moreover, the concept of supply price must be understood in the context of the specific structure of the industry. In industries with high fixed costs and long production periods, the supply price is highly inelastic in the short run. An increase in demand for investment goods may lead to a disproportionate rise in their supply price, thereby depressing the marginal efficiency of capital more rapidly than in industries with flexible production. This structural rigidity implies that the marginal efficiency of capital is not a smooth, continuous function, but one subject to discontinuities and bottlenecks. The specific conditions of the market—such as the degree of competition, the availability of skilled labor, and the regulatory environment—shape the supply price and, consequently, the marginal efficiency.

Another possible interpretation, often overlooked, is the role of the risk premium. The marginal efficiency of capital is a gross return, which includes a compensation for risk. The rate of interest, conversely, is often viewed as a pure return on liquidity, excluding risk. Therefore, the comparison between the two is not a simple comparison of apples and apples. The entrepreneur must assess the risk premium embedded in the expected yield. If the uncertainty of the future is high, the entrepreneur will demand a higher marginal efficiency to justify investment, effectively raising the hurdle rate above the nominal interest rate. This risk premium is not constant; it fluctuates with the general state of confidence. During periods of crisis, the risk premium may soar, causing the marginal efficiency of capital to appear insufficient even when the objective prospects for return are reasonable. Thus, the failure of investment may be a failure of confidence rather than a failure of physical opportunity.

In conclusion, the relationship between the expected returns of investment assets and the marginal efficiency of capital is not a static equation but a dynamic process mediated by the supply price of capital assets and the rate of interest. The marginal efficiency of capital is the discount rate that balances the prospective yield with the replacement cost. It is the primary determinant of the volume of investment. The rate of interest serves as the threshold against which this efficiency is measured. However, the classical assumption that a lower interest rate will automatically stimulate investment is flawed because it ignores the autonomous and volatile nature of the marginal efficiency of capital. The supply price and the expected yield are interdependent, and changes in one often offset changes in the other. Furthermore, the comparison is complicated by the risk premium and the psychological factors governing the preference for liquidity. Therefore, the level of investment in any economy is determined by the complex interaction of technological possibilities, cost structures, and, most importantly, the state of confidence in the future. Policy aimed at stimulating investment must therefore address not only the cost of borrowing but also the expectations of entrepreneurs and the stability of the economic environment. Only by recognizing the primacy of the marginal efficiency of capital can we understand the true causes of unemployment and the limitations of monetary policy in achieving full employment. The economy is not a self-correcting mechanism that naturally tends toward equilibrium at full capacity; it is a system prone to persistent deficiencies in effective demand, rooted in the fragility of the expectations that drive the marginal efficiency of capital.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，以第一次世界大战结束后的欧洲为背景，讨论公众对旧生活秩序的习惯如何影响对和平与重建的判断。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
THE power to become habituated to his surroundings is a marked characteristic of mankind. Very few of us realize with conviction the intensely unusual, unstable, complicated, unreliable, temporary nature of the economic organization by which Western Europe has lived for the last half century. We assume some of the most peculiar and temporary of our late advantages as natural, permanent, and to be depended on, and we lay our plans accordingly. On this sandy and false foundation we scheme for social improvement and dress our political platforms, pursue our animosities and particular ambitions, and feel ourselves with enough margin in hand to foster, not assuage, civil conflict in the European family. Moved by insane delusion and reckless self-regard, the German people overturned the foundations on which we all lived and built. But the spokesmen of the French and British peoples have run the risk of completing the ruin, which Germany began, by a Peace which, if it is carried into effect, must impair yet further, when it might have restored, the delicate, complicated organization, already shaken and broken by war, through which alone the Eu- ropean peoples can employ themselves and live.

In England the outward aspect of life does not yet teach us to feel or realize in the least that an age is over. We are busy picking up the threads of our life where we dropped them, with this difference only, that many of us seem a good deal richer than we were before. Where we spent millions before the war, we have now learnt that we can spend hundreds of millions and apparently not suffer for it. Evidently we did not exploit to the utmost the possibilities of our economic life. We look, therefore, not only to a return to the comforts of 1914, but to an immense broadening and intensification of them. All classes alike thus build their plans, the rich to spend more and save less, the poor to spend more and work less.

But perhaps it is only in England (and America) that it is possible to be so unconscious. In continental Europe the earth heaves and no one but is aware of the rumblings. There it is not just a matter of extravagance or “labor troubles”; but of life and death, of starvation and existence, and of the fearful convulsions of a dying civilization.

For one who spent in Paris the greater part of the six months which succeeded the Armistice an occasional visit to London was a strange experience. England still stands outside Europe. Europe's voiceless tremors do not reach her. Europe is apart and England is not of her flesh and body. But Europe is solid with herself. France, Germany, Italy, Austria and Holland, Russia and Roumania and Poland, throb together, and their structure and civilization are essentially one. They flourished together, they have rocked together in a war, which we, in spite of our enormous contributions and sacrifices (like though in a less degree than America), economically stood outside, and they may fall together. In this lies the destructive significance of the Peace of Paris. If the European Civil War is to end with France and Italy abusing their momentary victorious power to destroy Germany and Austria-Hungary now prostrate, they invite their own destruction also, being so deeply and inextricably intertwined with their victims by hidden psychic and economic bonds. At any rate an Englishman who took part in the Conference of Paris and was during those months a member of the Supreme Economic Council of the Allied Powers, was bound to become, for him a new experience, a European in his cares and outlook. There, at the nerve center of the European system, his British preoccupations must largely fall away and he must be haunted by other and more dreadful specters. Paris was a nightmare, and every one there was morbid. A sense of impending catastrophe overhung the frivolous scene; the futility and smallness of man before the great events confronting him; the mingled significance and unreality of the decisions; levity, blindness, insolence, confused cries from without,—all the elements of ancient tragedy were there. Seated indeed amid the theatrical trappings of the French Saloons of State, one could wonder if the extraordinary visages of Wilson and of Clemenceau, with their fixed hue and unchanging characterization, were really faces at all and not the tragi-comic masks of some strange drama or puppet-show.

The proceedings of Paris all had this air of extraordinary importance and unimportance at the same time. The decisions seemed charged with consequences to the future of human society; yet the air whispered that the word was not flesh, that it was futile, insignificant, of no effect, dissociated from events; and one felt most strongly the impression, described by Nikolai Berezin in War and Peace or by Hardy in The Dynasts, of events marching on to their fated conclusion uninfluenced and unaffected by the cerebrations of Statesmen in Council:

Observe that all wide sight and self-command Deserts these throngs now driven to demonry

By the Immanent Unrecking. Nought remains But vindictiveness here amid the strong, And there amid the weak an impotent rage.

Spirit of the Pities

Why prompts the Will so senseless-shaped a doing?

Spirit of the Years

I have told thee that It works unwittingly,

As one possessed not judging.
