In Paris, where those connected with the Supreme Economic Council received almost hourly the reports of the misery, disorder, and decaying organization of all Central and Eastern Europe, allied and enemy alike, and learnt from the lips of the financial representatives of Germany and Austria unanswerable evidence of the terrible exhaustion of their countries, an occasional visit to the hot, dry room in the President's house, where the Four fulfilled their destinies in empty and arid intrigue, only added to the sense of nightmare. Yet there in Paris the problems of Europe were terrible and clamant, and an occasional return to the vast unconcern of London a little disconcerting. For in London these questions were very far away, and our own lesser problems alone troubling. London believed that Paris was making a great confusion of its business, but remained uninterested. In this spirit the British people received the Treaty without reading it. But it is under the influence of Paris, not London, that this book has been written by one who, though an Englishman, feels himself a European also, and, because of too vivid recent experience, cannot dis- interest himself from the further unfolding of the great historic drama of these days which will destroy great institutions, but may also create a new world.
b:
The habit of the old order is not a mere inertia of sentiment, but a working premise of judgment; and in the Europe that emerged from the war it operated with peculiar force upon the question of peace and reconstruction. Men carried into the settlement of 1919 an unexamined picture of the world—of credit, of trade, of the mobility of labour and capital, of the ordinary continuities of production and exchange—which had been formed in the decades before 1914 and which the war had in fact destroyed. The practical consequence is that their estimates of what was possible, and of what was just, were made upon data that no longer existed. This is not to say that the statesmen were ignorant of the war; they knew its losses, its debts, its ruins. It is to say that they interpreted the post-war problem with the categories of the pre-war economy, and that the categories misled them.

Consider the matter of reparations. The habit of the old order suggested that a defeated nation could be treated as a going concern, that its industry would resume, that its exports would pay, that the transfer of great annual sums across the exchanges was a question of fiscal arrangement rather than of economic possibility. The old world had known large international payments, and had known them to be discharged by the movement of goods and services; and so it was assumed that the same mechanism would serve. But the conditions upon which that mechanism had depended—the free exchange of commodities, the willingness of creditor nations to receive payment in goods, the stability of currencies, the existence of a working system of international credit—were precisely the conditions the war had most gravely injured. To judge the reparations problem by the habits of 1913 was therefore to judge it by an analogy that had ceased to hold. The conclusion which follows is general in form: where the material conditions of an economy have been transformed, judgments formed upon the habits of the earlier order are liable to error, and the error is likely to be greatest where the sums at stake are largest and the mechanism least understood. But the particular application is not general: it does not follow that no reparations were payable, nor that the figures actually fixed were in every respect impossible. It follows only that the estimates of capacity and of transfer were made upon assumptions that required proof and did not receive it.

The same habit shows itself in the treatment of currency and prices. Before the war the value of money was, for practical men, a stable background; contracts, wages, rents and debts were framed upon the expectation that the unit of account would remain approximately constant. The war had taught a different lesson, but the lesson was slow to be learned, and the old habits of thought survived in the very quarters where they were most dangerous—in the drafting of treaties, in the fixation of indemnities, in the management of public finance. A statesman who assumes that a given sum of money will continue to mean what it meant when the obligation was contracted is not merely optimistic; he is applying a rule of thumb drawn from an order that has passed. The consequence is that obligations are fixed in nominal terms which, under the new conditions of depreciated currencies, bear no relation to the real burden intended. Here again the general proposition is safe: habits of mind formed under stable money are a poor guide to the conduct of affairs under unstable money. But the specific inference is conditional: it depends upon the degree of depreciation, upon the fiscal capacity of the country concerned, and upon the willingness of the creditor to accept payment in kind or in goods. Where these conditions are favourable, the old habits may do little harm; where they are unfavourable, they may produce a settlement that is neither just nor workable.

There is a further and subtler influence. The old order had accustomed men to think of Europe as a single economic organism, with a division of labour among its parts, and with a freedom of movement for persons, goods and capital that made the whole more productive than the sum of its members. The war had broken that organism into fragments, had raised new frontiers, had multiplied currencies and restrictions, and had destroyed the credit by which the parts had been held together. Yet the habit of the old order persisted in the form of a belief that the fragments could be reassembled by treaty, that the old channels would fill again of themselves, and that the restoration of the map would restore the economy. This belief was not unreasonable in itself; it was, indeed, the condition of any hopeful policy. But it led men to neglect the positive measures—the provision of credit, the relaxation of restrictions, the restoration of the means of exchange—by which alone the old organism could have been revived. They trusted to the habit, and the habit was not enough. The general lesson is that a community accustomed to a given economic order will tend to assume that the order will re-establish itself, and will underrate the deliberate effort required to restore it after a shock. The particular lesson is that in 1919 the effort required was greater than the habits of the time permitted men to conceive, and that the neglect of it was a principal cause of the subsequent disorder.

It is necessary, however, to distinguish between the habit as a source of error and the habit as a condition of sound judgment. Not all the assumptions of the old order were false. The belief that production must be restored before obligations can be met, that trade must be revived before debts can be paid, that confidence must be re-established before credit can flow—these are not prejudices of a vanished world; they are permanent truths of economic life, and the men who held them were right. The error lay not in holding them, but in supposing that they would operate automatically, and in framing the settlement upon the assumption that the old machinery was still in being. A judgment which recognises the continuity of economic law while insisting upon the discontinuity of economic circumstance is the judgment we require; and it is precisely the judgment which the habits of the old order made difficult to attain.

The alternative explanations of the settlement must also be weighed. It may be said that the errors of 1919 were due not to habit but to ignorance—that the statesmen did not know the facts, and that better information would have produced a better peace. This is partly true, and it is a more charitable explanation than the hypothesis of habit; but it does not displace it, for ignorance is itself shaped by habit, and men do not seek information which their habits tell them is unnecessary. It may be said, again, that the settlement was determined by political passion and the exigencies of democratic politics, and that economic habit was a minor influence. This too has force; the demands of electorates, the desire for security, the fear of a revived enemy, all played their part. But political passion operates upon the material presented to it by habit; men demanded what they believed to be possible, and their belief in what was possible was formed by the old order. The two explanations are not rival but complementary. A third explanation would emphasise the sheer novelty of the situation, and argue that no habits could have sufficed. This is the strongest of the alternatives, and it should be conceded that the post-war problem was in important respects without precedent. Yet even novelty is judged by analogy, and the analogies available were those of the old order; the failure was not that men lacked experience of the new, but that they applied the experience of the old without examining its conditions.

The conclusion, then, is twofold. In general, the habits of a settled economic order are indispensable to judgment, since without them no estimate of the future could be formed; but they become a source of error when the conditions that gave them meaning have been altered, and the error is greatest when the alteration is sudden and the habits are most deeply held. In the particular circumstances of post-war Europe, the habits of the old order led men to overestimate the automatic character of recovery, to underestimate the positive measures required, and to frame obligations upon assumptions of stability and transferability that the war had destroyed. The remedy is not to discard the habits, but to test them against the new conditions, and to ask in each case whether the analogy holds. A peace built upon unexamined habit is a peace built upon the past; and the past, in 1919, had already exacted its price.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，以战后法国财政与法郎问题为背景，分析税收负担、债权收入和工资调整之间的政策选择。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
MONSIEUR,—When I read in my daily paper the daily projects of yourself and your predecessors to draft new budgets and to fund old debts, I get the impression that Paris discusses very little what seems to me in London to be the technical analysis of your problem. May I, therefore, divert your attention for a moment from your Sisyphean task of rolling budgets up Parliament Hill back to certain fundamental calculations?

I have written about the French franc many times in recent years, and I do not find that I have changed my mind. More than two years ago I wrote: “The level of the franc is going to be settled in the long run, not by speculation or the balance of trade, or even the outcome of the Ruhr adventure, but by the proportion of his earned income which the French taxpayer will permit to be taken from him to pay the claims of the French rentier.” I still think that this is the root idea from which your plans ought to develop.

Now it is obvious that there are two methods of attaining the desired equilibrium. You can increase the burdens on the taxpayer, or you can diminish the claims of the rentier. If you choose the first alternative, taxation will absorb nearly a quarter of the national income of France. Is this feasible? If it is ever safe to speak about the political atmosphere of another country, I should judge from recent indications that the French public will certainly refuse to submit to the imposition of a burden of additional taxation sufficient to satisfy the claims of the rentier at their present level. And even if such taxation were politically possible, it would probably break down ad- ministratively. The pressing task of the French Treasury is not to devise additional taxes, but to construct an administrative machine capable of collecting those which exist. If, therefore, I were in your place, I should not, as a politician, give another minute's thought to new taxes, but would concentrate, so far as concerned the fiscal part of my office, on consolidating and administering the taxes already voted.

Since this by itself is not enough, your next business—provided you accept my conclusion as to the mind of the French public—is to consider coolly how best to reduce the claims of the rentier. Three methods offer themselves: first, a general capital levy; second, a forced reduction of the rate of interest on the public debt; third, a rise of prices which would reduce the real value of the rentier's money claims. Unquestionably, the first is preferable on grounds of virtue, justice, and theory. For Britain in a similar fix I should advocate it. But I think it so probable that such a project would be defeated in France to-day by the same political and administrative difficulties which stand in the way of further taxation, that I should not lose my time on it. The second method is attractive, if only because it offers no administrative difficulties. I believe that some authorities in France have favoured it. Nevertheless, I should decline this expedient also, if I were in your place, because, unlike a general capital levy or a depreciation of money, this species of discrimination is truly named Repudiation, and Repudiation of the National Debt is a departure from financial virtue so extreme and so dangerous as not to be undertaken but in the last emergency.

We are left, therefore, by a process of the exclusion of alternatives, with one Exit only—a rise of internal prices; which leads us away from the fiscal field to the price level, the foreign exchanges, the gold in the Bank of France, the volume of foreign investment, and the balance of trade. Here I must invite your particular attention to an interesting paradox.

Successive Finance Ministers have, in fact, done their utmost to find an escape through the Exit I indicate. They have inflated magnificently, and they have brought down the gold value of the franc by progressive stages with only temporary set-backs. What more could they have done?

I will tell you. The great army of your predecessors have failed, in spite of all their efforts, to depreciate adequately the internal purchasing power of the franc. Your present difficulties are due, not to the inflation of the notes or to the fall of the exchange (for these events are tending all the time to help you out of your troubles), but to the failure of these factors to diminish proportionately the internal purchasing power of the rentier's money claims.

The following figures present the essence of your problem. In December 1925, the gold value of the franc on the foreign exchanges was 19 per cent of its pre-war parity; world gold prices were about 158 per cent of their pre-war level; therefore on the pre-war basis a note circulation and a franc price level amounting to 830 per cent (for 158 ÷ 19 = 8·3) of their pre-war figures would be justified. Now the note circulation, being about 1000 per cent of its pre-war figure, roughly corresponds to the level of the foreign exchange—though, allowing for increased territory and the loss of gold and silver coin from the circulation, it is probably still too low in relation to the exchange, rather than too high, on a pre-war comparison.

When we come to the internal franc price level, on the other hand, we find an entirely different story. Imported raw materials have inevitably risen to their international parity. But the classes of goods such as food and other articles entering into the cost-of-living index number, which are dominated by home production, are far below their equilibrium value. Wholesale food prices in November 1925 were 490 per cent of pre-war, retail prices in Paris (thirteen items) were 433 per cent, and in the third quarter of 1925 the cost-of-living index for Paris stood at 401 per cent. These figures may understate the real rise of prices, but it certainly seems that French domestic costs are not above five times their pre-war figure. This means that the prices of purely home produce, converted at the present rate of exchange, are not much more than half world prices, and are actually below their pre-war level in terms of gold. Thus the Inflation of the currency has produced its full effect on the exchanges, and consequently on the prices of imported commodities, but has largely failed to do so on the prices of home produce.

Now the burden of the rentier on the taxpayer is measured by the internal purchasing power of the francs which have to be taken from the latter to be handed to the former. Thus if internal prices had risen as fast as the exchange has fallen, the real burden of the national debt service would be reduced by at least a third. I suggest to you, therefore, that, whilst the solution of your fiscal difficulties can come about in no other way than by a rise in the internal price level, it is not so clear that this need be accompanied either by further Inflation or by a further fall in the exchange.

It is for you to decide in your own mind at what level of internal prices you can hope to balance your budget. Your next step must be to bring about this rise in as orderly and scientific a way as you are able. Looking from outside, it appears to me that an internal price level between eight and nine times pre-war might be high enough. In this case there is no justification for any considerable further Inflation or fall in the franc exchange. All you have to do is to stabilise the note circulation and the franc exchange at near their present level and to allow time for internal prices to rise correspondingly.

What are the explanations of the present low level of franc prices? I think that they are: (1) the time element—internal prices move slowly, but will move as they should in time; (2) the hoarding of bank-notes on an even greater scale than formerly, leading to a sluggish circulation of the available currency; (3) excessive foreign investment by Frenchmen, due to lack of confidence, which drives the exchange down below the figure appropriate to the trading position; and (4) the legal restrictions on rents, etc.

These influences should be remediable as regards (1) by the mere lapse of time, and as regards (2) and (3) by the restoration of internal confidence. The right strategy, therefore, is to restore confidence and then just wait. And the way to restore confidence is, surely, not to heap up taxes, but to stabilise the franc exchange beyond doubt or criticism near its present level.

How to stabilise the franc exchange? Not so difficult as it is supposed to be. The balance of trade is strongly in favour of France. The present level of internal prices encourages exports and discourages imports. The metallic reserve of the Bank of France is worth (at the present exchange) nearly 40 per cent of the note issue. Nothing is required, I expect, but that the Bank of France should declare that for two years at least it will furnish dollar exchange against francs in unlimited amounts on terms not worse than some stated rate between dollars and francs, and that the Bank should be prepared, if necessary, to use its gold for the purpose. The rate selected should probably lie somewhere between 1 dollar for 25 francs and 1 dollar for 30 francs, and it would be safer to choose the latter ratio at first, with just a hope that the former might be achieved in the end.¹ The success of the scheme requires no more than that the Bank's undertaking should be believed. With this background of stability you will be able to borrow enough to carry you through the transitional period without further Inflation.

For the rest you can trust time. As the internal price level gradually rises to an equilibrium with the exchange and as the machinery for collecting the taxes is gradually improved, your budget receipts will grow month by month until they balance the expenses. Those taxes which are fixed in francs and are not ad valorem should, of course, be raised pari passu with the rise in prices.

There are two matters on which the Government of France needs to exercise an iron resolve — to fix the franc exchange at a minimum figure even if it costs gold to do so, and to collect the taxes in full. These are the indispensable measures. Heroic efforts to increase the rates of taxation are, at this stage, efforts in a wrong direction, and will not be successful.

What are the arguments against these courses? They are entirely political. A policy which will not be successful unless it raises prices by a heavy percentage will be open to the universal unpopularity of la vie chère. A policy of bringing about an equilibrium between internal and external prices must be injurious to the export interests which flourish on their disequilibrium. It may not be sufficient to reply that the first must happen in any case unless the taxpayer will sacrifice himself to the rentier, and that the second must happen some day unless the franc is to fall for ever.

But there are political considerations of some weight to set on the other side. A rise in the prices of agricultural produce will not be unpopular with farmers and peasant producers who have been selling their output much too cheap. Further, the Government must make it clear that wage-earners and officials are not intended to suffer, and will, if it is wise, pass a law providing for automatic quarterly increases of all wages and salaries throughout the next two years corresponding to every increase in the cost of living.
b:
The fiscal problem of post-war France presents itself, to the candid observer, less as a problem of rates than as a problem of the unit in which obligations are expressed. When the general level of prices has risen several-fold, every tax assessed in the depreciated unit, and every debt contracted in it, changes its economic meaning without any change in its legal form. The statesman who confines his attention to the nominal yield of the tax system will therefore mistake the character of his difficulty; for a burden which appears moderate when measured against the old money may be trivial or crushing when measured against the new, according to the movement of prices between assessment and payment. It is with this caution in mind that I would examine the three instruments—taxation, the service of the public debt, and the adjustment of wages—not as separable expedients but as parts of a single mechanism through which the community is asked to transfer real resources to the state.

Consider first the tax burden. A progressive income tax with rates fixed in law and brackets fixed in nominal francs suffers, under inflation, a double distortion. The taxpayer whose money income rises with prices is pushed into higher brackets; his real disposable income may fall even while his nominal tax is rising, and the state may collect a larger fraction of the national product without any legislative decision. This is not a tax imposed by Parliament but a tax imposed by the printer. It has the merit, from the Treasury's standpoint, of yielding revenue promptly; it has the defect of being arbitrary, of falling with particular severity on those whose incomes adjust slowly, and of generating a general sense that the fiscal system is a device for confiscation rather than a contribution to common purposes. Where the tax administration is weak and assessment lags, however, the opposite distortion may appear: the state collects in francs worth less than those in which the assessment was framed, and the real yield of the tax collapses precisely when expenditure is rising. The net effect in any given year is thus an empirical question, depending on the lag between assessment and collection, the indexation of brackets, and the elasticity of money incomes to prices. One cannot pronounce a general verdict on the French tax burden without specifying these conditions; what can be said is that a fiscal system which does not explicitly reckon with the changing value of its own unit will produce results that no one intended.

Turn now to the holders of the public debt. The rentier who lent to the state in a stable currency and is repaid in a depreciated one has suffered a capital levy without the formality of legislation. This is the classical objection to inflation, and it is a just one; but it is incomplete, because it treats the rentier's loss as a simple subtraction from national wealth, whereas the transfer is in fact a redistribution among living persons with different propensities to consume. The rentier, being typically a person of fixed habits and moderate means, spends a relatively stable proportion of his real income; the taxpayer relieved of debt service, and the wage-earner whose money income has risen, may spend more readily. The effect on effective demand is therefore not neutral, and the effect on the distribution of wealth is not the only consideration. Yet a government that allows the real value of its debt to be eroded cannot borrow again on reasonable terms except from those who are compelled to lend, and the destruction of the market for public securities is a lasting injury to the conduct of future finance. Here again the judgment must be conditional: where the debt is held largely by institutions whose liabilities are themselves expressed in the same depreciating unit, the injury is contained; where it is held by small savers and by foreign creditors, the injury is grave and the political consequences are incalculable.

The adjustment of wages occupies a middle position, and it is the point at which the other two instruments meet. If money wages rise in proportion to prices, the real burden of a given nominal tax is unchanged, but the yield of a progressive tax rises with the nominal income, and the state gains at the expense of wage-earners unless the brackets are revised. If money wages lag behind prices, real wages fall, and the wage-earner bears the burden of financing the state and the debt service through a reduction in his standard of life; this is the path of least resistance for a weak government, and it is the path that produces industrial unrest and, in the end, a wage explosion that restores the position with interest. The statesman who seeks to adjust wages by decree, in order to reconcile fiscal solvency with social peace, will find that the decree is effective only so long as the workers believe it will be enforced, and that belief is a function of the government's command over the currency. A wage policy and a monetary policy are not two policies but one.

From these considerations I draw a general conclusion and a particular one. The general conclusion is that in a period of substantial monetary disturbance the three instruments cannot be evaluated separately; the real burden of taxation, the real value of debt service, and the real wage are jointly determined by the movement of prices, and any policy which fixes two of them while leaving the third to the market will produce a result that is neither intended nor stable. The particular conclusion, applicable to France in the years after the war, is that the restoration of fiscal authority required first the restoration of a unit of account in which taxes could be assessed and debts contracted with some expectation of constancy; without that, the most ingenious tax schedule and the most equitable wage scale are merely nominal. I would add, as a caution against over-generalisation, that the particular conclusion depends on the assumption that the government can in fact stabilise the unit—an assumption which presupposes a political consensus that may not exist, and which in the French case was achieved only after a period of experiment and crisis. Where that consensus is absent, the alternative is not a well-ordered adjustment of the three instruments but a continuous struggle in which each group seeks to protect its own nominal position, and the general interest is served by none.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，讨论如何利用1919至1923年英美物价、购买力平价与实际汇率进行比较，明确指标口径和可回答的问题。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
b:
The comparison of American and British prices, purchasing-power parity, and actual exchange rates between 1919 and 1923 is a problem less of arithmetic than of interpretation; and the interpreter must begin by fixing his definitions, since the several series which may plausibly be called "prices" do not measure the same thing and do not answer the same question. Three distinct magnitudes are in question. First, the ratio of a British price index to an American price index, both computed on a common base period, gives what may be called the relative price level: it tells us how much more (or less) British goods in general cost than American goods in general, when each is measured in its own currency. Second, the purchasing-power parity of the two currencies is the exchange rate which would equate the two price levels, and is simply the ratio of the indices multiplied by the nominal parity (the pre-war mint parity of approximately $4.86 to the pound). Third, the actual market rate is the observed quotation, which in these years floated well above that parity. The comparison of the second with the third yields the "real" exchange rate—more precisely, a measure of the degree to which the actual rate diverged from the rate which relative prices would have justified. Each of these magnitudes answers a different question: the first, whether British prices rose more or less than American; the second, what rate would have preserved the pre-war relative purchasing power of the two currencies; the third, what the market in fact did.

The choice of index number is not a neutral technicality. A wholesale index, weighted toward internationally traded staples, will move with world commodity prices and will register the depreciation of the pound in terms of goods entering foreign trade; a cost-of-living index, weighted toward rents, services, and domestically produced articles, will behave differently, and the divergence between the two is itself evidence about the segmentation of markets. The base period must likewise be chosen with care: 1913 is the natural pre-war base, but the composition of output and the pattern of relative prices had been so disturbed by 1919 that a 1913-based comparison may exaggerate the disequilibrium. The investigator should therefore present his results for more than one index and more than one base, and should treat a conclusion which holds for all of them as robust, and one which depends on a single choice as provisional.

What questions can such a comparison answer? It can tell us whether, at the actual rate of exchange, British goods were cheap or dear in terms of American goods—that is, whether the pound was "overvalued" or "undervalued" relative to purchasing-power parity. It can tell us whether the movement of the exchanges tracked the movement of prices with a lag, and thus whether the market was forming expectations about future price levels. It can tell us whether the divergence between the two price levels was of a magnitude which the ordinary mechanisms of trade might be expected to correct. It cannot, by itself, tell us why the divergence existed; and it cannot tell us what rate of exchange was "correct," since no unique correct rate follows from price data alone.

Suppose, for illustration, that in 1920 the British wholesale index stood at 300 (1913 = 100) and the American at 220. The purchasing-power parity would then be $4.86 × 300/220, or about $6.63 to the pound. If the market rate was $3.95, the pound was depreciated in nominal terms but appreciated in real terms: British goods, converted at the market rate, were dearer than American goods, and the real exchange rate stood some 40 per cent above parity. The immediate inference—that British exports were handicapped and imports encouraged—is sound as far as it goes, but it depends on the assumption that the price indices are comparable in coverage and weighting, and that the goods entering trade are represented by the indices employed. If the British index is dominated by imported raw materials whose sterling price had risen with the exchange, the apparent appreciation is partly an artefact of the index's construction.

The further inference, that the divergence must be corrected by a fall in British prices or a rise in the exchange, depends on conditions which must be stated explicitly: that the divergence is not offset by tariffs, transport costs, or differences in the quality and variety of goods; that the elasticities of demand for exports and imports are such that a change in relative prices actually alters the trade balance in the expected direction; and that capital movements do not indefinitely sustain a rate which trade alone would not support. In the years in question, the last condition is of first importance: the return to gold at the pre-war parity in 1925 was a decision about the exchange rate taken in the face of a price level which purchasing-power parity would not have justified, and the subsequent strain on British industry is intelligible only when the real exchange rate is computed and its consequences traced.

The general conclusion, then, is this: purchasing-power parity is a useful first approximation and a serviceable organizing device, but it is not a theory of the exchange rate. It tells us what rate would equate price levels; it does not tell us what rate will obtain, since the actual rate is governed by capital movements, by expectations, by official intervention, and by the relative prices of those goods which do not enter international trade. The particular conclusion for 1919–1923 is that the pound was, on the evidence of the price indices, substantially overvalued in real terms for much of the period, and that this overvaluation was a principal cause of the difficulties of British export trades; but this conclusion is conditional on the indices chosen, on the assumption that the price data are comparable, and on the further assumption that the trade mechanism was free to operate. Where those conditions fail, the conclusion must be qualified; and the honest investigator will present his figures with the qualifications attached, rather than allow a precise-looking ratio to masquerade as a precise truth.

author: Henry Langford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，在严重失业和生产闲置的条件下，讨论节约、消费与经济恢复的关系，并比较私人和公共行动。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The slump in trade and employment and the business losses which are being incurred are as bad as the worst which have ever occurred in the modern history of the world. No country is exempt. The privation and—what is sometimes worse—the anxiety which exist to-day in millions of homes all over the world is extreme. In the three chief industrial countries of the world, Great Britain, Germany, and the United States, I estimate that probably 12,000,000 industrial workers stand idle. But I am not sure that there is not even more human misery to-day in the great agricultural countries of the world—Canada, Australia, and South America, where millions of small farmers see themselves ruined by the fall in the prices of their products, so that their receipts after harvest bring them in much less than the crops have cost them to produce. For the fall in the prices of the great staple products of the world such as wheat, wool, sugar, cotton, and indeed most other commodities has been simply catastrophic. Most of these prices are now below their pre-war level;

yet costs, as we all know, remain far above their pre-war level. A week or two ago, it is said, wheat in Liverpool sold at the lowest price recorded since the reign of Charles II. more than 250 years ago. How is it possible for farmers to live in such conditions? Of course it is impossible.

You might suppose—and some austere individuals do in fact believe—that cheapness must be an advantage. For what the producer loses, the consumer gains. But it is not so. For those of us who work—and we are in the great majority—can only consume so long as we produce. So that anything which interferes with the processes of production necessarily interferes also with those of consumption.

The reason for this is that there are all kinds of obstacles to the costs and prices of everything falling equally. For example, the wages-costs of most manufacturers are practically the same as they were. See how the vicious process works out. The prices of wool and wheat fall. Good for the British consumer of wheat and woollen garments—so one might suppose. But the producers of wool and wheat, since they receive too little for their products, cannot make their usual purchases of British goods. Consequently those British consumers who are at the same time workers who make these goods find themselves out of work. What is the use of cheapness when incomes are falling?

When Dr. Johnson, visiting the Island of Skye, was told that twenty eggs might be bought

And so the position gets worse and worse in a vicious circle.

The best guess I can make is that whenever you save five shillings, you put a man out of work for a day. Your saving that five shillings adds to unemployment to the extent of one man for one day—and so on in proportion. On the other hand, whenever you buy goods you increase employment—though they must be British, home-produced goods if you are to increase employment in this country. After all, this is only the plainest common sense. For if you buy goods, some one will have to make them. And if you do not buy goods, the shops will not clear their stocks, they will not give repeat orders, and some one will be thrown out of work.

Therefore, oh patriotic housewives, sally out to-morrow early into the streets and go to the wonderful sales which are everywhere advertised. You will do yourselves good—for never were things so cheap, cheap beyond your dreams. Lay in a stock of household linen, of sheets and blankets to satisfy all your needs. And have the added joy that you are increasing employment, adding to the wealth of the country because you are setting on foot useful activities, bringing a chance and a hope to Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Belfast.

These are only examples. Do whatever is necessary to satisfy the most sensible needs of yourself and your household, make improvements, build.

For what we need now is not to button up our waistcoats tight, but to be in a mood of expansion, of activity—to do things, to buy things, to make things. Surely all this is the most obvious common sense. For take the extreme case. Suppose we were to stop spending our incomes altogether, and were to save the lot. Why, every one would be out of work. And before long we should have no incomes to spend. No one would be a penny the richer, and the end would be that we should all starve to death—which would surely serve us right for refusing to buy things from one another, for refusing to take in one another's washing, since that is how we all live. The same is true, and even more so, of the work of a local authority. Now is the time for municipalities to be busy and active with all kinds of sensible improvements.

The patient does not need rest. He needs exercise. You cannot set men to work by holding back, by refusing to place orders, by inactivity. On the contrary, activity of one kind or another is the only possible means of making the wheels of economic progress and of the production of wealth go round again.

Nationally, too, I should like to see schemes of greatness and magnificence designed and carried through. I read a few days ago of a proposal to drive a great new road, a broad boulevard, parallel to the Strand, on the south side of the Thames, as a new thoroughfare joining Westminster to the City. That is the right sort of notion. But I should like to see something bigger still. For example, why not pull down the whole of South London from Westminster to Greenwich, and make a good job of it—housing on that convenient area near to their work a much greater population than at present, in far better buildings with all the conveniences of modern life, yet at the same time providing hundreds of acres of squares and avenues, parks and public spaces, having, when it was finished, something magnificent to the eye, yet useful and convenient to human life as a monument to our age. Would that employ men? Why, of course it would! Is it better that the men should stand idle and miserable, drawing the dole? Of course it is not.

These, then, are the chief observations which I want to leave with you now—first of all, to emphasise the extreme gravity of the situation, with about a quarter of our working population standing idle; next, that the trouble is a worldwide one which we cannot cure by ourselves; and, third, that we can all the same do something by ourselves and that something must take the form of activity, of doing things, of spending, of setting great enterprises afoot.

But I also have one final theme to put before you. I fancy that a reason why some people may be a little horrified at my suggestions is the fear that we are much too poor to be able to afford what they consider to be extravagance. They think that we are poor, much poorer than we were and that what we chiefly need is to cut our coat according to our cloth, by which they mean that we must curtail our consumption, reduce our standard of life, work harder and consume less; and that that is the way out of the wood. This view is not, in my judgement, in accordance with the facts. We have plenty of cloth and only lack the courage to cut it into coats. I want, therefore, to give you some cheerful facts to dispose you to take an ampler view of the economic strength of this country.

Let me first of all remind you of the obvious. The great mass of the population is living much better than it ever lived before. We are supporting in idleness, at a higher standard of life than is possible for those who are in work in most other countries, nearly a quarter of our employable population. Yet at the same time the national wealth is increasing year by year. After paying wages which are far higher than, for example, in France or in Germany, after supporting a quarter of our population in idleness, after adding to the country's equipment of houses and roads and electrical plant and so forth on a substantial scale, we still have a surplus available to be lent to foreign countries, which in 1929 was greater than the surplus for such purposes of any other country in the world, even of the United States.

How do we do it? If the pessimists were right who believe that we are terribly inefficient, overextravagant and getting poorer, obviously it would be impossible. We can only do it because the pessimists are quite wrong. We are not nearly so rich as we might be if we could manage our affairs better and not get them into such a muddle. But we are not inefficient, we are not poor, we are not living on our capital. Quite the contrary. Our labour and our plant are enormously more productive than they used to be. Our national income is going up quite quickly. That is how we do it.

Let me give you a few figures. As compared with so recent a date as 1924, our productive output per head has probably increased by 10 per cent. That is to say, we can produce the same amount of wealth with 10 per cent fewer men employed. As compared with pre-war the increase in output per head is probably as much as 20 per cent. Apart from changes in the value of money, the national income—even so recently as 1929 with a great mass of unemployment (it cannot, of course, be quite so good to-day)—was probably increasing by as much as £100,000,000 a year; and this has been going on year by year for a good many years. At the same time we have been quietly carrying through almost a revolution in the distribution of incomes in the direction of equality.

Be confident, therefore, that we are suffering from the growing pains of youth, not from the rheumatics of old age. We are failing to make full use of our opportunities, failing to find an outlet for the great increase in our productive powers and our productive energy. Therefore we must not draw in our horns; we must push them out. Activity and boldness and enterprise, both individually and nationally, must be the cure.
b:
The question of saving under conditions of severe unemployment and idle productive capacity is not a marginal refinement of economic doctrine but a test of its first principles. In such conditions the classical presumption that thrift is a private virtue and a public benefit loses its warrant, because the premises on which it rests—full employment of labour and equipment—are precisely what is absent. When resources lie idle, an act of saving does not release resources for alternative employment; it withdraws purchasing power from the stream of expenditure and leaves the idle resources more idle still. The argument I wish to develop is that the relation between saving, consumption, and recovery is not fixed but conditional: it depends on the level of employment and the state of expectations, and it differs systematically between private and public action. A general conclusion about thrift can therefore be stated only for the special case of full employment; for the case of underemployment, a different and conditional conclusion is required.

Begin with the elementary identities, which are not in dispute. Income is divided between consumption and saving; expenditure is divided between consumption and investment; and in equilibrium saving equals investment. These identities tell us nothing about causation, but they expose the fallacy of composition that governs popular and much professional reasoning about thrift. For an individual, saving is a way of adding to wealth; for a community, saving is a decision not to consume, and unless it is matched by a decision to invest, it is a decision that reduces incomes. The attempt to save more, undertaken simultaneously by many households, may fail to raise aggregate saving at all, because the reduced expenditure lowers incomes and thus the capacity to save. This is the paradox of thrift: it is not a paradox of arithmetic but of aggregation. The community cannot, by the sum of individual decisions to abstain from consumption, will itself to be richer in terms of employment and output; it can only redistribute and reduce the flow of income.

The mechanism is best seen through the multiplier. Let expenditure on consumption depend on income, with a marginal propensity to consume less than unity. Then an initial reduction in consumption expenditure reduces the incomes of those who would have supplied the goods, who in turn reduce their own expenditure, and so on in a diminishing series. The total contraction of income exceeds the initial saving by the multiplier, which is the reciprocal of the marginal propensity to save. If, for example, the community attempts to save an additional tenth of its income while investment remains unchanged, incomes must fall until saving out of the reduced income again equals the unchanged investment. The additional thrift is not realised; it is defeated by the fall in income. The same arithmetic runs in reverse for an increase in expenditure: a given increase in investment or in public outlay raises income by a multiple, and the resulting increase in saving out of the larger income is what finances the additional investment ex post. Saving is thus the child of investment, not its parent, in the short period; the classical sequence, in which saving precedes and finances investment, holds only in a condition where saving decisions and investment decisions are coordinated through the rate of interest at full employment.

That condition is exactly what fails in a slump. The rate of interest is not a market-clearing price that equates the supply of saving with the demand for investment at full employment; it is a monetary phenomenon, governed by liquidity preference and the quantity of money. When expectations are depressed, the desire to hold cash rises, and the rate of interest may be pushed to a level at which no worthwhile investment project is undertaken, or it may refuse to fall further because lenders will not part with cash except at a premium. In such circumstances the offer of additional saving does not call forth additional investment; it merely adds to the pool of idle funds and to the pressure on incomes. The idle equipment and unemployed labour are the visible evidence that the community's desire to save exceeds the inducement to invest. To urge more thrift in these conditions is to prescribe a remedy that aggravates the disease.

It is necessary, however, to distinguish the general proposition from the particular circumstances in which it holds. The proposition that saving is harmful is not a universal truth; it is a proposition about an economy operating below capacity, with rigid or sticky money wages, depressed expectations, and a deficiency of effective demand. Where resources are fully employed, an increase in saving may indeed release resources for investment, and thrift may be a virtue both private and public. The difference is not a matter of taste but of the state of the system: the same act has opposite effects according to whether the economy is at or below its productive frontier. A sound doctrine must therefore be stated conditionally, and the practical question is always: which case are we in? To mistake the underemployment case for the full-employment case is the characteristic error of orthodox finance, and it is an error with grave consequences, because it recommends contraction at the very moment when expansion is required.

Consider a concrete illustration. Suppose a community with unemployed labour and idle plant decides, on grounds of prudence, to increase its saving by a tenth of its income. If investment is unchanged, the multiplier ensures that incomes fall, employment falls further, and the intended saving is largely or wholly offset by the decline in income. The community is poorer, not richer; its capital equipment rusts, and its unemployed workers lose skills. Suppose instead that the same community directs a portion of its resources to public works—roads, housing, electrification—financed by borrowing. The expenditure creates incomes directly, and the recipients spend a fraction of those incomes on consumption, creating further incomes, and so on. The public outlay need not be "paid for" by prior saving; it creates the saving that finances it, through the increase in incomes and the consequent increase in the flow of saving out of those incomes. The borrowing is a transfer of claims, not a subtraction from a fixed fund. The true cost of the public works is the alternative use of the idle resources, and if those resources would otherwise have remained idle, the cost is small and the gain is the stream of useful output and the restoration of the community's productive capacity.

This comparison of private and public action must be made with care, for it is not a general licence for any public expenditure. Public action is superior in the underemployment case for three reasons: it can be undertaken on a scale and at a speed that private decisions cannot match when expectations are depressed; it can be directed to projects whose social return exceeds their private return, and which therefore would not be undertaken by private investors; and it can be financed in a way that does not depend on the prior accumulation of saving, which is precisely what is deficient. But public action is subject to its own conditions. It must be genuinely additional to private expenditure, not a substitute for it; it must be directed to useful projects, not to waste; and it must be withdrawn or moderated as full employment is approached, lest it generate inflationary pressure. The case for public works is a case for filling a gap in effective demand, not a case for the permanent substitution of public for private decision. Moreover, public action that is poorly designed, or that undermines confidence, or that is financed in a manner that raises the rate of interest and crowds out private investment, may fail to produce the intended effect. The argument is therefore conditional on the quality and the financing of the public programme, as well as on the state of employment.

There are other explanations of the slump that must be weighed, and the argument I have given is not the only possible one. One rival explanation attributes prolonged unemployment to rigid wages and to the resistance of labour to reductions in money wages; on this view the remedy is to make wages flexible, and the deficiency of demand is a symptom rather than a cause. Another explanation emphasises the disorganisation of the credit system and the failure of the banking mechanism to channel saving into investment; on this view the remedy is monetary reform rather than fiscal expansion. A third emphasises structural maladjustment—the decay of particular industries and the immobility of labour—and holds that general expansion would merely inflate prices without restoring employment in the affected trades. These explanations are not to be dismissed; each identifies a real obstacle, and in particular circumstances any of them may be dominant. But they do not overturn the central proposition, which is that when the desire to save exceeds the inducement to invest, the level of income and employment must fall until the two are brought into equality, and that in such a condition thrift is a public vice even though it remains a private prudence. The rival explanations describe the obstacles to recovery; they do not remove the need for an increase in effective demand, whether through private investment or public outlay, as the means of setting idle resources to work.

It is also necessary to distinguish the short period from the long. In the short period, the level of employment is determined by effective demand, and saving is a leakage that reduces it unless offset by investment. In the long period, the accumulation of capital depends on saving, and a community that consumes all its income will not grow rich. The reconciliation is that the long-period growth of capital requires that saving be matched by investment, and that in the short period the task of policy is to ensure that the inducement to invest is sufficient to absorb the community's desire to save at full employment. The error is to apply the long-period maxim to the short-period problem: to preach thrift in a slump is to confuse the conditions of growth with the conditions of recovery. A community that saves more than it invests will not grow; it will stagnate, because its saving is idle and its resources are unemployed. The virtue of thrift is conditional on the existence of an investment outlet, and the provision of that outlet is the proper object of public policy.

The practical conclusion, then, is not that saving is always harmful or that public expenditure is always beneficial. It is that the relation between saving, consumption, and recovery depends on the level of employment and on the state of expectations, and that the appropriate policy differs accordingly. In the underemployment case, the community should be encouraged to consume and the public authority should be prepared to spend, borrowing if necessary, until idle resources are re-employed; the objection that this involves debt is beside the point, since the debt is a transfer and the alternative is the waste of idle capacity. In the full-employment case, thrift resumes its classical role, and the task of policy is to ensure that saving is channelled into productive investment and that public expenditure does not outrun the available resources. The general conclusion is that saving and spending are not virtues or vices in themselves but functions of the state of the system; the specific conclusion is that in a slump the bias of policy should be toward expenditure, and that private thrift, however admirable in motive, must be offset by public action if the community is not to be made poorer by the sum of its prudent decisions. To recognise this is not to abandon sound finance but to understand that sound finance is a means to the employment of resources, not an end in itself; and that the first duty of the public authority in a slump is to restore the conditions in which private virtue and public benefit coincide.
