The modern university is conventionally spoken of as a single institution with a single function, and its friends and its critics alike proceed on that assumption. It is more serviceable to regard it as a concatenation of historically distinct enterprises that have been lodged, for reasons of convenience and prestige, under one roof and one charter. The oldest of these is the community of scholars devoted to the pursuit of learning for its own sake; the next in order of dignity, though not always in order of revenue, is the professional school; and the youngest and most numerous is the undergraduate college. These three do not share a common purpose, and their union is a matter of institutional convenience rather than of logical coherence. The strains that are commonly reported as "crises" in higher education are in the main the frictions incident to this forced cohabitation.

The historical formation of the university is instructive here. The medieval studium generale was not a teaching establishment in the modern sense but a guild of masters and scholars, organized for the certification of competence in the learned professions—theology, law, and medicine—and for the maintenance of a body of doctrine. Its charter was a privilege, its product a licensed practitioner, and its economy was one of fees, benefices, and, in time, endowment. The research function, in the sense of the systematic extension of knowledge by salaried investigators, is a late accretion, dating in its modern form from the nineteenth century and from the German example; the undergraduate college, in the sense of a general residential education for the sons of the prosperous, is later still in its full development, and is in some measure a by-product of the leisure and the pecuniary standards of the propertied classes. What we now call "the university" is therefore a composite of a guild of certified practitioners, a research institute, and a finishing school, each with its own lineage and its own criteria of success.

The pecuniary logic of the composite deserves attention, since it governs the relations among the parts more than the official pronouncements would suggest. Research is the most prestigious of the three activities, and prestige in this connection is convertible into endowment, into the goodwill of foundations and legislatures, and into the marketability of the institution's degrees. It is therefore rational, from the standpoint of the administrator, to subsidize research out of the revenues drawn from undergraduate instruction, and to justify the subsidy by the claim that instruction is improved by contact with investigators. This claim is not without foundation, but its foundation is narrower than the claim implies: the contact is effective chiefly for the small minority of students who are themselves candidates for the scholarly life, and for the remainder it is largely ceremonial. The undergraduate pays for the privilege of being present at an enterprise in which he has no productive part, and the prestige he purchases is the prestige of the enterprise, not of his own instruction. This is not a scandal; it is the ordinary working of a system in which repute is the chief article of sale.

The professional schools occupy an intermediate position and exhibit the tension most clearly. Their function is the certification of competence for practice, and their standards are set in some part by the practitioners themselves, organized in guilds of their own. The professional faculty is therefore under a double allegiance: to the discipline as a body of knowledge, and to the profession as a market. Where the two coincide, as in the more exacting branches of medicine and engineering, the arrangement works with tolerable smoothness. Where they diverge—as in schools of business, of journalism, of education, and of the various "service" professions—the school tends to become a purveyor of vocational technique and of the social connections that facilitate pecuniary success, and its claim to scholarly standing becomes increasingly a matter of nomenclature. The business school in particular is an instructive case: it is, in its origins, a school of accountancy and of commercial practice, and its later aspiration to the dignity of a "graduate school of administration" has been achieved chiefly by the importation of economic and statistical apparatus, not by any substantial addition to the discipline it professes. Its product is a certified man of affairs, and the certificate is its chief commodity.

The undergraduate college, again, has a function that is seldom stated in the official literature, and that function is best understood in terms of the pecuniary standards of the class it serves. It is, in its historic form, a place of residence and of general discipline, in which the young of the leisure class are initiated into the manners, the tastes, and the connections of their station. Its curriculum is accordingly a matter of less consequence than its social atmosphere; the Latin and the mathematics of the older scheme, and the "distribution requirements" and "areas of knowledge" of the newer, are in the main ceremonial observances, whose function is to mark the initiate as a person of cultivated leisure rather than to equip him for any productive employment. This is not to say that the instruction is worthless; it is to say that its worth is chiefly in the certification of a certain social standing, and that the demand for it is a demand for status rather than for knowledge. The growth of the undergraduate college, and the readiness of the prosperous to pay for its advantages, are to be explained on this footing rather than on the footing of any demonstrable addition to the student's industrial efficiency.

The relations among the three parts may now be stated in a general way. The research function supplies prestige; the professional schools supply revenue and social connection; the undergraduate college supplies numbers and the fees that accompany them. The prestige of research attracts endowment and able men; the able men lend distinction to the professional schools; the professional schools and the college together furnish the income by which the research is maintained. The system is stable so long as the prestige of research remains convertible, and so long as the demand for certification remains brisk. Its instabilities are of two sorts: a decline in the market value of the scholarly repute, or a decline in the willingness of the prosperous to pay for the ceremonial certification of their young. Both have occurred in the past, and both are capable of occurring again. The recent expansion of the undergraduate college, and the recent anxiety of the professional schools to acquire the trappings of research, are alike symptoms of a competitive struggle for prestige in which each part seeks to borrow the standing of the others.

It is necessary to distinguish the general conclusion from the particular circumstance. The general conclusion is that the university is a composite of incompatible enterprises, held together by a pecuniary logic that converts prestige into revenue and revenue into prestige, and that its internal arrangements are to be understood as the outcome of that logic rather than of any single educational purpose. The particular circumstance is that the balance among the parts varies with the legal and pecuniary constitution of the several national systems. In the German system, the research institute and the state bureaucracy dominate, and the undergraduate college in the English sense is wanting; in the English system, the residential college and the tutorial relation have historically dominated, and research has been a late and somewhat exotic import; in the American system, all three parts are present in a single corporation, and the competition among them is correspondingly acute. The American case is therefore the most instructive for the student of the composite, but its lessons are not to be transferred without allowance for the differing constitutions of the others.

An alternative explanation deserves notice, if only to be set aside. It is sometimes said that the university is a community of scholars and students united by a common love of learning, and that its organizational arrangements are mere machinery for the pursuit of that love. This explanation has the merit of describing the official ideal, and it is not wholly without foundation in the case of the older and smaller foundations. But it fails to account for the observable facts: for the subordination of instruction to research in the allocation of rewards, for the growth of vocational schools whose connection with learning is tenuous, for the ceremonial character of much of the undergraduate curriculum, and for the readiness of donors to endow buildings rather than investigators. An explanation that accounts for the ideal but not for the practice is, in the nature of the case, an incomplete explanation; and the pecuniary explanation here offered accounts for both, since the ideal itself is one of the assets by which the prestige of the enterprise is maintained.

The bearing of this analysis on the question of educational policy is indirect but not negligible. Proposals to "integrate" teaching and research, or to "restore" the primacy of undergraduate instruction, proceed on the assumption that the parts of the university are capable of being subordinated to a single purpose. If the analysis here given is sound, such proposals are likely to succeed only in so far as they alter the pecuniary logic that governs the relations among the parts; and since that logic is bound up with the whole scheme of pecuniary emulation in the society at large, the prospects of any substantial alteration are modest. The more feasible course is to recognize the composite character of the institution, to allocate its costs and its rewards with an eye to the actual functions performed rather than to the official ideal, and to cease to expect from a single corporation the coherence of purpose that belongs only to a single enterprise. Whether such a recognition is practicable in a society that values the certification of status as highly as it does, is a question on which the present inquiry does not undertake to pronounce. It is enough to have shown that the question is one of institutional economics rather than of educational theory, and that the answer depends on conditions that lie outside the university itself.

author: Edgar Norwick
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，比较勇武功绩与财富占有作为社会声望来源的作用，分析相对地位比较如何影响财富追求。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
Prowess and exploit may still remain the basis of award of the highest popular esteem, although the possession of wealth has become the basis of common place reputability and of a blameless social standing. The predatory instinct and the consequent approbation of predatory efficiency are deeply ingrained in the habits of thought of those peoples who have passed under the discipline of a protracted predatory culture. According to popular award, the highest honours within human reach may, even yet, be those gained by an unfolding of extraordinary predatory efficiency in war, or by a quasi-predatory efficiency in statecraft; but for the purposes of a commonplace decent standing in the community these means of repute have been replaced by the acquisition and accumulation of goods. In order to stand well in the eyes of the community, it is necessary to come up to a certain, somewhat indefinite, conventional standard of wealth; just as in the earlier predatory stage it is necessary for the barbarian man to come up to the tribe's standard of physical endurance, cunning, and skill at arms. A certain standard of wealth in the one case, and of prowess in the other, is a necessary condition of reputability, and anything in excess of this normal amount is meritorious.

Those members of the community who fall short of this, somewhat indefinite, normal degree of prowess or of property suffer in the esteem of their fellow-men; and consequently they suffer also in their own esteem, since the usual basis of self-respect is the respect accorded by one's neighbours. Only individuals with an aberrant temperament can in the long run retain their self-esteem in the face of the disesteem of their fellows. Apparent exceptions to the rule are met with, especially among people with strong religious convictions. But these apparent exceptions are scarcely real exceptions, since such persons commonly fall back on the putative approbation of some supernatural witness of their deeds.

So soon as the possession of property becomes the basis of popular esteem, therefore, it becomes also a requisite to the complacency which we call self-respect. In any community where goods are held in severalty it is necessary, in order to his own peace of mind, that an individual should possess as large a portion of goods as others with whom he is accustomed to class himself; and it is extremely gratifying to possess something more than others. But as fast as a person makes new acquisitions, and becomes accustomed to the resulting new standard of wealth, the new standard forthwith ceases to afford appreciably greater satisfaction than the earlier standard did. The tendency in any case is constantly to make the present pecuniary standard the point of departure for a fresh increase of wealth; and this in turn gives rise to a new standard of sufficiency and a new pecuniary classification of one's self as compared with one's neighbours. So far as concerns the present question, the end sought by accumulation is to rank high in comparison with the rest of the community in point of pecuniary strength. So long as the comparison is distinctly unfavourable to himself, the normal, average individual will live in chronic dissatisfaction with his present lot; and when he has reached what may be called the normal pecuniary standard of the community, or of his class in the community, this chronic dissatisfaction will give place to a restless straining to place a wider and ever-widening pecuniary interval between himself and this average standard. The invidious comparison can never become so favourable to the individual making it that he would not gladly rate himself still higher relatively to his competitors in the struggle for pecuniary reputability.

In the nature of the case, the desire for wealth can scarcely be satiated in any individual instance, and evidently a satiation of the average or general desire for wealth is out of the question. However widely, or equally, or "fairly", it may be distributed, no general increase of the community's wealth can make any approach to satiating this need, the ground of which is the desire of every one to excel every one else in the accumulation of goods. If, as is sometimes assumed, the incentive to accumulation were the want of subsistence or of physical comfort, then the aggregate economic wants of a community might conceivably be satisfied at some point in the advance of industrial efficiency; but since the struggle is substantially a race for reputability on the basis of an invidious comparison, no approach to a definitive attainment is possible.

What has just been said must not be taken to mean that there are no other incentives to acquisition and accumulation than this desire to excel in pecuniary standing and so gain the esteem and envy of one's fellow-men. The desire for added comfort and security from want is present as a motive at every stage of the process of accumulation in a modern industrial community; although the standard of sufficiency in these respects is in turn greatly affected by the habit of pecuniary emulation. To a great extent this emulation shapes the methods and selects the objects of expenditure for personal comfort and decent livelihood.

Besides this, the power conferred by wealth also affords a motive to accumulation. That propensity for purposeful activity and that repugnance to all futility of effort which belong to man by virtue of his character as an agent do not desert him when he emerges from the naive communal culture where the dominant note of life is the unanalysed and undifferentiated solidarity of the individual with the group with which his life is bound up. When he enters upon the predatory stage, where self-seeking in the narrower sense becomes the dominant note, this propensity goes with him still, as the pervasive trait that shapes his scheme of life. The propensity for achievement and the repugnance to futility remain the underlying economic motive. The propensity changes only in the form of its expression and in the proximate objects to which it directs the man's activity. Under the regime of individual ownership the most available means of visibly achieving a purpose is that afforded by the acquisition and accumulation of goods; and as the self-regarding antithesis between man and man reaches fuller consciousness, the propensity for achievement--the instinct of workmanship--tends more and more to shape itself into a straining to excel others in pecuniary achievement. Relative success, tested by an invidious pecuniary comparison with other men, becomes the conventional end of action. The currently accepted legitimate end of effort becomes the achievement of a favourable comparison with other men; and therefore the repugnance to futility to a good extent coalesces with the incentive of emulation. It acts to accentuate the struggle for pecuniary reputability by visiting with a sharper disapproval all shortcoming and all evidence of shortcoming in point of pecuniary success. Purposeful effort comes to mean, primarily, effort directed to or resulting in a more creditable showing of accumulated wealth. Among the motives which lead men to accumulate wealth, the primacy, both in scope and intensity, therefore, continues to belong to this motive of pecuniary emulation.

In making use of the term "invidious", it may perhaps be unnecessary to remark, there is no intention to extol or depreciate, or to commend or deplore any of the phenomena which the word is used to characterise. The term is used in a technical sense as describing a comparison of persons with a view to rating and grading them in respect of relative worth or value--in an aesthetic or moral sense--and so awarding and defining the relative degrees of complacency with which they may legitimately be contemplated by themselves and by others. An invidious comparison is a process of valuation of persons in respect of worth.
b:
The transition from a predatory culture to an industrial one is not merely a shift in the technology of production, but a fundamental reorientation of the psychological habits of men and the criteria by which they assess their own worth in the eyes of their fellows. In the earlier stages of social development, where the community was organized around the principle of force, the accumulation of honor was inextricably linked to the prowess of the individual in the field of battle or the hunt. The warrior and the hunter were the apex of the social hierarchy, not because they contributed to the sustenance of the group in any productive sense, but because they demonstrated an exemption from the drudgery of useful labor and a capacity for destruction that commanded awe. This status was derived from the visible evidence of strength and the ability to impose one’s will upon others. However, as the community advances toward a more settled, industrial order, the locus of prestige undergoes a subtle but profound migration. The valor of the sword is gradually supplanted by the valor of the purse. Wealth, rather than martial prowess, becomes the primary index of success, and the possession of goods becomes the definitive proof of one’s fitness to lead and to be revered.

This substitution is not arbitrary, nor is it a simple evolution of taste. It is rooted in the persistent human propensity for invidious comparison, that restless, restless instinct to measure one’s own standing against the standing of others. In the predatory phase, this comparison was conducted through the lens of physical dominance and the capacity for violence. The man who could kill more enemies or capture more captives was the man who stood higher in the estimation of his peers. As the struggle for existence shifts from physical combat to economic competition, the arena of comparison changes. The man who can acquire more wealth than his neighbor is now the one who demonstrates superior ability, superior cunning, and superior fitness. The wealth itself is not valued primarily for the physical comfort it affords, but for the relative advantage it confers in the social hierarchy. It is a badge of exemption from the common lot, a proof that one has succeeded in the struggle where others have failed.

Consider the case of the modern industrial magnate. His status is not derived from the utility he provides to the community through the efficient management of production, though he may claim such merit. Rather, his prestige is a function of the magnitude of his fortune relative to the fortunes of those around him. If his wealth were equal to that of his neighbors, the psychological satisfaction derived from it would vanish, for there would be no basis for invidious comparison. The drive to accumulate is therefore a drive to outstrip, to place oneself in a position of superiority that is visible and undeniable. This is the mechanism of conspicuous waste. The spending of wealth on non-productive ends—on lavish dwellings, on idle servants, on elaborate ceremonies—is not an irrational excess, but a calculated display of financial strength. It is a declaration that one has resources sufficient to afford the waste of resources without detriment to one’s standing. In this way, wealth serves the same social function that the trophies of war once served: it is evidence of power and of the ability to live without the necessity of labor.

However, one must distinguish between the general tendency of this development and the specific conditions under which it operates. In a society where the distribution of wealth is relatively stable and where the channels of social mobility are narrow, the reliance on wealth as a source of prestige is most intense. The established wealthy class uses its possessions to reinforce its status, while the aspiring class seeks to mimic these displays in order to gain admission to the higher circles. This creates a continuous cycle of emulation, where the definition of what constitutes sufficient wealth is constantly raised. The standard of living is not determined by physiological needs, but by the needs of the social comparison. What was once considered luxury becomes the baseline of respectability, and the pressure to accumulate intensifies as the baseline rises.

Yet, this analysis relies on the assumption that the industrial community has not yet fully developed the habits of the worker. In a truly industrial society, one might expect that prestige would be derived from skill, from the mastery of technical processes, and from the contribution to the common welfare. There are signs, though faint, that such a shift is possible. In certain technical professions, the recognition of expertise can confer a status that is independent of mere wealth. The engineer who solves a complex problem, or the scientist who discovers a new principle, may command respect that is not solely based on their financial success. However, these exceptions are often absorbed back into the pecuniary logic. The value of the scientist’s work is often measured by the grants they secure or the patents they hold, reducing their intellectual contribution to its monetary equivalent. Thus, the predatory habit of mind persists, even within the industrial sphere, corrupting the potential for a new, productive basis for prestige.

Furthermore, the role of relative status in driving wealth accumulation is contingent upon the visibility of that wealth. If wealth were hidden, its power to confer prestige would be diminished. This is why the forms of conspicuous consumption evolve to ensure visibility. In the early stages of the pecuniary culture, this visibility was achieved through the personal display of the owner—his clothing, his retinue, his feasts. As society becomes more complex and the distances between individuals increase, the visibility is maintained through institutional markers: the type of house one lives in, the neighborhood one occupies, the schools one’s children attend. These markers serve as signals of status that are legible to the community, allowing for the continuous process of comparison. The anxiety of the individual is thus not merely a fear of poverty, but a fear of invisibility, of being unrecognized, of falling below the threshold of notice.

It is also necessary to consider the alternative explanation that wealth accumulation is driven primarily by the desire for security and the fear of want. While this factor is undoubtedly present, it cannot account for the extent of the accumulation observed in advanced communities. The wealthy do not stop accumulating when their physical needs are met; they stop only when they have reached a point of relative saturation or when the effort of accumulation ceases to yield additional social returns. The security sought is not merely material, but social. The fear is of losing one’s place, of being displaced by those who have accumulated more. This fear is irrational from the standpoint of pure utility, but it is rational within the framework of a society organized around invidious comparison. The individual is trapped in a race where the finish line is constantly moving, and where the only way to win is to run faster than everyone else.

In conclusion, the shift from martial prowess to wealth possession as the primary source of social prestige is a manifestation of the enduring predatory instinct in a changed environment. The need to assert superiority and to distinguish oneself from the common herd remains constant, but the means of assertion have changed. Wealth has become the modern trophy, the proof of victory in the economic struggle. This transformation is driven by the relentless logic of relative status, where absolute gain is meaningless without relative advantage. While there are emerging forms of prestige based on productive contribution, they are largely overshadowed by the pecuniary standard. The result is a society in which the pursuit of wealth is not merely an economic activity, but a moral and social imperative, a necessary condition for self-respect and social recognition. To understand the modern man’s obsession with accumulation, one must look beyond the ledger and into the mirror of society, where his worth is reflected not in what he has made, but in what he has outdone.

author: Edgar Norwick
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，分析大型企业采用效率管理的条件，讨论商业收益、生产效率和社会技术利益之间的协调问题。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The businessmen in control of large industrial enterprises are beginning to appreciate something of their own unfitness to direct or oversee, or even to control, technological matters, and so they have, in a tentative way, taken to employing experts to do the work for them. Such experts are known colloquially as “efficiency engineers” and are presumed to combine the qualifications of technologist and accountant. In point of fact it is as accountants, capable of applying the tests of accountancy in a new field, that these experts commend themselves to the businessmen in control, and the “efficiency” which they look to is an efficiency counted in terms of net pecuniary gain. “Efficiency” in these premises means pecuniary efficiency, and only incidentally or in a subsidiary sense does it mean industrial efficiency,--only in so far as industrial efficiency conduces to the largest net pecuniary gain. All the while the businessmen retain the decisive superior discretion in their own incompetent hands, since all the while the whole matter remains a business proposition. The “staff organisation,” in which vests the superior control of these technological affairs, consistently remains an organisation of worldly wisdom, business enterprise--not of technological proficiency,--a state of things not to be remedied so long as industry is carried on for business profits.

Meantime the workmen of all kinds and grades--labourers, mechanics, operatives, engineers, experts--all imbued with the same pecuniary principles of efficiency, go about their work with more than half an eye to the pecuniary advantage of what they have in hand. The attitude of the trades-unions towards their work and towards the industrial concerns in whose employ their work is done illustrates something of the habitual frame of mind of these men, who are avowed experts in the matter of workmanship.

Latterly many inconveniences have beset the community at large as well as particular sections and classes of the industrial community, due in the main to a consistent adherence to these business principles in the management of industrial affairs. The capitalist-employers, on the one hand, have gone on the full powers with which the modern institution of ownership and its broad implications has vested them; with the result that the public at large, investors, consumers of industrial products, users of “public utility” agencies serving such needs as light, fuel, transportation, communication, amusement, etc., feel very much aggrieved; as do also and more particularly the workmen with whom the capitalist-employers do business on the lines laid down by the authentic business principles involved in the discretionary ownership of the industrial plant and resources. On the other hand the workmen, resting their case on the same common-sense view that the individual is a self-sufficient economic unit who owes nothing to the community at large beyond what he may freely undertake “for a good and valuable consideration in hand paid,”--the workmen stand likewise on the full powers given them by the current institutions of ownership and contractual discretion, and so work what mischief they can to their employers and to the public at large, always blamelessly within the rules of the game as laid down of old on the pecuniary principles of business discretion, and in the light of such sense as their training has given them with regard to efficiency in the industries that have fallen into their hands. And then the “money power” comes in as a third pecuniarily trained factor, with ever increasing force and incisiveness, to muddle the whole situation mysteriously and irretrievably by looking after their own pecuniary interests in a fashion even more soberly legitimate and authentic, if possible, than the workmen’s management of their own affairs.

Of course, all this working at cross purposes is not altogether due to trained incapacity on the part of the several contestants to appreciate the large and general requirements of the industrial situation; perhaps it is not even chiefly due to such inability, but rather to an habitual, and conventionally rightful, disregard of other than pecuniary considerations. It would doubtless appear that a trained inability to apprehend any other than the immediate pecuniary bearing of their manœuvres accounts for a larger share in the conduct of the businessmen who control industrial affairs than it does in that of their workmen, since the habitual employment of the former holds them more rigorously and consistently to the pecuniary valuation of whatever passes under their hands; and the like should be true only in a higher degree of those who have to do exclusively with the financial side of business. The state of the industrial arts requires that these several factors should coöperate intelligently and without reservation, with an eye single to the exigencies of this modern wide-sweeping technological system; but their habitual addiction to pecuniary rather than technological standards and considerations leaves them working at cross purposes. So also their (pecuniary) interests are at cross purposes; and since these interests necessarily rule in any pecuniary culture, they must decide the line of conduct for each of the several factors engaged.

These discrepancies, obstructive tactics and disserviceable practices are commonly deplored and are presumably deplorable, and they doubtless merit extensive discussion on these grounds, but their merits in this bearing do not properly come into consideration here. The matter has been brought in here not with any view of defence, denunciation or remedy, but because it is a matter of grave consequence as regards the training given by business experience to these men in whose hands the current scheme of institutions has placed the technological fortunes of the community. And whether these pecuniary tactics and practices that fill so large a place in the attention and sentiments of this generation come chiefly of a lack of insight into current technological exigencies, or of a deliberate choice of evils enforced by the pecuniary necessities of the case, still their disciplinary value as bearing on the sense of workmanship taken in its larger scope will be much the same in either case. Habituation to bargaining and to the competitive principles of business necessarily brings it about that pecuniary standards of efficiency invade (contaminate) the sense of workmanship; so that work, workmen, equipment and products come to be rated on a scale of money values, which has only a circuitous and often only a putative relation to their workmanlike efficiency or their serviceability. Those occupations and those aptitudes that yield good returns in terms of price are reputed valuable and commendable,--the accepted test of success, and even of serviceability, being the gains acquired. Workmanship comes to be confused with salesmanship, until tact, effrontery and prevarication have come to serve as a standard of efficiency, and unearned gain is accepted as the measure of productiveness.

Efficiency conduces to the common good, and is also a meritorious and commendable trait in the person who exercises it. But under the canons of self-help and pecuniary valuation the test of efficiency in economic matters has come to be, not technological mastery and productive effect, but proficiency in pecuniary management and the acquisition of wealth. Both in his own estimation and in the eyes of his fellows, the man who gains much does well; he is conceived to do well both as a matter of personal efficiency and in point of serviceability to the common good. To “do well” in modern phrase means to engross something appreciably more of the community’s wealth than falls to the common run. But since gains, and hence efficiency, are conceived in terms of price, it follows that the man, workman or businessman, who can induce his fellows to pay him well for his services or his goods is accounted efficient and serviceable; from which it follows that under this canon of pecuniary efficiency men are conceived to serve the common good somewhat in proportion as they are able to induce the community to pay more for their services than they are worth.

The businessman who gains much at little cost, who gets something for nothing, is rated, in his own as well as in his neighbours’ esteem, as a public benefactor indispensable to the community’s welfare, and as contributing to the common good in direct proportion to the amount which he has been able to draw out of the aggregate product. It is perhaps needless to call to mind that of this character are the main facts in the history of all the great fortunes; although the current accounts of their accumulation, being governed by pecuniary standards of efficiency and serviceability, dwell mainly on the services that have inured to the community from the traffic with which the great captains have interfered in their quest of gain. The prevalence of salesmanship, that is to say of business enterprise, and the consequent high repute of the salesmanlike activities and aptitudes in any community that is organised on a price system, is perhaps the most serious obstacle which the pecuniary culture opposes to the advance in workmanship. It intrudes into the most intimate and secret workings of the human spirit and contaminates the sense of workmanship in its initial move, and sets both the proclivity to efficient work and the penchant for serviceability at cross purposes with the common good.
b:
The question of efficiency management in the large enterprise is, properly understood, not a question of engineering but a question of the terms on which the industrial process is carried on. The machinery of systematic management—time study, standardization, cost accounting, the functional organization of the works—is in itself a body of technological expedients, and its bearing on output is a matter of the physical facts of the case. But its adoption by any given enterprise is governed by the pecuniary considerations that control the conduct of business, and these considerations are not identical with the technological ones, nor do they run parallel with them except under conditions that require to be specified. To speak of the "adoption" of efficiency management is therefore to speak of a bargain rather than of an engineering decision, and the analysis must proceed on that footing.

In the first place, the large enterprise is a going concern with an established capital account, and the introduction of a more exacting regimen of work and accounting is itself a pecuniary outlay that must be justified by the pecuniary return. The installation of the apparatus—the planning department, the routing of work, the records, the supervisory staff—entails a fixed charge, and this charge is not proportioned to the technical excellence of the methods but to their cost. Where the scale of operations is large, this fixed charge is spread thin and the inducement is correspondingly strong; where the scale is small, the same methods may be technically available and pecuniarily inadmissible. This is the first condition, and it is a condition of magnitude rather than of merit: the large enterprise can afford the apparatus of efficiency because it can afford many things that the small enterprise cannot, and the economy of the large scale is in this respect an economy of overhead rather than an economy of workmanship.

But magnitude alone is not sufficient. The second condition is the character of the output and of the market in which it is sold. Efficiency management, in its stricter forms, requires a standardized product and a steady, calculable demand, because its economies are economies of repetition and of the elimination of waste in the interstices of the process. Where the product is made to the order of the customer, in small lots and in shifting patterns, the apparatus of standardization is defeated by the variety of the work; where the demand is capricious, the enterprise that gears its plant to a precise and exacting routine carries a heavier burden of idle equipment in slack seasons than the enterprise that keeps its organization loose. The large enterprise in a stable and standardized line of production is therefore the favorable case; the large enterprise in a fashion trade or in a trade subject to sharp fluctuations is a less favorable case, and the difference is not a difference of managerial ability but of the pecuniary exigencies of the market. Here the general conclusion must be qualified by the particular circumstances, and the qualification is not a counsel of perfection but a statement of the conditions under which the general conclusion holds.

A third condition is the state of the labor supply and the terms on which labor is engaged. The efficiency of a given regimen of work is measured by output per unit of cost, and cost includes wages; but the wage is not a simple quantity. Where labor is scarce and the bargaining position of the workmen is strong, the enterprise may find it advantageous to substitute machinery and method for labor, and the introduction of efficiency management is then a phase of the general substitution of capital for labor. Where labor is abundant and cheap, the same methods may yield a smaller pecuniary return, since the saving in wages is less and the fixed charge of the apparatus is the same. This is a commonplace of the business man's reckoning, and it goes to show that the "efficiency" of a method is not a single fact but a ratio whose terms are pecuniary and whose value shifts with the market for labor. The technological gain in output per man-hour may be large and yet the pecuniary gain to the enterprise small, if the wage is low and the apparatus costly; and conversely, a modest technological gain may be highly profitable where wages are high. The two measures of efficiency—the technological and the pecuniary—are not the same measure, and their divergence is the crux of the matter.

It is at this point that the question of the coordination of business gain, industrial productivity, and the technological interest of the community becomes acute. The business man's interest is in the net pecuniary return, and this return is not maximized by the maximum output. It is maximized by the output that yields the largest margin between cost and price, and this output may be less than the plant is capable of producing. The large enterprise that has installed an exacting regimen of efficiency may therefore find it to its advantage to restrict the output, to withhold the full use of its equipment, or to divert its methods to the production of goods that yield a higher margin rather than a larger volume. This is not a matter of the personal turpitude of the managers; it is the logic of the business enterprise, which is a pecuniary institution and not an industrial one. The technological interest of the community is in the largest and cheapest output of the goods that serve human use; the business interest is in the largest net return; and where the two do not coincide, the business interest governs the conduct of the enterprise. The coordination of the two is therefore not automatic, and the conditions under which it occurs require to be stated with some care.

The conditions are, in the main, two. The first is the state of the industrial arts—the body of technological knowledge and equipment available to the community. Where the arts are advancing rapidly, the enterprise that adheres to an exacting regimen of efficiency is under a constant necessity of revising its methods, and the pecuniary advantage of the regimen is offset by the cost of obsolescence. The enterprise that keeps its organization loose and its equipment adaptable may fare better in a period of rapid change than the enterprise that has geared itself to a precise routine. This is the reason why the most highly systematized establishments are commonly found in industries where the arts are relatively stable, and why the industries of rapid change—the electrical, the chemical, the automotive—have developed forms of organization that are less rigid and more adaptable than the classical efficiency management of the machine shop. The general conclusion, then, that efficiency management is advantageous to the large enterprise must be qualified by the state of the arts: it holds most strongly where the arts are stable, and it holds less strongly, or not at all, where the arts are in flux.

The second condition is the state of the market for the product, and here the matter is one of the elasticity of demand and of the competitive situation. Where the demand is elastic, a reduction in cost may be passed on in a reduction of price and may be followed by an expansion of sales; in that case the pecuniary interest of the enterprise and the technological interest of the community may run together, since the enterprise gains by the expansion and the community gains by the cheaper goods. Where the demand is inelastic, the reduction in cost is more likely to be retained as a larger margin, and the community gains little or nothing in the way of cheaper goods; the gain is a gain of the enterprise, and the technological improvement is, from the community's standpoint, sterilized. The efficiency management of the large enterprise is therefore not a single phenomenon with a single effect; its effect on the community depends on the market in which the enterprise sells, and this is a circumstance that the business man does not control and that the community does not ordinarily take into account.

There is a further consideration that bears on the coordination of the three interests, and it is the consideration of the "conscientious" use of the apparatus. The methods of efficiency management are, in their technological character, capable of being applied with more or less thoroughness, and the degree of thoroughness is a matter of pecuniary calculation. The enterprise may install the apparatus and use it to the full, or it may install it and use it only so far as the pecuniary return requires; and the difference between the two is the difference between an industrial gain and a pecuniary one. The business man's reckoning is with the margin, not with the output, and the margin may be served by a partial use of the apparatus as well as by a full one. This is the point at which the technological interest of the community is most directly at odds with the business interest, and it is the point at which the "efficiency" of the enterprise is least to be trusted as a measure of its service to the community.

It is necessary, in conclusion, to distinguish between the general and the particular. The general conclusion is that the large enterprise is the favorable case for efficiency management, because it can afford the apparatus, because it can standardize its output, and because it can command the market and the labor supply on terms that make the pecuniary return calculable. But this general conclusion is subject to the particular conditions that have been stated: the stability of the arts, the elasticity of demand, the state of the labor market, and the degree of thoroughness with which the apparatus is used. Where these conditions are favorable, the business gain, the industrial productivity, and the technological interest of the community may run together, and the efficiency management of the large enterprise may be, in the phrase of the day, a public benefit as well as a private one. Where they are unfavorable, the business gain may be secured at the expense of the industrial productivity and of the community's interest, and the efficiency management may be a means of restricting output rather than of increasing it. The distinction is not a distinction between good men and bad men, but between the exigencies of the pecuniary institution and the exigencies of the industrial process; and the student of the matter will do well to keep the two apart, and to state the conditions under which the one serves the other, rather than to assume that the identity of the two is a fact of nature.

The alternative explanations of the observed facts are, in the main, two, and they should be noticed. The first is the explanation in terms of managerial capacity: the differences in the adoption and success of efficiency management are ascribed to the greater or less ability of the managers. This explanation has the merit of being simple, and it is not without force in particular cases; but it does not account for the regularity with which the large, standardized, stable-market enterprise adopts the methods and the small, variable, unstable-market enterprise does not. The regularity suggests that the conditions of the case, rather than the capacity of the managers, are the governing circumstance. The second alternative is the explanation in terms of the "natural" superiority of the methods: the methods are said to be efficient in themselves, and their adoption is said to follow from their efficiency. This explanation confounds the technological with the pecuniary, and it fails to account for the cases in which the methods are technically available and pecuniarily inadmissible, or in which they are adopted and used only in part. The explanation in terms of the pecuniary exigencies of the business enterprise, here advanced, is to be preferred because it accounts for the regularities and for the exceptions alike, and because it does not assume an identity between the business gain and the industrial gain which the facts do not warrant.

It may be added, as a matter of the logic of the inquiry, that the question of efficiency management is a question of the "conditions" in the strict sense—the circumstances under which a given result follows—and not a question of the merits of the persons concerned. The business man who declines to install an exacting regimen of efficiency in a small establishment with a variable output is not thereby convicted of backwardness; he is conducting his business on the terms on which it can be conducted. The business man who installs the regimen and then restricts the output to maintain his margin is not thereby convicted of dishonesty; he is conducting his business on the terms on which it can be conducted. The student who wishes to understand the matter will therefore address himself to the conditions, and will reserve his judgments of merit for the cases in which the conditions are fully known. This is the import of the analysis here offered, and it is offered as a contribution to the understanding of the business enterprise as a pecuniary institution, not as a plea for or against any particular policy.

author: Edgar Norwick
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，分析商品的实用性、昂贵程度与审美评价之间的关系，并讨论手工制作偏好如何获得社会意义。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
It is notorious that in their selection of serviceable goods in the retail market purchasers are guided more by the finish and workmanship of the goods than by any marks of substantial serviceability. Goods, in order to sell, must have some appreciable amount of labor spent in giving them the marks of decent expensiveness, in addition to what goes to give them efficiency for the material use which they are to serve. This habit of making obvious costliness a canon of serviceability of course acts to enhance the aggregate cost of articles of consumption. It puts us on our guard against cheapness by identifying merit in some degree with cost. There is ordinarily a consistent effort on the part of the consumer to obtain goods of the required serviceability at as advantageous a bargain as may be; but the conventional requirement of obvious costliness, as a voucher and a constituent of the serviceability of the goods, leads him to reject as under grade such goods as do not contain a large element of conspicuous waste.

It is to be added that a large share of those features of consumable goods which figure in popular apprehension as marks of serviceability, and to which reference is here had as elements of conspicuous waste, commend themselves to the consumer also on other grounds than that of expensiveness alone. They usually give evidence of skill and effective workmanship, even if they do not contribute to the substantial serviceability of the goods; and it is no doubt largely on some such ground that any particular mark of honorific serviceability first comes into vogue and afterward maintains its footing as a normal constituent element of the worth of an article. A display of efficient workmanship is pleasing simply as such, even where its remoter, for the time unconsidered, outcome is futile. There is a gratification of the artistic sense in the contemplation of skillful work. But it is also to be added that no such evidence of skillful workmanship, or of ingenious and effective adaptation of means to an end, will, in the long run, enjoy the approbation of the modern civilized consumer unless it has the sanction of the Canon of conspicuous waste.

The position here taken is enforced in a felicitous manner by the place assigned in the economy of consumption to machine products. The point of material difference between machine-made goods and the hand-wrought goods which serve the same purposes is, ordinarily, that the former serve their primary purpose more adequately. They are a more perfect product--show a more perfect adaptation of means to end. This does not save them from disesteem and deprecation, for they fall short under the test of honorific waste. Hand labor is a more wasteful method of production; hence the goods turned out by this method are more serviceable for the purpose of pecuniary reputability; hence the marks of hand labor come to be honorific, and the goods which exhibit these marks take rank as of higher grade than the corresponding machine product. Commonly, if not invariably, the honorific marks of hand labor are certain imperfections and irregularities in the lines of the hand-wrought article, showing where the workman has fallen short in the execution of the design. The ground of the superiority of hand-wrought goods, therefore, is a certain margin of crudeness. This margin must never be so wide as to show bungling workmanship, since that would be evidence of low cost, nor so narrow as to suggest the ideal precision attained only by the machine, for that would be evidence of low cost.

The appreciation of those evidences of honorific crudeness to which hand-wrought goods owe their superior worth and charm in the eyes of well-bred people is a matter of nice discrimination. It requires training and the formation of right habits of thought with respect to what may be called the physiognomy of goods. Machine-made goods of daily use are often admired and preferred precisely on account of their excessive perfection by the vulgar and the underbred who have not given due thought to the punctilios of elegant consumption. The ceremonial inferiority of machine products goes to show that the perfection of skill and workmanship embodied in any costly innovations in the finish of goods is not sufficient of itself to secure them acceptance and permanent favor. The innovation must have the support of the canon of conspicuous waste. Any feature in the physiognomy of goods, however pleasing in itself, and however well it may approve itself to the taste for effective work, will not be tolerated if it proves obnoxious to this norm of pecuniary reputability.

The ceremonial inferiority or uncleanness in consumable goods due to "commonness," or in other words to their slight cost of production, has been taken very seriously by many persons. The objection to machine products is often formulated as an objection to the commonness of such goods. What is common is within the (pecuniary) reach of many people. Its consumption is therefore not honorific, since it does not serve the purpose of a favorable invidious comparison with other consumers. Hence the consumption, or even the sight of such goods, is inseparable from an odious suggestion of the lower levels of human life, and one comes away from their contemplation with a pervading sense of meanness that is extremely distasteful and depressing to a person of sensibility. In persons whose tastes assert themselves imperiously, and who have not the gift, habit, or incentive to discriminate between the grounds of their various judgments of taste, the deliverances of the sense of the honorific coalesce with those of the sense of beauty and of the sense of serviceability--in the manner already spoken of; the resulting composite valuation serves as a judgment of the object's beauty or its serviceability, according as the valuer's bias or interest inclines him to apprehend the object in the one or the other of these aspects. It follows not infrequently that the marks of cheapness or commonness are accepted as definitive marks of artistic unfitness, and a code or schedule of aesthetic proprieties on the one hand, and of aesthetic abominations on the other, is constructed on this basis for guidance in questions of taste.

As has already been pointed out, the cheap, and therefore indecorous, articles of daily consumption in modern industrial communities are commonly machine products; and the generic feature of the physiognomy of machine-made goods as compared with the hand-wrought article is their greater perfection in workmanship and greater accuracy in the detail execution of the design. Hence it comes about that the visible imperfections of the hand-wrought goods, being honorific, are accounted marks of superiority in point of beauty, or serviceability, or both. Hence has arisen that exaltation of the defective, of which John Ruskin and William Morris were such eager spokesmen in their time; and on this ground their propaganda of crudity and wasted effort has been taken up and carried forward since their time. And hence also the propaganda for a return to handicraft and household industry. So much of the work and speculations of this group of men as fairly comes under the characterization here given would have been impossible at a time when the visibly more perfect goods were not the cheaper.
b:
In any attempt to reduce the aesthetic appraisal of goods to a stable relation among utility, cost, and beauty, one is met at the outset by the circumstance that these categories are not natural kinds but institutional facts, and that their mutual bearing is fixed, not by the intrinsic properties of the article, but by the habits of thought of the community that appraises it. The utility of an object, in the sense relevant to economic theory, is its serviceability for some end conceived by the user; but the ends themselves are largely conventional, and the canon of serviceability is therefore conventional too. The expensive article is not merely one that has cost much labor and materials; it is one whose costliness is known and is legible in its appearance. And the aesthetic judgment is not a simple report of sensory pleasure, but a trained response, saturated with the standards of the group and with the repute of the persons and practices with which the object is associated. To treat these three as independent variables whose correlation may be measured is to mistake the grammar of a social practice for a law of nature.

Consider first the relation of utility to beauty. It is a commonplace of the industrial arts that an implement may be praised for "honest" construction, for the evident adaptation of means to end, and that this praise carries an aesthetic coloring. But the aesthetic value here is derivative. The perception of fitness pleases because it is the perception of a purpose achieved, and purposes are socially furnished. Where the purpose is obsolete, the fitness ceases to please; a hand loom may be admired as a relic, but its admirers do not propose to weave upon it. The workmanship of the article, its "efficiency," is thus admired only so long as the end it serves is an end the community still owns. When the end is discarded, the same construction becomes quaint, and quaintness is a different aesthetic category from beauty. Hence the general conclusion: utility contributes to aesthetic appraisal only through the mediation of conventionally sanctioned ends; it is not a sufficient ground, nor even a necessary one, since the beautiful may be frankly useless, as in the case of the jewel or the flower.

The relation of expensiveness to beauty is more intimate and more instructive. The canon of taste in any community with a leisure class is not independent of the canon of expense. The beautiful is, in good part, the costly made visible. This is not because cost is itself beautiful, but because the marks of cost—the rarity of the material, the superfluity of the labor, the evident absence of any pressing need—are marks of that exemption from industrial usefulness which is the badge of repute. The article that is beautiful and expensive is doubly creditable; the article that is beautiful and cheap is a puzzle, and the puzzle is commonly resolved by denying its beauty. Here one may take the example of the hand-wrought silver spoon as against the machine-stamped one of identical form. The two are, to the eye trained in the industrial arts, nearly indistinguishable in point of design; yet the hand-wrought article commands a higher price and a higher esteem. The esteem is not reducible to a finer perception of the object's qualities, for the qualities are the same. It is the evidence of the hand that is esteemed, because the hand is the warrant of cost, and cost is the warrant of honor. The aesthetic judgment has been recruited into the service of invidious distinction.

Now the preference for hand manufacture, which is the special case before us, is commonly defended on the ground of a superior beauty inhering in the irregularities of the hand. This defense is not without force, but its force is conditional. The irregularity pleases where it is read as the signature of the craftsman, that is, where the craftsman's skill is itself a mark of distinction. In communities where labor is cheap and plentiful, the hand-wrought article is the common article, and its irregularities are read as defects, not as beauties; the machine-made article, being scarcer and costlier, is then the object of esteem. The aesthetic preference thus follows the direction of the honorific, not the reverse. The general conclusion is that the hand-made preference is a function of the repute of hand labor, not of any constant sensory superiority in hand-wrought surfaces. The specific recognition is that in a society where the machine has become the vulgar instrument and the hand the aristocratic one, the irregularities of the hand acquire a borrowed beauty, which they lose the moment the hand ceases to be honorific.

The social meaning of this preference is therefore to be sought in the logic of status rather than in the logic of perception. To possess the hand-wrought article is to advertise that one can afford to dispense with the economies of machine production; it is to exhibit what may be called conspicuous waste in the sphere of taste. The preference is not a fraud consciously practiced; it is a habit of thought, formed under the pressure of emulation, which has come to seem self-evident to those who hold it. The connoisseur who detects a finer "quality" in the hand-wrought spoon is not lying; he is reporting, in good faith, a difference that his training has made real to him. But the difference is real only within the institutional setting that makes the hand honorable. Outside that setting, the report would be different, and the same connoisseur, trained otherwise, would detect the opposite.

It is necessary, however, to distinguish this general account from certain specific situations in which it does not hold. Where the hand-wrought article is genuinely more serviceable—as in the case of a tool whose balance and weight must be adjusted to the individual user—the preference may rest on utility, and its aesthetic coloring may be a rational accompaniment of a real fitness. Where the hand-wrought article embodies a technique not reproducible by machinery—as in certain textiles and ceramics—the preference may rest on a genuine novelty of effect, which is an aesthetic good independent of its cost. And where the community is small and its standards are those of craft rather than of pecuniary emulation, the hand may be esteemed for its skill and not for its cost, in which case the aesthetic judgment is relatively free of the invidious element. These are limiting cases, and they serve to mark the boundaries of the general conclusion rather than to refute it. The general conclusion is that in a society organized about pecuniary emulation, the aesthetic appraisal of goods is systematically contaminated by the canon of expense, and the hand-made preference is one of the channels through which that contamination is effected. The specific recognition is that the contamination is not uniform; it varies with the repute of the hand, with the genuineness of the utility, and with the presence or absence of a leisure-class standard of taste.

A further complication deserves notice. The aesthetic appraisal is not merely passive before the canon of expense; it reacts upon it. The article that has been long esteemed as beautiful becomes, by that very esteem, expensive; its cost is raised by the demand which its beauty creates, and its beauty is then confirmed by its cost. The relation is circular, and the circle is stable only so long as the underlying habits of thought remain undisturbed. When machinery cheapens the article, the circle is broken: the article remains beautiful in form but loses its honorific character, and its beauty is presently discovered to be vulgar. This is the history of many ornaments and many stuffs. The process is not a change in the object but a change in the institutional facts that sustain the appraisal. Hence any attempt to fix the aesthetic value of an article by reference to its intrinsic properties alone is foredoomed; the properties are constant, the appraisal is not.

The upshot of the argument is that utility, expensiveness, and beauty are not three independent quantities whose relations may be stated once for all, but three moments in a single institutional process. The process is the emulative organization of taste. Within that process, the general rule holds that the expensive is esteemed as beautiful and the beautiful is esteemed as expensive, and that the hand-made preference is a special case of this rule, operating wherever hand labor is honorific. But the rule is a rule of tendency, not a law of nature; it is subject to the limiting conditions already noted, and it is liable to reversal when the underlying repute of labor or of machinery changes. The analyst who would understand the aesthetic appraisal of goods must therefore begin, not with the goods, but with the scheme of status in which they are appraised; and he must be prepared to find that the same object, in different institutional settings, is beautiful, vulgar, or merely useful, without any change in its physical constitution. This is not a paradox but the ordinary working of the human habit of judgment, which is a social habit and takes its color from the society that entertains it.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_after: That such is the case should by no means be taken as intentionally reflecting anything like dispraise on those persons who have this (unavoidable) work of stultification in hand. Rather, it is dispassionately to be gathered from the run of the facts as set out above that those persons on whom these exigencies impinge will, by force of habituation, necessarily come to take the bent which these current conditions enforce, and without which this work could not well be done; all on the supposition — and it is by no means an extravagant assumption — that these persons so exposed to these agencies of spiritual disintegration are by native gift endowed with the commonplace traits of human nature, no more and no less. It is the duties of the office, not a run of infirmities peculiar to the incumbents of office, that make the outcome. Very much like that of the medicine-man, the office is one which will not abide a tolerant and in-genuous incumbent.
a: These remarks on the typical traits of the academic executive have unavoidably taken the colour of personalities.
b: It is the office that makes the man, not the man the office.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_after: The two main canons of truth on which the science proceeded, and with which the inquiry is here concerned, were: (a) a hedonistic-associational psychology, and (b) an uncritical conviction that there is a meliorative trend in the course of events, apart from the conscious ends of the individual members of the community. This axiom of a meliorative developmental trend fell into shape as a belief in an organic or quasi-organic (physiological) life process on the part of the economic community or of the nation; and this belief carried with it something of a constraining sense of self-realising cycles of growth, maturity and decay in the life history of nations or communities.
a: Seen through modern eyes and without effort to turn past gains to modern account, the metaphysical or preconceptional furniture of political economy as it stood about the middle of this century may come to look quite curious.
b: It is the office of the present inquiry to displace these canons by an appeal to the facts of economic life

author: Edgar Norwick
context_before: Along with the habits of thought peculiar to the technology of handicraft, modern science also took over and assimilated much of the institutional preconceptions of the era of handicraft and petty trade. The "natural laws," with the formulation of which this early modern science is occupied, are the rules governing natural "uniformities of sequence"; and they punctiliously formulate the due procedure of any given cause creatively working out the achievement of a given effect, very much as the craft rules sagaciously specified the due routine for turning out a staple article of merchantable goods. But these "natural laws" of science are also felt to have something of that integrity and prescriptive moral force that belongs to the principles of the system of "natural rights" which the era of handicraft has contributed to the institutional scheme of later times.
context_after: They were looked upon as intrinsically meritorious and beneficent, and were held to carry a sanction of their own. This habit of uncritically imputing merit and equity to the "natural laws" of science continued in force through much of the nineteenth century; very much as the habitual acceptance of the principles of "natural rights" has held on by force of tradition long after the exigencies of experience out of which these "rights" sprang ceased to shape men's habits of life. This traditional attitude of submissive approval toward the "natural laws" of science has not yet been wholly lost, even among the scientists of the passing generation, many of whom have uncritically invested these "laws" with a prescriptive rectitude and excellence; but so far, at least, has this animus progressed toward disuse that it is now chiefly a matter for expatiation in the pulpit, the accredited vent for the exudation of effete matter from the cultural organism.
a: The natural laws were not only held to be true to fact, but they were also felt to be right and good.
b: These "natural laws" were conceived in the image of the natural rights of man.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_before: But all these are matters chiefly of interior arrangement, appliances and materials, and they are all of a relatively inconspicuous character.
context_after: In meeting all these material requirements of the work in hand a very large expenditure of funds might advantageously be made — advantageously to the academic use which they are to serve — without much visible effect as seen in perspective from the outside. And so far as bears on this academic use, the exterior of the buildings is a matter of altogether minor consequence, as are also the decorative appointments of the interior.
a: Except as detailed in printed statistics they do not ordinarily lend themselves with appreciable effect to the art of advertising.
b: The exterior of the buildings, however, is what chiefly strikes the eye and forms the impression of the place.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_after: The Imperial establishment has shown itself to be wise, indeed more wise than amiable, but wise at least in its intentions, in the use which it has made of subject peoples hitherto. It is true, a somewhat accentuated eagerness on the part of the Imperial establishment to get the maximum service in a minimum of time and at a minimum cost from these subject populations,--as, e.g., in Silesia and Poland, in Schleswig-Holstein, in Alsace-Lorraine, or in its African and Oceanic possessions,--has at times led to practices altogether dubious on humanitarian grounds, at the same time that in point of thrifty management they have gone beyond "what the traffic will bear." Yet it is not to be overlooked--and in this connection it is a point of some weight--that, so far as the predatory traditions of its statecraft will permit, the Imperial establishment has in all these matters been guided by a singularly unreserved attention to its own material advantage. Where its management in these premises has yielded a less profitable usufruct than the circumstances would reasonably admit, the failure has been due to an excess of cupidity rather than the reverse.
a: Yet it should not be overlooked that any presumptive hard usage which the vassal peoples might look for at the hands of the German dynasty would necessarily be tempered with considerations of expediency as dictated by the exigencies of usufruct.
b: The institutional machinery of the Empire, while exhibiting a certain pragmatic astuteness in its administrative conduct, has consistently subordinated the welfare of its subject populations to the exigencies of pecuniary gain and efficient extraction.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_before: So far the argument has run on the pecuniary incidence of this projected Imperial dominion as it falls on the underlying community as a whole, with no attempt to discriminate between the divergent interests of the different classes and conditions of men that go to make up any modern community.
context_after: In all these modern nations that now stand in the article of decision between peace by submission or a doubtful and melancholy alternative,--in all of them men are by statute and custom inviolably equal before the law, of course; they are ungraded and masterless men before the law. But these same peoples are also alike in the respect that pecuniary duties and obligations among them are similarly sacred and inviolable under the dispassionate findings of the law. This pecuniary equality is, in effect, an impersonal equality between pecuniary magnitudes; from which it follows that these citizens of the advanced nations are not ungraded men in the pecuniary respect; nor are they masterless, in so far as a greater pecuniary force will always, under this impersonal equality of the law, stand in a relation of mastery toward a lesser one.
a: The question in hand is a question of pecuniary burdens, and therefore of the pecuniary interests of these several distinguishable classes or conditions of men.
b: A discrimination of these classes and conditions is necessary to any adequate apprehension of the case.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_before: The growth and mutations of the institutional fabric are an outcome of the conduct of the individual members of the group, since it is out of the experience of the individuals, through the habituation of individuals, that institutions arise; and it is in this same experience that these institutions act to direct and define the aims and end of conduct. It is, of course, on individuals that the system of institutions imposes those conventional standards, ideals, and canons of conduct that make up the community's scheme of life.
context_after: But such an inquiry can serve the purposes of a genetic theory only if and in so far as this individual conduct is attended to in those respects in which it counts toward habituation, and so toward change (or stability) of the institutional fabric, on the one hand, and in those respects in which it is prompted and guided by the received institutional conceptions and ideals on the other hand. The postulates of marginal utility, and the hedonistic preconceptions generally, fail at this point in that they confine the attention to such bearings of economic conduct as are conceived not to be conditioned by habitual standards and ideals and to have no effect in the way of habituation. They disregard or abstract from the causal sequence of propensity and habituation in economic life and exclude from theoretical inquiry all such interest in the facts of cultural growth, in order to attend to those features of the case that are conceived to be idle in this respect. All such facts of institutional force and growth are put on one side as not being germane to pure theory; they are to be taken account of, if at all, by afterthought, by a more or less vague and general allowance for inconsequential disturbances due to occasional human infirmity. Certain institutional phenomena, it is true, are comprised among the premises of the hedonists, as has been noted above; but they are included as postulates a priori. So the institution of ownership is taken into the inquiry not as a factor of growth or an element subject to change, but as one of the primordial and immutable facts of the order of nature, underlying the hedonistic calculus. Property, ownership, is presumed as the basis of hedonistic discrimination and it is conceived to be given in its finished (nineteenth-century) scope and force. There is no thought either of a conceivable growth of this definitive nineteenth-century institution out of a cruder past or of any conceivable cumulative change in the scope and force of ownership in the present or future. Nor is it conceived that the presence of this institutional element in men's economic relations in any degree affects or disguises the hedonistic calculus, or that its pecuniary conceptions and standards in any degree standardize, color, mitigate, or divert the hedonistic calculator from the direct and unhampered quest of the net sensuous gain. While the institution of property is included in this way among the postulates of the theory, and is even presumed to be ever-present in the economic situation, it is allowed to have no force in shaping economic conduct, which is conceived to run its course to its hedonistic outcome as if no such institutional factor intervened between the impulse and its realization. The institution of property, together with all the range of pecuniary conceptions that belong under it and that cluster about it, are presumed to give rise to no habitual or conventional canons of conduct or standards of valuation, no proximate ends, ideals, or aspirations. All pecuniary notions arising from ownership are treated simply as expedients of computation which mediate between the pain-cost and the pleasure-gain of hedonistic choice, without lag, leak, or friction; they are conceived simply as the immutably correct, God-given notation of the hedonistic calculus.
a: Scientific inquiry in this field, therefore, must deal with individual conduct and must formulate its theoretical results in terms of individual conduct.
b: An inquiry into the economic conduct of individuals is therefore indispensable to any genetic account of institutions.

author: Edgar Norwick
context_after: The vogue of the corset offers an apparent exception from the rule of which it has here been cited as an illustration. A closer examination, however, will show that this apparent exception is really a verification of the rule that the vogue of any given element or feature in dress rests on its utility as an evidence of pecuniary standing. It is well known that in the industrially more advanced communities the corset is employed only within certain fairly well defined social strata. The women of the poorer classes, especially of the rural population, do not habitually use it, except as a holiday luxury.
