They had often attempted to do it before, but it was a subject on which Mrs. Bennet was beyond the reach of reason, and she continued to rail bitterly against the cruelty of settling an estate away from a family of five daughters, in favour of a man whom nobody cared anything about.
b: Clara Fenwick, Pride and Prejudice, Chapter 13. Mrs. Bennet is lamenting the entail of Longbourn to Mr. Collins. Jane and Elizabeth attempt to reason with her, but she remains inconsolable, declaring that she cannot bear to hear Mr. Collins mentioned. Mr. Bennet then observes that the affair is iniquitous and that nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn, but suggests that his letter may soften her.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: Not yet, however, in spite of her disappointment in her husband, did Mrs. Bennet give up the point. She talked to Elizabeth again and again; coaxed and threatened her by turns. She endeavoured to secure Jane in her interest; but Jane, with all possible mildness, declined interfering; and Elizabeth, sometimes with real earnestness, and sometimes with playful gaiety, replied to her attacks. Though her manner varied, however, her determination never did.
context_after: While the family were in this confusion, Charlotte Lucas came to spend the day with them. She was met in the vestibule by Lydia, who, flying to her, cried in a half whisper, “I am glad you are come, for there is such fun here! What do you think has happened this morning? Mr. Collins has made an offer to Lizzy, and she will not have him.”
a: Mr. Collins, meanwhile, was meditating in solitude on what had passed. He thought too well of himself to comprehend on what motives his cousin could refuse him; and though his pride was hurt, he suffered in no other way. His regard for her was quite imaginary; and the possibility of her deserving her mother's reproach prevented his feeling any regret.
b: Mr. Collins, meanwhile, was meditating in solitude on what had passed. He thought too well of himself to comprehend on what motive his cousin could refuse him; and though his pride was hurt, he suffered in no other way. His regard for her was quite imaginary; and the possibility of her deserving her mother’s reproach prevented his feeling any regret.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: Elizabeth hesitated, but her knees trembled under her and she felt how little would be gained by her attempting to pursue them. Calling back the servant, therefore, she commissioned him, though in so breathless an accent as made her almost unintelligible, to fetch his master and mistress home instantly.
context_after: “No, I thank you,” she replied, endeavouring to recover herself. “There is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well; I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn.”
a: On his quitting the room she sat down, unable to support herself, and looking so miserably ill, that it was impossible for Darcy to leave her, or to refrain from saying, in a tone of gentleness and commiseration, “Let me call your maid. Is there nothing you could take to give you present relief? A glass of wine; shall I get you one? You are very ill.”
b: On his coming in, he immediately advanced towards her, and, with a look of great surprise, said, “Good God! what is the matter?”—but recollecting himself, he added, “I am afraid you are ill; you look very pale. Pray sit down and compose yourself.”

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: They travelled as expeditiously as possible, and, sleeping one night on the road, reached Longbourn by dinner time the next day. It was a comfort to Elizabeth to consider that Jane could not have been wearied by long expectations.
context_after: Elizabeth jumped out; and, after giving each of them a hasty kiss, hurried into the vestibule, where Jane, who came running down from her mother's apartment, immediately met her.
a: The little Gardiners, attracted by the sight of a chaise, were standing on the steps of the house as they entered the paddock; and, when the carriage drove up to the door, the joyful surprise that lighted up their faces, and displayed itself over their whole bodies, in a variety of capers and frisks, was the first pleasing earnest of their welcome.
b: The little Gardiners, attracted by the sight of a chaise, were standing on the steps of the house as they entered the paddock; and when the carriage drove up to the door, the joyful surprise that lighted up their faces, and displayed itself over their whole bodies, in a variety of capers and frisks, was the first pleasing earnest of their welcome.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: “But my dear Elizabeth,” she added, “what sort of girl is Miss King? I should be sorry to think our friend mercenary.”
context_after: “If you will only tell me what sort of girl Miss King is, I shall know what to think.”
a: “Pray, my dear aunt, what is the difference in matrimonial affairs, between the mercenary and the prudent motive? Where does discretion end, and avarice begin? Last Christmas you were afraid of his marrying me, because it would be imprudent; and now, because he is trying to get a girl with only ten thousand pounds, you want to find out that he is mercenary.”
b: “Pray, my dear aunt, what is the difference in matrimonial affairs between the mercenary and the prudent motive? Where does discretion end, and avarice begin? Last Christmas you were afraid of his marrying me, because it would be imprudent; and now, because he is trying to get a girl with only ten thousand pounds, you want to find out that he is mercenary.”

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a conversation in which Wickham tells Elizabeth about a disputed bequest and presents himself as the victim of someone else's failure of honor.
a:
“There was just such an informality in the terms of the bequest as to give me no hope from law. A man of honour could not have doubted the intention, but Mr. Darcy chose to doubt it--or to treat it as a merely conditional recommendation, and to assert that I had forfeited all claim to it by extravagance, imprudence--in short anything or nothing. Certain it is, that the living became vacant two years ago, exactly as I was of an age to hold it, and that it was given to another man; and no less certain is it, that I cannot accuse myself of having really done anything to deserve to lose it. I have a warm, unguarded temper, and I may have spoken my opinion _of_ him, and _to_ him, too freely. I can recall nothing worse. But the fact is, that we are very different sort of men, and that he hates me.”

“This is quite shocking! He deserves to be publicly disgraced.”

“Some time or other he _will_ be--but it shall not be by _me_. Till I can forget his father, I can never defy or expose _him_.”

Elizabeth honoured him for such feelings, and thought him handsomer than ever as he expressed them.
b:
"Pray, Miss Elizabeth, do not think me forward if I speak of a matter that weighs heavily upon my spirits. You have been so kind as to listen to me before, and I find in you a sympathy rare among your sex."

"I am sure I should be sorry to hear of any injustice done you, Mr. Wickham."

"You are goodness itself. Then I shall be brief. My late godfather, the elder Mr. Darcy, promised me a living in the church—a promise made, I may say, upon his deathbed, and confirmed by every expression of affection. Yet his son, upon inheriting, found it convenient to forget the obligation, and bestowed the preferment elsewhere. A man of honor would have honored his father's word; but pride and fortune are poor substitutes for principle."

"Indeed, that is a grave charge."

"It is a charge I would rather bury than utter, but truth will out. I have been made to feel the want of powerful friends, and must earn my bread as best I can, while others enjoy what was meant for me. But I trouble you too much."

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a scene at a country ball where Elizabeth looks in vain for a man she expected to see, and what she hears about his absence colors her view of another guest.
a: Till Elizabeth entered the drawing-room at Netherfield, and looked in vain for Mr. Wickham among the cluster of red coats there assembled, a doubt of his being present had never occurred to her. The certainty of meeting him had not been checked by any of those recollections that might not unreasonably have alarmed her. She had dressed with more than usual care, and prepared in the highest spirits for the conquest of all that remained unsubdued of his heart, trusting that it was not more than might be won in the course of the evening. But in an instant arose the dreadful suspicion of his being purposely omitted for Mr. Darcy's pleasure in the Bingleys' invitation to the officers; and though this was not exactly the case, the absolute fact of his absence was pronounced by his friend Denny, to whom Lydia eagerly applied, and who told them that Wickham had been obliged to go to town on business the day before, and was not yet returned; adding, with a significant smile, “I do not imagine his business would have called him away just now, if he had not wanted to avoid a certain gentleman here.”
b:
The evening promised everything that a country ball could offer, and Elizabeth entered the assembly rooms with an expectancy she was half ashamed to own. She had been assured that Mr. Harville would be present, and she found herself, as the hours wore on, scanning every new arrival with an eagerness she could not entirely suppress. Yet the quadrilles came and went, and still he did not appear.

It was while she stood near the refreshments, affecting an interest in the negus, that she overheard the two ladies beside her. “Poor Mr. Harville,” said one, with a sigh of great satisfaction, “detained in town upon business of the most tedious kind. He wrote to say he could not possibly get away.” Elizabeth felt the disappointment settle upon her spirits, and she turned away before her countenance could betray her.

It was then that her eye fell upon Mr. Ashford, who stood across the room in easy conversation, laughing with that careless confidence she had always found so trying. His presence, which she had before merely disliked, now seemed to her a positive affront; for had he not been heard to say, only last week, that no gentleman of sense would neglect a prior engagement for the sake of business? She could not but feel that his very ease was a reproach to the absent, and she resolved to think no better of him than she had always done.

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a domestic scene in which a father reveals a social visit he had kept secret, prompting his wife's surprise and eager speculation among his daughters.
a:
The astonishment of the ladies was just what he wished; that of Mrs. Bennet perhaps surpassing the rest; though, when the first tumult of joy was over, she began to declare that it was what she had expected all the while.

“How good it was in you, my dear Mr. Bennet! But I knew I should persuade you at last. I was sure you loved your girls too well to neglect such an acquaintance. Well, how pleased I am! and it is such a good joke, too, that you should have gone this morning and never said a word about it till now.”

“Now, Kitty, you may cough as much as you choose,” said Mr. Bennet; and, as he spoke, he left the room, fatigued with the raptures of his wife.

“What an excellent father you have, girls!” said she, when the door was shut. “I do not know how you will ever make him amends for his kindness; or me, either, for that matter. At our time of life it is not so pleasant, I can tell you, to be making new acquaintances every day; but for your sakes, we would do anything. Lydia, my love, though you _are_ the youngest, I dare say Mr. Bingley will dance with you at the next ball.”
b:
The tea-things were scarcely removed, and Mr. Bennet seated with his usual book, when he observed, with an air of studied indifference, “I hope, my dear, you have ordered a good dinner to-day, because I have reason to expect an addition to our family party.”

“Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope my dinners are good enough for her.”

“The person of whom I speak is a gentleman, and a stranger.”

Mrs. Bennet’s eyes sparkled. “A gentleman and a stranger! It must be Mr. Bingley, I am sure. Why, Jane, you never said a word of it. Well, I shall be glad to see him; but I wish you had told me before, that I might have had a bit of fish.”

“It is not Mr. Bingley,” said her husband. “It is a person whom I never saw in the whole course of my life.”

This roused curiosity in every quarter. The girls pressed round him, entreating to know whether he came in a chaise or a chair, and whether he was tall or short. “About a month ago,” said he, “I received this letter; and about a fortnight ago I answered it, for I thought it a case of some delicacy.”

Elizabeth, watching him closely, perceived a slyness in his look which promised something of moment. “Let me read it aloud,” cried Mrs. Bennet, “for I long to know who it is from.” But he folded it away, declaring that he would keep his own counsel until the gentleman arrived; and though his wife protested that it was very hard, and the younger girls teased without ceasing, he would say no more, leaving them all to wonder, and Elizabeth to suspect that the visit would prove neither so agreeable nor so simple as her mother hoped.

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a drawing-room conversation in which a mother boasts of a daughter's advantageous marriage while lamenting that the couple must live far away.
a:
“It is a delightful thing, to be sure, to have a daughter well married,” continued her mother, “but at the same time, Mr. Bingley, it is very hard to have her taken such a way from me. They are gone down to Newcastle, a place quite northward, it seems, and there they are to stay I do not know how long. His regiment is there; for I suppose you have heard of his leaving the ----shire, and of his being gone into the regulars. Thank Heaven! he has _some_ friends, though perhaps not so many as he deserves.”

Elizabeth, who knew this to be levelled at Mr. Darcy, was in such misery of shame, that she could hardly keep her seat. It drew from her, however, the exertion of speaking, which nothing else had so effectually done before; and she asked Bingley whether he meant to make any stay in the country at present. A few weeks, he believed.

“When you have killed all your own birds, Mr. Bingley,” said her mother, “I beg you will come here, and shoot as many as you please on Mr. Bennet's manor. I am sure he will be vastly happy to oblige you, and will save all the best of the covies for you.”
b:
"My dear Mrs. Ashford, you cannot conceive what a comfort it is to me that dear Louisa has secured such a gentleman as Mr. Pemberton. Ten thousand a year, and a house in Surrey, though I am sure I never boasted of it."

"Indeed, ma'am, you have every reason to be satisfied."

"Satisfied! I am transported. Though I own it grieves me that they must remove so far as Northumberland. A mother's heart, you know. But what is distance when affection is so amply provided for? He is everything that is obliging, and Louisa writes that she is quite the mistress of her own establishment already."

"You must be very proud."

"Proud and desolate by turns, I assure you. But we must not repine. A daughter well settled is a blessing not every mother is granted, and I would not exchange my felicity for the world—though I confess I shall miss her sadly at Michaelmas."

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a domestic scene in which Mrs. Bennet eagerly interprets two gentlemen's recent behavior and makes plans for their next visit.
a:
They did not see the gentlemen again till Tuesday; and Mrs. Bennet, in the meanwhile, was giving way to all the happy schemes, which the good humour and common politeness of Bingley, in half an hour's visit, had revived.

On Tuesday there was a large party assembled at Longbourn; and the two who were most anxiously expected, to the credit of their punctuality as sportsmen, were in very good time. When they repaired to the dining-room, Elizabeth eagerly watched to see whether Bingley would take the place, which, in all their former parties, had belonged to him, by her sister. Her prudent mother, occupied by the same ideas, forbore to invite him to sit by herself. On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look round, and happened to smile: it was decided. He placed himself by her.

Elizabeth, with a triumphant sensation, looked towards his friend. He bore it with noble indifference, and she would have imagined that Bingley had received his sanction to be happy, had she not seen his eyes likewise turned towards Mr. Darcy, with an expression of half-laughing alarm.
b: Mrs. Bennet could think of nothing but the two gentlemen’s visit to Longbourn, and she was in a flutter of spirits which no breakfast could compose. “My dear Mr. Bennet,” said she, “you must observe how Mr. Bingley looked at Jane—there is no mistaking such attentions; and as for Mr. Darcy, though he is so high and so proud, he asked after Lizzy’s health twice, which I call very particular indeed. I dare say he is beginning to feel the worth of her. We must have the carriage out on Thursday, for I am resolved they shall find us at home; and Jane must wear her new muslin, and Lizzy must not be so saucy, but speak a little more than she does. I shall order a good dinner—a couple of dishes more than common—for gentlemen are always hungry, and a full table puts them in spirits. If Mr. Bingley comes early, he may walk with Jane in the shrubbery; and I shall contrive that Mr. Darcy sits by Lizzy at cards. Only think, my dear, if we should have two daughters married before Michaelmas! I declare I shall hardly be able to sleep for joy.”

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write an after-visit conversation among neighbors and young women about an aloof gentleman at a ball. Show how his position affects their judgments of his pride.
a:
“I believe, ma'am, I may safely promise you _never_ to dance with him.”

“His pride,” said Miss Lucas, “does not offend _me_ so much as pride often does, because there is an excuse for it. One cannot wonder that so very fine a young man, with family, fortune, everything in his favour, should think highly of himself. If I may so express it, he has a _right_ to be proud.”

“That is very true,” replied Elizabeth, “and I could easily forgive _his_ pride, if he had not mortified _mine_.”

“Pride,” observed Mary, who piqued herself upon the solidity of her reflections, “is a very common failing, I believe. By all that I have ever read, I am convinced that it is very common indeed; that human nature is particularly prone to it, and that there are very few of us who do not cherish a feeling of self-complacency on the score of some quality or other, real or imaginary. Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us.”
b:
“My dear,” cried Mrs. Bennet to her neighbour, “you will hardly believe it, but Mr. Darcy stood about the room in the most forbidding manner, and would not be prevailed upon to dance above twice, though there were a dozen young ladies in want of a partner.”
“La, ma’am,” replied her daughter Kitty, “I am sure he is very proud. He looked as if he thought nobody good enough for him.”
“Nay, child,” said Mary, “his fortune must be considered. A man of ten thousand a year may be excused a little reserve; it is not pride so much as propriety.”
“I cannot agree,” said Elizabeth. “Had he been merely reserved, he might have been civil; but he was silent, and looked displeased, and that is pride in any station.”
“Well,” said Mrs. Bennet, “if he had danced with our Jane, I daresay we should have found him agreeable enough; but as he did not, I shall think him as proud as Lucifer.”

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a scene from Elizabeth's point of view as she meets Miss Darcy and revises an impression formed from other people's descriptions.
a:
Miss Darcy was tall, and on a larger scale than Elizabeth; and, though little more than sixteen, her figure was formed, and her appearance womanly and graceful. She was less handsome than her brother; but there was sense and good humour in her face, and her manners were perfectly unassuming and gentle. Elizabeth, who had expected to find in her as acute and unembarrassed an observer as ever Mr. Darcy had been, was much relieved by discerning such different feelings.

They had not long been together before Mr. Darcy told her that Bingley was also coming to wait on her; and she had barely time to express her satisfaction, and prepare for such a visitor, when Bingley's quick step was heard on the stairs, and in a moment he entered the room. All Elizabeth's anger against him had been long done away; but had she still felt any, it could hardly have stood its ground against the unaffected cordiality with which he expressed himself on seeing her again. He inquired in a friendly, though general way, after her family, and looked and spoke with the same good-humoured ease that he had ever done.
b:
Elizabeth had heard enough of Miss Darcy, before ever entering the room, to have settled her opinion very decidedly. From Mr. Wickham she had received the account of a proud, disagreeable girl; from Miss Bingley, a portrait of sullen haughtiness and ill-bred reserve; and from the general voice of Meryton, a confirmation of fortune and consequence that could hardly fail to produce insolence. She had prepared herself, therefore, for cold looks and a distant manner, and had resolved to bear them with becoming composure.

But the lady who rose to receive her was nothing of the kind. Miss Darcy was tall and womanly, and though but sixteen, her figure was formed and her appearance dignified; yet there was a gentleness in her countenance, and a shyness in her address, that spoke rather of diffidence than pride. She coloured, she hesitated, and seemed almost afraid of her own voice; and when she did speak, it was with a modesty so unaffected, and a wish to please so evident, that Elizabeth could scarcely credit the descriptions she had been given.

She was not handsome in the striking way of her brother, but there was sense and sweetness in her face; and her manners, though retiring, were perfectly unassuming. Elizabeth, who had come prepared to dislike, found herself disarmed; and she began to suspect that the reports she had trusted were the offspring rather of prejudice than of truth. She remembered that Mr. Wickham's account had been given with a warmth that might colour it, and that Miss Bingley's praise or blame was seldom to be relied upon. The discovery gave her a sensation of shame, and she resolved to judge for herself hereafter, and to let no second-hand report decide the character of a stranger.

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a novel scene about two young women stopping at relatives' house on a journey home. Use their arrival and family conversation to convey changes in their circumstances.
a:
Their journey was performed without much conversation, or any alarm; and within four hours of their leaving Hunsford they reached Mr. Gardiner's house, where they were to remain a few days.

Jane looked well, and Elizabeth had little opportunity of studying her spirits, amidst the various engagements which the kindness of her aunt had reserved for them. But Jane was to go home with her, and at Longbourn there would be leisure enough for observation.

It was not without an effort, meanwhile, that she could wait even for Longbourn, before she told her sister of Mr. Darcy's proposals. To know that she had the power of revealing what would so exceedingly astonish Jane, and must, at the same time, so highly gratify whatever of her own vanity she had not yet been able to reason away, was such a temptation to openness as nothing could have conquered but the state of indecision in which she remained as to the extent of what she should communicate; and her fear, if she once entered on the subject, of being hurried into repeating something of Bingley which might only grieve her sister further.
b:
The carriage had scarcely halted before the door of the parsonage flew open, and the two young ladies were handed down with all the bustle that a long journey’s end allows. Mrs. Ferrars received them in the hall with an embrace that was warm but searching, her eyes travelling over their pelisses and their countenances alike, as though she would read in the one the cost of the other. “My dear girls, you are cold and weary, I am sure; come to the fire directly.”

Elinor, the elder, returned her aunt’s greeting with composure, but there was a gravity in her manner that had not been there at Michaelmas, and she spoke of their lodgings at Bath with a brevity that discouraged inquiry. Harriet, by contrast, was all animation, yet her colour rose too quickly and her laugh came a little too often, as if she feared a pause might invite questions she could not answer.

“And your father?” said Mrs. Ferrars, when they were seated. “He writes that the estate is much encumbered.”

“It is,” said Elinor quietly. “We are come home to be of use, and to be economical.”

“Economical!” cried their aunt. “Then it is as I feared. Well, well—we must none of us be ashamed of prudence.” She rang for tea, and the conversation turned to lesser matters; but the two sisters exchanged a look which said that their changed fortunes were already understood, and that the remainder of the evening would be spent in explaining what could not be concealed.

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a restrained drawing-room scene in which Elizabeth and her aunt call on Georgiana Darcy, who struggles to receive them while other visitors watch.
a:
In this house they were received by Miss Darcy, who was sitting there with Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley, and the lady with whom she lived in London. Georgiana's reception of them was very civil, but attended with all the embarrassment which, though proceeding from shyness and the fear of doing wrong, would easily give to those who felt themselves inferior the belief of her being proud and reserved. Mrs. Gardiner and her niece, however, did her justice, and pitied her.

By Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley they were noticed only by a curtsey; and, on their being seated, a pause, awkward as such pauses must always be, succeeded for a few moments. It was first broken by Mrs. Annesley, a genteel, agreeable-looking woman, whose endeavour to introduce some kind of discourse proved her to be more truly well-bred than either of the others; and between her and Mrs. Gardiner, with occasional help from Elizabeth, the conversation was carried on. Miss Darcy looked as if she wished for courage enough to join in it; and sometimes did venture a short sentence when there was least danger of its being heard.
b:
The drawing-room at Darcy House was elegant without ostentation, and Elizabeth entered it with her aunt, Mrs. Gardiner, sensible of the honour of the invitation and curious as to its reception. Miss Darcy rose to greet them, her colour heightened, her curtsy correct to the inch, yet her eyes betrayed a flutter that no accomplishment of manner could quite conceal. She offered seats by the fire, enquired after their health, and spoke of the weather with the desperate composure of one reciting a lesson.

Nor was the trial hers alone. Two ladies of consequence, seated at the farther window, had suspended their discourse to observe the newcomers with that leisure which politeness lends to scrutiny. One inclined her head to the other; a fan moved; a smile, faint and uncharitable, passed between them. Georgiana perceived it all, and her voice, already low, sank almost to a whisper. She turned her questions to Mrs. Gardiner with an earnestness meant to exclude the room, yet her fingers worked at her handkerchief, and once, when a low murmur reached her from the window, she lost the thread of her own sentence entirely.

Elizabeth, pitying her, supplied the want of discourse with easy observations upon the park and the season, and asked after Miss Darcy's music with so much warmth that the girl's gratitude showed plainly in her face. Still the visit was short, as such visits must be; and when they rose to go, Georgiana attended them to the door with a haste that spoke relief, and pressed Elizabeth's hand at parting with a sincerity that more than atoned for every awkwardness within.

author: Clara Fenwick
task: Write a scene in which a young woman's private distress can pass unnoticed under the cover of a family crisis, and show how the household responds to news from London.
a:
The present unhappy state of the family rendered any other excuse for the lowness of her spirits unnecessary; nothing, therefore, could be fairly conjectured from _that_, though Elizabeth, who was by this time tolerably well acquainted with her own feelings, was perfectly aware that, had she known nothing of Darcy, she could have borne the dread of Lydia's infamy somewhat better. It would have spared her, she thought, one sleepless night out of two.

When Mr. Bennet arrived, he had all the appearance of his usual philosophic composure. He said as little as he had ever been in the habit of saying; made no mention of the business that had taken him away, and it was some time before his daughters had courage to speak of it.

It was not till the afternoon, when he had joined them at tea, that Elizabeth ventured to introduce the subject; and then, on her briefly expressing her sorrow for what he must have endured, he replied, “Say nothing of that. Who should suffer but myself? It has been my own doing, and I ought to feel it.”

“You must not be too severe upon yourself,” replied Elizabeth.
b:
The letter from London arrived at breakfast, and within a quarter-hour the whole house was in motion. Mrs. Ellworth had gone quite pale over the second paragraph—her brother's affairs, it seemed, were in dreadful disorder, and his wife was to be sent down to them at once with the children—and the servants were dispatched hither and thither, and the carriage bespoke, and everyone talking of beds and broth and the shame of it.

Amelia alone said nothing. She stood by the window with her hands folded, and when her mother cried, "Amelia, do not stand there like a post!" she answered, "Yes, Mama," and moved to fetch the linen, and was praised for her composure. No one observed that her fingers shook upon the cupboard latch, nor that she had read the letter twice and found in it, between the lines, the name of a gentleman whose silence had been growing these three weeks past, and who was now reported to be upon the point of marriage with another.

The household, being wholly occupied with the ruin of Uncle Henry, had no leisure to perceive that Miss Ellworth ate no dinner, and attributed her paleness to the fatigue of preparing rooms; and her aunt, arriving in a flurry of tears, declared her the best of nieces, and kissed her, and never saw that the kiss was received as one receives a kindness from a stranger.

a: “You must be surprised, very much surprised--so lately as Mr. Collins was wishing to marry you.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: But why Mr. Darcy came so often to the Parsonage, it was more difficult to understand. He seldom appeared really animated. Mrs. Collins knew not what to make of him. Colonel Fitzwilliam's occasionally laughing at his stupidity, proved that he was generally different, which her own knowledge of him could not have told her; and as she would liked to have believed this change the effect of love, and the object of that love her friend Eliza, she set herself seriously to work to find it out. She watched him whenever they were at Rosings, and whenever he came to Hunsford; but without much success.
context_after: It was an earnest, steadfast gaze, but she often doubted whether there were much admiration in it, and sometimes it seemed nothing but absence of mind.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: “I beg your pardon, I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I ever saw--and if he becomes really attached to me--I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence of it. Oh! _that_ abominable Mr. Darcy!
context_after: My father, however, is partial to Mr. Wickham. In short, my dear aunt, I should be very sorry to be the means of making any of you unhappy; but since we see every day that where there is affection, young people are seldom withheld by immediate want of fortune from entering into engagements with each other, how can I promise to be wiser than so many of my fellow-creatures if I am tempted, or how am I even to know that it would be wisdom to resist? All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short, I will do my best.”
a: My father's opinion of me does me the greatest honour, and I should be miserable to forfeit it.
b: He is the cause of my exposing myself to your reproof.

author: Clara Fenwick

context_after: But our visitor was very obstinate. I fancy, Lizzy, that obstinacy is the real defect of his character, after all. He has been accused of many faults at different times, but _this_ is the true one. Nothing was to be done that he did not do himself; though I am sure (and I do not speak it to be thanked, therefore say nothing about it), your uncle would most readily have settled the whole.
a: It was not all settled before Monday: as soon as it was, the express was sent off to Longbourn.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: But Elizabeth was not formed for ill-humour; and though every prospect of her own was destroyed for the evening, it could not dwell long on her spirits; and having told all her griefs to Charlotte Lucas, whom she had not seen for a week, she was soon able to make a voluntary transition to the oddities of her cousin, and to point him out to her particular notice.
context_after: Mr. Collins, awkward and solemn, apologising instead of attending, and often moving wrong without being aware of it, gave her all the shame and misery which a disagreeable partner for a couple of dances can give. The moment of her release from him was ecstasy.
a: The first two dances, however, brought a return of distress; they were dances of mortification.

author: Clara Fenwick
context_before: Elizabeth, to whom Jane very soon communicated the chief of all this, heard it in silent indignation.
