It is my belief that the ethical and religious motives in spite of the splendidly imaginative systems to which they have given rise, have been on the whole a hindrance to the progress of philosophy, and ought now to be consciously thrust aside by those who wish to discover philosophical truth. Science, originally, was entangled in similar motives, and was thereby hindered in its advances. It is, I maintain, from science, rather than from ethics and religion, that philosophy should draw its inspiration.

But there are two different ways in which a philosophy may seek to base itself upon science. It may emphasise the most general results of science, and seek to give even greater generality and unity to these results. Or it may study the methods of science, and seek to apply these methods, with the necessary adaptations, to its own peculiar province. Much philosophy inspired by science has gone astray through preoccupation with the results momentarily supposed to have been achieved. It is not results, but methods that can be transferred with profit from the sphere of the special sciences to the sphere of philosophy. What I wish to bring to your notice is the possibility and importance of applying to philosophical problems certain broad principles of method which have been found successful in the study of scientific questions.

The opposition between a philosophy guided by scientific method and a philosophy dominated by religious and ethical ideas may be illustrated by two notions which are very prevalent in the works of philosophers, namely the notion of the universe, and the notion of good and evil. A philosopher is expected to tell us something about the nature of the universe as a whole, and to give grounds for either optimism or pessimism. Both these expectations seem to me mistaken. I believe the conception of "the universe" to be, as its etymology indicates, a mere relic of pre-Copernican astronomy: and I believe the question of optimism and pessimism to be one which the philosopher will regard as outside his scope, except, possibly, to the extent of maintaining that it is insoluble.

In the days before Copernicus, the conception of the "universe" was defensible on scientific grounds: the diurnal revolution of the heavenly bodies bound them together as all parts of one system, of which the earth was the centre. Round this apparent scientific fact, many human desires rallied: the wish to believe Man important in the scheme of things, the theoretical desire for a comprehensive understanding of the Whole, the hope that the course of nature might be guided by some sympathy with our wishes. In this way, an ethically inspired system of metaphysics grew up, whose anthropocentrism was apparently warranted by the geocentrism of astronomy. When Copernicus swept away the astronomical basis of this system of thought, it had grown so familiar, and had associated itself so intimately with men's aspirations, that it survived with scarcely diminished force--survived even Kant's "Copernican revolution," and is still now the unconscious premiss of most metaphysical systems.

The oneness of the world is an almost undiscussed postulate of most metaphysics. "Reality is not merely one and self-consistent, but is a system of reciprocally determinate parts"--such a statement would pass almost unnoticed as a mere truism. Yet I believe that it embodies a failure to effect thoroughly the "Copernican revolution," and that the apparent oneness of the world is merely the oneness of what is seen by a single spectator or apprehended by a single mind. The Critical Philosophy, although it intended to emphasise the subjective element in many apparent characteristics of the world, yet, by regarding the world in itself as unknowable, so concentrated attention upon the subjective representation that its subjectivity was soon forgotten. Having recognised the categories as the work of the mind, it was paralysed by its own recognition, and abandoned in despair the attempt to undo the work of subjective falsification. In part, no doubt, its despair was well founded, but not, I think, in any absolute or ultimate sense. Still less was it a ground for rejoicing, or for supposing that the nescience to which it ought to have given rise could be legitimately exchanged for a metaphysical dogmatism.

As regards our present question, namely, the question of the unity of the world, the right method, as I think, has been indicated by William James. "Let us now turn our backs upon ineffable or unintelligible ways of accounting for the world's oneness, and inquire whether, instead of being a principle, the 'oneness' affirmed may not merely be a name like 'substance' descriptive of the fact that certain specific and verifiable connections are found among the parts of the experiential flux.... We can easily conceive of things that shall have no connection whatever with each other. We may assume them to inhabit different times and spaces, as the dreams of different persons do even now. They may be so unlike and incommensurable, and so inert towards one another, as never to jostle or interfere. Even now there may actually be whole universes so disparate from ours that we who know ours have no means of perceiving that they exist. We conceive their diversity, however; and by that fact the whole lot of them form what is known in logic as 'a universe of discourse.' To form a universe of discourse argues, as this example shows, no further kind of connexion. The importance attached by certain monistic writers to the fact that any chaos may become a universe by merely being named, is to me incomprehensible." We are thus left with two kinds of unity in the experienced world; the one what we may call the epistemological unity, due merely to the fact that my experienced world is what one experience selects from the sum total of existence: the other that tentative and partial unity exhibited in the prevalence of scientific laws in those portions of the world which science has hitherto mastered. Now a generalisation based upon either of these kinds of unity would be fallacious. That the things which we experience have the common property of being experienced by us is a truism from which obviously nothing of importance can be deducible: it is clearly fallacious to draw from the fact that whatever we experience is experienced the conclusion that therefore everything must be experienced. The generalisation of the second kind of unity, namely, that derived from scientific laws, would be equally fallacious, though the fallacy is a trifle less elementary. In order to explain it let us consider for a moment what is called the reign of law. People often speak as though it were a remarkable fact that the physical world is subject to invariable laws. In fact, however, it is not easy to see how such a world could fail to obey general laws. Taking any arbitrary set of points in space, there is a function of the time corresponding to these points, i.e. expressing the motion of a particle which traverses these points: this function may be regarded as a general law to which the behaviour of such a particle is subject. Taking all such functions for all the particles in the universe, there will be theoretically some one formula embracing them all, and this formula may be regarded as the single and supreme law of the spatio-temporal world. Thus what is surprising in physics is not the existence of general laws, but their extreme simplicity. It is not the uniformity of nature that should surprise us, for, by sufficient analytic ingenuity, any conceivable course of nature might be shown to exhibit uniformity. What should surprise us is the fact that the uniformity is simple enough for us to be able to discover it. But it is just this characteristic of simplicity in the laws of nature hitherto discovered which it would be fallacious to generalise, for it is obvious that simplicity has been a part cause of their discovery, and can, therefore, give no ground for the supposition that other undiscovered laws are equally simple.

The fallacies to which these two kinds of unity have given rise suggest a caution as regards all use in philosophy of general results that science is supposed to have achieved. In the first place, in generalising these results beyond past experience, it is necessary to examine very carefully whether there is not some reason making it more probable that these results should hold of all that has been experienced than that they should hold of things universally. The sum total of what is experienced by mankind is a selection from the sum total of what exists, and any general character exhibited by this selection may be due to the manner of selecting rather than to the general character of that from which experience selects. In the second place, the most general results of science are the least certain and the most liable to be upset by subsequent research. In utilizing these results as the basis of a philosophy, we sacrifice the most valuable and remarkable characteristic of scientific method, namely, that, although almost everything in science is found sooner or later to require some correction, yet this correction is almost always such as to leave untouched, or only slightly modified, the greater part of the results which have been deduced from the premiss subsequently discovered to be faulty. The prudent man of science acquires a certain instinct as to the kind of uses which may be made of present scientific beliefs without incurring the danger of complete and utter refutation from the modifications likely to be introduced by subsequent discoveries. Unfortunately the use of scientific generalisations of a sweeping kind as the basis of philosophy is just that kind of use which an instinct of scientific caution would avoid, since, as a rule, it would only lead to true results if the generalisation upon which it is based stood in no need of correction.

We may illustrate these general considerations by means of two examples, namely, the conservation of energy and the principle of evolution.
b:
The motives which lead men to philosophise are various, and the value of a philosophy depends very largely upon the motive from which it springs. There is, first, the motive of curiosity—the desire to understand the world, to render it coherent, and to escape from the bewilderment produced by fragmentary and disconnected knowledge. This is the scientific motive, and where it is dominant philosophy is conceived as a branch of knowledge, continuous with the sciences, differing from them rather in the generality of its problems than in the methods by which it hopes to solve them. There is, secondly, the motive of consolation—the wish to find in the universe a home for the affections, to believe that reality is akin to what we value, and to persuade ourselves that the apparent indifference of nature is but a veil. This is the religious motive, and it is responsible for much of the metaphysical construction that has been offered as philosophy. There is, thirdly, the motive of moral and social reform—the desire to discover a rational basis for conduct, to justify or to undermine institutions, and to furnish men with a creed by which they may live together. This is the practical motive, and it is apt to colour the whole of a thinker's speculation, sometimes without his knowledge. And there is, fourthly, the motive of logical clarification—the wish to understand what we mean by our assertions, to disentangle confusions, and to exhibit the structure of the concepts we employ. These motives are seldom found in isolation; most philosophies are composites, and the difficulty of estimating them is increased by the fact that a philosopher commonly believes himself to be actuated by curiosity alone, whereas his conclusions may be dictated by hopes and fears of which he is scarcely conscious.

The scientific motive, when it is genuine and not merely professed, imposes upon philosophy a discipline which the other motives do not. It requires that every assertion shall be capable of being brought into relation with fact, and that where fact is wanting the assertion shall be held tentatively, as an hypothesis, not asserted as a revelation. It is a consequence of this discipline that the results of scientific philosophy are modest in proportion to its pretensions. The man who seeks consolation will not be satisfied with a universe which may be indifferent to his aspirations; the man who seeks a creed will not be satisfied with an analysis which dissolves his creed into a set of propositions whose truth cannot be ascertained. Hence there arises a perpetual conflict between those who value philosophy for what it can prove and those who value it for what it can make men feel. It is important to observe that this conflict is not merely temperamental; it turns upon a question of fact, namely, what philosophy can actually accomplish. If philosophy can establish a synoptic view of the universe which is more than a summary of the sciences, then the consolatory and practical motives may be justified in seeking its aid. If it cannot, then those who seek consolation through it are seeking it where it is not to be found, and are likely to be deceived.

Let us consider, then, the claim that philosophy can furnish a view of the universe as a whole. The claim is ancient and has been made in many forms. It appears in the systems of the pre-Socratics, who sought a single principle from which the multiplicity of things might be derived; in the theological synthesis of the Middle Ages, which exhibited the world as a hierarchy culminating in God; in the grandiose constructions of the German idealists, who professed to deduce the whole of reality from the nature of thought; and in the more recent attempts to exhibit the universe as an evolving process with a direction and a goal. In each case the synoptic view is offered as knowledge, and it is claimed that the parts of the world are intelligible only when seen in their relation to the whole. Now it must be admitted that there is a legitimate sense in which philosophy may aim at a synoptic view. The sciences are many, and their results are scattered; the philosopher may attempt to arrange them in an order, to exhibit their mutual bearings, and to indicate the gaps which remain. This is a work of synthesis, and it is valuable, but it is not knowledge of a new kind; it is knowledge of the relations between knowledge. It does not add to our information about the world; it adds to our command of the information we possess. And it is subject to the limitation that the synthesis is provisional, since the sciences are in process of growth and the arrangement which suits one stage may be superseded at the next.

The claim to a synoptic view of a more ambitious kind—the claim to know the universe as a whole, to pronounce upon its ultimate nature, its purpose, and its destiny—stands upon a different footing. Such knowledge, if it were attainable, would be of a kind altogether different from the knowledge which the sciences supply. The sciences proceed by analysis and by the correlation of particulars; they tell us how one part of the world behaves in relation to another, and their laws are laws of connection, not of essence. From such knowledge the nature of the whole cannot be inferred, unless we assume that the whole is of the same character as the parts, which is precisely the point at issue. The inference from the parts to the whole is legitimate only where we have independent reason to believe that the whole is homogeneous with the parts; and in the case of the universe we have no such reason. The universe is not a large sample of which the parts are small samples; it is the totality of things, and the relation of the parts to the whole is not the relation of one part to another. Hence the synoptic view, in so far as it professes to be knowledge, is not knowledge but a construction of the imagination, valuable perhaps as poetry, but not to be confounded with science.

It is worth while to examine the arguments by which the possibility of such knowledge has been defended, since they exhibit the conditions upon which the judgment depends. It is said, in the first place, that the whole is more than the sum of its parts, and that the understanding of the parts requires the understanding of the whole. This is true in a sense, but the sense is not that which the argument requires. In the case of a living organism, or of a work of art, or of a social institution, the parts have a character which depends upon their place in the whole, and the whole has a character which is not the mere aggregate of the parts. But this dependence is a matter of fact, to be established by observation; it is not a universal principle which can be applied to the universe without further inquiry. Moreover, even where the dependence holds, our knowledge of the whole is derived from our knowledge of the parts and of their relations, not from an intuition of the whole as a whole. The biologist does not begin with an intuition of the organism; he begins with observation of its parts and their functions, and his conception of the whole is a construction from these observations. To say that the whole is prior to the parts in the order of knowledge is to reverse the actual procedure of science.

It is said, in the second place, that the universe must be rational, and that philosophy, as the science of reason, can therefore deduce its fundamental character. This argument depends upon an equivocation. The rationality of the universe may mean that it is governed by laws, in the sense that events occur in accordance with uniformities which can be formulated; or it may mean that it is such as to satisfy the demands of our reason, in the sense that its character is what we should desire it to be. The first sense is a hypothesis of science, to be verified by the discovery of laws; the second is a postulate of the affections, not a conclusion of logic. From the fact that the world is intelligible in the first sense nothing follows as to its character in the second sense. A world of blind mechanism may be perfectly intelligible, and a world governed by a benevolent purpose may be so complex as to baffle our understanding. Hence the argument from rationality, when it is examined, is found to rest upon the assumption that the universe must be such as to satisfy our demands, which is precisely the assumption which a scientific philosophy is bound to question.

It is said, in the third place, that the synoptic view is necessary for the conduct of life, since without it we cannot know what to pursue and what to avoid. This argument has a practical force which the others lack, but it does not establish the truth of the view; it establishes only its utility, and even its utility is doubtful. For the conduct of life depends upon a knowledge of particular facts and of the consequences of particular actions, and upon the strength of our desires, rather than upon a theory of the universe. Men have acted wisely and virtuously without any such theory, and men have acted foolishly and cruelly with the aid of the most elaborate systems. The belief that a metaphysical creed is necessary for morals is one of the errors which the study of history should correct. It is true that a creed may give coherence and stability to a moral code, and may supply the emotional force which carries it into practice; but the creed is not the source of the code, and the code may survive the creed. The practical motive, therefore, does not justify the claim to knowledge; it justifies at most the cultivation of a certain attitude of mind, which may be valuable as a discipline, though it is not knowledge.

The conclusion which these considerations suggest is that the synoptic view, in so far as it claims to be knowledge, must be distinguished from the scientific investigation of the world, and that the two cannot be combined into a single enterprise without confusion. The scientific investigation proceeds by the analysis of particular problems, by the formulation of hypotheses, and by the testing of these hypotheses against fact. Its results are partial, provisional, and cumulative; it does not aim at a final view of the whole, and it would not recognise such a view if it were offered, since it has no method of testing it. The synoptic view, on the other hand, proceeds by the construction of a system which shall satisfy the demands of the intellect and the affections; it is not capable of verification, and its value lies in its coherence and in its power to give unity to our thoughts and feelings, not in its correspondence with fact. To confound the two is to do injury to both: to the scientific investigation, because it imposes upon it a task which it cannot perform and a standard by which it must fail; to the synoptic view, because it claims for it a kind of authority which it cannot sustain, and exposes it to the criticism which is appropriate only to science.

It should be observed, however, that the distinction which has been drawn is not a distinction between two kinds of men, but between two kinds of interest which may coexist in the same mind. The same philosopher may be a rigorous analyst in one department and a constructor of systems in another; and the history of philosophy affords many examples of this combination. The question is not whether a man may legitimately pursue both interests, but whether he may legitimately transfer the results of the one to the credit of the other. The answer is that he may not. The results of analysis are knowledge; the results of construction are not knowledge, but something else, which may be called wisdom, or vision, or poetry, according to the temper of the constructor. It is important to recognise this, because the confusion of the two has been the source of much dogmatism and much disillusionment. The man who expects from philosophy a revelation of the meaning of the universe will be disappointed; the man who expects from it a clarification of his ideas and a discipline of his imagination will not be disappointed, provided he does not ask for more than it can give.

The conditions upon which this judgment depends should be stated explicitly. It depends, in the first place, upon the assumption that knowledge is distinguished from other modes of apprehension by its relation to fact, and that the relation to fact is established by the methods of observation and experiment. If this assumption is rejected, and if it is held that there is a mode of apprehension—call it intuition, or intellectual vision, or what you will—which yields knowledge of the whole independently of the sciences, then the conclusion which has been drawn does not follow. It is therefore necessary to consider what can be said for such a mode of apprehension. The claim has been made by many philosophers, and it has been supported by the argument that the sciences are abstract, that they deal with aspects of reality rather than with reality itself, and that the concrete whole can be grasped only by a sympathetic insight which is not discursive. There is force in the contention that the sciences are abstract; they are so by their very nature, since they select certain features of things for study and ignore others. But it does not follow that the concrete whole can be grasped by a mode of insight which dispenses with analysis. The insight, if it occurs, is a private experience, and the assertions to which it gives rise are not capable of being tested by others; hence they cannot be incorporated into the body of knowledge, which is essentially public. The mystic may be right, but he cannot prove that he is right, and the philosopher who adopts his method must abandon the claim to give reasons.

It depends, in the second place, upon the assumption that the universe is not such that its nature can be inferred from the nature of the parts by any process of analogy or extrapolation. If the universe were a whole of the same kind as the wholes with which we are acquainted—an organism, say, or a machine—then the inference from the parts to the whole might be legitimate. But the universe is not a whole of this kind; it is the totality of things, and the categories which apply to wholes within the world do not apply to the world itself. This is a point upon which Kant insisted, and his insistence was justified, though his own construction of a system transcending experience was inconsistent with it. The world is not an object among objects; it is the horizon within which objects appear. Hence the attempt to treat it as an object, and to pronounce upon its character, is doomed to failure, not because our knowledge is incomplete, but because the question is not one which can be answered by the methods of knowledge.

It depends, in the third place, upon the assumption that the value of a philosophy is not to be measured solely by its power to console or to inspire. If the value of philosophy were solely of this kind, then the synoptic view would be justified by its effects, and the question of its truth would be irrelevant. But this is not the case. The value of philosophy, in so far as it is a branch of knowledge, lies in the clarity and rigour of its analyses, and in the extent to which it renders explicit the assumptions of the sciences and of common sense. Its power to console is a by-product, not a criterion; and a philosophy which consoles at the expense of clarity is, from the point of view of knowledge, a corruption. It may be objected that this is to underestimate the importance of the emotional and practical needs which philosophy has traditionally satisfied. The objection is just, but it does not affect the conclusion. The needs exist, and they must be satisfied in some way; but they are not satisfied by being confounded with the needs of knowledge. The man who seeks consolation would do better to seek it in religion or in poetry, where it is offered without the pretence of proof, than in a philosophy which claims to prove what it can only assert.

It remains to consider the bearing of these conclusions upon the particular sciences, and upon the relation of philosophy to them. The sciences, as has been said, proceed by analysis; they do not aim at a synoptic view, and they are not disturbed by the absence of one. But the sciences are not independent of one another, and the problems which arise at their boundaries—the problems of the relation of mind to body, of the nature of causality, of the status of mathematical entities—are philosophical problems, and they are dealt with by philosophical methods. In dealing with them, the philosopher is not constructing a system of the universe; he is analysing concepts, and his results are subject to the same tests as those of the sciences. It is here that philosophy can make its most solid contribution, and it is here that the scientific motive is most clearly justified. The synoptic view, on the other hand, has its place, but its place is at the end, not at the beginning; it is a vision which may arise when the analyses have been made, and which may give unity to their results, but it is not a substitute for them, and it cannot be used to justify them.

The distinction between general conclusion and particular application should be kept in mind. The general conclusion is that the synoptic view of the universe, in so far as it claims to be knowledge, is not attainable by the methods of philosophy, and that the attempt to attain it has been a source of confusion. This conclusion is general, and it holds for any philosophy which makes the claim. But the particular application of it depends upon the particular philosophy under consideration. A system which is offered as poetry, or as a confession of faith, or as a programme of action, is not to be judged by the standard of knowledge, and the criticism which has been directed against the synoptic view does not apply to it. It is only when the system claims to be knowledge that the criticism is in place. Hence the judgment which has been formed is not a judgment upon the value of the synoptic view in all its aspects, but upon its value as knowledge. The distinction is important, because it leaves open the possibility that the synoptic view may be valuable in other ways, and it avoids the dogmatism which would condemn it wholesale.

It may be added, finally, that the recognition of the limits of knowledge is not a counsel of despair. The man who renounces the hope of a final view of the universe does not thereby renounce the pursuit of understanding; he exchanges a dream for a task. The task is the clarification of ideas, the analysis of concepts, and the criticism of assumptions; it is a task which is never finished, and it is a task which yields a satisfaction of its own—the satisfaction of intellectual honesty. The dream is the vision of a system which shall explain all things; it is a dream which has inspired much noble work, and it would be foolish to deny its value. But the dream is not knowledge, and the man who mistakes it for knowledge is led into dogmatism, into intolerance, and into the persecution of those who do not share his vision. The history of philosophy affords abundant evidence of this danger, and the evidence should make us cautious in estimating the claims of any system which professes to have solved the riddle of the universe. The riddle remains, and it is probable that it will always remain; but the attempt to solve it, if it is conducted with honesty and with a sense of its limitations, is not without its reward. It teaches us to distinguish what we know from what we hope, and to value knowledge for its own sake, even when it is knowledge of our own ignorance.

author: Adrian Hartwell
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察日常知觉能提供何种确定知识，区分感觉呈现与物理对象，并提出物质存在和性质的问题。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really one of the most difficult that can be asked. When we have realized the obstacles in the way of a straightforward and confident answer, we shall be well launched on the study of philosophy--for philosophy is merely the attempt to answer such ultimate questions, not carelessly and dogmatically, as we do in ordinary life and even in the sciences, but critically, after exploring all that makes such questions puzzling, and after realizing all the vagueness and confusion that underlie our ordinary ideas.

In daily life, we assume as certain many things which, on a closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great amount of thought enables us to know what it is that we really may believe. In the search for certainty, it is natural to begin with our present experiences, and in some sense, no doubt, knowledge is to be derived from them. But any statement as to what it is that our immediate experiences make us know is very likely to be wrong. It seems to me that I am now sitting in a chair, at a table of a certain shape, on which I see sheets of paper with writing or print. By turning my head I see out of the window buildings and clouds and the sun. I believe that the sun is about ninety-three million miles from the earth; that it is a hot globe many times bigger than the earth; that, owing to the earth's rotation, it rises every morning, and will continue to do so for an indefinite time in the future. I believe that, if any other normal person comes into my room, he will see the same chairs and tables and books and papers as I see, and that the table which I see is the same as the table which I feel pressing against my arm. All this seems to be so evident as to be hardly worth stating, except in answer to a man who doubts whether I know anything. Yet all this may be reasonably doubted, and all of it requires much careful discussion before we can be sure that we have stated it in a form that is wholly true.

To make our difficulties plain, let us concentrate attention on the table. To the eye it is oblong, brown and shiny, to the touch it is smooth and cool and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Any one else who sees and feels and hears the table will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as we try to be more precise our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of the same colour all over, the parts that reflect the light look much brighter than the other parts, and some parts look white because of reflected light. I know that, if I move, the parts that reflect the light will be different, so that the apparent distribution of colours on the table will change. It follows that if several people are looking at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, because no two can see it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the light is reflected.

For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we have already the beginning of one of the distinctions that cause most trouble in philosophy--the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality', between what things seem to be and what they are. The painter wants to know what things seem to be, the practical man and the philosopher want to know what they are; but the philosopher's wish to know this is stronger than the practical man's, and is more troubled by knowledge as to the difficulties of answering the question.

To return to the table. It is evident from what we have found, that there is no colour which pre-eminently appears to be the colour of the table, or even of any one particular part of the table--it appears to be of different colours from different points of view, and there is no reason for regarding some of these as more really its colour than others. And we know that even from a given point of view the colour will seem different by artificial light, or to a colour-blind man, or to a man wearing blue spectacles, while in the dark there will be no colour at all, though to touch and hearing the table will be unchanged. This colour is not something which is inherent in the table, but something depending upon the table and the spectator and the way the light falls on the table. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we only mean the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator from an ordinary point of view under usual conditions of light. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and therefore, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that, in itself, the table has any one particular colour.

The same thing applies to the texture. With the naked eye one can see the grain, but otherwise the table looks smooth and even. If we looked at it through a microscope, we should see roughnesses and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to the naked eye. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real, but that in turn would be changed by a still more powerful microscope. If, then, we cannot trust what we see with the naked eye, why should we trust what we see through a microscope? Thus, again, the confidence in our senses with which we began deserts us.

The shape of the table is no better. We are all in the habit of judging as to the 'real' shapes of things, and we do this so unreflectingly that we come to think we actually see the real shapes. But, in fact, as we all have to learn if we try to draw, a given thing looks different in shape from every different point of view. If our table is 'really' rectangular, it will look, from almost all points of view, as if it had two acute angles and two obtuse angles. If opposite sides are parallel, they will look as if they converged to a point away from the spectator; if they are of equal length, they will look as if the nearer side were longer. All these things are not commonly noticed in looking at a table, because experience has taught us to construct the 'real' shape from the apparent shape, and the 'real' shape is what interests us as practical men. But the 'real' shape is not what we see; it is something inferred from what we see. And what we see is constantly changing in shape as we move about the room; so that here again the senses seem not to give us the truth about the table itself, but only about the appearance of the table.

Similar difficulties arise when we consider the sense of touch. It is true that the table always gives us a sensation of hardness, and we feel that it resists pressure. But the sensation we obtain depends upon how hard we press the table and also upon what part of the body we press with; thus the various sensations due to various pressures or various parts of the body cannot be supposed to reveal directly any definite property of the table, but at most to be signs of some property which perhaps causes all the sensations, but is not actually apparent in any of them. And the same applies still more obviously to the sounds which can be elicited by rapping the table.

Thus it becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if there is one, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence, two very difficult questions at once arise; namely, (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be?

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of 'sense-data' to the things that are immediately known in sensation: such things as colours, sounds, smells, hardnesses, roughnesses, and so on. We shall give the name 'sensation' to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever we see a colour, we have a sensation of the colour, but the colour itself is a sense-datum, not a sensation. The colour is that of which we are immediately aware, and the awareness itself is the sensation. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the table, it must be by means of the sense-data--brown colour, oblong shape, smoothness, etc.--which we associate with the table; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the table is the sense-data, or even that the sense-data are directly properties of the table. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the sense-data to the real table, supposing there is such a thing.

The real table, if it exists, we will call a 'physical object'. Thus we have to consider the relation of sense-data to physical objects. The collection of all physical objects is called 'matter'. Thus our two questions may be re-stated as follows: (1) Is there any such thing as matter? (2) If so, what is its nature?
b:
The question before us is not whether we know this or that particular fact about the furniture of the world, but what, if anything, the ordinary exercise of perception can yield in the way of certainty; and the answer, I shall argue, is both less and more than is commonly supposed. Less, because the greater part of what we take ourselves to know through the senses is inference, and inference of a precarious kind; more, because there remains a residue of immediate knowledge which, though narrow and in a sense trivial, is yet immune to the doubts that beset our beliefs about physical things. It is necessary, in the first place, to distinguish with some care between what is given in sensation and what is judged or inferred on the occasion of sensation. When I look at a table, there is present to me a certain patch of colour, of a particular shade and shape, surrounded by other patches; when I pass my hand over it, there is a certain sensation of resistance and smoothness; and these, together with similar data of touch and sight, are what I shall call sense-data, or the appearances of the table. The table itself, the physical object, is not given in this way. It is something inferred, or at least something believed, as possessing a unity and a permanence which no single sense-datum possesses. The colour which is present to me varies with the light, with the angle of vision, with the condition of my eye; the shape varies with perspective; the smoothness varies with the pressure of my fingers and the temperature of my hand. Yet we believe that there is one object, persisting through these variations, which is the cause of them and which possesses a definite colour, shape, and texture of its own. It is this belief that constitutes the ordinary conviction of the existence of a physical world, and it is this belief whose grounds I wish to examine.

Now it must be observed that the distinction between sense-data and physical objects is not a distinction between two kinds of thing given with equal immediacy. Only the sense-datum is immediate; the physical object is reached by a process which, however rapid and habitual, is nevertheless an inference. When I see a table, I do not first see a coloured patch and then infer a table, in the explicit manner of the philosopher; but the logical relation is nevertheless one of inference, and the inference is of the same general character as that by which I conclude that a friend is in the room because I hear his voice. The difference is that in the case of perception the inference has become so automatic that its conclusion is confounded with its premise. This confusion is the source of no small part of the difficulties of philosophy. If we once recognise that the physical object is not given but inferred, we shall be in a position to ask what warrant the inference possesses, and whether that warrant is sufficient to justify the confidence with which we ordinarily affirm the existence of an external world.

Let us consider what can be said for the inference. The sense-data which we attribute to a single object exhibit a certain order and coherence. They recur in regular sequences; they are connected with one another by relations of similarity and difference which are not arbitrary; and, above all, they are connected with our own movements and with the movements of other bodies in a manner which enables us to predict them. The colour which I now see will be replaced by another if I move my head; the resistance which I now feel will cease if I withdraw my hand; and these transitions are themselves regular and predictable. It is this regularity which leads us to postulate a permanent cause of our transient sensations, and the postulate is justified, in the first instance, by its success in enabling us to anticipate and control the course of our experience. But success in prediction is not the same thing as proof of existence. A systematic dream may possess the utmost coherence, and a consistent fiction may be as serviceable for prediction as a truth. The hypothesis of a physical world is thus, at best, the simplest and most convenient of the hypotheses which account for the order of our sensations; and simplicity and convenience, though they are the grounds upon which we act, are not grounds upon which we can claim absolute certainty.

It is necessary here to distinguish between two questions which are commonly confounded. The first is whether there exists anything beyond our sense-data; the second is what is the nature of that something. To the first question, I think we must answer that the existence of something independent of our sensations is highly probable, though not demonstrable. The order of our sensations is not wholly within our control; we cannot, by an act of will, cause the table to appear where no table is, nor prevent it from appearing where it is. This involuntary character of perception suggests a cause external to ourselves, and the hypothesis of a physical world is the most natural and fruitful explanation of that cause. But when we pass to the second question, and ask what the physical object is in itself, we find ourselves in far greater difficulty. We know the object only through the sense-data which it causes in us, and these sense-data are relative to our organs and our position. The colour which we see is not in the object, but is the effect of the object upon our eyes; the sound is not in the object, but is the effect of its vibrations upon our ears. What the object is apart from these effects, we cannot know; we can only describe it as the unknown cause of our sensations, or, more cautiously, as a system of relations which we construct for the purpose of predicting them. The physical world, in short, is known to us only in its structure, not in its intrinsic quality; and even its structure is known only so far as it is reflected in the structure of our sensations.

It follows that the certainty which we possess in perception is confined within very narrow limits. What is certain is the existence of the sense-datum at the moment of its occurrence. When I see a patch of colour, it is certain that I see it, and certain, further, that there is a seeing, a subject to whom the colour appears. This is the foundation upon which all empirical knowledge rests, and it is a foundation which no subsequent discovery can undermine. But the moment we pass from the sense-datum to the object which we believe to cause it, we pass from certainty to probability, and from probability of the highest kind to probability which may be diminished by reflection. The belief in the existence of the table is a belief which no sane man can seriously doubt in the conduct of life; but it is a belief which, in the study, we must recognise as an inference, and an inference which is not logically coercive. The difference between the two attitudes is not a difference in the strength of our conviction, but a difference in the kind of evidence upon which the conviction rests. In action, we are justified in acting upon the hypothesis which has the greatest predictive success; in reflection, we are bound to acknowledge that the hypothesis remains a hypothesis.

It is worth while to illustrate this by an example which brings out the conditions upon which our judgments depend. Suppose that I see a straight stick half immersed in water, and that the stick appears bent. I have here two sense-data which are in conflict: the visual datum of the bent stick, and the tactual datum, obtained by running my hand along the stick, of a straight stick. The ordinary man resolves the conflict by saying that the stick is really straight, and that the appearance of bending is due to refraction. But this resolution is itself an inference, and it depends upon a knowledge of the laws of optics which is not given in the sense-data themselves. If I were ignorant of these laws, I might equally well conclude that the stick is really bent, and that the tactual datum is illusory; or that there are two sticks, one bent and one straight; or that the water has the power of producing a bent appearance without any corresponding object. Each of these hypotheses would account for the facts, though some would be less convenient than others. The judgment that the stick is straight is thus seen to depend upon a body of general knowledge, and upon a preference for the hypothesis which fits into the widest system of our beliefs. It is not a judgment which is forced upon us by the sense-data alone. And what is true of the stick is true of the table and of the whole physical world. Our judgments about physical objects are always relative to a system of assumptions, and the certainty which they possess is the certainty of coherence within that system, not the certainty of immediate intuition.

This conclusion may appear to be a scepticism, but it is not a scepticism of the kind which paralyses action. It is rather an analysis of the kind of knowledge which perception affords, and an acknowledgment of its limits. The man who says that he knows the table exists is saying something which is true in the ordinary sense of knowledge, but he is not saying something which is immune to philosophical doubt. The man who says that he knows the table is a fiction is saying something which is false in the ordinary sense, but he is not saying something which can be refuted by an appeal to the sense-data alone. Between these two positions there is a middle ground, which is the ground of the philosopher: the recognition that the physical world is a construction, necessary for action and justified by its success, but not given in intuition and not capable of demonstration. The certainty of the sense-datum is the certainty of the moment; the certainty of the physical object is the certainty of a well-tested hypothesis. To confuse the two is to misunderstand the nature of empirical knowledge; to deny the first is to deny the foundation of all knowledge; to deny the second is to deny the possibility of science. The wise man will accept both, but he will accept them with a clear understanding of the different grounds upon which they rest.

It remains to consider whether the general conclusion which I have stated is to be regarded as a conclusion about knowledge in general, or only about knowledge in a particular situation. I think it must be regarded as general in one respect and particular in another. It is general in that it applies to all our perceptual knowledge of physical objects, whatever the object and whatever the sense. There is no physical object whose existence can be demonstrated from sense-data alone; there is no perceptual judgment which is not in some degree an inference. But it is particular in that the degree of probability which attaches to any given judgment depends upon the particular circumstances in which it is made, and upon the particular system of beliefs within which it is embedded. The judgment that there is a table before me is more probable when I am in good light, when I have just touched the table, and when I am in a state of normal health, than when I am in darkness, when I have no tactual evidence, and when I am fatigued or feverish. The general conclusion is that all such judgments are inferences; the particular conclusion is that this inference is more or less warranted according to the coherence of the sense-data with one another and with the rest of our experience. It is this double character of perceptual knowledge—general in its logical form, particular in its degree of warrant—that makes it so difficult to classify, and that has led philosophers alternately to exaggerate and to disparage its certainty.

I shall conclude, then, with a statement of the position which seems to me to be warranted by the foregoing analysis. The sense-datum is the only element in perception which is immediately certain; and even this certainty is confined to the moment of its occurrence, and to the bare fact that it occurs. The physical object is an inference from sense-data, justified by the order and coherence of those data, and by the success of the inference in enabling us to predict and control our experience. The existence of the physical world is therefore probable, but not certain; and its nature is known to us only in its relational structure, not in its intrinsic quality. The judgments which we make about particular physical objects are inferences within a system, and their warrant varies with the circumstances and with the coherence of the system. To recognise this is not to abandon the belief in an external world, but to understand the kind of belief which it is. It is a belief which we are justified in holding, but not a belief which we can claim to have proved; and the man who holds it with a clear consciousness of its grounds is in a better position than the man who holds it dogmatically, even though the practical conduct of both may be the same. For philosophy, as I have elsewhere remarked, is not a body of doctrines but a habit of mind; and the habit of mind which perceives the difference between the certainty of the moment and the probability of the inference is the beginning of wisdom.

author: Adrian Hartwell
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，评估独立于个人经验的物质世界是否存在，区分直接确定的经验与支持公共世界的证据。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
In this chapter we have to ask ourselves whether, in any sense at all, there is such a thing as matter. Is there a table which has a certain intrinsic nature, and continues to exist when I am not looking, or is the table merely a product of my imagination, a dream-table in a very prolonged dream? This question is of the greatest importance. For if we cannot be sure of the independent existence of objects, we cannot be sure of the independent existence of other people's bodies, and therefore still less of other people's minds, since we have no grounds for believing in their minds except such as are derived from observing their bodies. Thus if we cannot be sure of the independent existence of objects, we shall be left alone in a desert--it may be that the whole outer world is nothing but a dream, and that we alone exist. This is an uncomfortable possibility; but although it cannot be strictly proved to be false, there is not the slightest reason to suppose that it is true. In this chapter we have to see why this is the case.

Before we embark upon doubtful matters, let us try to find some more or less fixed point from which to start. Although we are doubting the physical existence of the table, we are not doubting the existence of the sense-data which made us think there was a table; we are not doubting that, while we look, a certain colour and shape appear to us, and while we press, a certain sensation of hardness is experienced by us. All this, which is psychological, we are not calling in question. In fact, whatever else may be doubtful, some at least of our immediate experiences seem absolutely certain.

Descartes (1596-1650), the founder of modern philosophy, invented a method which may still be used with profit--the method of systematic doubt. He determined that he would believe nothing which he did not see quite clearly and distinctly to be true. Whatever he could bring himself to doubt, he would doubt, until he saw reason for not doubting it. By applying this method he gradually became convinced that the only existence of which he could be quite certain was his own. He imagined a deceitful demon, who presented unreal things to his senses in a perpetual phantasmagoria; it might be very improbable that such a demon existed, but still it was possible, and therefore doubt concerning things perceived by the senses was possible.

But doubt concerning his own existence was not possible, for if he did not exist, no demon could deceive him. If he doubted, he must exist; if he had any experiences whatever, he must exist. Thus his own existence was an absolute certainty to him. 'I think, therefore I am,' he said (Cogito, ergo sum); and on the basis of this certainty he set to work to build up again the world of knowledge which his doubt had laid in ruins. By inventing the method of doubt, and by showing that subjective things are the most certain, Descartes performed a great service to philosophy, and one which makes him still useful to all students of the subject.

But some care is needed in using Descartes' argument. 'I think, therefore I am' says rather more than is strictly certain. It might seem as though we were quite sure of being the same person to-day as we were yesterday, and this is no doubt true in some sense. But the real Self is as hard to arrive at as the real table, and does not seem to have that absolute, convincing certainty that belongs to particular experiences. When I look at my table and see a certain brown colour, what is quite certain at once is not 'I am seeing a brown colour', but rather, 'a brown colour is being seen'. This of course involves something (or somebody) which (or who) sees the brown colour; but it does not of itself involve that more or less permanent person whom we call 'I'. So far as immediate certainty goes, it might be that the something which sees the brown colour is quite momentary, and not the same as the something which has some different experience the next moment.

Thus it is our particular thoughts and feelings that have primitive certainty. And this applies to dreams and hallucinations as well as to normal perceptions: when we dream or see a ghost, we certainly do have the sensations we think we have, but for various reasons it is held that no physical object corresponds to these sensations. Thus the certainty of our knowledge of our own experiences does not have to be limited in any way to allow for exceptional cases. Here, therefore, we have, for what it is worth, a solid basis from which to begin our pursuit of knowledge.

The problem we have to consider is this: Granted that we are certain of our own sense-data, have we any reason for regarding them as signs of the existence of something else, which we can call the physical object? When we have enumerated all the sense-data which we should naturally regard as connected with the table, have we said all there is to say about the table, or is there still something else--something not a sense-datum, something which persists when we go out of the room? Common sense unhesitatingly answers that there is. What can be bought and sold and pushed about and have a cloth laid on it, and so on, cannot be a mere collection of sense-data. If the cloth completely hides the table, we shall derive no sense-data from the table, and therefore, if the table were merely sense-data, it would have ceased to exist, and the cloth would be suspended in empty air, resting, by a miracle, in the place where the table formerly was. This seems plainly absurd; but whoever wishes to become a philosopher must learn not to be frightened by absurdities.

One great reason why it is felt that we must secure a physical object in addition to the sense-data, is that we want the same object for different people. When ten people are sitting round a dinner-table, it seems preposterous to maintain that they are not seeing the same tablecloth, the same knives and forks and spoons and glasses. But the sense-data are private to each separate person; what is immediately present to the sight of one is not immediately present to the sight of another: they all see things from slightly different points of view, and therefore see them slightly differently. Thus, if there are to be public neutral objects, which can be in some sense known to many different people, there must be something over and above the private and particular sense-data which appear to various people. What reason, then, have we for believing that there are such public neutral objects?

The first answer that naturally occurs to one is that, although different people may see the table slightly differently, still they all see more or less similar things when they look at the table, and the variations in what they see follow the laws of perspective and reflection of light, so that it is easy to arrive at a permanent object underlying all the different people's sense-data. I bought my table from the former occupant of my room; I could not buy his sense-data, which died when he went away, but I could and did buy the confident expectation of more or less similar sense-data. Thus it is the fact that different people have similar sense-data, and that one person in a given place at different times has similar sense-data, which makes us suppose that over and above the sense-data there is a permanent public object which underlies or causes the sense-data of various people at various times.

Now in so far as the above considerations depend upon supposing that there are other people besides ourselves, they beg the very question at issue. Other people are represented to me by certain sense-data, such as the sight of them or the sound of their voices, and if I had no reason to believe that there were physical objects independent of my sense-data, I should have no reason to believe that other people exist except as part of my dream. Thus, when we are trying to show that there must be objects independent of our own sense-data, we cannot appeal to the testimony of other people, since this testimony itself consists of sense-data, and does not reveal other people's experiences unless our own sense-data are signs of things existing independently of us. We must therefore, if possible, find, in our own purely private experiences, characteristics which show, or tend to show, that there are in the world things other than ourselves and our private experiences.
b:
The question whether a material world exists independently of individual experience is not, as it is sometimes supposed, a question of fact to be settled by experiment, but a question concerning the interpretation of evidence and the logical status of the inferences we make from it. To answer it, we must first distinguish with care between what is directly given in experience and what is inferred; for confusion upon this point is the source of most of the traditional perplexities.

What is directly certain, in the strict sense, is the existence of particular sensible data—colours, sounds, tactual qualities, and the like—together with the relations among them at the moment of their occurrence. When I see a table, what is indubitable is that a certain patch of colour, of a certain shape, is present to my view. That the table exists as a physical object, possessing a surface and a back and an interior, is not given in the same immediate manner; it is an inference, though an inference so habitual that it has come to seem like a datum. The distinction is not merely verbal. It marks the boundary between propositions which it would be absurd to doubt and propositions which, however firmly we may believe them, rest upon grounds capable of being stated and examined.

Now the evidence which supports belief in a public material world is of a peculiar kind. It consists, first, in the coherence and orderliness of sensible data: the appearances I call the table follow one another according to rules, and these rules connect them with appearances of other kinds—with tactual and muscular sensations, with the testimony of other persons, and with the success of predictions. Secondly, there is the fact that sensible data are not private in the manner one might at first suppose; for I find that other persons report data which, though not identical with mine, are correlated with mine in a systematic way, and that the correlations hold irrespective of my wishes. Thirdly, there is the enormous simplification effected by the hypothesis of a public world: a single system of physical objects, obeying uniform laws, accounts for the whole manifold of actual and possible experience, whereas any attempt to dispense with it leaves us with a chaotic succession of private appearances and no principle of connection.

These considerations, however, do not amount to a demonstration. It is important to observe that the argument from coherence and simplification is of the nature of an inference to the best explanation, not a deduction. Other hypotheses are logically possible. One may conceive, for instance, that the order of our experience is produced directly by a deity or by some impersonal principle, without the intervention of anything resembling matter; or that the whole is a dream of unusual consistency; or, more subtly, that what we call the physical world is a construction out of actual and possible sensible data, so that the "independent" world is not an entity over and above experience but a systematic way of describing the connections among experiences. Each of these hypotheses can be framed so as to save the appearances. The question is therefore not whether the material world can be proved to exist—in the strict sense it cannot—but whether the hypothesis of an independent material world is the most reasonable among the alternatives, and upon what conditions that reasonableness depends.

Here we must note the conditions upon which our judgment rests. The inference presupposes the uniformity of nature, or at least a sufficient regularity in the succession of data to make prediction possible; it presupposes the trustworthiness of memory, without which no accumulation of evidence could occur; and it presupposes the general reliability of testimony, since the public character of the world is established in large part by the agreement of different observers. If these presuppositions were undermined—if, for example, memory were systematically deceptive, or if the reports of different observers were found to be wholly uncorrelated—the inference would lose its force. It is therefore a mistake to regard the belief in an external world as either a self-evident truth or a groundless prejudice; it is a reasoned hypothesis, whose warrant is empirical and whose certainty is of a different order from that of the immediate data.

A further distinction must be drawn between the general conclusion and the particular knowledge we claim in specific situations. The general conclusion is that there exists, with a very high degree of probability, a system of physical objects independent of any particular observer, and that this system is the best available explanation of the order of experience. But in any particular case—when I judge that the table before me is a real table and not a hallucination—the grounds are more specific: the agreement of sight with touch, the persistence of the appearance when I look again, the corroboration of other persons, and the absence of any indication of abnormal conditions. A man who has taken a drug, or who is delirious, may have data qualitatively similar to those of a waking man, yet we rightly discount his testimony because we know that in his condition the usual correlations fail. Thus the general hypothesis of a material world, and the particular judgment that this or that object is material, are supported by different considerations and are liable to different kinds of doubt.

It may be objected that this account leaves the existence of the external world hanging upon a probability, and that common sense demands something more. To this the reply is that common sense itself, when examined, rests upon precisely such probabilities; the confidence of the plain man is the confidence of a habit which has never been analysed. The philosopher does not diminish the practical certainty of the belief by exhibiting its grounds; he merely refuses to confound a high degree of rational warrant with logical indubitability. The world of physics, indeed, is not the world of immediate appearance; it is a construction, inferred and corrected, whose entities—atoms, fields, and the rest—are known only through their effects upon sensible data. Yet the construction is justified by its power to unify and predict, and it is this justification, rather than any immediate intuition, which gives the belief in an independent world its rational standing.

I conclude, then, that the existence of a material world independent of individual experience cannot be demonstrated with the certainty belonging to the data of sense, but that it is a hypothesis of overwhelming rational probability, supported by the coherence, the public corroboration, and the predictive fertility of experience. The distinction between the immediate and the inferred is essential to any clear statement of the problem; and the recognition that our conclusion is general and probable, while our particular judgments depend upon specific correlations and conditions, preserves us alike from dogmatism and from the barren scepticism which confounds the absence of demonstration with the absence of reasonable grounds.

author: Adrian Hartwell
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察通过事件关系界定时刻的方法，讨论同时性与连续性假设如何适用于经验。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
If a relational theory of instants is constructed, in which an "instant" is defined as a group of events simultaneous with each other and not all simultaneous with any event outside the group, then if our resulting series of instants is to be compact, it must be possible, if x wholly precedes y, to find an event z, simultaneous with part of x, which wholly precedes some event which wholly precedes y. Now this requires that the number of events concerned should be infinite in any finite period of time. If this is to be the case in the world of one man's sense-data, and if each sense-datum is to have not less than a certain finite temporal extension, it will be necessary to assume that we always have an infinite number of sense-data simultaneous with any given sense-datum. Applying similar considerations to space, and assuming that sense-data are to have not less than a certain spatial extension, it will be necessary to suppose that an infinite number of sense-data overlap spatially with any given sense-datum. This hypothesis is possible, if we suppose a single sense-datum, e.g. in sight, to be a finite surface, enclosing other surfaces which are also single sense-data. But there are difficulties in such a hypothesis, and I do not know whether these difficulties could be successfully met. If they cannot, we must do one of two things: either declare that the world of one man's sense-data is not continuous, or else refuse to admit that there is any lower limit to the duration and extension of a single sense-datum. I do not know what is the right course to adopt as regards these alternatives. The logical analysis we have been considering provides the apparatus for dealing with the various hypotheses, and the empirical decision between them is a problem for the psychologist.

(3) We have now to consider the logical answer to the alleged difficulties of the mathematical theory of motion, or rather to the positive theory which is urged on the other side. The view urged explicitly by Bergson, and implied in the doctrines of many philosophers, is, that a motion is something indivisible, not validly analysable into a series of states. This is part of a much more general doctrine, which holds that analysis always falsifies, because the parts of a complex whole are different, as combined in that whole, from what they would otherwise be. It is very difficult to state this doctrine in any form which has a precise meaning. Often arguments are used which have no bearing whatever upon the question. It is urged, for example, that when a man becomes a father, his nature is altered by the new relation in which he finds himself, so that he is not strictly identical with the man who was previously not a father. This may be true, but it is a causal psychological fact, not a logical fact. The doctrine would require that a man who is a father cannot be strictly identical with a man who is a son, because he is modified in one way by the relation of fatherhood and in another by that of sonship. In fact, we may give a precise statement of the doctrine we are combating in the form: There can never be two facts concerning the same thing. A fact concerning a thing always is or involves a relation to one or more entities; thus two facts concerning the same thing would involve two relations of the same thing. But the doctrine in question holds that a thing is so modified by its relations that it cannot be the same in one relation as in another. Hence, if this doctrine is true, there can never be more than one fact concerning any one thing. I do not think the philosophers in question have realised that this is the precise statement of the view they advocate, because in this form the view is so contrary to plain truth that its falsehood is evident as soon as it is stated. The discussion of this question, however, involves so many logical subtleties, and is so beset with difficulties, that I shall not pursue it further at present.

When once the above general doctrine is rejected, it is obvious that, where there is change, there must be a succession of states. There cannot be change--and motion is only a particular case of change--unless there is something different at one time from what there is at some other time. Change, therefore, must involve relations and complexity, and must demand analysis. So long as our analysis has only gone as far as other smaller changes, it is not complete; if it is to be complete, it must end with terms that are not changes, but are related by a relation of earlier and later. In the case of changes which appear continuous, such as motions, it seems to be impossible to find anything other than change so long as we deal with finite periods of time, however short. We are thus driven back, by the logical necessities of the case, to the conception of instants without duration, or at any rate without any duration which even the most delicate instruments can reveal. This conception, though it can be made to seem difficult, is really easier than any other that the facts allow. It is a kind of logical framework into which any tenable theory must fit--not necessarily itself the statement of the crude facts, but a form in which statements which are true of the crude facts can be made by a suitable interpretation. The direct consideration of the crude facts of the physical world has been undertaken in earlier lectures; in the present lecture, we have only been concerned to show that nothing in the crude facts is inconsistent with the mathematical doctrine of continuity, or demands a continuity of a radically different kind from that of mathematical motion.
b:
The proposal to define an instant by its relations to events is attractive because it replaces a mysterious entity with a structure of observable relations. We may say, roughly, that two events are simultaneous when neither precedes the other, and that an instant is a maximal class of mutually simultaneous events. Yet this definition is not a simple report of experience; it already presupposes a logical apparatus and a decision about how relations are to be treated. The question is therefore not whether the definition is convenient, but what assumptions it conceals and under what conditions those assumptions are justified.

Consider first the relational scheme. Let events be related by a relation of precedence, and let simultaneity be defined as the absence of precedence in either direction. For this to yield instants rather than a confused heap, the relation must be transitive and must exclude circularity: if A precedes B and B precedes C, then A precedes C, and no event may precede itself. Given such an ordering, we may group events into classes whose members are mutually simultaneous and which are maximal with respect to that property. An instant is then not a thing but a logical construction out of events. This construction has the merit of economy, but its merit depends upon the ordering being sufficiently determinate. Where the relation is vague or incomplete, the classes may overlap, and the supposed instants may fail to be unique.

The assumption of continuity is more delicate. To speak of a continuous series of instants is to suppose that between any two instants there is another, and that the series has the order of the real numbers rather than of the integers. Experience, however, presents us with events that are extended and often overlapping; it does not present us with points of time. The continuity of time is thus an idealisation, useful for the mathematician and indispensable for the physicist who employs differential equations, but not directly given. We may justify it by its success in coordinating observations, yet we must not mistake a successful convention for a discovered fact. The same caution applies to simultaneity: if simultaneity is defined by the absence of a causal relation, then events at a distance may be neither earlier nor later in any observable sense, and the assignment of a common instant may depend upon a convention of signalling. In such a case the definition records a decision about how to coordinate observations rather than a property inherent in the events themselves.

An example will make the point. Suppose two flashes of light are observed at different places, and suppose we have no means of deciding whether one preceded the other except by the arrival of signals. If the signals travel with finite velocity, the judgement of simultaneity will depend upon the frame from which the observations are coordinated. We may, if we wish, define a universal simultaneity by choosing a preferred frame, but the choice is not forced by the observations. What is forced is a relation of causal connectibility: some pairs of events can be connected by a signal, others cannot. The former may be ordered; the latter may be treated as simultaneous by convention. Thus the relational definition, when applied to empirical material, yields a structure that is partly determined and partly stipulated.

The general conclusion is that defining instants by event relations is legitimate as a logical construction, provided the ordering relation is transitive, irreflexive, and sufficiently determinate. Continuity, however, is an idealisation that experience supports only indirectly, through the success of the theories that employ it. In particular circumstances—for instance, where signals of finite velocity are the only means of coordination—simultaneity may be conventional rather than factual. The distinction between what is given and what is constructed is not always sharp, but it is essential if we are to avoid attributing to the world the simplicity of our own definitions.

author: Adrian Hartwell
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，区分连续性在逻辑、感觉与物理层面的不同问题，讨论经验能否验证连续世界的假设。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
(a) Are series possessing mathematical continuity logically
 possible?

 (b) Assuming that they are possible logically, are they not
 impossible as applied to actual sense-data, because, among actual
 sense-data, there are no such fixed mutually external terms as are
 to be found, e.g., in the series of fractions?

 (c) Does not the assumption of points and instants make the whole
 mathematical account fictitious?

 (d) Finally, assuming that all these objections have been answered,
 is there, in actual empirical fact, any sufficient reason to believe
 the world of sense continuous?

Let us consider these questions in succession.

(a) The question of the logical possibility of the mathematical continuum turns partly on the elementary misunderstandings we considered at the beginning of the present lecture, partly on the possibility of the mathematical infinite, which will occupy our next two lectures, and partly on the logical form of the answer to the Bergsonian objection which we stated a few minutes ago. I shall say no more on this topic at present, since it is desirable first to complete the psychological answer.

(b) The question whether sense-data are composed of mutually external units is not one which can be decided by empirical evidence. It is often urged that, as a matter of immediate experience, the sensible flux is devoid of divisions, and is falsified by the dissections of the intellect.
