Where the aristocracy is a closed body, with a monopoly of office and a distinct corporate interest, it is apt to govern in its own favour, and its administrative capacity, however great in the routine of business, is liable to be perverted by the desire to preserve its own privileges. The history of aristocratic governments is full of instances of great administrative ability combined with a systematic disregard of the interests of the majority; and the reason is not far to seek. The governing body, having a common interest in maintaining its position, develops a high degree of esprit de corps, and this esprit de corps, while it promotes efficiency in the execution of measures, also promotes a disposition to resist all measures which would diminish the power of the body. The professional element is here strong, but the competitive element is weak, and the conflict of interests is not sufficiently provided for.

In a democracy, the conditions are different. The administrative capacity of a democratic government depends upon the existence of a body of trained officials, upon the extent to which the public is capable of forming a judgment upon administrative questions, and upon the degree in which the interests of the administrators are separated from the interests of the majority. Where the democratic government is based upon a wide suffrage, and where the offices are filled by election, the tendency is to select persons for their popularity rather than for their capacity, and to make the tenure of office depend upon the favour of the multitude. This tendency is a real danger to administrative capacity; but it is not inseparable from democracy. The experience of some democratic governments shows that it is possible to combine popular control with the existence of a permanent and trained civil service, and that the two are not only compatible but mutually supporting. The permanent official supplies the knowledge which the elected person cannot be expected to possess; the elected person supplies the control which the permanent official cannot be trusted to exercise over himself. The competition of parties, moreover, supplies a stimulus to efficiency, in so far as each party is compelled to justify its conduct before the public; but it also supplies a temptation to sacrifice the permanent interests of the administration to the exigencies of party warfare. The conflict of interests, therefore, is present in a democracy in a different form from that which it assumes in an aristocracy; it is not the conflict between the governing body and the community, but the conflict between the parties, and between the administrators and the public.

These considerations lead me to distinguish between the general conclusions which may be affirmed of all governments, and the particular conclusions which depend upon the circumstances of each. The general conclusions are these: that administrative capacity requires a body of persons possessing the requisite knowledge; that it requires a stimulus to exertion, which is best supplied by competition and publicity; and that it requires such an adjustment of interests as shall prevent the administrators from using their power for their own advantage. These conditions are universal, in the sense that no government can permanently retain administrative capacity without them. But the particular conclusions, as to how these conditions are to be secured, depend upon the form of government and upon the state of society. In a country where the general level of education is low, and where the public is incapable of forming a judgment upon administrative questions, the control of the administrators must be exercised by some body of persons who are capable of understanding the business, and who have an interest in maintaining efficiency; and this body may be an hereditary aristocracy, or a body of proprietors, or a council of persons selected for their knowledge. In a country where education is widely diffused, and where public opinion is capable of exercising a real control, the control may be exercised by the public itself, through its representatives, provided that the permanent officials are protected from the pressure of momentary opinion. The same general principle, therefore, leads to different conclusions in different circumstances; and it is a mark of the empirical spirit in politics to recognise that the question is not which form of government is absolutely best, but which form is best adapted to the circumstances of the case.

It is necessary, however, to guard against a possible misinterpretation. The doctrine that administrative capacity depends upon the adjustment of interests is not to be confounded with the doctrine that it depends upon the mere multiplication of checks. A government may be so checked that it can do nothing; and a government which can do nothing has no administrative capacity. The object of the adjustment of interests is not to paralyse the administration, but to prevent it from being perverted. There is a balance to be struck between the vigour which comes from unity of direction and the security which comes from the division of power; and the balance is not the same in all circumstances. In time of war, or of great national emergency, the need of unity is greater, and the checks may be relaxed with advantage; in time of peace, and in the ordinary course of administration, the checks are more necessary. The judgment of the statesman consists in discerning the degree of each which the circumstances require; and this judgment cannot be reduced to a rule, but must be formed by the exercise of a cultivated understanding, instructed by experience and by the comparison of different governments.

I may add, as a further illustration, the case of a government which is administered by a body of persons selected by examination, and who hold office during good behaviour. Such a body possesses the professional knowledge which is the first condition of administrative capacity; and it is protected from the pressure of momentary opinion, which is a security against corruption. But it is exposed to the danger of becoming a caste, and of using its knowledge to resist improvement. The remedy is to be found in the publicity of its proceedings, in the comparison of its conduct with that of other bodies, and in the existence of a power of control exterior to itself. Where these remedies are absent, the professional body is apt to become narrow and self-sufficient; where they are present, it may be made one of the most efficient instruments of government. The example shows that the same institution may be a source of strength or of weakness, according to the conditions with which it is surrounded; and it confirms the general conclusion that administrative capacity is not a matter of form, but of the relation between the administrators, the public, and the interests which they are called upon to regulate.

I have confined myself in this discourse to the conditions of administrative capacity, and have not attempted to determine the question of the best form of government. That question is distinct, and requires a separate consideration. But I may observe, in conclusion, that the analysis which I have given suggests a criterion by which forms of government may be compared. The form of government which, in a given state of society, is most likely to secure the conditions of administrative capacity, is, pro tanto, the best; and the form which is least likely to secure them is, pro tanto, the worst. This criterion is not the only one; for government has other ends besides the efficient conduct of business, and the cultivation of the intelligence and virtue of the people is an end not less important than the execution of measures. But it is a criterion which is often neglected, and which deserves to be kept in view; for a government which is incapable of conducting business with knowledge and integrity will fail in all its other ends, and the most excellent constitution will be of little value if it is not supported by an administration capable of carrying its provisions into effect.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，比较政府的能力不足与积极危害，考察代议制度面临的知识水平和利益偏向问题。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The defects of any form of government may be either negative or positive. It is negatively defective if it does not concentrate in the hands of the authorities power sufficient to fulfill the necessary offices of a government, or if it does not sufficiently develop by exercise the active capacities and social feelings of the individual citizens. On neither of these points is it necessary that much should be said at this stage of our inquiry.

The want of an amount power in the government adequate to preserve order and allow of progress in the people is incident rather to a wild and rude state of society generally than to any particular form of political union. When the people are too much attached to savage independence to be tolerant of the amount of power to which it is for their good that they should be subject, the state of society (as already observed) is not yet ripe for representative government. When the time for that government has arrived, sufficient power for all needful purposes is sure to reside in the sovereign assembly; and if enough of it is not intrusted to the executive, this can only arise from a jealous feeling on the part of the assembly toward the administration, never likely to exist but where the constitutional power of the assembly to turn them out of office has not yet sufficiently established itself. Wherever that constitutional right is admitted in principle and fully operative in practice, there is no fear that the assembly will not be willing to trust its own ministers with any amount of power really desirable; the danger is, on the contrary, lest they should grant it too ungrudgingly, and too indefinite in extent, since the power of the minister is the power of the body who make and who keep him so. It is, however, very likely, and is one of the dangers of a controlling assembly, that it may be lavish of powers, but afterwards interfere with their exercise; may give power by wholesale, and take it back in detail, by multiplied single acts of interference in the business of administration. The evils arising from this assumption of the actual function of governing, in lieu of that of criticising and checking those who govern, have been sufficiently dwelt upon in the preceding chapter. No safeguard can in the nature of things be provided against this improper meddling, except a strong and general conviction of its injurious character.

The other negative defect which may reside in a government, that of not bringing into sufficient exercise the individual faculties, moral, intellectual, and active, of the people, has been exhibited generally in setting forth the distinctive mischiefs of despotism. As between one form of popular government and another, the advantage in this respect lies with that which most widely diffuses the exercise of public functions; on the one hand, by excluding fewest from the suffrage; on the other, by opening to all classes of private citizens, so far as is consistent with other equally important objects, the widest participation in the details of judicial and administrative business; as by jury-trial, admission to municipal offices, and, above all, by the utmost possible publicity and liberty of discussion, whereby not merely a few individuals in succession, but the whole public, are made, to a certain extent, participants in the government, and sharers in the instruction and mental exercise derived from it. The further illustration of these benefits, as well as of the limitations under which they must be aimed at, will be better deferred until we come to speak of the details of administration.

The positive evils and dangers of the representative, as of every other form of government, may be reduced to two heads: first, general ignorance and incapacity, or, to speak more moderately, insufficient mental qualifications, in the controlling body; secondly, the danger of its being under the influence of interests not identical with the general welfare of the community.

The former of these evils, deficiency in high mental qualifications, is one to which it is generally supposed that popular government is liable in a greater degree than any other. The energy of a monarch, the steadiness and prudence of an aristocracy, are thought to contrast most favorably with the vacillation and shortsightedness of even the most qualified democracy. These propositions, however, are not by any means so well founded as they at first sight appear.

Compared with simple monarchy, representative government is in these respects at no disadvantage. Except in a rude age, hereditary monarchy, when it is really such, and not aristocracy in disguise, far surpasses democracy in all the forms of incapacity supposed to be characteristic of the last. I say, except in a rude age, because in a really rude state of society there is a considerable guaranty for the intellectual and active capacities of the sovereign. His personal will is constantly encountering obstacles from the willfulness of his subjects, and of powerful individuals among their number. The circumstances of society do not afford him much temptation to mere luxurious self-indulgence; mental and bodily activity, especially political and military, are his principal excitements; and among turbulent chiefs and lawless followers he has little authority, and is seldom long secure even of his throne, unless he possesses a considerable amount of personal daring, dexterity, and energy. The reason why the average of talent is so high among the Henries and Edwards of our history may be read in the tragical fate of the second Edward and the second Richard, and the civil wars and disturbances of the reigns of John and his incapable successor. The troubled period of the Reformation also produced several eminent hereditary monarchs--Elizabeth, Henri Quatre, Gustavus Adolphus; but they were mostly bred up in adversity, succeeded to the throne by the unexpected failure of nearer heirs, or had to contend with great difficulties in the commencement of their reign. Since European life assumed a settled aspect, any thing above mediocrity in an hereditary king has become extremely rare, while the general average has been even below mediocrity, both in talent and in vigor of character. A monarchy constitutionally absolute now only maintains itself in existence (except temporarily in the hands of some active-minded usurper) through the mental qualifications of a permanent bureaucracy. The Russian and Austrian governments, and even the French government in its normal condition, are oligarchies of officials, of whom the head of the state does little more than select the chiefs. I am speaking of the regular course of their administration; for the will of the master of course determines many of their particular acts.
b:
The question, whether a government is more to be dreaded for its incapacity or for its positive mischiefs, is not to be resolved by any absolute preference, but by a comparison of the specific evils incident to each, and of the conditions under which either is likely to predominate. Incapacity in a government is chiefly dangerous where much is required of it: where the security of person and property, the administration of justice, the conduct of foreign relations, or the execution of measures necessary to public welfare demand continuous and concerted action. In such circumstances, a feeble government does not merely fail to confer benefits; it leaves evils unredressed which, in the absence of any authority capable of redressing them, harden into custom and are ultimately defended as rights. The positive mischiefs of government, on the other hand, consist in the abuse of power to serve particular interests, to restrain opinion, to favour one class at the expense of another, or to pursue objects which the community has not sanctioned. These are of a different character: they are not omissions but acts, and they corrupt the sources of improvement rather than merely obstruct its course.

The distinction is important, because the two evils are frequently confounded in popular argument. It is common to hear a weak government defended on the ground that it does little harm, and a vigorous government condemned on the ground that it may do much. But weakness is itself a species of harm, and vigour is not necessarily oppressive. The proper test is not the quantity of action, but its direction and its responsibility. A government which does much, but does it under the constant scrutiny of a free press and a representative assembly, and with full liability to dismissal for misconduct, may be far less dangerous than one which does nothing, but does nothing because it is unable to do anything, and therefore leaves every abuse to grow unchecked. The incapacity of a government, moreover, is rarely neutral in its effects: it commonly operates as a premium upon the arts of private influence and corruption, since where public authority cannot perform its functions, private persons will perform them for their own advantage.

In considering the knowledge and the interest-bias of representative institutions, we must observe that these two defects are not of equal significance, and that they are frequently mistaken for one another. The want of knowledge in a legislature is a defect which, in some measure, admits of remedy: it may be supplied by the evidence of skilled witnesses, by permanent administrative staffs, by the reports of commissions, and by the gradual education of public opinion. The interest-bias of a legislature is a more serious matter, because it operates not merely upon the judgment but upon the will, and because those who are influenced by it are commonly the last to perceive it. A representative assembly composed of persons of moderate information, but honestly desirous of the public good, may be instructed and may improve; an assembly in which a dominant class legislates for its own advantage may possess abundant knowledge and yet employ it systematically against the community.

The connection between these defects and the form of representative government is intimate. Representation, as I have elsewhere maintained, is valuable not because it secures the wisest rulers, but because it secures the responsibility of rulers to the ruled, and because it affords a channel for the expression of grievances and the correction of abuses. Its characteristic danger is not so much the ignorance of the representative body as the tendency of that body to reflect the interests of the most numerous or the most organised portion of the community, to the neglect of those whose voice is weak. Hence the necessity of securities: a widely extended suffrage, minority representation, publicity of proceedings, and an independent judicature. Where these securities are wanting, the assembly may be both ignorant and interested; where they are present, its ignorance is corrigible and its interest-bias is checked.

The judgment we form must therefore depend upon conditions. In a community where the administrative service is tolerably honest and the judiciary independent, the incapacity of the central government is a less evil than a vigorous government directed by a narrow class; for the ordinary business of life may proceed under local and customary arrangements, and the positive mischiefs of a class government are cumulative and corrupting. In a community, on the other hand, where no such subsidiary safeguards exist, and where the security of life and property depends upon the energy of the central authority, incapacity is the greater evil; for it is the parent of anarchy, and anarchy is the parent of despotism. The general conclusion, therefore, is that positive mischief is in itself the more dangerous of the two, because it is an active principle of deterioration; but that incapacity becomes the more dangerous in proportion as the functions which government is called upon to perform are extensive and indispensable, and in proportion as the community is destitute of those independent arrangements which can supply, in some degree, the place of a vigorous executive.

It is necessary, however, to guard against a too exclusive reliance upon this conclusion. Other explanations of the same phenomena are possible. The apparent incapacity of a government may be the effect, not of want of knowledge or of power, but of a deliberate policy of non-interference, adopted from a just jealousy of authority; and the apparent vigour of a government may be the effect of a temporary emergency rather than of a settled disposition to tyranny. The character of the public service, again, depends less upon the form of government than upon the moral habits of the people and the state of opinion; and a representative assembly which is ignorant to-day may be enlightened to-morrow by the progress of education and the freedom of discussion. These considerations should make us cautious in pronouncing upon particular cases, while they do not impair the general doctrine, that the positive mischiefs of government are to be feared chiefly as they corrupt the sources of improvement, and that the incapacity of government is to be feared chiefly as it leaves the field open to private oppression and to the disorders which invite despotism.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，评估公共权力压制意见的正当性，讨论个人和时代的可错性对言论自由的意义。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The time, it is to be hoped, is gone by, when any defence would be necessary of the "liberty of the press" as one of the securities against corrupt or tyrannical government. No argument, we may suppose, can now be needed, against permitting a legislature or an executive, not identified in interest with the people, to prescribe opinions to them, and determine what doctrines or what arguments they shall be allowed to hear. This aspect of the question, besides, has been so often and so triumphantly enforced by preceding writers, that it need not be specially insisted on in this place. Though the law of England, on the subject of the press, is as servile to this day as it was in the time of the Tudors, there is little danger of its being actually put in force against political discussion, except during some temporary panic, when fear of insurrection drives ministers and judges from their propriety; and, speaking generally, it is not, in constitutional countries, to be apprehended that the government, whether completely responsible to the people or not, will often attempt to control the expression of opinion, except when in doing so it makes itself the organ of the general intolerance of the public. Let us suppose, therefore, that the government is entirely at one with the people, and never thinks of exerting any power of coercion unless in agreement with what it conceives to be their voice. But I deny the right of the people to exercise such coercion, either by themselves or by their government. The power itself is illegitimate. The best government has no more title to it than the worst. It is as noxious, or more noxious, when exerted in accordance with public opinion, than when in or opposition to it. If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind. Were an opinion a personal possession of no value except to the owner; if to be obstructed in the enjoyment of it were simply a private injury, it would make some difference whether the injury was inflicted only on a few persons or on many. But the peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it. If the opinion is right, they are deprived of the opportunity of exchanging error for truth: if wrong, they lose, what is almost as great a benefit, the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.

It is necessary to consider separately these two hypotheses, each of which has a distinct branch of the argument corresponding to it. We can never be sure that the opinion we are endeavouring to stifle is a false opinion; and if we were sure, stifling it would be an evil still.

First: the opinion which it is attempted to suppress by authority may possibly be true. Those who desire to suppress it, of course deny its truth; but they are not infallible. They have no authority to decide the question for all mankind, and exclude every other person from the means of judging. To refuse a hearing to an opinion, because they are sure that it is false, is to assume that their certainty is the same thing as absolute certainty. All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. Its condemnation may be allowed to rest on this common argument, not the worse for being common.

Unfortunately for the good sense of mankind, the fact of their fallibility is far from carrying the weight in their practical judgment, which is always allowed to it in theory; for while every one well knows himself to be fallible, few think it necessary to take any precautions against their own fallibility, or admit the supposition that any opinion, of which they feel very certain, may be one of the examples of the error to which they acknowledge themselves to be liable. Absolute princes, or others who are accustomed to unlimited deference, usually feel this complete confidence in their own opinions on nearly all subjects. People more happily situated, who sometimes hear their opinions disputed, and are not wholly unused to be set right when they are wrong, place the same unbounded reliance only on such of their opinions as are shared by all who surround them, or to whom they habitually defer: for in proportion to a man's want of confidence in his own solitary judgment, does he usually repose, with implicit trust, on the infallibility of "the world" in general. And the world, to each individual, means the part of it with which he comes in contact; his party, his sect, his church, his class of society: the man may be called, by comparison, almost liberal and large-minded to whom it means anything so comprehensive as his own country or his own age. Nor is his faith in this collective authority at all shaken by his being aware that other ages, countries, sects, churches, classes, and parties have thought, and even now think, the exact reverse. He devolves upon his own world the responsibility of being in the right against the dissentient worlds of other people; and it never troubles him that mere accident has decided which of these numerous worlds is the object of his reliance, and that the same causes which make him a Churchman in London, would have made him a Buddhist or a Confucian in Pekin. Yet it is as evident in itself as any amount of argument can make it, that ages are no more infallible than individuals; every age having held many opinions which subsequent ages have deemed not only false but absurd; and it is as certain that many opinions, now general, will be rejected by future ages, as it is that many, once general, are rejected by the present.
b:
The question whether public authority may rightly suppress an opinion is commonly decided by the assumption that the opinion is false and pernicious; but this manner of deciding it begs the very point in dispute. For the authority which assumes infallibility in its judgment of the opinion’s falsity is composed of fallible men, and the history of human progress is largely a record of the correction of authoritative errors. If the whole human race minus one were of one opinion, and that one of the contrary, the race would be no more justified in silencing that one than he, had he the power, would be in silencing the race. The justification for suppressing an opinion must rest, not upon the certainty of the suppressors, but upon the conditions under which the suppression occurs; and these conditions are rarely such as to warrant the conclusion that the opinion is certainly false and certainly harmful.

The fallibility of individuals is not merely a contingent fact about particular persons; it is a structural feature of human cognition and of the social transmission of knowledge. Every age has held opinions which later ages have rejected, and every individual holds many opinions upon insufficient evidence, acquired by custom, education, or the influence of those around him. The recognition of this general fallibility does not, however, lead to the conclusion that all opinions are equally probable; it leads rather to the conclusion that the grounds of an opinion’s truth are always open to examination, and that the examination is impeded when the expression of contrary opinions is prohibited. The suppression of opinion does not merely deprive the world of the suppressed opinion; it deprives the received opinion of the conditions under which its truth can be rationally held. An opinion which is protected from attack is held as a prejudice, not as a reasoned conviction; and the mind which holds it is deprived of the exercise by which its grounds are understood.

It is important to distinguish the general conclusion from the particular judgments which may be made in specific circumstances. The general conclusion is that the suppression of opinion is not justified by the mere fact that the opinion is believed to be false, nor by the fact that it is believed to be pernicious, because the belief in its falsity or perniciousness may itself be mistaken, and because the suppression removes the means by which the error might be corrected. But this does not entail that every expression of opinion must be permitted in every circumstance. There are conditions in which the expression of an opinion is so intimately connected with an incitement to violence, or with a fraud practised upon the ignorant, that the expression and the harm are not separable; and in such cases the justification for restraint rests upon the prevention of harm, not upon the suppression of opinion as such. The distinction is between the expression of an opinion, which is to be permitted because its truth or falsity is to be tested by discussion, and the commission of an act which is harmful independently of the opinion it expresses. The boundary between the two is not always easy to draw, and the difficulty of drawing it is itself a reason for caution in extending the authority of restraint.

The significance of the fallibility of the age is closely connected with the significance of the fallibility of the individual. An age which is confident of its own opinions is apt to regard the opinions of the past as errors and the opinions of the future as not yet formed; but the confidence is itself an opinion, and the history of opinion affords no ground for supposing that the present age is exempt from the errors of its predecessors. The opinions which are now regarded as settled may be revised, and the revision is more likely to be effected if the opinions which are now regarded as settled are kept open to challenge. The individual who holds an opinion which is generally rejected may be mistaken, but the probability of his being mistaken is not a sufficient reason for suppressing his opinion, because the probability of the majority being mistaken is also not zero, and the suppression removes the means by which either error might be discovered. The argument is not that the minority is likely to be right, but that the conditions under which truth is discovered require that the minority be heard.

The connection between the fallibility of the individual and the fallibility of the age is thus not merely an analogy but a relation of mutual support. The individual’s opinions are formed by the age, and the age’s opinions are formed by individuals; the correction of error in either depends upon the free exchange of opinions between them. The suppression of opinion by public authority interrupts this exchange, and the interruption is harmful not only because it may suppress a true opinion, but because it weakens the grounds upon which the received opinion is held. The harm is therefore twofold: the loss of the suppressed opinion, if it is true, and the degeneration of the received opinion into a prejudice, even if it is true. The first harm is contingent upon the truth of the suppressed opinion; the second is independent of it, and is sufficient by itself to condemn the suppression.

An objection may be made that the free expression of opinion is itself a source of harm, because it unsettles received opinions and encourages doubt. But the unsettling of received opinions is not a harm if the opinions are held upon insufficient grounds; it is rather the condition of their being held upon sufficient grounds. The doubt which is encouraged by discussion is not a doubt which prevents action, but a doubt which accompanies action and which is resolved by the consideration of reasons. The mind which has been accustomed to the free exchange of opinions is not less capable of decision, but more capable of rational decision, because it has learned to distinguish the grounds of its opinions from the accidents of their acquisition. The objection therefore rests upon a confusion between the unsettlement of prejudice and the unsettlement of knowledge.

The judgment that public authority ought not to suppress opinion depends, then, upon certain conditions. It depends upon the existence of a public which is capable of considering reasons, and upon the existence of institutions which permit the expression of contrary opinions without the disruption of the conditions of social order. Where these conditions are absent, the argument for liberty of opinion is not that the suppression is always wrong, but that the suppression is a remedy which is likely to be worse than the disease, because it removes the means by which the conditions of rational discussion might be gradually established. The argument is therefore not an absolute prohibition of restraint, but a presumption against restraint which can be overborne only by the clearest evidence of immediate and inseparable harm. The presumption rests upon the general fallibility of those who restrain, and upon the general utility of discussion as the means by which error is corrected.

It may be said that the argument from fallibility proves too much, because it would justify the toleration of opinions which are not merely false but which are held upon no evidence at all. But the argument does not rest upon the equal probability of all opinions; it rests upon the impossibility of separating the process of correction from the process of discussion. An opinion which is held upon no evidence is best corrected by the exhibition of the evidence which is against it, and the exhibition is prevented by suppression. The suppression of an opinion which is held upon no evidence does not correct the opinion; it merely removes it from the field of discussion, where it might have been corrected, and leaves the habit of holding opinions upon no evidence undisturbed. The argument from fallibility is therefore not an argument for the equal value of all opinions, but an argument for the conditions under which opinions may be rationally held and rationally revised.

The particular judgments which are made in specific circumstances must therefore be distinguished from the general conclusion. The general conclusion is that the suppression of opinion is not justified by the certainty of the suppressors, because that certainty is fallible, nor by the perniciousness of the opinion, because the perniciousness may be inseparable from the expression only in specific circumstances which must be shown and not assumed. The particular judgment in a given circumstance must consider the nature of the opinion, the manner of its expression, the likelihood of immediate harm, and the availability of other means of correction. The general conclusion provides a presumption against suppression; the particular judgment may, in rare circumstances, overbear the presumption, but the burden of proof lies upon those who would restrain. The distinction between the general and the particular is not a distinction between the certain and the probable, but a distinction between the grounds of a presumption and the grounds of its being overborne.

The fallibility of the individual and the fallibility of the age thus converge upon the same conclusion: that the free expression of opinion is a condition of the rational holding of opinions, and that the suppression of opinion is a remedy which is justified, if at all, only by the clearest evidence of harm which cannot be otherwise prevented. The conclusion is not that truth is always to be found in the minority, nor that all opinions are equally true, but that the conditions under which truth is discovered and error corrected require that opinions be permitted to be expressed and examined. The judgment which depends upon these conditions is a judgment of presumption and burden, not a judgment of certainty; and it is in the recognition of this distinction that the argument for liberty of opinion finds its strength.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，讨论研究逻辑错误的目的与分类，区分证据不足、推论失误及不依赖推论的错误来源。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
It is a maxim of the school-men, that “contrariorum eadem est scientia:” we never really know what a thing is, unless we are also able to give a sufficient account of its opposite. Conformably to this maxim, one considerable section, in most treatises on Logic, is devoted to the subject of Fallacies; and the practice is too well worthy of observance, to allow of our departing from it. The philosophy of reasoning, to be complete, ought to comprise the theory of bad as well as of good reasoning.

We have endeavored to ascertain the principles by which the sufficiency of any proof can be tested, and by which the nature and amount of evidence needful to prove any given conclusion can be determined beforehand. If these principles were adhered to, then although the number and value of the truths ascertained would be limited by the opportunities, or by the industry, ingenuity, and patience, of the individual inquirer, at least error would not be embraced instead of truth. But the general consent of mankind, founded on their experience, vouches for their being far indeed from even this negative kind of perfection in the employment of their reasoning powers.

In the conduct of life—in the practical business of mankind—wrong inferences, incorrect interpretations of experience, unless after much culture of the thinking faculty, are absolutely inevitable; and with most people, after the highest degree of culture they ever attain, such erroneous inferences, producing corresponding errors in conduct, are lamentably frequent. Even in the speculations to which eminent intellects have systematically devoted themselves, and in reference to which the collective mind of the scientific world is always at hand to aid the efforts and correct the aberrations of individuals, it is only from the more perfect sciences, from those of which the subject-matter is the least complicated, that opinions not resting on a correct induction have at length, generally speaking, been expelled. In the departments of inquiry relating to the more complex phenomena of nature, and especially those of which the subject is man, whether as a moral and intellectual, a social, or even as a physical being; the diversity of opinions still prevalent among instructed persons, and the equal confidence with which those of the most contrary ways of thinking cling to their respective tenets, are proof not only that right modes of philosophizing are not yet generally adopted on those subjects, but that wrong ones are; that inquirers have not only in general missed the truth, but have often embraced error; that even the most cultivated portion of our species have not yet learned to abstain from drawing conclusions which the evidence does not warrant.

The only complete safeguard against reasoning ill, is the habit of reasoning well; familiarity with the principles of correct reasoning, and practice in applying those principles. It is, however, not unimportant to consider what are the most common modes of bad reasoning; by what appearances the mind is most likely to be seduced from the observance of true principles of induction; what, in short, are the most common and most dangerous varieties of Apparent Evidence, whereby persons are misled into opinions for which there does not exist evidence really conclusive.

A catalogue of the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence, is an enumeration of Fallacies. Without such an enumeration, therefore, the present work would be wanting in an essential point. And while writers who included in their theory of reasoning nothing more than ratiocination, have in consistency with this limitation, confined their remarks to the fallacies which have their seat in that portion of the process of investigation; we, who profess to treat of the whole process, must add to our directions for performing it rightly, warnings against performing it wrongly in any of its parts: whether the ratiocinative or the experimental portion of it be in fault, or the fault lie in dispensing with ratiocination and induction altogether.

In considering the sources of unfounded inference, it is unnecessary to reckon the errors which arise, not from a wrong method, nor even from ignorance of the right one, but from a casual lapse, through hurry or inattention, in the application of the true principles of induction. Such errors, like the accidental mistakes in casting up a sum, do not call for philosophical analysis or classification; theoretical considerations can throw no light upon the means of avoiding them. In the present treatise our attention is required, not to mere inexpertness in performing the operation in the right way (the only remedies for which are increased attention and more sedulous practice), but to the modes of performing it in a way fundamentally wrong; the conditions under which the human mind persuades itself that it has sufficient grounds for a conclusion which it has not arrived at by any of the legitimate methods of induction—which it has not, even carelessly or overhastily, endeavored to test by those legitimate methods.

There is another branch of what may be called the Philosophy of Error, which must be mentioned here, though only to be excluded from our subject. The sources of erroneous opinions are twofold, moral and intellectual. Of these, the moral do not fall within the compass of this work. They may be classed under two general heads: Indifference to the attainment of truth, and Bias; of which last the most common case is that in which we are biased by our wishes; but the liability is almost as great to the undue adoption of a conclusion which is disagreeable to us, as of one which is agreeable, if it be of a nature to bring into action any of the stronger passions. Persons of timid character are the more predisposed to believe any statement, the more it is calculated to alarm them. Indeed it is a psychological law, deducible from the most general laws of the mental constitution of man, that any strong passion renders us credulous as to the existence of objects suitable to excite it.

But the moral causes of opinions, though with most persons the most powerful of all, are but remote causes; they do not act directly, but by means of the intellectual causes; to which they bear the same relation that the circumstances called, in the theory of medicine, predisposing causes, bear to exciting causes. Indifference to truth can not, in and by itself, produce erroneous belief; it operates by preventing the mind from collecting the proper evidences, or from applying to them the test of a legitimate and rigid induction; by which omission it is exposed unprotected to the influence of any species of apparent evidence which offers itself spontaneously, or which is elicited by that smaller quantity of trouble which the mind may be willing to take. As little is Bias a direct source of wrong conclusions. We can not believe a proposition only by wishing, or only by dreading, to believe it. The most violent inclination to find a set of propositions true, will not enable the weakest of mankind to believe them without a vestige of intellectual grounds—without any, even apparent, evidence. It acts indirectly, by placing the intellectual grounds of belief in an incomplete or distorted shape before his eyes. It makes him shrink from the irksome labor of a rigorous induction, when he has a misgiving that its result may be disagreeable; and in such examination as he does institute, it makes him exert that which is in a certain measure voluntary, his attention, unfairly, giving a larger share of it to the evidence which seems favorable to the desired conclusion, a smaller to that which seems unfavorable. It operates, too, by making him look out eagerly for reasons, or apparent reasons, to support opinions which are conformable, or resist those which are repugnant, to his interests or feelings; and when the interests or feelings are common to great numbers of persons, reasons are accepted and pass current, which would not for a moment be listened to in that character if the conclusion had nothing more powerful than its reasons to speak in its behalf. The natural or acquired partialities of mankind are continually throwing up philosophical theories, the sole recommendation of which consists in the premises they afford for proving cherished doctrines, or justifying favorite feelings; and when any one of these theories has been so thoroughly discredited as no longer to serve the purpose, another is always ready to take its place. This propensity, when exercised in favor of any widely-spread persuasion or sentiment, is often decorated with complimentary epithets; and the contrary habit of keeping the judgment in complete subordination to evidence, is stigmatized by various hard names, as skepticism, immorality, coldness, hard-heartedness, and similar expressions according to the nature of the case. But though the opinions of the generality of mankind, when not dependent on mere habit and inculcation, have their root much more in the inclinations than in the intellect, it is a necessary condition to the triumph of the moral bias that it should first pervert the understanding. Every erroneous inference, though originating in moral causes, involves the intellectual operation of admitting insufficient evidence as sufficient; and whoever was on his guard against all kinds of inconclusive evidence which can be mistaken for conclusive, would be in no danger of being led into error even by the strongest bias. There are minds so strongly fortified on the intellectual side, that they could not blind themselves to the light of truth, however really desirous of doing so; they could not, with all the inclination in the world, pass off upon themselves bad arguments for good ones. If the sophistry of the intellect could be rendered impossible, that of the feelings, having no instrument to work with, would be powerless. A comprehensive classification of all those things which, not being evidence, are liable to appear such to the understanding, will, therefore, of itself include all errors of judgment arising from moral causes, to the exclusion only of errors of practice committed against better knowledge.

To examine, then, the various kinds of apparent evidence which are not evidence at all, and of apparently conclusive evidence which do not really amount to conclusiveness, is the object of that part of our inquiry into which we are about to enter.

The subject is not beyond the compass of classification and comprehensive survey. The things, indeed, which are not evidence of any given conclusion, are manifestly endless, and this negative property, having no dependence on any positive ones, can not be made the groundwork of a real classification. But the things which, not being evidence, are susceptible of being mistaken for it, are capable of a classification having reference to the positive property which they possess of appearing to be evidence. We may arrange them, at our choice, on either of two principles; according to the cause which makes them appear to be evidence, not being so; or according to the particular kind of evidence which they simulate. The Classification of Fallacies which will be attempted in the ensuing chapter, is founded on these considerations jointly.
b:
In the pursuit of a rigorous and sound methodology for the acquisition of truth, it is incumbent upon the philosopher to direct a vigilant scrutiny toward the sources of human error. It is not sufficient merely to ascertain what is true; we must equally understand the mechanisms by which we are led astray, for the mind is not a passive vessel awaiting the impression of facts, but an active agent prone to systematic distortions. The study of logical fallacies, or more broadly, the anatomy of error, serves a dual purpose: it acts as a negative criterion, warning us against the snares of false reasoning, and it functions as a positive instrument for clarifying the precise conditions under which belief is justified. To navigate the labyrinth of human cognition, we must distinguish with acute precision between those errors arising from a deficiency of evidence, those stemming from a defect in the process of inference itself, and those errors which, paradoxically, occur without any reliance upon inference at all. This tripartite division is not merely a taxonomic convenience but a necessity for the epistemologist who seeks to map the boundaries of human knowledge.

First, let us consider the class of errors attributable to insufficient evidence. It is a common misconception that error arises primarily from the misapplication of logic to adequate premises. In reality, a far greater proportion of human error stems from the premature acceptance of propositions that are not sufficiently supported by the phenomena they purport to explain. When we form a belief, we are, in effect, making a prediction about the constancy of nature or the reliability of our sensory apparatus. If the evidence before us is sparse, unrepresentative, or derived from a single, isolated instance, the conclusion we draw is not necessarily logically invalid in its structure, but it is epistemically precarious. The error here is one of haste and overconfidence, a failure to recognize that the uniformity of nature, which is the ultimate foundation of all inductive reasoning, is itself a generalization derived from experience, not an intuitive certainty. For instance, if one observes that several swans in a particular locality are white and concludes that all swans are white, the syllogistic structure may be flawless: "These swans are white; these swans are members of the species swan; therefore, members of the species swan are white." However, the error lies in the assumption that the sample is representative of the whole. The insufficiency of evidence is a failure to account for the possibility of counter-instances lying beyond the horizon of observation. To guard against this, we must employ the method of difference and agreement with greater rigor, seeking not only to confirm our hypotheses but to falsify them by looking for conditions that might disrupt the observed correlation. This requires a humility of intellect, an acknowledgment that our current state of knowledge is provisional and subject to revision upon the arrival of new data.

Secondly, we must examine errors that arise from defects in inference, where the evidence may be sufficient, but the mental operation connecting the evidence to the conclusion is flawed. This is the domain of traditional logic, where the structure of the argument is compromised. Here, the mind fails to adhere to the laws of association or the rules of deductive validity. A common example is the fallacy of affirming the consequent: if P implies Q, and Q is observed, it does not follow that P is true. Consider the proposition: "If it rains, the ground will be wet." If one observes that the ground is wet, it is a logical error to conclude definitively that it has rained, for the ground may have been wetted by a hose, a sprinkler, or a burst pipe. The inference is invalid because it ignores alternative explanations that are equally consistent with the observed effect. The error here is not a lack of data—the data of wet ground is present—but a failure to consider the full range of possible causes. This highlights the critical importance of the condition of exclusivity in causal reasoning. For a cause to be established with certainty, one must demonstrate that no other plausible cause could have produced the effect. In complex social or psychological phenomena, this is notoriously difficult, leading to frequent errors of oversimplification where a single factor is credited with effects that are the result of a confluence of causes. The student of logic must therefore cultivate the habit of enumerating alternative hypotheses and testing each one against the available evidence, rather than settling for the first explanation that comes to mind.

Thirdly, and perhaps most subtly, there are errors that do not depend upon inference at all. These are errors of perception, memory, or immediate intuition, where the mind accepts a sensation or an idea as true without any process of reasoning. One might argue that if there is no inference, there is no logic to be broken, and thus no logical error. However, this is a narrow view of logic. If logic is the science of the conditions of belief, then errors that precede the formation of a belief are equally relevant. Consider the optical illusion where a straight stick appears bent when placed in water. The observer does not infer that the stick is bent; the appearance is immediate. Yet, if the observer acts upon this appearance, they commit an error. The source of the error is the failure to distinguish between the subjective appearance and the objective reality, a distinction that requires an act of judgment, which, while not a syllogism, is a cognitive operation subject to the same standards of accuracy. Similarly, errors of memory involve the acceptance of a past mental state as a current fact. One may vividly recall an event that never occurred, or misremember the details of an event that did. This is not a failure of deductive logic, but a failure of the faculty of retention and the trustworthiness of introspection. These errors remind us that the foundation of all knowledge, sensory experience and memory, is itself fallible. Therefore, the verification of truth cannot rest solely on the vividness of an idea or the clarity of a perception, but must be corroborated by external consistency and intersubjective agreement.

In analyzing these three sources of error, we must also consider the interplay between them. An error of insufficient evidence can lead to a faulty inference, which in turn can distort perception. For example, a person who holds a strong prejudice (an error of belief formation) may selectively attend to evidence that confirms their bias (an error of perception) and ignore disconfirming evidence (an error of evaluation), leading to a conclusion that is logically coherent within their distorted framework but false in reality. This demonstrates that the classification of errors is not rigid; they often cascade, each exacerbating the other. The general conclusion we may draw is that the reliability of our beliefs is proportional to the rigor with which we interrogate each stage of the cognitive process: the acquisition of data, the processing of that data, and the formation of the final judgment.

However, we must distinguish between general principles and specific contexts. In the natural sciences, where phenomena are relatively isolated and controllable, the methods of inductive logic can be applied with high precision, and errors of insufficient evidence can be minimized through repeated experimentation. In the moral and social sciences, where variables are numerous and human agency introduces unpredictability, the risk of error is magnified. Here, the reliance on simple induction is particularly dangerous, as the complexity of human motives and social structures means that correlations are rarely causal. In such contexts, the "insufficient evidence" error is endemic, and the "inference" error is often a matter of oversimplifying complex systems. Therefore, while the general logic of avoiding error remains the same, the application of that logic must be adapted to the peculiarities of the subject matter. We must be more cautious, more tolerant of ambiguity, and more willing to hold our conclusions tentatively when dealing with the intricate web of human affairs.

Ultimately, the study of logical errors is not an exercise in pedantry, but a moral and intellectual imperative. It requires us to confront our own cognitive limitations with honesty and to recognize that the path to truth is fraught with traps laid by our own psychology. By distinguishing between errors of evidence, inference, and non-inferential acceptance, we equip ourselves with the tools to diagnose the specific nature of our mistakes and to correct them. We learn that truth is not a static possession but a dynamic process of verification, requiring constant vigilance against the seductive ease of false certainty. In this endeavor, the logician serves not merely as a critic of arguments, but as a guardian of the integrity of human thought, ensuring that our beliefs are not merely comfortable, but justified.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察以社会秩序约束纯粹研究的主张，讨论知识自由、政治组织和领导权继承的联系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
It is no exaggeration to say, that M. Comte gradually acquired a real hatred for scientific and all purely intellectual pursuits, and was bent on retaining no more of them than was strictly indispensable. The greatest of his anxieties is lest people should reason, and seek to know, more than enough. He regards all abstraction and all reasoning as morally dangerous, by developing an inordinate pride (orgueil), and still more, by producing dryness (scheresse). Abstract thought, he says, is not a wholesome occupation for more than a small number of human beings, nor of them for more than a small part of their time. Art, which calls the emotions into play along with and more than the reason, is the only intellectual exercise really adapted to human nature. It is nevertheless indispensable that the chief theories of the various abstract sciences, together with the modes in which those theories were historically and logically arrived at, should form a part of universal education: for, first, it is only thus that the methods can be learnt, by which to attain the results sought by the moral and social sciences: though we cannot perceive that M. Comte got at his own moral and social results by those processes. Secondly, the principal truths of the subordinate sciences are necessary to the systematization (still systematization!) of our conceptions, by binding together our notions of the world in a set of propositions, which are coherent, and are a sufficiently correct representation of fact for our practical wants. Thirdly, a familiar knowledge of the invariable laws of natural phaenomena is a great elementary lesson of submission, which, he is never weary of saying, is the first condition both of morality and of happiness. For these reasons, he would cause to be taught, from the age of fourteen to that of twenty-one, to all persons, rich and poor, girls or youths, a knowledge of the whole series of abstract sciences, such as none but the most highly instructed persons now possess, and of a far more systematic and philosophical character than is usually possessed even by them. (N.B.--They are to learn, during the same years, Greek and Latin, having previously, between the ages of seven and fourteen, learnt the five principal modern languages, to the degree necessary for reading, with due appreciation, the chief poetical compositions in each.) But they are to be taught all this, not only without encouraging, but stifling as much as possible, the examining and questioning spirit. The disposition which should be encouraged is that of receiving all on the authority of the teacher. The Positivist faith, even in its scientific part, is la foi demontrable, but ought by no means to be la foi toujours demontree. The pupils have no business to be over-solicitous about proof. The teacher should not even present the proofs to them in a complete form, or as proofs. The object of instruction is to make them understand the doctrines themselves, perceive their mutual connexion, and form by means of them a consistent and systematized conception of nature. As for the demonstrations, it is rather desirable than otherwise that even theorists should forget them, retaining only the results. Among all the aberrations of scientific men, M. Comte thinks none greater than the pedantic anxiety they show for complete proof, and perfect rationalization of scientific processes. It ought to be enough that the doctrines afford an explanation of phaenomena, consistent with itself and with known facts, and that the processes are justified by their fruits. This over-anxiety for proof, he complains, is breaking down, by vain scruples, the knowledge which seemed to have been attained; witness the present state of chemistry. The demand of proof for what has been accepted by Humanity, is itself a mark of "distrust, if not hostility, to the sacerdotal order" (the naivete of this would be charming, if it were not deplorable), and is a revolt against the traditions of the human race. So early had the new High Priest adopted the feelings and taken up the inheritance of the old. One of his favourite aphorisms is the strange one, that the living are more and more governed by the dead. As is not uncommon with him, he introduces the dictum in one sense, and uses it in another. What he at first means by it, is that as civilization advances, the sum of our possessions, physical and intellectual, is due in a decreasing proportion to ourselves, and in an increasing one to our progenitors. The use he makes of it is, that we should submit ourselves more and more implicitly to the authority of previous generations, and suffer ourselves less and less to doubt their judgment, or test by our own reason the grounds of their opinions. The unwillingness of the human intellect and conscience, in their present state of "anarchy," to sign their own abdication, lie calls "the insurrection of the living against the dead." To this complexion has Positive Philosophy come at last!

Worse, however, remains to be told. M. Comte selects a hundred volumes of science, philosophy, poetry, history, and general knowledge, which he deems a sufficient library for every positivist, even of the theoretic order, and actually proposes a systematic holocaust of books in general--it would almost seem of all books except these. Even that to which he shows most indulgence, poetry, except the very best, is to undergo a similar fate, with the reservation of select passages, on the ground that, poetry being intended to cultivate our instinct of ideal perfection, any kind of it that is less than the best is worse than none. This imitation of the error, we will call it the crime, of the early Christians--and in an exaggerated form, for even they destroyed only those writings of pagans or heretics which were directed against themselves--is the one thing in M. Comte's projects which merits real indignation. When once M. Comte has decided, all evidence on the other side, nay, the very historical evidence on which he grounded his decision, had better perish. When mankind have enlisted under his banner, they must burn their ships. There is, though in a less offensive form, the same overweening presumption in a suggestion he makes, that all species of animals and plants which are useless to man should be systematically rooted out. As if any one could presume to assert that the smallest weed may not, as knowledge advances, be found to have some property serviceable to man. When we consider that the united power of the whole human race cannot reproduce a species once eradicated--that what is once done, in the extirpation of races, can never be repaired; one can only be thankful that amidst all which the past rulers of mankind have to answer for, they have never come up to the measure of the great regenerator of Humanity; mankind have not yet been under the rule of one who assumes that he knows all there is to be known, and that when he has put himself at the head of humanity, the book of human knowledge may be closed.

Of course M. Comte does not make this assumption consistently. He does not imagine that he actually possesses all knowledge, but only that he is an infallible judge what knowledge is worth possessing. He does not believe that mankind have reached in all directions the extreme limits of useful and laudable scientific inquiry. He thinks there is a large scope for it still, in adding to our power over the external world, but chiefly in perfecting our own physical, intellectual, and moral nature. He holds that all our mental strength should be economized, for the pursuit of this object in the mode leading most directly to the end. With this view, some one problem should always be selected, the solution of which would be more important than any other to the interests of humanity, and upon this the entire intellectual resources of the theoretic mind should be concentrated, until it is either resolved, or has to be given up as insoluble: after which mankind should go on to another, to be pursued with similar exclusiveness. The selection of this problem of course rests with the sacerdotal order, or in other words, with the High Priest. We should then see the whole speculative intellect of the human race simultaneously at work on one question, by orders from above, as a French minister of public instruction once boasted that a million of boys were saying the same lesson during the same half-hour in every town and village of France. The reader will be anxious to know, how much better and more wisely the human intellect will be applied under this absolute monarchy, and to what degree this system of government will be preferable to the present anarchy, in which every theorist does what is intellectually right in his own eyes. M. Comte has not left us in ignorance on this point. He gives us ample means of judging. The Pontiff of Positivism informs us what problem, in his opinion, should be selected before all others for this united pursuit.

What this problem is, we must leave those who are curious on the subject to learn from the treatise itself. When they have done so, they will be qualified to form their own opinion of the amount of advantage which the general good of mankind would be likely to derive, from exchanging the present "dispersive speciality" and "intellectual anarchy" for the subordination of the intellect to the coeur, personified in a High Priest, prescribing a single problem for the undivided study of the theoretic mind.

We have given a sufficient general idea of M. Comte's plan for the regeneration of human society, by putting an end to anarchy, and "systematizing" human thought and conduct under the direction of feeling. But an adequate conception will not have been formed of the height of his self-confidence, until something more has been told. Be it known, then, that M. Comte by no means proposes this new constitution of society for realization in the remote future. A complete plan of measures of transition is ready prepared, and he determines the year, before the end of the present century, in which the new spiritual and temporal powers will be installed, and the regime of our maturity will begin. He did not indeed calculate on converting to Positivism, within that time, more than a thousandth part of all the heads of families in Western Europe and its offshoots beyond the Atlantic. But he fixes the time necessary for the complete political establishment of Positivism at thirty-three years, divided into three periods, of seven, five, and twenty-one years respectively. At the expiration of seven, the direction of public education in France would be placed in M. Comte's hands. In five years more, the Emperor Napoleon, or his successor, will resign his power to a provisional triumvirate, composed of three eminent proletaires of the positivist faith; for proletaires, though not fit for permanent rule, are the best agents of the transition, being the most free from the prejudices which are the chief obstacle to it. These rulers will employ the remaining twenty-one years in preparing society for its final constitution; and after duly installing the Spiritual Power, and effecting the decomposition of France into the seventeen republics before mentioned, will give over the temporal government of each to the normal dictatorship of the three bankers. A man may be deemed happy, but scarcely modest, who had such boundless confidence in his own powers of foresight, and expected so complete a triumph of his own ideas on the reconstitution of society within the possible limits of his lifetime. If he could live (he said) to the age of Pontenelle, or of Hobbes, or even of Voltaire, he should see all this realized, or as good as realized. He died, however, at sixty, without leaving any disciple sufficiently advanced to be appointed his successor. There is now a College, and a Director, of Positivism; but Humanity no longer possesses a High Priest.
b:
The proposition that the pursuit of pure research ought to be restrained by considerations of social order is one which, in its general form, appears at first sight to rest upon a prudent maxim, namely that no man has a right to scatter firebrands through a crowded assembly merely because he is curious to observe the conflagration. Yet when the proposition is examined more closely, it will be found to confound two very different questions: whether a given inquiry is likely to produce mischievous consequences, and whether any authority is competent to pronounce upon that likelihood beforehand. The first is a question of fact, always difficult and often impossible to determine in advance; the second is a question of right, upon which the friends of liberty have, I think, uniformly held that the burden of proof lies with those who would prohibit.

It is necessary, in the first place, to distinguish between the restraint of conduct and the restraint of speculation. Conduct is amenable to general rules, because its consequences fall upon others in ways that may be foreseen and computed; and society may justly punish or prevent those acts which, upon the ordinary principles of jurisprudence, are held to be injurious. But speculation, so long as it remains speculation, affects others only through the medium of persuasion; and the persuasion of one mind by another is precisely the operation which it is the office of a free community to protect rather than to obstruct. He who would suppress an inquiry because of the use to which its conclusions may be turned is in the position of the man who would prohibit the study of chemistry lest some person should employ the knowledge so acquired to poison a well. The remedy for the abuse of knowledge is more knowledge, and the remedy for dangerous conclusions is the free confrontation of those conclusions with the evidence and the reasonings by which they may be refuted. It is only where the inquiry passes into the act—where the publication of a doctrine is accompanied by an incitement to immediate violence, or where the possession of a particular instrument of knowledge is itself equivalent to the possession of a weapon—that the ordinary grounds of restraint become applicable.

But it must be acknowledged that the matter is not so simple as this statement may appear to make it. The friends of intellectual liberty have sometimes been too ready to assume that knowledge is always, in the long run, a public benefit, and that the truth, once discovered, will make its own way. This assumption is true only under conditions which it is the business of the political philosopher to specify. It is true where there exists a public capable of weighing evidence, where the channels of communication are open, where the holders of power have no interest in suppressing inconvenient conclusions, and where the institutions of the country afford a means of correcting error without the violent overthrow of the whole fabric of society. Where these conditions are wanting, the discovery of a new truth may be, not a benefit, but an instrument in the hands of a faction. The question, therefore, whether pure research should be restrained by considerations of social order resolves itself, in great measure, into the question whether the society in which the research is conducted possesses the means of assimilating new knowledge without disruption.

Now it is here that the connexion between intellectual liberty and the forms of political organization becomes apparent. A society which vests authority in a single person, or in a narrow body of persons, has an interest in the suppression of inquiry which a society of a different constitution does not possess. For where power is hereditary or self-appointed, the grounds upon which it rests are not open to discussion without danger to the power itself; and consequently the ruling few are tempted to treat every speculation which touches upon the foundations of their authority as a matter of police rather than of philosophy. In such a society, the restraint of pure research is not an exceptional measure adopted for the prevention of a particular mischief, but a permanent principle of government; and it is precisely in such societies that the mischief which the restraint is intended to prevent is most likely to arise, because the suppression of inquiry drives speculation underground, where it ferments without the corrective of public criticism, and associates itself with the passions of discontent rather than with the sober pursuit of truth.

In a society, on the other hand, where the holders of authority are removable, where the grounds of their title are matters of open debate, and where the succession to power is determined by rules which no single faction can alter at will, the interest of the governors in the suppression of inquiry is greatly diminished. They may be annoyed by criticism, but they are not endangered by it; for the tenure of their office does not depend upon the maintenance of a particular opinion, but upon the observance of a known rule. It is under such a constitution that the restraint of pure research may safely be reduced to the narrowest limits, because the community possesses within itself the means of turning new knowledge to account, and of correcting the errors which new knowledge may for a time engender. The liberty of speculation, therefore, is not a good in the abstract, independent of political conditions; it is a good which the constitution of a free state renders practicable, and which the constitution of a despotism renders dangerous to concede and impossible to maintain.

The same consideration applies to the question of leadership and the succession to authority. Every political society must provide for the transmission of power from one generation to another; and the manner in which that transmission is provided for determines, in a great degree, the attitude which the society will adopt towards intellectual innovation. Where the succession is determined by birth, the occupant of power is placed in a position which he cannot defend by argument, and which he is therefore tempted to defend by the suppression of argument. Where the succession is determined by election or by some other principle which admits of public discussion, the candidates for power are compelled to submit their pretensions to the judgment of the community; and a community accustomed to judge of the pretensions of its rulers is a community accustomed to the free examination of opinions. The habit of free inquiry in matters of speculation and the habit of free election in matters of politics are, indeed, closely allied; for both rest upon the same principle, namely that the grounds of belief and the grounds of authority are alike fit subjects for examination, and that no conclusion is to be imposed upon men by any other means than the force of reason and the weight of evidence.

It may be objected that this reasoning proves too much; for if the liberty of research is to be measured by the political conditions of the society, it would seem to follow that in a society imperfectly constituted the restraint of research may be justified as a means of preserving order. To this objection I answer, that the restraint of research is never justified as a permanent principle, but only, if at all, as a temporary expedient, and that even as a temporary expedient it is attended with consequences which commonly outweigh the evils it is designed to avert. The suppression of an inquiry does not destroy the causes which produce it; it merely prevents those causes from being understood. The discontent which expresses itself in a dangerous doctrine is not removed by silencing the doctrine; it is driven to seek other channels, and it is precisely when the channels of legitimate expression are closed that it seeks the channels of violence. History, so far as I am able to judge, affords no instance of a society which has been preserved from revolution by the suppression of speculation; but it affords many instances of societies in which the suppression of speculation has been the immediate precursor of revolution.

There is, however, a class of cases in which the connexion between research and social order is more direct, and in which the argument for restraint deserves a more careful examination. I refer to those inquiries which are not merely speculative, but which are immediately connected with the means of physical power—the discovery of new instruments of destruction, the investigation of the secrets of nature which may be turned to the purposes of war, and the like. Here the ordinary presumption in favour of liberty may be rebutted, not because the inquiry is dangerous to opinion, but because the knowledge, once obtained, cannot be confined to those who are capable of using it wisely. The distinction is between knowledge which operates through the mind, and knowledge which operates through the material world; and it is a distinction which the friends of liberty would do well to mark, for it is by confounding the two that the enemies of liberty have often contrived to justify the restraint of the one by arguments which are applicable only to the other.
