Even in this class of cases, however, the restraint, to be justifiable, must be exercised by a authority competent to judge of the danger, and must be accompanied by securities against abuse; and the history of such restraints is not encouraging, for the authority which is empowered to suppress a dangerous discovery is commonly found, in practice, to suppress discoveries which are merely inconvenient to itself.

It is further to be observed that the connexion between pure research and social order is not a simple relation of cause and effect, but is mediated by a variety of circumstances which may vary indefinitely. The same doctrine which is harmless in one society may be dangerous in another; the same inquiry which is encouraged in one age may be prohibited in the next. The conclusion, therefore, which I would draw is not that pure research should be unrestrained in all circumstances, but that the presumption is always in favour of liberty, and that the burden of proof lies upon those who would restrain. This presumption is not a mere prejudice; it rests upon the consideration that the restraint of inquiry is itself an evil of a peculiar kind, because it destroys the only means by which error can be corrected and truth established. The man who suppresses an inquiry is not merely preventing the discovery of a particular truth; he is striking at the root of the habit of inquiry itself, and thereby diminishing the capacity of the community to deal with the very dangers which he professes to apprehend.

The general conclusion, then, may be stated as follows: that the pursuit of pure research ought not to be restrained by considerations of social order, except where the research is of such a nature that its results cannot be confined to the sphere of opinion, and where the authority imposing the restraint is so constituted as to afford a reasonable security that the restraint will be exercised for the public good and not for the advantage of a faction. This conclusion is general, and is subject to the qualifications which I have stated. But the application of it to any particular society depends upon circumstances which no general proposition can anticipate: upon the degree of intelligence and public spirit in the community, upon the openness of the channels of communication, upon the character of the government, and upon the manner in which the succession to authority is determined. In a society where these circumstances are favourable, the restraint of research is unnecessary; in a society where they are unfavourable, the restraint of research is likely to be both ineffective and mischievous. The friends of order, therefore, and the friends of liberty, have a common interest in the improvement of political institutions; for it is only under institutions which render the holders of power responsible to the community, and which provide for the peaceful succession of authority, that the liberty of research can be safely enjoyed and the order of society effectually maintained.

It may be added, that the question is not merely one of policy, but of morals. The man who suppresses an opinion which he believes to be false is guilty of a presumption which no human being is entitled to make; for he assumes that he is infallible, and that the opinion which he suppresses is certainly erroneous. The history of opinion affords abundant evidence that the conclusions which have been most confidently held, and most vigorously enforced, have often been reversed by subsequent inquiry; and the recollection of this should make us slow to employ the arm of authority in matters of speculation. The only security which we can have for the correctness of our opinions is the constant submission of them to the test of free discussion; and the society which denies that test to any portion of its members is, in so far, deprived of the means of correcting its own errors. It is for this reason that the liberty of research is not merely a privilege of the individual, but a condition of the improvement of society; and that the restraint of it, however plausible the pretext, is commonly found to be a barrier to that progress which it is the interest of every community to promote.

I am sensible that these observations do not exhaust the subject, and that the connexion between intellectual liberty and political organization might be traced through many other particulars. But I have endeavoured to show that the question of the restraint of pure research cannot be decided by any general rule applicable alike to all societies and all circumstances; that the presumption is in favour of liberty, and that the burden of proof lies upon those who would restrain; that the restraint of research is most dangerous, and most likely to be resorted to, in societies where the succession to authority is not determined by open and peaceful means; and that the improvement of political institutions is the surest means of rendering the liberty of research both safe and beneficial. These conclusions, I think, are warranted by the considerations which I have stated, and are consistent with that regard for order which no friend of liberty can afford to disregard, since liberty without order is but the liberty of the stronger to oppress the weaker.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察道德规则产生约束力的依据，讨论内在情感、外部动机和道德能力的培养。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
The question is often asked, and properly so, in regard to any supposed moral standard--What is its sanction? what are the motives to obey it? or more specifically, what is the source of its obligation? whence does it derive its binding force? It is a necessary part of moral philosophy to provide the answer to this question; which, though frequently assuming the shape of an objection to the utilitarian morality, as if it had some special applicability to that above others, really arises in regard to all standards. It arises, in fact, whenever a person is called on to adopt a standard or refer morality to any basis on which he has not been accustomed to rest it. For the customary morality, that which education and opinion have consecrated, is the only one which presents itself to the mind with the feeling of being in itself obligatory; and when a person is asked to believe that this morality derives its obligation from some general principle round which custom has not thrown the same halo, the assertion is to him a paradox; the supposed corollaries seem to have a more binding force than the original theorem; the superstructure seems to stand better without, than with, what is represented as its foundation. He says to himself, I feel that I am bound not to rob or murder, betray or deceive; but why am I bound to promote the general happiness? If my own happiness lies in something else, why may I not give that the preference?

If the view adopted by the utilitarian philosophy of the nature of the moral sense be correct, this difficulty will always present itself, until the influences which form moral character have taken the same hold of the principle which they have taken of some of the consequences--until, by the improvement of education, the feeling of unity with our fellow creatures shall be (what it cannot be doubted that Christ intended it to be) as deeply rooted in our character, and to our own consciousness as completely a part of our nature, as the horror of crime is in an ordinarily well-brought-up young person. In the mean time, however, the difficulty has no peculiar application to the doctrine of utility, but is inherent in every attempt to analyse morality and reduce it to principles; which, unless the principle is already in men's minds invested with as much sacredness as any of its applications, always seems to divest them of a part of their sanctity.

The principle of utility either has, or there is no reason why it might not have, all the sanctions which belong to any other system of morals. Those sanctions are either external or internal. Of the external sanctions it is not necessary to speak at any length. They are, the hope of favour and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe, along with whatever we may have of sympathy or affection for them or of love and awe of Him, inclining us to do His will independently of selfish consequences. There is evidently no reason why all these motives for observance should not attach themselves to the utilitarian morality, as completely and as powerfully as to any other. Indeed, those of them which refer to our fellow creatures are sure to do so, in proportion to the amount of general intelligence; for whether there be any other ground of moral obligation than the general happiness or not, men do desire happiness; and however imperfect may be their own practice, they desire and commend all conduct in others towards themselves, by which they think their happiness is promoted. With regard to the religious motive, if men believe, as most profess to do, in the goodness of God, those who think that conduciveness to the general happiness is the essence, or even only the criterion, of good, must necessarily believe that it is also that which God approves. The whole force therefore of external reward and punishment, whether physical or moral, and whether proceeding from God or from our fellow men, together with all that the capacities of human nature admit, of disinterested devotion to either, become available to enforce the utilitarian morality, in proportion as that morality is recognized; and the more powerfully, the more the appliances of education and general cultivation are bent to the purpose.

So far as to external sanctions. The internal sanction of duty, whatever our standard of duty may be, is one and the same--a feeling in our own mind; a pain, more or less intense, attendant on violation of duty, which in properly cultivated moral natures rises, in the more serious cases, into shrinking from it as an impossibility. This feeling, when disinterested, and connecting itself with the pure idea of duty, and not with some particular form of it, or with any of the merely accessory circumstances, is the essence of Conscience; though in that complex phenomenon as it actually exists, the simple fact is in general all encrusted over with collateral associations, derived from sympathy, from love, and still more from fear; from all the forms of religious feeling; from the recollections of childhood and of all our past life; from self-esteem, desire of the esteem of others, and occasionally even self-abasement. This extreme complication is, I apprehend, the origin of the sort of mystical character which, by a tendency of the human mind of which there are many other examples, is apt to be attributed to the idea of moral obligation, and which leads people to believe that the idea cannot possibly attach itself to any other objects than those which, by a supposed mysterious law, are found in our present experience to excite it. Its binding force, however, consists in the existence of a mass of feeling which must be broken through in order to do what violates our standard of right, and which, if we do nevertheless violate that standard, will probably have to be encountered afterwards in the form of remorse. Whatever theory we have of the nature or origin of conscience, this is what essentially constitutes it.

The ultimate sanction, therefore, of all morality (external motives apart) being a subjective feeling in our own minds, I see nothing embarrassing to those whose standard is utility, in the question, what is the sanction of that particular standard? We may answer, the same as of all other moral standards--the conscientious feelings of mankind. Undoubtedly this sanction has no binding efficacy on those who do not possess the feelings it appeals to; but neither will these persons be more obedient to any other moral principle than to the utilitarian one. On them morality of any kind has no hold but through the external sanctions. Meanwhile the feelings exist, a feet in human nature, the reality of which, and the great power with which they are capable of acting on those in whom they have been duly cultivated, are proved by experience. No reason has ever been shown why they may not be cultivated to as great intensity in connection with the utilitarian, as with any other rule of morals.

There is, I am aware, a disposition to believe that a person who sees in moral obligation a transcendental fact, an objective reality belonging to the province of "Things in themselves," is likely to be more obedient to it than one who believes it to be entirely subjective, having its seat in human consciousness only. But whatever a person's opinion may be on this point of Ontology, the force he is really urged by is his own subjective feeling, and is exactly measured by its strength. No one's belief that Duty is an objective reality is stronger than the belief that God is so; yet the belief in God, apart from the expectation of actual reward and punishment, only operates on conduct through, and in proportion to, the subjective religious feeling. The sanction, so far as it is disinterested, is always in the mind itself; and the notion, therefore, of the transcendental moralists must be, that this sanction will not exist in the mind unless it is believed to have its root out of the mind; and that if a person is able to say to himself, That which is restraining me, and which is called my conscience, is only a feeling in my own mind, he may possibly draw the conclusion that when the feeling ceases the obligation ceases, and that if he find the feeling inconvenient, he may disregard it, and endeavour to get rid of it. But is this danger confined to the utilitarian morality? Does the belief that moral obligation has its seat outside the mind make the feeling of it too strong to be got rid of? The fact is so far otherwise, that all moralists admit and lament the ease with which, in the generality of minds, conscience can be silenced or stifled. The question, Need I obey my conscience? is quite as often put to themselves by persons who never heard of the principle of utility, as by its adherents. Those whose conscientious feelings are so weak as to allow of their asking this question, if they answer it affirmatively, will not do so because they believe in the transcendental theory, but because of the external sanctions.

It is not necessary, for the present purpose, to decide whether the feeling of duty is innate or implanted. Assuming it to be innate, it is an open question to what objects it naturally attaches itself; for the philosophic supporters of that theory are now agreed that the intuitive perception is of principles of morality, and not of the details. If there be anything innate in the matter, I see no reason why the feeling which is innate should not be that of regard to the pleasures and pains of others. If there is any principle of morals which is intuitively obligatory, I should say it must be that. If so, the intuitive ethics would coincide with the utilitarian, and there would be no further quarrel between them. Even as it is, the intuitive moralists, though they believe that there are other intuitive moral obligations, do already believe this to be one; for they unanimously hold that a large portion of morality turns upon the consideration due to the interests of our fellow creatures. Therefore, if the belief in the transcendental origin of moral obligation gives any additional efficacy to the internal sanction, it appears to me that the utilitarian principle has already the benefit of it.

On the other hand, if, as is my own belief, the moral feelings are not innate, but acquired, they are not for that reason the less natural. It is natural to man to speak, to reason, to build cities, to cultivate the ground, though these are acquired faculties. The moral feelings are not indeed a part of our nature, in the sense of being in any perceptible degree present in all of us; but this, unhappily, is a fact admitted by those who believe the most strenuously in their transcendental origin. Like the other acquired capacities above referred to, the moral faculty, if not a part of our nature, is a natural outgrowth from it; capable, like them, in a certain small degree, of springing up spontaneously; and susceptible of being brought by cultivation to a high degree of development. Unhappily it is also susceptible, by a sufficient use of the external sanctions and of the force of early impressions, of being cultivated in almost any direction: so that there is hardly anything so absurd or so mischievous that it may not, by means of these influences, be made to act on the human mind with all the authority of conscience. To doubt that the same potency might be given by the same means to the principle of utility, even if it had no foundation in human nature, would be flying in the face of all experience.
b:
The question, what it is that gives binding force to a moral rule, is often confounded with the quite different question, what it is that in fact induces men to obey it. The confusion is natural, since the same word, obligation, is employed for both; yet the two inquiries lead to conclusions which, if not carefully distinguished, mutually obscure one another. A rule may be binding in the strict sense—that is, a valid demand upon the agent's conduct which he is not at liberty to set aside at pleasure—while the motives which actually secure his conformity to it are of the most various and, in themselves, morally indifferent character. Conversely, an agent may be strongly moved to a course of conduct by feelings which have all the warmth of conscience, while the rule he obeys has no genuine authority, being either a superstition of his age or a prejudice of his class. The analysis of moral obligation therefore requires that we separate three things: the ground of the rule's authority, the psychological causes of our susceptibility to that authority, and the discipline by which the susceptibility is cultivated and made reliable.

Let us begin with the first. When we say that a moral rule binds, we mean, I take it, that there is a reason for acting in conformity with it which is independent of the agent's present desires, and which survives even when those desires run counter to it. Now the only reason of this description which can be exhibited in the last resort is the tendency of the rule to promote the general happiness, or, in the more comprehensive phrase, the greatest amount of well-being of which the circumstances admit, considered impartially among all who are affected. This is the doctrine of utility, and I am aware that it is commonly met with the objection that it makes obligation a matter of calculation, and thus substitutes a cold arithmetic of consequences for the living voice of duty. The objection appears to me to rest upon a misapprehension. To say that the ultimate ground of obligation is utility is not to say that the agent, on each occasion, performs a sum in addition before he acts, any more than to say that the ultimate ground of the truth of an arithmetical proposition is the definitions of number is to say that the calculator rehearses those definitions at every step. The principle is the justification of the rule, not the mental process of the person who obeys it. In the ordinary case the rule has been received from education, confirmed by the approbation of those whose approbation we value, and is applied with the rapidity of habit; the appeal to utility is made, if at all, only when rules conflict, or when some new case arises for which the received rule provides no clear direction.

But here a difficulty presents itself which has been urged with great force by writers of a different school. If obligation depends upon consequences, it would seem to follow that the obligation varies with every variation in the probable consequences, and that no rule can be more than a rough memorandum of the results of past experience, to be disregarded whenever the particular case appears to promise a better issue. This is the doctrine sometimes called, by its friends, casuistry, and by its enemies, the doctrine of expediency in the bad sense. I answer that the moral rules which mankind has adopted, such as the prohibition of murder, of theft, of breach of faith, and the like, are not arbitrary generalizations, but are supported by the whole weight of human experience; and that the utility of maintaining them, as rules, is itself one of the most important of the consequences which the utilitarian is bound to consider. The question, in any given case, is not merely whether a departure from the rule would in this instance produce a balance of good, but whether the general observance of the rule is not so indispensable to the security and confidence of society that a departure, even though it should seem to be attended with immediate benefit, tends to weaken the fabric upon which all benefit depends. It is this consideration which gives to the received rules their peculiar stringency, and which justifies us in treating them, in ordinary cases, as authoritative without a fresh calculation. The rule, then, is binding because of its utility; but its utility is the utility of a rule, and not merely of the particular act.

I am sensible that this account will appear to many to leave the essence of obligation unexplained. They will say that when a man feels himself bound, he is conscious of a peculiar sentiment, the sentiment of duty, which is not resolvable into any anticipation of pleasure or pain, and that this sentiment is itself the voice of the moral law within him. Now I am far from denying the existence of this sentiment, or its immense practical importance. The question is whether the sentiment is the ground of the obligation, or the obligation the ground of the sentiment. Those who maintain the former view are, I think, led to it by a natural but fallacious transition. They find in their own minds a strong and disinterested feeling of approbation towards certain conduct, and of disapprobation towards the contrary; they find that this feeling is not derived from any calculation of their own personal advantage; and they conclude that it is a simple, ultimate, and inexplicable fact of our nature, which reveals to us a law independent of all considerations of happiness. But the inference is not warranted. A feeling may be disinterested, in the sense of not being directed to the agent's private advantage, and yet may be the product of a long course of social discipline, and may be explained by the operation of the principle of association. We are formed by education and by the usages of society to connect certain acts with the ideas of approbation and blame; the connection, once established, is strengthened by repetition, by sympathy with others, and by the powerful influence of early impressions; and at last the feeling of approbation or blame appears in consciousness as if it were an original and underived element of our constitution. This is precisely what we should expect, if the utilitarian account be true; for the utility of the rules is so great, and the necessity of their observance so constant, that nature, or rather the course of human society, has taken care to implant the sentiment strongly, and to make it, in the ordinary mind, independent of the calculation which originally justified it. The sentiment is thus not the foundation, but the safeguard, of the rule; and the proof of this is that when we examine the sentiment closely, we find it to be precisely proportioned, in the main, to the importance of the rule to human welfare, and to vary, in different ages and nations, in a manner which no theory of an immutable moral sense can explain.

I pass now to the second of the three inquiries, namely, the nature of the external motives which secure conformity to moral rules. These are of two principal kinds: the hope of reward and the fear of punishment, whether in this life or in another; and the desire of the approbation, and the dread of the disapprobation, of our fellow-creatures. Of these, the latter is by far the more powerful in the ordinary course of human conduct, and it is the one which the legislator and the moralist have chiefly to rely upon. The love of praise and the fear of blame are among the strongest of our social feelings; and they operate, in the greater number of cases, without any distinct reference to the ultimate utility of the rules whose observance they enforce. A man refrains from theft, not because he has calculated that the institution of property is necessary to the general good, but because he would be ashamed to be thought a thief, and because he has been accustomed from childhood to regard theft with aversion. The external motive, in this case, is the disapprobation of others; the internal motive is the disapprobation of himself, or, as we commonly say, his conscience. Both are, in the utilitarian account, derived from the same source; for the disapprobation of others is itself a consequence of the utility of the rule, and the internal sentiment is the result of the external disapprobation, gradually absorbed into the mind by the operation of sympathy and association.

It is here that the question of the cultivation of the moral capacity becomes important. If the sentiment of duty is not an original and independent element of our nature, but a product of education and social discipline, it follows that it may be cultivated, and that the manner of its cultivation is a matter of the highest practical concern. The cultivation is of two kinds: the formation of habits of obedience to the received rules, and the enlightenment of the understanding as to the grounds of those rules. The first is the work of early education, of the family, of the school, and of the general tone of society. The second is the work of reflection and of a cultivated intelligence. Now it is a common error to suppose that the one is sufficient without the other. Habits formed without intelligence are liable to be broken by the first strong temptation, or, if they hold, they hold as blind prejudices, which may be attached to rules that have no utility, and may be wanting to rules that have. On the other hand, intelligence without habit is weak in the moment of action; the man who has never been trained to obey may see clearly the reasons for obedience, and yet may yield to the solicitation of the passing desire. The moral capacity, therefore, is best cultivated when the two are combined: when the young are trained to conform to the received rules before they are capable of understanding their grounds, and are afterwards led, as their reason unfolds, to perceive why the rules are binding. This is the method which nature herself suggests; for the child must obey before he can comprehend, and the comprehension, when it comes, confirms and elevates the obedience.

But I must notice a further point, which is often overlooked. The cultivation of the moral capacity is not merely the cultivation of the individual; it is also the cultivation of the society. The rules which bind the individual are sustained by the general opinion of the community; and the general opinion is itself a product of the moral condition of the community. If the community is enlightened, its approbation will be attached to rules which are really useful, and its disapprobation to conduct which is really pernicious. If it is ignorant or corrupt, its approbation may be attached to the most absurd and mischievous rules, and its disapprobation to the most innocent and beneficial conduct. Hence the reformer who seeks to improve the moral condition of mankind must address himself not only to individuals, but to the general tone of opinion; and he must be prepared to encounter the resistance of those whose conscience has been formed upon rules which he believes to be erroneous. This is the explanation of the fact, which has often perplexed the historians of morals, that men of the purest conscience have sometimes persecuted and slain their fellows for the sake of opinions which we now regard as indifferent or absurd. Their conscience was formed upon the rules which their age had received; and the disapprobation which they felt towards the heretic was as genuine a sentiment of duty as any which we feel ourselves. The sentiment was the same in kind; the rule was different; and the difference was due to the difference in the enlightenment of the community.

From these considerations I draw the following conclusions, which I offer as general, subject to the qualifications which particular circumstances may require. First, the binding force of a moral rule consists in its tendency to promote the general happiness, and the rule is binding as a rule, and not merely as a particular act; so that the utility of maintaining the rule is itself one of the consequences which must be taken into account. Secondly, the sentiment of duty, which is the internal motive to conformity, is not an original and independent element of our nature, but a product of education and association, and is therefore capable of cultivation, and liable to be perverted when the rules to which it is attached are erroneous. Thirdly, the external motives, namely, the approbation and disapprobation of others, are the most powerful in ordinary cases, and are the means by which the internal sentiment is chiefly formed; and hence the improvement of the moral tone of society is a condition of the improvement of individual character. Fourthly, the cultivation of the moral capacity requires both the formation of habits and the enlightenment of the understanding, and neither is sufficient without the other.

I am aware that these conclusions will not satisfy those who demand a more absolute and unconditional ground of obligation. They will say that if the rule is binding only because of its utility, it is binding only so long as it is useful; and that if the sentiment of duty is a product of education, it may be educated away. To this I answer, that the utility of the rules is not a matter of doubt or of arbitrary opinion, but is founded upon the whole experience of mankind; and that the sentiment of duty, when it has been formed upon rules which are really useful, is confirmed, and not weakened, by the progress of intelligence. The man who has been trained to regard the happiness of others as the object of his conduct, and who has learned to understand the reasons of the rules which he obeys, is not less but more firmly bound than the man who obeys from blind habit; for he has the habit still, and he has also the conviction that the habit is reasonable. The apparent conflict between the two grounds of obligation is thus resolved; and the utilitarian account, so far from undermining the authority of the moral law, supplies it with a foundation more solid than any which the theory of an intuitive moral sense can afford.

It remains to add a word upon the conditions under which our judgments of particular cases are to be formed. The general conclusions above stated are, I conceive, true of all times and places; but their application to particular cases depends upon circumstances which vary indefinitely. The same rule which is useful in one state of society may be pernicious in another; and the same sentiment of duty which is a safeguard of morality in an enlightened community may be an instrument of oppression in a community which is benighted. Hence the reformer must be cautious in applying the general conclusions to the particular case; he must consider the actual condition of the society which he seeks to improve, the strength of the prejudices which he opposes, and the probable consequences of the change which he recommends. He must not expect that the mere demonstration of the utility of a rule will be sufficient to secure its adoption; for the sentiment of duty, which is the internal motive, may be attached to the opposite rule, and may resist the demonstration. He must address himself to the formation of a new sentiment, as well as to the enlightenment of the understanding; and he must be content to wait for the slow operation of education and of the general progress of society. This is the lesson which the history of moral reform teaches; and it is a lesson which the utilitarian, of all men, is most bound to lay to heart. For if the ground of obligation is utility, the reformer who would change the rules of conduct must show that the change is useful; and the proof of utility is not always obvious, and is never irresistible at once. The general conclusion, therefore, must be held with a firm conviction, but the particular application must be made with a cautious and discriminating judgment, which takes account of the actual condition of the society and of the sentiments of those whom it is proposed to improve.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察未经讨论而接受正确观点的后果，讨论理由理解、反对意见和信念意义之间的联系。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
There is a class of persons (happily not quite so numerous as formerly) who think it enough if a person assents undoubtingly to what they think true, though he has no knowledge whatever of the grounds of the opinion, and could not make a tenable defence of it against the most superficial objections. Such persons, if they can once get their creed taught from authority, naturally think that no good, and some harm, comes of its being allowed to be questioned. Where their influence prevails, they make it nearly impossible for the received opinion to be rejected wisely and considerately, though it may still be rejected rashly and ignorantly; for to shut out discussion entirely is seldom possible, and when it once gets in, beliefs not grounded on conviction are apt to give way before the slightest semblance of an argument. Waiving, however, this possibility--assuming that the true opinion abides in the mind, but abides as a prejudice, a belief independent of, and proof against, argument--this is not the way in which truth ought to be held by a rational being. This is not knowing the truth. Truth, thus held, is but one superstition the more, accidentally clinging to the words which enunciate a truth.

If the intellect and judgment of mankind ought to be cultivated, a thing which Protestants at least do not deny, on what can these faculties be more appropriately exercised by any one, than on the things which concern him so much that it is considered necessary for him to hold opinions on them? If the cultivation of the understanding consists in one thing more than in another, it is surely in learning the grounds of one's own opinions. Whatever people believe, on subjects on which it is of the first importance to believe rightly, they ought to be able to defend against at least the common objections. But, some one may say, "Let them be taught the grounds of their opinions. It does not follow that opinions must be merely parroted because they are never heard controverted. Persons who learn geometry do not simply commit the theorems to memory, but understand and learn likewise the demonstrations; and it would be absurd to say that they remain ignorant of the grounds of geometrical truths, because they never hear any one deny, and attempt to disprove them." Undoubtedly: and such teaching suffices on a subject like mathematics, where there is nothing at all to be said on the wrong side of the question. The peculiarity of the evidence of mathematical truths is, that all the argument is on one side. There are no objections, and no answers to objections. But on every subject on which difference of opinion is possible, the truth depends on a balance to be struck between two sets of conflicting reasons. Even in natural philosophy, there is always some other explanation possible of the same facts; some geocentric theory instead of heliocentric, some phlogiston instead of oxygen; and it has to be shown why that other theory cannot be the true one: and until this is shown, and until we know how it is shown, we do not understand the grounds of our opinion. But when we turn to subjects infinitely more complicated, to morals, religion, politics, social relations, and the business of life, three-fourths of the arguments for every disputed opinion consist in dispelling the appearances which favour some opinion different from it. The greatest orator, save one, of antiquity, has left it on record that he always studied his adversary's case with as great, if not with still greater, intensity than even his own. What Cicero practised as the means of forensic success, requires to be imitated by all who study any subject in order to arrive at the truth. He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. His reasons may be good, and no one may have been able to refute them. But if he is equally unable to refute the reasons on the opposite side; if he does not so much as know what they are, he has no ground for preferring either opinion. The rational position for him would be suspension of judgment, and unless he contents himself with that, he is either led by authority, or adopts, like the generality of the world, the side to which he feels most inclination. Nor is it enough that he should hear the arguments of adversaries from his own teachers, presented as they state them, and accompanied by what they offer as refutations. That is not the way to do justice to the arguments, or bring them into real contact with his own mind. He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them. He must know them in their most plausible and persuasive form; he must feel the whole force of the difficulty which the true view of the subject has to encounter and dispose of; else he will never really possess himself of the portion of truth which meets and removes that difficulty. Ninety-nine in a hundred of what are called educated men are in this condition; even of those who can argue fluently for their opinions. Their conclusion may be true, but it might be false for anything they know: they have never thrown themselves into the mental position of those who think differently from them, and considered what such persons may have to say; and consequently they do not, in any proper sense of the word, know the doctrine which they themselves profess. They do not know those parts of it which explain and justify the remainder; the considerations which show that a fact which seemingly conflicts with another is reconcilable with it, or that, of two apparently strong reasons, one and not the other ought to be preferred. All that part of the truth which turns the scale, and decides the judgment of a completely informed mind, they are strangers to; nor is it ever really known, but to those who have attended equally and impartially to both sides, and endeavoured to see the reasons of both in the strongest light. So essential is this discipline to a real understanding of moral and human subjects, that if opponents of all important truths do not exist, it is indispensable to imagine them, and supply them with the strongest arguments which the most skilful devil's advocate can conjure up.

To abate the force of these considerations, an enemy of free discussion may be supposed to say, that there is no necessity for mankind in general to know and understand all that can be said against or for their opinions by philosophers and theologians. That it is not needful for common men to be able to expose all the misstatements or fallacies of an ingenious opponent. That it is enough if there is always somebody capable of answering them, so that nothing likely to mislead uninstructed persons remains unrefuted. That simple minds, having been taught the obvious grounds of the truths inculcated on them, may trust to authority for the rest, and being aware that they have neither knowledge nor talent to resolve every difficulty which can be raised, may repose in the assurance that all those which have been raised have been or can be answered, by those who are specially trained to the task.

Conceding to this view of the subject the utmost that can be claimed for it by those most easily satisfied with the amount of understanding of truth which ought to accompany the belief of it; even so, the argument for free discussion is no way weakened. For even this doctrine acknowledges that mankind ought to have a rational assurance that all objections have been satisfactorily answered; and how are they to be answered if that which requires to be answered is not spoken? or how can the answer be known to be satisfactory, if the objectors have no opportunity of showing that it is unsatisfactory? If not the public, at least the philosophers and theologians who are to resolve the difficulties, must make themselves familiar with those difficulties in their most puzzling form; and this cannot be accomplished unless they are freely stated, and placed in the most advantageous light which they admit of. The Catholic Church has its own way of dealing with this embarrassing problem. It makes a broad separation between those who can be permitted to receive its doctrines on conviction, and those who must accept them on trust. Neither, indeed, are allowed any choice as to what they will accept; but the clergy, such at least as can be fully confided in, may admissibly and meritoriously make themselves acquainted with the arguments of opponents, in order to answer them, and may, therefore, read heretical books; the laity, not unless by special permission, hard to be obtained. This discipline recognises a knowledge of the enemy's case as beneficial to the teachers, but finds means, consistent with this, of denying it to the rest of the world: thus giving to the elite more mental culture, though not more mental freedom, than it allows to the mass. By this device it succeeds in obtaining the kind of mental superiority which its purposes require; for though culture without freedom never made a large and liberal mind, it can make a clever nisi prius advocate of a cause. But in countries professing Protestantism, this resource is denied; since Protestants hold, at least in theory, that the responsibility for the choice of a religion must be borne by each for himself, and cannot be thrown off upon teachers. Besides, in the present state of the world, it is practically impossible that writings which are read by the instructed can be kept from the uninstructed. If the teachers of mankind are to be cognisant of all that they ought to know, everything must be free to be written and published without restraint.

If, however, the mischievous operation of the absence of free discussion, when the received opinions are true, were confined to leaving men ignorant of the grounds of those opinions, it might be thought that this, if an intellectual, is no moral evil, and does not affect the worth of the opinions, regarded in their influence on the character. The fact, however, is, that not only the grounds of the opinion are forgotten in the absence of discussion, but too often the meaning of the opinion itself. The words which convey it, cease to suggest ideas, or suggest only a small portion of those they were originally employed to communicate. Instead of a vivid conception and a living belief, there remain only a few phrases retained by rote; or, if any part, the shell and husk only of the meaning is retained, the finer essence being lost. The great chapter in human history which this fact occupies and fills, cannot be too earnestly studied and meditated on.
b:
The question I propose to consider is not whether a true opinion be preferable to a false one—concerning that there can be no rational dispute—but what is the worth of a true opinion when it is held without examination, and what are the consequences, both for the understanding and for the character, of receiving it on authority while the grounds upon which it rests remain unconsidered. It is a common supposition that the holding of correct conclusions is the whole end of mental discipline, and that so long as a man believes what is true, it matters little how he came by his belief. I shall endeavour to show that this supposition is erroneous; that the mere possession of a right conclusion, unaccompanied by any comprehension of the reasons which justify it, is of small value in itself, and is attended with positive disadvantages, both intellectual and moral, which it is the purpose of a liberal education to counteract.

Let me first distinguish with care the several things which are commonly confounded under the name of belief. There is, in the first place, the proposition believed—the conclusion itself, considered as a matter of fact, true or false. There is, secondly, the evidence or grounds upon which it is believed, which may be understood or not understood by the believer. There is, thirdly, the manner in which the belief was acquired—whether by the exercise of the believer's own faculties of observation and reasoning, or by implicit adoption from others. And there is, fourthly, the influence which the belief exercises upon the believer's conduct and character. Now it is a striking peculiarity of the human mind, that these four things are continually disjoined; and it is the business of the philosopher to inquire what is the value of a true conclusion when the three last conditions are wanting or defective.

Consider, then, the case of a person who holds a true opinion, but who has never heard, or has never considered, the objections which may be urged against it, and who is ignorant of the arguments by which it is supported. Such a person is in a condition which, with respect to the opinion itself, may be compared to that of a man who possesses a valuable instrument without knowing its use. He has the right word, but he has not the meaning; he has the conclusion, but he has not the premises. And here I must observe, that the strength of a belief, considered as a mental habit, depends not upon the truth of the proposition, but upon the manner in which it is held. A man may hold a true opinion with the same blind tenacity with which another holds a false one; and the former, though his conclusion be correct, is not one whit more rational than the latter. The difference between them is a difference of accident, not of principle. The one has happened to light upon truth, the other upon error; but neither has any ground for his assurance which he could render to himself or to others. It is evident that such a belief, however true, is not a rational belief; it is a prejudice, and though a prejudice in favour of truth, it is not the less a prejudice.

Now, the consequences of this state of mind are twofold. In the first place, the understanding is not strengthened, but rather weakened, by the unexamined reception of true opinions. For the faculty of reason, like every other faculty, is improved by exercise and impaired by disuse. He who receives his opinions ready-made, without troubling himself to inquire into their grounds, acquires a habit of passive acquiescence which is fatal to all vigour of thought. He may be right in his conclusions, but he has not learned to think; and when a new question arises, for which his accustomed formulas afford no answer, he is helpless. He has the appearance of knowledge without the reality; and the appearance is often more mischievous than avowed ignorance, because it imposes upon himself and upon others.

In the second place, the moral character suffers no less than the understanding. For the man who holds his opinions without knowing why, holds them not as truths which he has verified, but as dogmas which he has inherited. His belief is not a part of himself; it is a foreign substance, which may be detached by any accident. And hence it is that persons of this description are often found to abandon their opinions upon the slightest provocation, or to retain them with a bigotry proportioned to their ignorance. In either case, the opinion is not a living principle of action, but a dead formula. The man who has never doubted, it has been said, is not to be trusted in his convictions; and the saying is profoundly true. For conviction, in the proper sense of the term, implies a conflict overcome; it is the result of a struggle with difficulties, and it derives its strength from the victory. He who has never encountered an objection has never known the force of his own belief.

But it will be said, perhaps, that the unexamined reception of true opinions is at least harmless, since the opinions themselves are true, and the conduct which they prescribe is right. To this I answer, that the harm lies precisely in the separation of the opinion from its grounds. For the opinion, thus held, is liable at any moment to be shaken by the first plausible objection; and when it is shaken, the man has nothing to fall back upon. He has not learned to distinguish between the essential and the accidental, between the principle and its applications; and therefore, when the application is shown to be erroneous, he abandons the principle also. Hence it is that great and salutary truths, when held in this manner, are continually passing into their opposites; and the history of opinion affords numerous examples of doctrines which, having been received without examination, have been rejected without reason.

Let me illustrate this by an example. Suppose a man who has been taught from his childhood that veracity is a duty, but who has never considered the grounds of the obligation, nor the exceptions which the complex affairs of life may require. So long as he moves in a narrow circle, his rule serves him well; but let him be placed in a situation where truth would inflict a cruel and unnecessary injury, and he is at a loss. He has no principle by which to discriminate; his rule is a mere formula, and he either applies it with a rigid and mischievous literalism, or, finding it inapplicable, he concludes that the obligation itself is not absolute, and so passes to the opposite extreme of laxity. Had he understood the grounds of the duty—had he perceived that veracity is binding because of the reliance which society places upon it, and that the obligation is suspended only where the reliance itself is absent or forfeited—he would have been able to reconcile the rule with the exception, and to preserve his principle while adapting it to circumstances. The difference between the two men is not a difference in the conclusion, but in the comprehension of the conclusion; and this difference is precisely what constitutes the value of a rational belief.

I am aware that it may be objected, that the greater part of mankind have neither leisure nor capacity for such inquiries, and that it is better for them to receive true opinions upon authority than to remain in ignorance or to fall into error. This objection is not without weight, and I do not deny that, in the present condition of society, a large portion of the community must necessarily receive many of their opinions at second hand. But the objection, when examined, will be found to confirm rather than to weaken the principle which I am maintaining. For the question is not whether men shall receive opinions from others, but whether they shall receive them in a manner which admits of subsequent examination, or in a manner which precludes it. The most unlettered person may be taught to know that there are reasons for his belief, even though he be unable to comprehend them fully; and the habit of referring his opinions to reasons, so far as his capacity extends, is itself the most important part of his education. The mischief arises when the opinion is imposed as a dogma, and the very possibility of doubt is excluded. It is not the reception of truth upon authority that I condemn, but the reception of it in such a manner as to destroy the disposition to inquire.

And here I must notice a distinction which is of the utmost importance in the present inquiry—the distinction between the general conclusion and the particular application. The general conclusion, that a certain opinion is true, may be established by evidence which is conclusive; but the particular application of it to a given case may depend upon circumstances which are known only to those who have studied the case. Now, when a man receives a general conclusion without understanding its grounds, he is apt to apply it indiscriminately to all cases, without regard to the circumstances which may modify or suspend its operation. Hence arises a great part of the errors and mischiefs which are attributed to opinion itself, but which in truth belong to the manner in which it is held. The opinion is true in the abstract; but the man who holds it without comprehension applies it in the concrete, where it may be false. And thus it happens that the same doctrine which, in the hands of a philosopher, is a principle of order and progress, becomes, in the hands of a bigot, a principle of confusion and reaction.

The connection, then, between the understanding of reasons, the consideration of objections, and the significance of belief, may be stated as follows. A belief has significance—that is to say, it is a living and operative principle in the mind—only when it is held with a consciousness of the grounds upon which it rests, and with a recognition of the objections which may be urged against it. For the significance of a belief consists not in the mere fact of assent, but in the relation which it bears to the other parts of our knowledge, and in the influence which it exercises upon our conduct. A belief which is held without reasons is isolated; it has no connection with the rest of our mental furniture; it is not a principle from which we can reason, but a formula which we repeat. And a belief which has never encountered an objection is untested; it has not been proved in the only way in which a belief can be proved—by surviving the trial of adverse criticism. Hence it is that the consideration of objections is not merely a means to the correction of error, but a necessary condition of the vitality of truth. He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. His reasons may be good, and no one may have been able to refute them; but if he is equally unable to refute the reasons on the opposite side, and does not even know what they are, he has no ground for preferring either opinion.

I am far from asserting that a man should never hold an opinion until he has personally examined all the arguments for and against it. Such a demand would be impracticable, and, if practicable, would be inconsistent with the division of labour which is necessary to the progress of knowledge. What I maintain is, that the opinion should be held in a manner which admits of examination; that the man should be conscious that there are reasons for it, and should be ready, when the occasion arises, to inquire into them; and that he should never confound the mere fact of his believing a thing with the proof that it is true. The distinction is between a belief which is closed and a belief which is open; between a mind which has made up its mind once for all, and a mind which, while it holds its conclusions firmly, is prepared to revise them upon evidence.

The consequences of neglecting this distinction are nowhere more visible than in the sphere of morals and politics. A man who has been trained to hold his moral and political opinions without examination is, in the first place, incapable of defending them against a skilful adversary; and, in the second place, he is incapable of applying them to new circumstances. He has learned his lesson by rote, and he can repeat it; but he cannot reason from it. And hence it is that, in times of change, such a man is either a blind adherent of the past or a blind follower of the new; he has no principle of discrimination, because he has never understood the principle of his own creed. The man, on the contrary, who has been accustomed to examine the grounds of his opinions, and to consider the objections which may be urged against them, is able to distinguish between the substance and the form; he can retain the principle while he abandons the application; he can adjust his conduct to circumstances without abandoning his convictions.

It may be asked, finally, what is the practical remedy for the evil which I have described. The remedy is not to be found in the substitution of one set of unexamined opinions for another, but in the cultivation of the habit of examining opinions, and in the diffusion of the knowledge of the grounds upon which the most important of them rest. It is the business of education, not to implant opinions, but to form the faculty of judging; not to furnish the mind with conclusions, but to teach it how to arrive at conclusions. And it is the business of the press, and of all who influence public opinion, to present truth in such a manner that it may be examined, and to refrain from the imposition of dogmas which cannot be questioned. For truth, to be operative, must be not merely received, but digested; and it is digested only when it has been subjected to the scrutiny of the understanding, and has been found to survive the test of objection.

I conclude, therefore, that the unexamined reception of true opinions is, in the strict sense of the term, irrational, and that its consequences are injurious both to the understanding and to the character. The value of a belief depends not upon the truth of the conclusion alone, but upon the manner in which it is held; and the manner in which it is held depends upon the comprehension of its grounds and the consideration of the objections to it. The general conclusion, that truth is better than error, remains unshaken; but the particular conclusion, that the mere possession of truth, apart from the comprehension of its grounds, is a good, must be rejected. And the practical lesson is, that in the education of the young, and in the formation of public opinion, the cultivation of the habit of inquiry is of more importance than the inculcation of any particular conclusions; since the former is the condition of all rational belief, while the latter, without the former, is but the semblance of knowledge, which, like a counterfeit coin, may pass current for a time, but is found wanting when it is brought to the test.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，评估政府优劣的判断标准，讨论公民品质、制度组织和社会能力之间的相互作用。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
If we ask ourselves on what causes and conditions good government in all its senses, from the humblest to the most exalted, depends, we find that the principal of them, the one which transcends all others, is the qualities of the human beings composing the society over which the government is exercised.

We may take, as a first instance, the administration of justice; with the more propriety, since there is no part of public business in which the mere machinery, the rules and contrivances for conducting the details of the operation, are of such vital consequence. Yet even these yield in importance to the qualities of the human agents employed. Of what efficacy are rules of procedure in securing the ends of justice if the moral condition of the people is such that the witnesses generally lie, and the judges and their subordinates take bribes? Again, how can institutions provide a good municipal administration if there exists such indifference to the subject that those who would administer honestly and capably can not be induced to serve, and the duties are left to those who undertake them because they have some private interest to be promoted? Of what avail is the most broadly popular representative system if the electors do not care to choose the best member of Parliament, but choose him who will spend most money to be elected? How can a representative assembly work for good if its members can be bought, or if their excitability of temperament, uncorrected by public discipline or private self-control, makes them incapable of calm deliberation, and they resort to manual violence on the floor of the House, or shoot at one another with rifles? How, again, can government, or any joint concern, be carried on in a tolerable manner by people so envious that, if one among them seems likely to succeed in any thing, those who ought to cooperate with him form a tacit combination to make him fail? Whenever the general disposition of the people is such that each individual regards those only of his interests which are selfish, and does not dwell on, or concern himself for, his share of the general interest, in such a state of things good government is impossible. The influence of defects of intelligence in obstructing all the elements of good government requires no illustration. Government consists of acts done by human beings; and if the agents, or those who choose the agents, or those to whom the agents are responsible, or the lookers-on whose opinion ought to influence and check all these, are mere masses of ignorance, stupidity, and baleful prejudice, every operation of government will go wrong; while, in proportion as the men rise above this standard, so will the government improve in quality up to the point of excellence, attainable but nowhere attained, where the officers of government, themselves persons of superior virtue and intellect, are surrounded by the atmosphere of a virtuous and enlightened public opinion.

The first element of good government, therefore, being the virtue and intelligence of the human beings composing the community, the most important point of excellence which any form of government can possess is to promote the virtue and intelligence of the people themselves. The first question in respect to any political institutions is how far they tend to foster in the members of the community the various desirable qualities, moral and intellectual, or rather (following Bentham's more complete classification) moral, intellectual, and active. The government which does this the best has every likelihood of being the best in all other respects, since it is on these qualities, so far as they exist in the people, that all possibility of goodness in the practical operations of the government depends.

We may consider, then, as one criterion of the goodness of a government, the degree in which it tends to increase the sum of good qualities in the governed, collectively and individually, since, besides that their well-being is the sole object of government, their good qualities supply the moving force which works the machinery. This leaves, as the other constituent element of the merit of a government, the quality of the machinery itself; that is, the degree in which it is adapted to take advantage of the amount of good qualities which may at any time exist, and make them instrumental to the right purposes. Let us again take the subject of judicature as an example and illustration. The judicial system being given, the goodness of the administration of justice is in the compound ratio of the worth of the men composing the tribunals, and the worth of the public opinion which influences or controls them. But all the difference between a good and a bad system of judicature lies in the contrivances adopted for bringing whatever moral and intellectual worth exists in the community to bear upon the administration of justice, and making it duly operative on the result. The arrangements for rendering the choice of the judges such as to obtain the highest average of virtue and intelligence; the salutary forms of procedure; the publicity which allows observation and criticism of whatever is amiss; the liberty of discussion and cinsure through the press; the mode of taking evidence, according as it is well or ill adapted to elicit truth; the facilities, whatever be their amount, for obtaining access to the tribunals; the arrangements for detecting crimes and apprehending offenders-all these things are not the power, but the machinery for bringing the power into contact with the obstacle; and the machinery has no action of itself, but without it the power, let it be ever so ample, would be wasted and of no effect. A similar distinction exists in regard to the constitution of the executive departments of administration. Their machinery is good, when the proper tests are prescribed for the qualifications of officers, the proper rules for their promotion; when the business is conveniently distributed among those who are to transact it, a convenient and methodical order established for its transaction, a correct and intelligible record kept of it after being transacted; when each individual knows for what he is responsible, and is known to others as responsible for it; when the best-contrived checks are provided against negligence, favoritism, or jobbery in any of the acts of the department. But political checks will no more act of themselves than a bridle will direct a horse without a rider. If the checking functionaries are as corrupt or as negligent as those whom they ought to check, and if the public, the mainspring of the whole checking machinery, are too ignorant, too passive, or too careless and inattentive to do their part, little benefit will be derived from the best administrative apparatus. Yet a good apparatus is always preferable to a bad. It enables such insufficient moving or checking power as exists to act at the greatest advantage; and without it, no amount of moving or checking power would be sufficient. Publicity, for instance, is no impediment to evil, nor stimulus to good, if the public will not look at what is done; but without publicity, how could they either check or encourage what they were not permitted to see? The ideally perfect constitution of a public office is that in which the interest of the functionary is entirely coincident with his duty. No mere system will make it so, but still less can it be made so without a system, aptly devised for the purpose.

What we have said of the arrangements for the detailed administration of the government is still more evidently true of its general constitution. All government which aims at being good is an organization of some part of the good qualities existing in the individual members of the community for the conduct of its collective affairs. A representative constitution is a means of bringing the general standard of intelligence and honesty existing in the community, and the individual intellect and virtue of its wisest members, more directly to bear upon the government, and investing them with greater influence in it than they would have under any other mode of organization; though, under any, such influence as they do have is the source of all good that there is in the government, and the hindrance of every evil that there is not. The greater the amount of these good qualities which the institutions of a country succeed in organizing, and the better the mode of organization, the better will be the government.
b:
The question of what constitutes a good government is not one that admits of a single, simple answer, for the criteria by which we judge governments are several, and they do not always point in the same direction. It is necessary, therefore, at the outset to distinguish the different grounds upon which a government may be approved or condemned, and to consider how these grounds are related to one another.

The first and most obvious criterion is the degree to which a government promotes the good qualities of its citizens. A government is good, in this view, insofar as it tends to make the governed better men and women—more intelligent, more virtuous, more public-spirited, more capable of acting on reasoned conviction rather than mere custom or impulse. This is not a merely ornamental consideration appended to the more substantial business of government; it is, I would argue, among the most important tests by which any political arrangement must be tried. For the character of a people is not fixed by nature; it is formed, in great measure, by the institutions under which they live, and by the manner in which those institutions call upon them to act. A government which treats its subjects as children, deciding everything for them and requiring no exercise of judgment or public spirit, will produce a people incapable of self-direction; while a government which entrusts them with responsibilities, and holds them answerable for the manner in which those responsibilities are discharged, will tend to produce a people capable of discharging them well. The evidence for this proposition is to be found in the observable differences between nations and between periods: peoples who have enjoyed a share in the management of their own affairs have generally exhibited a greater degree of intelligence and public virtue than those who have been mere passive recipients of the commands of others. Yet this criterion, taken alone, is incomplete, for a government might conceivably cultivate the qualities of its citizens at the expense of the efficient conduct of public business, and a nation of virtuous men who cannot maintain order or defend themselves is not, in the ordinary sense, well governed.

The second criterion is the quality of the machinery of government itself—the degree to which it organizes the moral and intellectual resources of the community for the conduct of public affairs, and the degree to which it secures the honest and efficient administration of justice and of the various branches of public business. A government must possess sufficient organization to maintain order, to protect persons and property, to raise and expend revenue with integrity, and to conduct the relations of the community with other communities. These are matters of contrivance and arrangement; and it is possible to conceive of a government which, whatever its effects upon the character of the people, is admirably adapted to the dispatch of business. The history of administration affords many examples of governments which have been efficient in this narrow sense while remaining indifferent or hostile to the improvement of the governed. But here too the criterion is insufficient when taken by itself, for a government may be well organized and yet be so organized as to concentrate power in a manner that renders it dangerous, or so as to exclude from all share in public affairs those whose cooperation is necessary to the stability of the whole.

The third criterion is the degree to which the government secures the obedience and cooperation of the governed—the extent to which it rests upon consent rather than upon force, and the extent to which it is able to call forth the voluntary cooperation of the community in the execution of its measures. This is a matter of social capacity as much as of institutional form: a government may be excellent in design and yet fail because the community lacks the habits and dispositions necessary to sustain it, or because the government has not taken pains to cultivate those habits. The interaction between these three considerations—the quality of citizens, the organization of institutions, and the social capacity of the community—is of the first importance, and it is a mistake to treat them as independent variables. Institutions shape character; character in turn determines what institutions can be worked; and the working of institutions over time either confirms or undermines the social capacity upon which all government ultimately depends. A people trained in self-government acquires the capacity for it; a people denied all share in public affairs loses even the desire for it. The relation is reciprocal, and it is this reciprocity that makes the judgment of governments so difficult, for a government may be praised for the qualities it has fostered while being condemned for the inefficiency of its administration, and the two judgments may both be true.

It is necessary also to distinguish between the general conclusions that may be affirmed of governments in the abstract and the particular judgments that must be formed of particular governments under particular circumstances. In general, it may be affirmed that a government which secures the participation of the governed in public affairs, which holds its officers to account, and which cultivates the intelligence and public spirit of the people, is better than one which does none of these things. But the application of this general truth to any particular case depends upon conditions that cannot be assumed in advance: upon the degree of civilization the community has attained, upon its previous political experience, upon the external dangers to which it is exposed, and upon the peculiar character of its institutions. A form of government that is excellent for a community of long political experience may be premature for one that has never known self-rule; and a measure of authority that would be intolerable in a settled and peaceful society may be necessary for the preservation of order in a society emerging from disorder. The judgment that a government is good, therefore, is always a judgment relative to circumstances, even when the general principles upon which it rests are universally true.

It should be added that there are other explanations of political success and failure besides the quality of the government itself. The prosperity of a nation may be due to its natural advantages, to the character of its people independently of its institutions, or to the accidents of its position among other nations; and the failure of a government may be due to causes beyond its control. The wise observer, therefore, will not attribute to the form of government every difference that he observes between nations, but will endeavor to distinguish the effects of institutions from the effects of other causes, and will form his judgment of governments with a due sense of the complexity of the subject and the fallibility of his own conclusions.

author: Julian Wrenford
task: 请用英文撰写一段相对完整的学术论述，考察人对自然一致性的预期如何形成，比较日常概括与严格归纳所需的证据和方法。围绕相关概念和问题之间的联系展开分析，结合适当的论据或自拟例子，说明判断所依赖的条件及其他可能解释。使论述能够独立理解，并区分一般结论与特定情境下的认识。
a:
Every person’s consciousness assures him that he does not always expect uniformity in the course of events; he does not always believe that the unknown will be similar to the known, that the future will resemble the past. Nobody believes that the succession of rain and fine weather will be the same in every future year as in the present. Nobody expects to have the same dreams repeated every night. On the contrary, every body mentions it as something extraordinary, if the course of nature is constant, and resembles itself, in these particulars. To look for constancy where constancy is not to be expected, as for instance that a day which has once brought good fortune will always be a fortunate day, is justly accounted superstition.

The course of nature, in truth, is not only uniform, it is also infinitely various. Some phenomena are always seen to recur in the very same combinations in which we met with them at first; others seem altogether capricious; while some, which we had been accustomed to regard as bound down exclusively to a particular set of combinations, we unexpectedly find detached from some of the elements with which we had hitherto found them conjoined, and united to others of quite a contrary description. To an inhabitant of Central Africa, fifty years ago, no fact probably appeared to rest on more uniform experience than this, that all human beings are black. To Europeans, not many years ago, the proposition, All swans are white, appeared an equally unequivocal instance of uniformity in the course of nature. Further experience has proved to both that they were mistaken; but they had to wait fifty centuries for this experience. During that long time, mankind believed in a uniformity of the course of nature where no such uniformity really existed.

According to the notion which the ancients entertained of induction, the foregoing were cases of as legitimate inference as any inductions whatever. In these two instances, in which, the conclusion being false, the ground of inference must have been insufficient, there was, nevertheless, as much ground for it as this conception of induction admitted of. The induction of the ancients has been well described by Bacon, under the name of “Inductio per enumerationem simplicem, ubi non reperitur instantia contradictoria.” It consists in ascribing the character of general truths to all propositions which are true in every instance that we happen to know of. This is the kind of induction which is natural to the mind when unaccustomed to scientific methods. The tendency, which some call an instinct, and which others account for by association, to infer the future from the past, the known from the unknown, is simply a habit of expecting that what has been found true once or several times, and never yet found false, will be found true again. Whether the instances are few or many, conclusive or inconclusive, does not much affect the matter: these are considerations which occur only on reflection; the unprompted tendency of the mind is to generalize its experience, provided this points all in one direction; provided no other experience of a conflicting character comes unsought. The notion of seeking it, of experimenting for it, of interrogating nature (to use Bacon’s expression) is of much later growth. The observation of nature, by uncultivated intellects, is purely passive: they accept the facts which present themselves, without taking the trouble of searching for more: it is a superior mind only which asks itself what facts are needed to enable it to come to a safe conclusion, and then looks out for these.

But though we have always a propensity to generalize from unvarying experience, we are not always warranted in doing so. Before we can be at liberty to conclude that something is universally true because we have never known an instance to the contrary, we must have reason to believe that if there were in nature any instances to the contrary, we should have known of them. This assurance, in the great majority of cases, we can not have, or can have only in a very moderate degree. The possibility of having it, is the foundation on which we shall see hereafter that induction by simple enumeration may in some remarkable cases amount practically to proof.(111) No such assurance, however, can be had, on any of the ordinary subjects of scientific inquiry. Popular notions are usually founded on induction by simple enumeration; in science it carries us but a little way. We are forced to begin with it; we must often rely on it provisionally, in the absence of means of more searching investigation. But, for the accurate study of nature, we require a surer and a more potent instrument.

It was, above all, by pointing out the insufficiency of this rude and loose conception of Induction, that Bacon merited the title so generally awarded to him, of Founder of the Inductive Philosophy. The value of his own contributions to a more philosophical theory of the subject has certainly been exaggerated. Although (along with some fundamental errors) his writings contain, more or less fully developed, several of the most important principles of the Inductive Method, physical investigation has now far outgrown the Baconian conception of Induction. Moral and political inquiry, indeed, are as yet far behind that conception.
